body:
Table 110 "Entries in a Type 3 font dictionary" states about the /Resources entry: "Optional but **should** be used".

On the other hand, 7.8.3 "Resource dictionaries" states in the second bulleted item

"Content streams that define the glyph descriptions of a Type 3 font **shall** include a Resources entry in the Type 3 font dictionary specifying all the resources used by all the content streams in the CharProcs dictionary of a Type 3 font."

Here "shall" contradicts "should" in Table 110.

Possible solutions (given inconsistent conditions it's hard to decide compatibility issues):
- Might be considered incompatible: change "Optional but should be used" to "Required" for Resources in Table 110.
- Weaker, but compatible: change "shall" to "should" in 7.8.3.

A better approach would be to require the Resources dictionary only if there actually are resources (i.e. don't require empty /Resources), but this would further complicate the compatibility issue.

A minor wording problem in 7.8.3 is that a content stream shall specify something in another location, which is weird phrasing for "if dictionary A is present, dictionary B shall contain X" (the content stream doesn't contain the resources, but actually the font does). Actually, since a Type 3 font without "Content streams that define the glyph descriptions" doesn't make sense this boils down to "/Resources is required in a Type 3 font dict", a statement which is redundant with the (corrected) entry in Table 110. The relevant information is that the Resources dictionary collects the resources in all CharProcs.
title: Inconsistent conditions for Type 3 font resources

body:
Both PDF/X-6 and PDF/X-4 are based on 32000-2:2020, but neither make any comments about the Extensions dictionary. At present there are numerous extensions standards in development, many of which would make a file that uses them incompatible with readers that do not implement the extension.

Each of those extensions specifications requires that appropriate data be filled in the Extensions dictionary in a PDF file (32000-2:2020 7.12).

So we may soon find ourselves in a situation where a file is completely compliant with PDF/A-4 or PDF/X-6, but that cannot be read by the majority of readers for those formats.

On the up-side, at least those readers should be able to look in the Extensions dictionary and at least understand why they can’t read the file (and possibly provide that information to the user/operator).

It’s not clear what could/should be done about this now that the standards are published. I’m opening an issue here just to publicise the situation a bit more widely so that it comes as a surprise to fewer people when a valid file using a new image codec, or a non-rectangular link or whatever is encountered.
title: Future challenge for PDF subset standards from Extensions

body:
_This issue is originally reported by [faceless2](https://github.com/faceless2 ) at PDF/A TWG. Moving it here for discussion, as it concerns also other PDF substandards, such as PDF/X-6._

The attached PDF is considered valid PDF/A-3u, despite the /Widths array for the embeded Type 3 font making the first glyph (a square) 3 times wider than it should be.

[FontWidths.pdf](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/files/7511444/FontWidths.pdf)

If the Widths array was correct, the square would be touching the circle.

The problem is that the Type3 font uses a very small em-box - instead of the usual 1000x1000 units, it defines each glyph on a 0.1x0.1 grid and uses a large font size. Which means that even though the glyph specifies its width as 0.1 and the Widths array specifies the width as 0.3 - three times wider - the PDF still meets the requirements of the text in PDF/A:

> For every font embedded in a conforming file and used for rendering, the glyph width information in the font dictionary and in the embedded font program shall be consistent. For this International Standard, consistent is defined to be a difference of no more than 1/1000 unit.

By defining the tolerance in terms of absolute units, rather than (say) a difference of no more than 0.1%, cases where the absolute size of the glyph is very small but the width is very different are not going to be caught.

A slightly different problem occurs at the other end of the scale. We have some sample documents (eg PDF_2428_525738.pdf from the "Govdocs" corpus) where the glyphs are enormous floating point values, say 500000 x 500000. Converting these to and from floating point values results in the difference sometimes being more than 0.1 absolute unit, just because 32-bit floats just don't have the resolution to preserve "0.1 unit" after the numbers have been multiplied a few times and the result written to the PDF with a normal number of significant figures.

I think the best solution is to rephrase the test as a percentage: "a difference of no more than 0.1%", which is exactly the same test for all non-Type3 fonts (and the vast majority of Type3s that are based on a 1000x1000 grid).
title: FontWidths must be consistent "to within 1/1000 unit" doesn't scale

body:
For certification signatures with _no-changes-allowed_ ISO 32000-2 clearly says that incremental updates with only DSS and/or DTS are allowed:

>_(Optional)_ The access permissions granted for this document. Changes to a PDF that are incremental updates which include only the data necessary to add DSS’s 12.8.4.3, "Document Security Store (DSS)" and/or document timestamps 12.8.5, "Document timestamp (DTS) dictionary" to the document shall not be considered as changes to the document as defined in the choices below.
>
>Valid values shall be:
>_1_ No changes to the document shall be permitted; any change to the document shall invalidate the signature.
>_2_ Permitted changes shall be filling in forms, instantiating page templates, and signing; other changes shall invalidate the signature.
>_3_ Permitted changes shall be the same as for 2, as well as annotation creation, deletion, and modification; other changes shall invalidate the signature.
>
>Default value: _2_.

*(Table 257 — Entries in the DocMDP transform parameters dictionary — entry for key **P**)*

(Last time I tried Adobe Acrobat still incorrectly reported such changes as invalidating the certification but Leonard had confirmed [here](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/PDFBOX-3017?focusedCommentId=17224930&page=com.atlassian.jira.plugin.system.issuetabpanels%3Acomment-tabpanel#comment-17224930) that this is an Acrobat bug and will be addressed in a future release.)

But there is a second mechanism changing permissions to _no-changes-allowed_ via signatures, the signature field **Lock** dictionaries. Since PDF-2.0 these **Lock** dictionaries can contain a similar entry, also with the key **P**, but here DSS and DTS additions are not explicitly exempted; the full entry is:

>*(Optional; PDF 2.0)* The access permissions granted for this document. Valid values shall be:
>_1_ No changes to the document are permitted; any change to the document shall invalidate the signature.
>_2_ Permitted changes shall be filling in forms, instantiating page templates, and signing; other changes shall invalidate the signature.
>_3_ Permitted changes are the same as for 2, as well as annotation creation, deletion, and modification; other changes shall invalidate the signature.
>
>There is no default value; absence of this key shall result in no effect on signature validation rules.
>
>If **MDP** permission is already in effect from an earlier incremental save section or the original part of the document, the number shall specify permissions less than or equal to the permissions already in effect based on signatures earlier in the document. That is, permissions can be denied but not added. If the number specifies greater permissions than an **MDP** value already in effect, the new number is ignored.
>
>If the document does not have an author signature, the initial permissions in effect are those based on the number 3.
>
>The new permission applies to any incremental changes to the document following the signature of which this key is part.

*(Table 236 — Entries in a signature field lock dictionary — entry for key **P**)*

Apparently both entries work with the same underlying settings, the second one referring to the former value as the "_**MDP** permission already in effect from_ an earlier incremental save section or _the original part of the document_".

Thus, I have the impression that the _intent_ here is that the latter permission values shall have the same meaning as the former ones, they in particular also shall always allow DSS & DTS. On the other hand strict interpretation of the specification exempts DSS & DTP only when certifying, not when locking.

Which interpretation is correct? And could that interpretation made be clear in the specification?
title: Clarification on signature field Lock dictionary permissions and DSS/DTS incremental updates

body:
To @petervwyatt's point on #131: it's true that the DocMDP permission levels for updates to signed files are only defined in very vague terms. I also appreciate that the validation of such incremental updates is not within the scope of ISO 32000, and that there's an ongoing ETSI project to standardise some of that.

However, would it be in scope for ISO 32000 to make the requirements more explicit on the _file format_ side of things? For example, ISO 32000 could say things like:


 * "Incremental updates to a PDF document containing a DocMDP level 1 signature shall (should?) only override dictionaries X, Y and Z."

 * "Incremental updates to a PDF with any certifying signature shall not redefine any object IDs that reference stream objects."


This is not a proposal to add specific text, but rather an example of what such requirements _might_ look like. What validators do with this information is of course up to them, but it would make this area of the specification amenable to formalisation in something like the Arlington PDF model, for example.

Thoughts?
title: Add explicit file format requirements for incremental updates on signed files?

body:
Section 14.8.4.7.2 defines the **Link** structure element type.  Table 368 provides the primary guidance on how to use the element, but in the paragraphs below Table 368 are additional restrictions and requirements for the children of **Link** structure elements.  These are fundamentally wrong, not only contradicting early specifications, but requiring setting requirements that make no sense in the context (and are impossible).

The specification provides the following text:

> The following items may be children of a link element:
> - One or more content items or other ILSEs (except other links) if **A**, **Dest** and **PA** keys of all of them have identical values
> - One object reference (see 14.7.5.3, "PDF objects as content items") to one link annotation associated with the content

Neither of the bullets describe correct requirements for the children of **Link** structure elements.

Addressing the issues for the first bullet:

> - One or more content items or other ILSEs (except other links) if **A**, **Dest** and **PA** keys of all of them have identical values

The **A**, **Dest** and **PA** are related to Link annotations, so cannot exist for content items or child ILSEs.  The equivalent from ISO 32000-1 stops at the end of the parenthetical, correctly having no opinion on these non-existent entries.

**Recommendation:** strike the text after the parenthetical, leaving the text to match ISO 32000-1:2008:
> One or more content items or other ILSEs (except other links)

Addressing the issues for the second bullet:
> - One object reference (see 14.7.5.3, "PDF objects as content items") to one link annotation associated with the content

If a link spans a page, the only mechanism to connect that spanning link is a parent **Link** structure element enclosing the content from both pages and both link annotations.  This has always been permissible and was part of the PDF standards ever since the introduction of links in structure.

** Recommendation:** Restore the original text from ISO 32000-1 and PDF 1.7:
> - Object references (see 14.7.5.3, “PDF Objects as Content Items”) to one or more link annotations associated with the content

Additionally, a lot of text was removed from ISO 32000-1 and PDF 1.7.  We would recommend the inclusion of that.
title: Requirements for Link elements are incorrect (section 14.8.4.7.2)

body:
ISO32000-2:2020 Table 145 in "11.6.6 Transparency group XObjects" specifies for the blend color space (CS entry) in a group entry of an isolated transparency group in a Form XObject, that it can be remapped (to an ICCBased color space):
"Device colour spaces shall be subject to remapping according to the DefaultGray, DefaultRGB, and DefaultCMYK entries in the ColorSpace subdictionary of the current resource dictionary (see 8.6.5.6, "Default colour spaces")."

The question is whether the "current resource dictionary" is the one of the respective Form XObject or of the parent object (the page or a parent Form XObject).

It is clear that for any default colors in the _content stream_ of the respective Form XObject the "current resource dictionary" is the one of this Form XObject (if present, otherwise inherited).
But that is not as clear for the blending color space that is defined in the group entry. This blend color space is used for two color conversions (if needed): 
1. "all painting operators shall convert source colours in a colour space (that are not equivalent to the group colour space) to the group colour space before compositing objects" (below Table 145, 4th bullet: "Group colour spaces", first sub bullet).
2. "The group’s shape [...] shall then be painted into the parent group or page, using the group’s accumulated colour and opacity at each point. If colour conversion needs to take place in order to composite the group into its parent, the rendering intent and black point compensation from the graphics state at the point of invocation of the Do operator shall be used for the conversion." (below Table 145, 5th bullet). In other words for this conversion the parent context is applicable.

The first conversion suggests that the "current resource dictionary" is the one of the group.
The second conversion will use the blend color space of the group in order to convert the content of the group into the parent context and then it would be more logical to use the resource dictionary of he parent object.

This [sample file](https://www.dropbox.com/s/zql8999qgbk61ry/DefaultCMYK%20XObject%20Question.pdf?dl=0) has originally been created by some layout software which seems to imply that the DefaultCMYK color space of the page is applied to the blend color space of the Form XObject (DeviceCMYK). (The attached PDF has been massively reduced and modified, but still demonstrates the question.)

Recommendation

The first conversion mentioned above explicitly mentions the blend color space of the group and if that would be the only color conversion the "current resource dictionary" would clearly be the one of the Form XObject itself. 
The second color conversion does not explicitly refer to the blend color space. 

Therefore I think the "current resource dictionary" is indeed the one of the Form XObject itself.

But I think this should somehow be clarified in the standard, even more so since existing applications seem to assume otherwise.
title: Which default color space is applicable to the blend color space of an isolated transparency group Form XObject?

body:
ISO 32000-2, 14.9.2.1 describes the /Lang entry in the document catalog as "the document’s default language" which "applies to both content within content streams and any text string".

The main entry for /Lang in ISO 32000-2, Table 29 describes /Lang as "natural language for all text in the document except where overridden by language specifications for structure elements or marked-content. If this entry is absent, the language shall be considered unknown". This contradicts 14.9.2.1 on two accounts:

- In the absence of /Lang the language isn't necessarily unknown, it's just that no document-wide default is available.
- The exemption is too strict as it covers only structure elements and marked content, but not text strings, e.g. in bookmarks.

### Suggestion
Align the /Lang description in Table 29 to 14.9.2.1 by avoiding the incomplete "except..." repetition and the "unknown" clause:

> Lang
> (Optional; PDF 1.4) A language identifier that shall specify the default value of the natural language for all text in the document except where overridden by language specifications in any of several possible locations (see 14.9.2, "Natural language specification").
title: Inconsistent description of /Lang entry in the catalog

> The escape sequence shall consist of the following elements, in order:
> a) The Unicode value ESCAPE (U+001B) (that is, for strings encoded in UTF-16BE, the byte sequence 0 followed by 27; for strings encoded in UTF-8 the byte value 27).
> b) A 2- byte BCP 47 language code.

Item b) is wrong since BCP 47 is not restricted to 2-byte codes. In the unlikely case that this restriction is intentional it should be pointed out and explained as it would exclude all three-byte ISO 639-2 codes.

body:
The understanding at the National Archives and Records Administration is that there are three ways to scan a document into the PDF format. One is to simply put the scan into the PDF, all bits included. The other two methods involve adding OCR'ed data to the file. They are "Searchable Image - Exact" and "Formatted Text and Graphics and PDF Normal". 

Is there a way to determine programatically on a page by page basis which method was used for any given scan?

The "Formatted Text and Graphics and PDF Normal" version of the data is not acceptable as a permanent record because it discards image data and replaces it with, sometimes imperfect, OCR'ed data.

It would be very helpful in the archival world to be able to analyze a PDF file and determine which of the three methods the file was created with. Yes, we have seen federal agency data which appear to have all three methods in the same file!

Thanks.
title: Wishlist - Ability to identify different methods of producing OCR'ed PDF from scanned document

"Table 151 — Entries in an outline item dictionary" states:

* for **Prev**: (_Required for all but the first item at each level_; ...
* for **Next**: (_Required for all but the last item at each level_; ...

It is arguably ambiguous if **Prev**/**Next** are prohibited or just optional for the first/last item at each level respectively. Here are some trivial test PDFs:

[OutlinesGood.pdf](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/files/7798402/OutlinesGood.pdf)  - no **Prev**/**Next** key for first/last outline items. Works everywhere AFAICT.

[OutlinesBad.pdf](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/files/7798404/OutlinesBad.pdf)  - "optional" **Prev**/**Next** keys for first/last outline items. Causes various popular implementations to lock-up/hang(!!) or display "Outline A" twice.

I would interpret the current wording as implying the keys are optional for the inverse of the required statement, as there is no explicit prohibition, but experimenting with various popular implementations causes them to lock up and hang, hence this is a question. I could also see nothing helpful in the prose of clause 12.3.3 Document outlines.

Wording can be improved by the addition of "_optional otherwise_" to the parenthetical.
title: Are Outline Item (Table 151) Prev/Next optional or prohibited when not required?

body:
Currently Table 202 in 12.6.4.2 Go-To actions defines **D** entry as:  

> The destination to jump to (see 12.3.2, "Destinations").

Section 12.3.2 specifies three ways to define destinations: 
- 12.3.2.2 Explicit destinations
- 12.3.2.3 Structure destinations
- 12.3.2.4 Named destinations

So, as it is written now, one may use a Structure destination as a value of **D** entry.

It looks like the original intention was to keep the definition of **D** entry fully compatible with PDF 1.7 and allow Structure destinations only as values of the newly introduced **SD** entry.  

One additional issue is that according to the same Table 202 the value of **SD** can only be of _array_ type, which does not permit the use of Named destinations here, which have type _name_ or _byte string_.  On the other hand, section 12.3.2.4 on Named destinations does provide the text on how to use Structure destinations via Named destinations. So, again, the current text permits **D** entry of the GoTo action to have Named destination wrapping a Structure element as its value. Was this really intended?
title: Not clear if D entry in GoTo actions can define a structure destination

This one has been bothering me for a while, so I thought I'd ask here.

Table 365 (Grouping level structure types) in ISO 32000-2:2020 has the following to say about **Part**:

> Encloses a grouping of structure elements without consideration for their hierarchy.
> NOTE 1: **Part** is the semantic equivalent of **Div**.
> (rest of table cell omitted)

I think there are several ways to read that note:

 - **Part** is semantically equivalent to **Div** (this interpretation clearly doesn't make sense, otherwise there's no point in having two separate SEs)
 - **Part** is like **Div** applied to semantics[, as opposed to something else?] (layout?)
 - **Part** is like **Div** [in that it is non-hierarchical], but unlike **Div** it has semantic [grouping] value[, whereas **Div** is just a vehicle for attributes or inserted for layout convenience]

I believe the 3rd reading is the intended one, but I end up doing a double take every time I read that note, and the interpretation of **Part** comes up in meetings occasionally. My question is twofold:

 - Is my reading consistent with the intention of the note?
 - Can we rephrase the note to make said intention more obvious to the reader?

Tagging this as a question rather than a bug for now.
title: Potentially confusing note in definition of *Part* structure element

Adobe PDF 1.7, Table 3.17: "**XRefStm** integer (_Optional_) The byte offset from the beginning of the file of a cross-reference stream"

ISO 32000-1:2008 and ISO 32000-1:2017, Table 19: "**XRefStm** integer (_Optional_) The byte offset in the decoded stream from the beginning of the file of a cross-reference stream."

ISO ISO 32000-2:2020, Table 19: "XRefStm integer (_Optional_) The byte offset in the decoded stream from the beginning of the PDF file of a cross-reference stream."

The **XRefStm** key is in a trailer dict so I'm unclear what "... in the decoded stream" is referring to. That is clearly wrong.

And I also find the phrasing "from the beginning of the PDF file of a cross-reference stream" confusing: "of a" cross reference stream?? Surely "to the" cross reference stream or "to a" cross reference stream? 

So then there is the question of which cross reference stream to help resolve "to the" vs "to a" as this might be ambiguous... 
Clearly it is the last cross reference stream that is associated with the hybrid-reference file’s trailer dictionary and there can only be one of those so we can say "the". 

So I think it should be described as: 
 "**XRefStm** integer (_Optional_) The byte offset from the beginning of the PDF file to the cross-reference stream."
title: XRefStm key (Table 19) description is confusing / wrong

body:
In the case where an incremental update ONLY updates a direct trailer entry (e.g. `/ID`) what, if any, are the requirements for the object number in the xref sub-section line (that consists of just 2 integers)?
 * is `xref 0 0` valid or does the first 'object number' need to be strictly greater than zero (i.e. a valid PDF object number, and never the special "start of freelist" object zero)?
* Or is it a "don't care" because the second value is a zero and thus the supposed object number is not relevant? Would that mean `xref -1 0` is then acceptable?

The ISO TC 171 SC 2 WG 8 "Securing PDF" discussion group has discussed this and recommends that both the integers in all xref sub-section lines be specified as non-negative integers. The following changes (in bold) are proposed in clause 7.5.4 Cross-reference table:

> The subsection shall begin with a line containing only two **non-negative** integers separated by a SPACE (20h) and terminated by an end-of-line marker (see 7.2.3, "Character set").

- Delete the last sentence of NOTE 3: "_This also means that cross reference subsections of incremental updates can never have an object number of zero_.", since an incremental update that changes only the trailer dictionary can be like this with no objects added or freed.
title: Clarification on xref sub-section line syntax (clause 7.5.4)

body:
The semantics for use of Table 16 object stream dictionary `Extends` key are insufficient as to what a PDF reader is expected to do when encountering this key when parsing, or how a PDF writer/modifier software might need to do to maintain, add or remove this key.

This was discussed in the ISO TC 171 SC 2 WG 8 "Securing PDF" discussion group:

The `Extends` key is effectively a hint for a PDF reader that a "_collection_" of object streams (as a "_directed acyclic graph_") has some unspecified relationship and that caching the collection of related object streams _may_ provide some benefit. Obviously any decision to cache/pre-process or not is entirely up to each PDF processor, as the collection may be large, and/or the unspecified relationship may not be relevant to the PDF processor in question. The term "collection" here has nothing to do with clause 12.3.5 "Collections".

General suggestions for improvement:
* generally disambiguate "collections" in clause 7.5.7 from clause 12.3.5 by replacing with the phrase "collections of object streams"
* incorporate the term "hint" into Table 16
* extend NOTE 4 that the `Extends` key forms a hint to PDF processors for improving performance (since this is where performance is already mentioned)

Any other suggestions?
title: The semantics for use of Table 16 ObjStm /Extends key are unclear / insufficient

body:
Referring to Table 15 Trailer, `Size` entry: "_The total number of entries in the PDF file’s cross-reference table, as defined by the combination of the original section and all update sections. Equivalently, this value shall be 1 greater than the highest object number defined in the PDF file_.":

* the term _entry_ (as in "The total number of entries...") is the terminology used in clause 7.5.4 for each 20-byte line in cross reference tables. But because xref sub-section lines in incremental updates can start object numbering anywhere, there is no guarantee that the "_The total number of entries ..._" is the same as the highest object number.

Thus "_Equivalently_" is technically incorrect because these two sentences are not necessarily equivalent until things are more precisely defined:

* It would be nice to more formally define "_defined by the combination of the original section and all update sections_" and/or "_defined in the PDF file._" - so if the last _N_ objects in a PDF are in the free list does this count or not? What if they are just in the xrefs and there are no actual objects with those numbers in the body of the PDF (is that what makes them "defined in the PDF file"?

* It should be made clear whether the `Size` value needs to be: 
    - 1 bigger than all object numbers defined in any update, or 
    - 1 bigger than all object numbers in the final/combined xref table.

Note also from clause 7.5.4: "_The cross-reference table (comprising the original cross-reference section and all update sections) shall contain one entry for each object number from 0 to the maximum object number defined in the PDF file, even if one or more of the object numbers in this range do not actually occur in the PDF file._"

This was discussed in the ISO TC 171 SC 2 WG 8 "Securing PDF" discussion group where it was agreed that a clearer definition would be helpful as `Size` can be used for memory allocation by some processors, and it also influences when an object might be considered undefined (as per Table 15: "_Any object in a cross-reference section whose number is greater than this value shall be ignored and defined to be missing by a PDF reader._" and clause 7.3.10 statement: "_An indirect reference to an undefined object shall not be considered an error by a PDF processor; it shall be treated as a reference to the **null** object._")

So what is a more formal, accurate but nice and succinct definition for `Size`?
title: Table 15 Trailer Size entry definition is described inaccurately/ambiguously

body:
In the Subtype entry of Table 44 (section 7.4.11.1), we have:
"_The value of this entry shall conform to the MIME media type names defined in Internet RFC 2046, with the provision that characters not permitted in names shall use the 2-character hexadecimal code format described in 7.3.5, "Name objects"_."

The problem with this is that RFC 2046 defined (in 1996) an initial hierarchy of media type names with a note that: "It should be noted that the list of media type values given here may be augmented in time, via the mechanisms described above, and that the set of subtypes is expected to grow substantially."

The normative grammar of the media types was actually given in RFC 2045, however, that has since been restricted somewhat in section 4.2 of [RFC 6838](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6838#section-4.2) "Media Type Specifications and Registration Procedures".

Current best(?) practice with PDF is to use both IANA-registered media types: https://www.iana.org/assignments/media-types/media-types.xhtml
But also not-currently-registered media types like: "model/u3d" and "model/prc"
Such unregistered (or perhaps pre-registered) media types should probably conform to the RFC6838 registration requirements to the extent possible rather than RFC2046.

Also note that revision of this entry should take [RFC6657](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6657) into consideration, without which non-UTF8 plain-text attachments are just bit-rot.
title: Embedded File Stream dictionary (table 44)  Subtype definition is bad.

body:
**N** entry in 3D nodes dictionary (Table 323) specifies node ID, to which these node properties (transformation matrix, opacity, etc) should be applied. 

The format of node ID depends on the embedded 3D model formal and is different for U3D and PRC, as specified now in the definition of **N** entry. However, this definition assumes the presence of the 3D stream (Table 311), which does not exist in case of 3D model embedded into PDF as a RichMedia annotation.

In case of RichMedia the 3D model is embedded not as a 3D stream, but as an asset referenced from the RichMediaContent dictionary (Table 341). The only available mechanism today to determine the **Subtype** of an asset (=file format of the embedded 3D model) is a **Subtype** entry in the embedded file dictionary, which is optional at the moment. If this **Subtype** entry is not present in the embedded 3D asset, the only other mechanism available to distinguish between U3D and PRC is to read the header of the embedded file and use magic number technique.

One possible way to fix this issue would be:
 - require MIME type defined (via **Subtype** entry of the embedded file) for all assets referenced by the RichMediaContent dictionary (this would be useful not only for RichMedia 3D annotations, but also for Audio and Video ones). In case of embedded U3D and PRC this is related to #155 
 - update the definition of **N** entry in Table 323 to use either **Subtype** entry in the 3D steam dictionary or a **Subtype** entry of the embedded file dictionary for the embedded 3D asset to determine the format of the 3D model
title: definition of N entry in 3D nodes dictionary ambiguous in case of RichMedia 3D annotations

> "An indirect object reference (see 7.3.10, "Indirect objects") to a nonexistent object shall be treated the same as a null object."
"Specifying the null object as the value of a dictionary entry (7.3.7, "Dictionary objects") shall be equivalent to omitting the entry entirely."

> "A dictionary entry whose value is null (see 7.3.9, "Null object") shall be treated the same as if the entry does not exist."

and noting that no similar statement about null handling for arrays is made in clause 7.3.6.

If there is a `Kids` array (for example, such as in a name or number tree, or the Kids of a page tree node, or in the StructTree) that has an indirect reference to a "nonexistent object" and there are no other errors then is it correct to interpret that this as NOT an error because:

1. the non-existent object is equivalent to the null object
2. because the `Kids` array (in the cases listed) is not specified to be a fixed length nor does it need to be explicitly indexed numerically so when traversing the array the null object can be skipped over?

However if the array in question needs to have an explicit number of entries, such as an RGB color triplet, then it would be an error? Or does null not count as an indexable array element so if there was a 4th element then it would be valid?

In other words: what are the semantics for supporting null objects in arrays in PDF? 
Are there any differences between an explicit **null** (keyword) versus an implicit null (such as the "nonexistent object" case)?
title: What are the semantics for supporting null objects in arrays in PDF?

body:
**Describe the bug**

Table 237 (Entries in a digital signature seed value dictionary) contains the following text in the row defining the **DigestMethod** entry:

> This property is only applicable if the digital credential signing contains
> RSA public/private keys. If it contains DSA public/ private keys, the digest
> algorithm is always SHA-1 and this attribute shall be ignored.

ECDSA also allows the user to specify a digest, so **DigestMethod** should presumably also apply to ECDSA.  On the other hand, with EdDSA (for which we add support in ISO 32002) the choice of digest function is baked into the signing algorithm, which means that **DigestMethod** should not apply at all.

(EDIT: I'm of course making the tacit assumption here that we generally want the digest function used in the signing algorithm to be the same as the one used to digest the document.)

For the record, I also wasn't able to find any other language in the standard restricting the use of DSA to SHA-1. So at the very least, that provision isn't in the right place here. If anything, it should be somewhere in or around Table 260. Granted, the corresponding key size recommendations to make good use of anything "bigger" than SHA-256 with DSA get a bit ridiculous, but there's no real technical reason to stick to SHA-1.


Proposed solution:

Strike the cited portion of Table 237, and replace it with the following text:

> Some signature mechanisms require a specific digest function to be used. In such cases, the value of this entry shall be ignored.

If this change is agreed to, I'm happy to have the discussion on what to do with DSA in another issue. If we end up saying anything about digest algorithms for use with DSA in another subclause, we could of course still add a reference in Table 237.
title: DigestMethod seed value makes too many assumptions on the signing algorithm

body:
Table 237, DigestMethod array is defined as:

> An array of names indicating acceptable digest algorithms to use while signing. The value shall be one of ...

"_The value shall be one of_" implies this can only be a single-element array which I believe is not correct.

It would be better stated as "Values in this array shall be ..."

Then there is a separate question of whether the array is ordered or unordered. With help from @MatthiasValvekens, we think it is unordered so proposed solution:

> An unordered array of names indicating acceptable digest algorithms to use while signing. Values in this array shall be ...
title: Table 237 DigestMethod array definition is ambiguous

body:
**Describe the bug**
1. In 9.10.2 Paragraph 1 there's this sentence: "A PDF processor can use these methods, in the priority given, to map a character code to a Unicode value." Should be, "to map a character code to a Unicode character sequence"(following the wording in 9.10.3 ToUnicode CMaps clauses). 

    This is because it is possible to specify multiple multiple Unicode values or `UTF16-BE` encoding code units in a row in `ToUnicode` CMaps and `mapping-resources-pdf` CMaps, thus a Unicode character sequence. This new wording also covers the AGLFN cases well.

2. Also in paragraph 1, there's this sentence: "Tagged PDF documents, in particular, shall provide at least one of these methods." I believe this sentence is misleading and/or incorrect. First providing methods is the duty of processors not documents. Second, it's totally fine for a Tagged PDF document that doesn't exercise the following methods at all in that section if the document is fully annotated by `AltText` mechanism.

3. In paragraph 9 there's this sentence: "Map the CID obtained in step (a) according to the CMap obtained in step (d), producing a Unicode value.". This wording is correct at the moment but not future-proof. It is definitely possible and useful in the future that  `mapping-resources-pdf` CMaps use Unicode character sequences, for cases like UVSs. (Ken Lunde has expressed interest in doing so in the past in https://github.com/adobe-type-tools/mapping-resources-pdf/issues/6#issuecomment-496705666, which references https://ccjktype.fonts.adobe.com/2019/05/to-uvs-or-not-to-uvs.html , we all know this work has stalled, but i think the direction is correct and it's a useful provision.)
title: Wording in 9.10.2 is misleading and strictly saying incorrect.

Note 4 in 7.9.2.2.1 says 

> This mechanism precludes beginning a string using PDFDocEncoding with the three characters **dieresis**, guillemotright, questiondown, which is unlikely to be a meaningful beginning of a word or phrase.

body:
Clause 12.3.2.4 Named destinations states in para below NOTE 1:
> In PDF 1.1, the correspondence between name objects and destinations shall be defined by the **Dests** entry in the document catalog dictionary. The value of this entry shall be a dictionary in which each key is a destination name and the corresponding value is either an array defining the destination, using the syntax shown in "Table 149 — Destination syntax", or a dictionary with a **D** entry whose value is such an array and may optionally contain an **SD** entry as defined in "Table 201 — Action types".

The **SD** entry is described very ambiguously. **SD** was added in PDF 2.0  (2017 edition) so ISO 32000-1:2008 is no help here.

If we have a DocCatalog as follows:
```
<<
  /Type /Catalog ...
  /Names << 
     /Dests << % /Dests is a minimalistic name tree
       /Names [ (MyNamedDest) 10 0 R ]
     >> 
>>
```

then what are all the valid forms for object 10?

1. `[ 20 0 R /XYZ ... ]` or anything else from Table 149. This is OK.  

1. `<< /D [ 20 0 R /XYZ ... ] >>` this is the **D** entry "_whose value is such an array_" assuming that really means "...  an array defining the destination, using the syntax shown in "Table 149 — Destination syntax". This is as per ISO 32000-1:2008 and OK;

1. `<< /D [ 20 0 R /XYZ ... ] /SD ??? >>`  - "Table 201 — Action types" is effectively an index to all the other tables defining action dictionaries and doesn't directly mention any **/SD** entry. And not all the action dictionaries referenced from Table 201 have **SD** keys...

I then wondered if "Table 201" was a rotted reference meant for Table 201 from ISO 32000-1:2008, which is "Table 201 – Additional entries specific to an embedded go-to action". This became Table 204 in both ISO 32000-2:2017 and ISO 32000-2:2020, but that does not have an **/SD** key either. I also checked the Adobe Extensions to ISO 32000-1 and couldn't see anything...

So what is the correct specification and reference for the optional **/SD** key in Named Destinations?
title: Named Destination /SD entry added in PDF 2.0 is not sufficiently defined

body:
Clause 13.7.2.1 RichMedia annotations / General, paragraph 1 makes this factual statement:

> The _RichMediaSettings dictionary_ is unique to each annotation, while the _RichMediaContent dictionary_ can be shared across rich-media annotations.

Table 333 "Additional entries specific to a RichMedia annotation" **RichMediaSettings** has no stated requirements regarding uniqueness.

AFAICT there is also nothing technical (like a required indirect reference to something) that makes this a necessary requirement.

So is this a statement an actual enforceable "shall" requirement or purely descriptive/informative (e.g. "Typically ...")?
I believe it is the latter.
title: Are RichMediaSettings dictionaries mandated to be "unique to each annotation" (clause 13.7.2.1)?

body:
I noticed this one while prototyping the cryptography-related extensions to PDF that are currently in the ISO pipeline (ISO 32003 and 32004). These each come with an extension dictionary to describe the extension, but since some of the values in that dictionary are strings (to wit, **URL** and **ExtensionRevision**), they are (by default) subject to encryption as well!

This is a little awkward when dealing with extensions that _themselves_ add new encryption capabilities to the file format (like ISO 32003, which defines a whole new crypt filter). When dealing with a document using that sort of extension, a processor might simply not understand all of the entries in the extension dictionary, unless it already supported the extension in the first place! And of course, at that point, the processor probably has little use for the contents of the extensions dictionary.

Was that behaviour intended when the **URL** and **ExtensionRevision** entries were added in PDF 2.0?
title: Values in extension dictionary can potentially be encrypted

body:
In section *9.4.3 Text showing operators* we can read about the string argument (bold emphasis is mine)

> The strings shall conform to the syntax for string objects. When a string is written by enclosing the data in parentheses, bytes whose values are equal to those of the ASCII characters LEFT PARENTHESIS (28h), RIGHT PARENTHESIS (29h), and REVERSE SOLIDUS (5Ch) (backslash) shall be preceded by a REVERSE SOLIDUS character. **All other byte values between 0 and 255 may be used in a string object**. These rules apply to each individual byte in a string object, whether the string is interpreted by the text-showing operators as single-byte or multiple-byte character codes.

While this is true it is very misleading because in *7.3.4.2 String Literals* we can read (bold emphasis is mine) 

> An end-of-line marker appearing within a literal string without a preceding REVERSE SOLIDUS **shall be treated as a byte value of (0Ah)**, irrespective of whether the end-of-line marker was a CARRIAGE RETURN (0Dh), a LINE FEED (0Ah), or both.

This effectively mean that an `0Dh` byte value in the argument of a text showing operator will be interpreted as `0Ah` byte which is unlikely to be what you want :–) 

I suggest changing the text of 9.4.3 to mandate backslash escaping of `CARRIAGE RETURN (0Dh)` aswell.
title: Misleading text in 9.4.3 Text showing operators

body:
This bug lists a number of inconsistencies on the optional / required state of some of the objects within the **RichMedia** annotation, as well as the minimal array lengths for some of the cases.

If needed, I can split these issues into individual GitHub issues. I also attach a diagram visualizing the relationship between various object types used within RichMedia annotations: [RichMedia annotation.pdf](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/files/8285843/RichMedia.annotation.pdf)

1.  **Assets** entry in the **RichMediaContent** dictionary (Table 341) is currently optional. But it is difficult to imagine a **RichMedia** annotation without a single asset. Having no assets makes also problematic the definition of **RichMediaInstance** type (Table 343), which has **Asset** as a required entry pointing to one of the **RichMedia** assets.

Suggestion: change optional to required.

2. **RichMediaActivation** and **RichMediaDeactivation** entries in the Rich Media Settings dictionary are both optional, with no defualt value specified. On the other hand, both **RichMediaActivation** dictionary (Table 335) and **RichMediaDeactivation** dictionary (Table 336) have all entries optional with well-defined default values. It should also be noted that both **RichMediaActivation** and **RichMediaDeactivation** entries are important for the consistent behavior of RichMedia annotations across different implementations, as they specify when exactly the Rich Media should be activated / deactivated (e.g, upon an explicit user action such as mouse click or when the page with this RichMedia becomes visible). 

Suggestion: define default values for both  **RichMediaActivation** and **RichMediaDeactivation** entries as empty dictionaries except for the correctly specified Type value.

3. Same as above for **Animation** and **Presentation** entries  in the  **RichMediaActivation** dictionary (Table 335). Both **RichMediaAnimation** dictionary (Table 337) and **RichMediaPresentation** dictionary (Table 338) have all entries marked as optional and all having well-defined default values.

Suggestion: define default values for both  **Animation** and **Presentation** entries as empty dictionaries except for the correctly specified Type value.

4. **Configuration** entry in the **RichMediaActivation** dictionary (Table 335) specifies its default value as the first element in the **Configurations** array of the **RichMediaContent** dictionary (Table 341). But this entry is marked as optional in Table 341. So, it is not clear how the processor should behave if there is no **Configurations** entry in the  **RichMediaContent** dictionary or if it is present, but is an empty array.

Suggestion: make **Configurations** entry in the  **RichMediaContent** dictionary required and non-empty.

Alternatively, one can define a default configuration for the **RichMedia** annotation as an array of Instances wrapping all assets (=embedded files with 3D, Sound or Video content) within a given **RichMedia** annotation. But this probably needs to be double checked with the existing implementations.
title: Inconsistences in the data model of the RichMedia annotation

body:
This is the mirror of the issue https://github.com/pdf-association/pdfa-twg/issues/9 discussed and resolved at the PDF/A TWG.

The following PDF/A-4 requirements on JPEG 2000 (and only they) are related to **colr** box in JPX stream and shall be ignored in presence of **ColorSpace** entry in the parent Image XObject dictionary (ISO 19005-4, 6.2.7.3 JPEG2000) :

> If the number of colour space specifications in the JPEG2000 data is greater than 1, there shall be exactly
one colour space specification that has the value 0x01 in the APPROX field. If the specified colour space
specification uses an ICC profile, then that profile shall conform to the requirements of ISO 32000-2:2020,
8.6.5.5.

> The value of the METH entry in its ‘colr’ box shall be 0x01, 0x02 or 0x03. A conforming processor shall
use only that colour space and shall ignore all other colour space specifications.

> JPEG2000 enumerated colour space 19 (CIEJab) shall not be used.

> JPEG2000 enumerated colour space 12 (CMYK) which is part of JPX but not JPX baseline, may be used.

All other requirement from ISO 19005-4:2020, 6.2.7.3 such as the number of colour channels and the bit-depth of the JPEG2000 data are defined in other box types and stay independently of absence or presence of the **ColorSpace** entry in the Image XObject dictionary.
title: JPX ColorSpace can be overridden, but the rules for its "colr" box still apply

body:
This is the mirror of the issue https://github.com/pdf-association/pdfa-twg/issues/7 discussed and resolved at the PDF/A TWG.

The question is: are the **All** and **None** separations exempt from the requirements that their ColorSpace/Transforms should be consistent throughout the document (as specified in ISO 19005-4, 6.2.4.4);

> All **Separation** arrays within a single conforming PDF/A-4 file (including those in **Colorants**
dictionaries) that have the same name shall have the same _tintTransform_ and _alternateSpace_. In
evaluating equivalence, the PDF objects shall be compared, rather than the computational result of the
use of those PDF objects. Compression and whether or not an object is direct or indirect shall be ignored.

I believe they are, and the justification for this is this paragraph from ISO32000-2 (clause 8.6.6.4, the text below NOTE 6)

> A PDF reader shall support Separation colour spaces with the colourant names **All** and **None** on all
devices, even if the devices are not capable of supporting any others. When processing Separation
spaces with either of these colourant names PDF readers shall ignore the _alternateSpace_ and
_tintTransform_ parameters (discussed below), although valid values shall still be provided.

The proposed resolution: add a NOTE 4 right after NOTE 3 in 6.2.4.4 saying that **All** and **None** Separation names are not subject to the above requirement on _tintTransform_ and _alternateSpace_.
title: Separations All and None are exempt from ColorSpace requirements?

body:
Based on recent SafeDocs research, it is apparent that the vast majority of PDF processors silently support UTF-16LE encoded strings as well as UTF-16BE, resulting in significantly different visual appearances for things like outlines and OCG layer names. Over 18 PDF processors were tested with only 2 "correctly" processing UTF-16LE as PDFDocEncoding (being Slim PDF Reader and iText). Real PDFs in the wild with UTF-16LE do also exist, such as mentioned [here](https://github.com/pikepdf/pikepdf/issues/288). Also, no validators seem to detect (reject or warn) about PDFs with UTF-16LE. 

Thus the PDF spec should be updated to acknowledge this reality by permitting UTF-16LE

I have created a PDF test file here that uses non-trivial UTF-16LE strings: 
https://github.com/pdf-association/safedocs/tree/main/Miscellaneous%20Targeted%20Test%20PDFs#utf16le-testpdf
title: UTF-16LE strings are supported by vast majority of PDF processors and should be permitted

body:
For a check boxes the standard defines the following:

> The appearance for the off state is optional but, if present, shall be stored in the appearance dictionary under the name Off.

But for radio buttons this sentence is missing which could indicate that other names for the `Off` state are possible. 

There is a mentioning of the `Off` state in the context of the radio button  `V` dictionary:

> The parent field’s V entry holds a name object corresponding to the appearance state of whichever child field is currently in the on state; the default value for this entry is Off.

But still I would like to suggest that this is clarified by adding the same sentence from the check box also to the radio button chapter ...

body:
There is a discussion with the LateX guys about the interpretation of the PDF standard regarding radio button form fields. I would highly appreciate if the PDF community could shed some light on the matter.

According to the standard the Opt array is defined as:
> An array containing **one entry for each widget annotation** in the Kids array of the radio button or check box field. [...] When this entry is present, the names used to represent the on state in the AP dictionary of each annotation may use numerical position (starting with 0) of the annotation in the Kids array, encoded as a name object (for example: /0, /1). This allows distinguishing between the annotations even if two or more of them have the same value in the Opt array.

This basically means a 1:1 mapping (for me):

```
/Kids[ 2 0 R  3 0 R   4 0 R  5 0 R  6 0 R  7 0 R ] 
         |      |       |      |      |      |
/Opt [  (A)    (B)     (C)    (A)    (B)    (C) ]
         |      |       |      |      |      |
N-App[  /0     /1      /2     /3     /4     /5 ]      
```

The `RadiosInUnison` flag is defined as:
> If set, a group of radio buttons within a radio button field that use the same value for the on state will turn on and off in unison; that is if one is checked, they are all checked. If clear, the buttons are mutually exclusive [...].

**But how does both play together?**

*crobat generates the following structure:

```
1 0 obj
<</FT/Btn/Ff 33587200/Kids[2 0 R 3 0 R 4 0 R 5 0 R 6 0 R 7 0 R]/Opt[(A)(B)(C)(A)(B)(C)]/T(radio)>>
endobj
2 0 obj
<</AP <</N <</0 19 0 R/Off 20 0 R>>>>...omitted...>>
endobj
3 0 obj
<</AP <</N <</1 34 0 R/Off 35 0 R>>>>...omitted...>>
endobj
4 0 obj
<</AP <</N <</2 43 0 R/Off 44 0 R>>>>...omitted...>>
endobj
5 0 obj
<</AP <</N <</0 53 0 R/Off 54 0 R>>>>...omitted...>>
endobj
6 0 obj
<</AP <</N <</1 67 0 R/Off 68 0 R>>>>...omitted...>>
endobj
7 0 obj
<</AP <</N <</2 81 0 R/Off 82 0 R>>>>...omitted...>>
endobj
```

**Observations:**
Until now I considered the numerical position (=index) only a tool to resolve the actual value for the on state (which is then located in the `Opt` array).
However the usage of `/0 /1 /2 /0 /1 /2` instead of `/0 /1 /2 /3 /4 /5` indicates that this is not the case and when the `Radiosinunison` is set, the index turns into the name for the on state which must be the same for same-checked widgets.
But this raises another set of questions:

1. What is the use of the `Opt` array in that case if it is not a 1:1 mapping? Then /4 /5 /6 could also be skipped and defined like this `/Opt[(A)(B)(C)]` (argument from the LateX guys)? But when I changed the child normal appearance names from `/0 /1 /2 /0 /1 /2` to `/0 /1 /2 /3 /4 /5` the `Radiosinunison` behaviour  stopped working in the viewers I tried.
2. But if only 3 elements are specified what about the export values of the other elements?
3. When omitting the `Radiosinunison` flag the document still shows the `Radiosinunison` behaviour. Ok this might be an implementation specific thing, however what should win in this situation?
title: Radio button form field confusion when using Radiosinunison and Opt array

In Table 355  “Entries in a structure element dictionary” the **A** key defines an attribute object: “_Each attribute object shall be either a dictionary or a stream_”  This is then repeated in the 1st paragraph in 14.7.6.1: “_An attribute object shall be a dictionary or stream that includes an **O** entry (see "Table 360 — Entries common to all attribute object dictionaries") identifying the conforming product that owns the attribute information_.” along with a note: “_NOTE Earlier versions of PDF also provided for the use of streams as attributes._”.  I can see roughly the same wording in the Adobe PDF 1.4 reference but with no further explanation of how or why a stream might be used, what the stream data itself is used for, or if the stream has to be a particular type of stream (such as a content stream / Form XObject). 

Can others who are more experienced with Logical Structure (particularly its early use) please explain attribute objects as streams?

Given the NOTE in 14.7.6.1, atrribute objects as streams distinctly feel like something that should also be marked as “Deprecated in PDF 2.0” as it is certainly under-specified.
title: Table 355 Structure Element dictionary - attribute objects as streams?

body:
In Table 242 — Flag for reset-form actions, the meaning of the
Include/Exclude flag for internal fields is not evident (emphasis is mine):

> **If clear**, the Fields array (see "Table 241 — Additional
> entries specific to a reset-form action") specifies which fields
> to reset. (_All descendants of the specified fields in the field
> hierarchy are reset as well._) **If set**, the Fields array indicates
> which fields to exclude from resetting; that is, all fields in the
> document’s interactive form shall be reset except those listed
> in the Fields array. 

For internal fields it is obvious that when the flag is clear the
parenthesized text applies and all descendant fields will be reset.

But if the flag is **set**, despite the phrase after the semicolon,
it is not obvious what happens to descendant fields. My own
interpretation is that, symmetrically, all descendant fields will
also be exempt from being reset. If PDF TWG agrees, may I
suggest an additional clarification:

> If clear, the Fields array (see "Table 241 — Additional
> entries specific to a reset-form action") specifies which fields
> to reset. (All descendants of the specified fields in the field
> hierarchy are reset as well.) If set, the Fields array indicates
> which fields to exclude from resetting; that is, all fields in the
> document’s interactive form shall be reset except those listed
> in the Fields array. **_(All descendants of the specified fields
> in the field hierarchy are also exempt from being reset.)_**

---

In the unlikely event that PDF TWG does not agree with me, I
would _still_ like to see an addition clarifying the case of
internal fields, perhaps something like this:

> If set, the Fields array indicates which fields to exclude from
> resetting; that is, all fields in the document’s interactive form
> shall be reset except those listed in the Fields array.
> **_(If the flag is set, only terminal fields may be specified in the
> Fields array and those will be exempt from being reset. Any
> internal fields are ignored and their descendants will still be reset.)_**
title: Clarification concerning internal fields in ResetForm actions

body:
First sentence of the last paragraph of 12.7.8.1 says "_FDF shall use the MIME media type application/vnd.fdf._"

As FDF is defined in all parts of ISO 32000, it is no longer a vendor-specific format so the IANA MIME media type has been updated to `application/fdf` as defined at https://www.iana.org/assignments/media-types/media-types.xhtml. IANA doco also acknowledges the alias `application/vnd.fdf` so can just correct to:

> "_FDF shall use the MIME media type application/fdf._"
title: Update FDF MIME media type

body:
There is a problem in how to draw line endings for free text annotations.

First consider Table 179 - Line ending styles
 * It shows example appearances of line ending types, e.g. Square.
 * Some types use the interior colour to fill an enclosed area, if the interior colour is present.

If the interiour color is not present, the line endings should not be filled in.
Currently this behaviour is implied, but not explicitly stated (which would be better).

This applies to line annotations in Table 178 - Additional entries specific to a line annotation:
 * LE is used to specify the line ending type for the annotations.
 * IC specifies the interior color that applies to the line endings.

It is unclear how it applies to free text annotations in Table 177 - Additional entries specific to a free text annotation
 * Assume that IT is FreeTextCallout and that CL has an array of six numbers.
 * Assume further more that LE has the value Square.
 * There is no IC key specifying the interior color of the line ending.
 * This implies that the interior color of the line ending can not be set.

Does this mean that the line endings of callouts will never be filled?

Figure 79 shows a yellow freetext box with a callout with an OpenArrow line ending.
How would this be rendered if the line ending was Square?

My expectation is that free text annotations work similar to square 
annotations in that C is used to specify the border color and that 
IC is used to specify the interior colour of both the box itself, 
and (in the case of free text annotations also) the line ending fill color.
Thus I propose the following addition to Table 177 (similar to the IC key in Table 178):

| Key  | Type | Value |
| ------------- | ------------- | ------------- |
| **IC**  | array  | (Optional; meaningful only if CL is present; PDF 1.6) An array of numbers in the range 0.0 to 1.0 specifying the interior colour that shall be used to fill both the annotation’s rectangle and line ending (see "Table 179 — Line ending styles"). The number of array elements shall determine the colour space in which the colour is defined: 0 — No colour; transparent, 1 — DeviceGray, 3 — DeviceRGB, 4 — DeviceCMYK 

For reference, if I render a similar example in Adobe Acrobat Reader it uses
the color given in C (see Table 166) to fill in both the box itself and the
line ending (any specified IC is ignored). This contradicts interior colour 
being used for filling line endings in Table 179.
title: Unclear how to set fill color of line ending for free text annotations with callout

body:
See also Issue #152 Consider changing several dictionary entry types from unnecessary number to integer.

Table 120 — Entries common to all font descriptors: there are a lot of legacy extant PDFs that have a **FontWeight** value that is NOT one of the pre-defined "multiples of 100" (typically they are a multiple of 50 so land in between 2 of the predefined values). AFAICT all PDF processors seem to handle this OK.

Proposal is to permit any integer value between 100 and 900 (the current lower and upper bounds), with a recommendation for multiples of 100 (i.e. as per the existing spec).
title: Font Descriptor FontWeight should reflect extant data not using the set of predefined integer values

body:
This issue is somewhat similar to #127 

Table 345 defines PDF 2.0 extension of 3D node dictionary (Table 323) adding two new entries to it. In fact, these new entries are already present in Table 323. 

But the original text of Section 13.7.2.3.6 and Table 345 speaks about new entries in the _View Params dictionary_, which actually does not exist in PDF 2.0 (the closest would be 3D view dictionary).

I would suggest to replace "View Params" by "3D node" everywhere in Section 13.7.2.3.6 as well as in Table 323, **Data** entry description.

There are also other problems in Section 13.7.2.3.6, which might require more rewording:
- 13.7.2.3.6.1 General is confusing, as it speaks about some general purpose mechanism to pass custom **Data** to the 3D instance. However, further text explains that **Data** is used solely to store and load opaque data. 
- The format how this **Data** is serialized is not specified, which might cause interoperability issues
-  the section uses a boldface term  **View**, which is reserved for predefined names in PDF spec. But in fact it means just a general concept of a 3D view (or just a view) as used in Section 13.6.4.1 3D views - General.
title: Table 345 references View Params dictionary instead of 3D node dictionary

body:
The intro to 32000-2:2020 says “ISO 15076-1:2010 dated reference for ICC.1 can be supplemented by the Errata list and approved revisions available from the ICC website (http://color.org/icc_specs2.xalter) – see 8.6.5.5, "ICCBased colour spaces"”, but:

- There is no reference to ICC.1 in either normative references or in the bibliography, except in the name of 15076-1 in normative references. Neither is there anything under terms and definitions or notations to establish “ICC.1” as an indirection to anything.

- 7.4.9 (JPXDecode filter) says images may use “An input ICC profile of any sort defined by ICC.1.” This is normative text, so surely ICC.1 should be in normative references … or this reference needs replacing with 15076.

- 8.6.5.5 (ICCBased colour spaces) uses dated references in Table 66 and the bullet points under it. Specifically the row in the table for PDF 2.0 says it supports “ICC.1:2010 (ISO 15076-1:2010)”, and the bullets say that “A PDF reader shall support ICC.1:2010” and “A PDF writer should use ICC 1:2010 profiles”. These requirements seem to assume that the line in the table establishes a synonym for ICC.1 that can be used in the bullets below it. I don’t see that it does. So the same options for correction as for JPXDecode above would apply.

The simplest solution for those last two might be to define “ICC.1:2010” as a synonym for 15076-1:2010 in terms and definitions.

But that still doesn’t deliver the claim in the intro about approved revisions from the ICC website. I’m not sure how to do that, unless that is rolled into the terms & definitions entry?

And in all of this I haven’t touched on the long discussion in the last JWG7 call about whether there should be a dated revision of 15076-1 or whether an amendment would be better!
title: A few clean-ups to ICC spec references

body:
I am trying to locate the requirement ("shall"/"shall not") in PDF which requires an "indirect object" (as referenced by an "indirect reference") to always be a single basic PDF object and not anything else. But I can't...

Consider an array: `[ /a /b /c 10 0 R ]`
I hope everyone would agree that object 10 0 can only be a **_single_** PDF basic object type such as:
```
10 0 obj
/d
endobj
```
resulting in the array having 4 elements.

And that an indirect reference is **_not_** some form of expansion or continuation - so this would be invalid syntax and the array would **_not_** have 6 elements:
```
10 0 obj
/d /e /f 
endobj
```

The informal-ish definition of a PDF type of object comes from clause 7.3.1 which states:
> PDF syntax includes nine basic types of objects: boolean values, integers, real numbers, strings, names, arrays, dictionaries, streams, and the null object.

Can someone identify the requirement?
title: Indirect objects need to be single PDF basic objects only - where stated?

body:
**Describe the bug**

Table 25 currently has this to say about the **Length** key in encryption dictionaries:

>(Required; deprecated in PDF 2.0) Security handlers may define their own use of the Length entry and should use it to define the bit length of the file encryption key. The bit length of the file encryption key shall be a multiple of 8 in the range of 40 to 256. The standard security handler expresses the Length entry in bytes (e.g., 32 means a length of 256 bits) and public-key security handlers express it as is (e.g., 256 means a length of 256 bits).
> When CFM is AESV2, the Length key shall have the value of 128. When CFM is AESV3, the Length key shall have a value of 256.

> NOTE (2020) The Length key was corrected to be required and the descriptive text updated.

While I'm fully aware of the fact that this key has a complicated past ("Required/deprecated") and is mostly a vestige of history at this point as far as PDF 2.0 is concerned, I think the description still contains a contradiction, even after the 2020 edits. More to the point, this sentence

>  When CFM is AESV2, the Length key shall have the value of 128. When CFM is AESV3, the Length key shall have a value of 256.

is not compatible with the previous one. The V4/V5 _standard_ security handlers also use crypt filters, which would imply a length in bytes instead of bits. I believe that should read

> When **CFM** is _AESV2_, the Length key shall have a value of 128 for public-key security handlers, and 16 for the standard security handler. When **CFM** is _AESV3_, the Length key shall have a value of 256 for public-key security handlers, and 32 for the standard security handler.

Again, in both of these cases the correct length can be inferred from the crypt filter method name anyhow, so I doubt any real-world implementations actually use the **Length** key for that, but the current text is still unclear as to what PDF producing software has to put there.
title: Text around **Length** key for encryption dictionary is still confusing

body:
ISO 21757-1:2020 (ECMAScript for PDF 2.0) normatively references (as a **DATED** reference): "_ISO/IEC 22275:2018, Information technology — Programming languages, their environments, and system software interfaces — ECMAScript® Specification Suite_".

ISO/IEC 22275:2018 (https://www.iso.org/standard/73002.html) is freely available from https://standards.iso.org/ittf/PubliclyAvailableStandards/index.html as https://standards.iso.org/ittf/PubliclyAvailableStandards/c073002_ISO_IEC_22275_2018.zip

ISO/IEC 22275:2018 is a VERY short ISO/IEC standard which just normative references ECMA-262 and ECMA-402 using **UNDATED** references. As all ISO standards state: "_For undated references, the latest edition of the referenced document (including any amendments) applies_."

"_ECMA-262, ECMAScript® Language Specification_" is available from https://www.ecma-international.org/publications-and-standards/standards/ecma-262/ with the latest version being ECMAScript 2021. All older ECMAScript specification editions are still available from this URL.

I believe the root cause of this issue is probably ISO insisting that ISO specs are always used in preference to supposedly equivalent standards from other SDOs - but in this case the ISO standard is clearly NOT technically equivalent to a specific version of JS! 

Referring back to ISO 32000-1:2008 (PDF 1.7) which normatively referenced "_Client-Side JavaScript Reference, (May 1999), Mozilla Foundation_.".  I cannot locate this but I suspect was supposed to be ECMA-262 4th edition however this was never released by ECMA. This theory would also align with the previous support for E4X (now agreed deprecated for PDF 2.0).

The latest Adobe documentation for "_Acrobat JavaScript API Reference_" from https://opensource.adobe.com/dc-acrobat-sdk-docs/acrobatsdk/ provides this information on p.33:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/26521615/173211534-bac9d9d1-60a8-4dcf-9d64-5e4b4eb1b2f1.png)

This is also confusing as I cannot find references to JavaScript versions as "1.x" but only "ESx" with "ES5" being ECMAScript 5 (2009) and I'm not sure what JavaScript "1.8" is in terms of ECMAScript editions since after ES6 the year is the version...

I do not believe PDF should allow a moving target for JS language support. So the question is: what version(s) of ECMAScript can be used with PDF 2.0, and what are the correct normative references for that fixed version(s)?
title: In ISO 21757, the ECMAScript version for use with PDF 2.0 is not specified or constrained

body:
The **Placement** attribute is defined in 14.8.5.4.2 General layout attributes, Table 378 — Standard layout attributes common to all standard structure types. The definition says:

> Default value: _Block_ for BLSEs, _Inline_ for ILSEs.

Some structure elements can be either a BLSE or an ILSE, for example **Figure** and **Formula**. It's unclear at this point in the text whether such a structure element is a BLSE or an ILSE. The default value of **Placement** is thus also unclear. The BLSE vs ILSE determination is specified in 14.8.4.1, "General", about 20 pages back.

This issue was discussed in today's meeting of the Reuse TWG of the PDF Association. One expert explained how BLSE vs ILSE could be determined from context. Several other experts in the meeting found that explanation extremely helpful in clarifying the default value of **Placement** for those elements. The meeting participants developed that explanation into an informative note and two examples. I've modified the note slightly. The suggestion is to add this note and those examples after **Placement**'s default value text, so the text would read:

> Default value: _Block_ for BLSEs, _Inline_ for ILSEs.
> NOTE The default value depends on the context in which the structure element is used (see 14.8.4.1, "General").
> EXAMPLE 1 A **Figure** structure element occurring within a **P** structure element is an ILSE, and therefore has a default value of _Inline_. 
> EXAMPLE 2 A **Figure** structure element occurring within a **Sect** structure element is an BLSE, and therefore has a default value of _Block_.
title: Placement attribute default in Table 378 unclear for structure elements that can be either block or inline

to
