body:
Table 120 for Font Descriptors defines **Descent** as:
> (_Required, except for Type 3 fonts_) The maximum depth below the baseline reached by glyphs in this font. The value shall be a negative number.

Examining millions of PDFs shows that **Descent** 0 (zero) is extremely common even tho' the negative requirement was originally stated back in Adobe PDF 1.0.  So why is **Descent** strictly negatively (i.e. the smallest valid value for Descent is thus -1) and zero not allowed? Not all glyph sets or typefaces have descenders that project _below_ the baseline...

PS. I am ignoring the sizable collection of invalid PDFs that have **Descent** with very large _positive_ values!
title: Why is Font Descriptor Descent strictly negative? Why is zero Descent not permitted?

body:
As noted in Issue #190, the use of phrasing such "negative", "positive", "non-negative", etc. can have a regional understanding as to whether or not zero is included or excluded.

Discussions in the PDF TWG suggested a review of all such terms throughout ISO 32000-2:2020 and to always explicitly state if zero is included or excluded. Defining new formal T&Ds was felt to be *not* a good solution because it is not as immediately obvious for developers when picking over the PDF spec and may also unintentionally apply elsewhere in ISO 32000. 

This issue is to track this review.
title: Review use of "negative", "positive", "non-negative", etc. phrases for clear and consistent understanding

body:
**Describe the bug**

PDF/A-4 (like PDF/A-2 and PDF/A-3 before it) contains the following provision:

> Except for annotation dictionaries whose Subtype value is Popup, all annotation dictionaries shall contain the F key. If present, the F key’s Print flag bit shall be set to 1 and its Hidden, Invisible, ToggleNoView, and NoView flag bits shall be set to 0.

Note that invisible (=zero-size **Rect**) signature fields are _not_ exempt from this requirement! To understand why this is an issue, allow me to take a brief detour through PDF 1.7-land.


PDF/UA-1 contains the following provision in the general annotation requirements:

> The requirements of this clause shall not apply to annotations whose hidden flag is set or whose
rectangle is outside the CropBox or whose Subtype is Popup.

This means that, in order for an invisible signature field to be exempt from the tagging requirements in PDF/UA-1, it must have its hidden flag set (possible workaround: put them outside the cropbox?). Ergo, in a file that declares compliance with PDF/A-2 (or PDF/A-3) _and_ PDF/UA-1, all invisible signature fields are subject to tagging requirements.

In practice, this standard is impossible to meet: the classic example is PAdES-B-LTA document timestamp updates, which require a potentially unbounded number of signature fields to be added for timestamps. Under PDF/UA+PDF/A, that implies having to add all these document timestamp fields to the structure tree, which creates a royal mess for signature validation.

The effect is that it's impractical to use PAdES-B-LTA signatures effectively in PDF 1.7 documents that need to comply with both PDF/A and PDF/UA. I think we can all agree that that's not a good state of affairs.

--------------

Why does this story matter at all in a PDF 2.0 context? Because PDF/A-4 contains the same requirement on annotation flags as PDF/A-2 and PDF/A-3. Fortunately, widgets with zero width and height are considered artifacts in PDF/UA-2 (at least according to the current draft), so there's an escape hatch for (future) software seeking to comply with both. It's not particularly intuitive, though.

I would therefore (still) like to ask the PDF/A experts  here whether they would consider adding an exemption to 6.3.2 of ISO 19005-4 for "annotations where the value of the Rect key consists of an array where value 1 is equal to value 3 and value 2 is equal to value 4" (such an exemption does apply to appearance streams, interestingly enough).

Regardless of the outcome of that discussion, this clearly warrants a very loud, obnoxious note in PDF/UA-2... ;)

--------------

TL;DR: In current standards derived from PDF 1.7, the combined requirements of PDF/A and PDF/UA w.r.t. invisible signature fields are too onerous to enable modern (PAdES-style) digital signing workflows. Since PDF/A-4 did not change course on that issue, we either need to amend PDF/A-4 to allow the **Hidden** flag on invisible signature fields, or make it _crystal clear_ to future PDF/UA-2 users what they have to do. Ideally, both.
title: Invisible signature fields and PDF/A-4 restrictions on flags, and what that means for PDF/UA-2

body:
**Describe the bug**

Clause 7.2.2 contains the following text:

> A non-encrypted PDF file can be entirely represented using byte values corresponding to the visible printable subset of the ASCII character set defined in INCITS 4-1986 (R2017), plus white-space characters. However, a PDF file is not restricted to the ASCII character set; it may contain arbitrary bytes, subject to the following considerations: 
> - [...]
> - A PDF file containing binary data shall be transported as a binary file rather than as a text file to ensure that all bytes of the file are faithfully preserved.

Clearly, _all_ PDF files, not just the ones that happen to contain invisible/non-printable ASCII characters, should be saved and transported as binary files. For example, platform differences in line ending conventions can mess up byte offsets in the cross-reference table of _any_ PDF file if the file is transported as text, even if it doesn't contain any "exotic" characters.


**Proposed solution**

Strike the words "containing binary data" from that last bullet point:

> A PDF file shall be transported as a binary file rather than as a text file to ensure that all bytes of the file are faithfully preserved.
title: Minor nitpick on PDF representation as text

body:
Where does the spec state how to interpret a reference to an object in an object stream when that stream (itself an indirect object) is the null object, especially if it is considered null due to its cross-reference entry being of an unknown type?

Context:

The spec states that in cross-reference streams, entries of an unknown type are to be treated as valid entries that point to the null object (7.5.8.3 Cross-reference stream data).

It also states that references to non-existent objects are to be treated as references to the null object (7.3.9 Null object). This presumably covers the case where cross-reference data points to an object stream but that stream does not in fact contain the object in question. It would also cover the case where the stream itself does not exist. It does not seem to cover the case where the stream is null, because being null is not the same as being non-existent, cf. the rules for null objects in arrays.
title: What if a stream is null?

body:
This issue and proposed solution arose from the PDF/A TWG discussion on July 11 related to https://github.com/pdf-association/pdfa-twg/issues/19.

ISO 32000-2, Table 275 declares requirement type PRC (and similarly for U3D) with the following wording:

> PRC - Requires support for 3D data streams conforming to the PRC specification. This shall apply to the use of PRC in either 3D (13.6.3, "3D streams") or RichMedia annotations (13.7.2.2, "RichMediaSettings dictionary"). This also includes support for associated ECMAScripts.

The "_shall_" statement here for U3D and PRC are not correct as this would imply that Document Requirements would be needed for all PDF/A-4e (for example). ISO 32000-2 describes Doc Requirements not as file format requirements, but as hints to a processor. The best way to avoid confusion is to modify the wording to reword as a factual statement (applies to both U3D and PRC cells in Table 275) as is done with the ECMAScript statement:

> PRC - Requires support for 3D data streams conforming to the PRC specification. **This applies to the use of PRC** in either 3D (13.6.3, "3D streams") or RichMedia annotations (13.7.2.2, "RichMediaSettings dictionary"). This also includes support for associated ECMAScripts.
title: Document Requirements are processor hints, not file format requirements, for U3D and PRC

Clause 7.6.5.2 "Public-key encrypt dictionary" paragraph 1 states that it is made up of Table 20 + Table 23. Yet Table 24 talks about permissions, but neither Table 20 or Table 23 have a permissions key anymore as it was removed (as per the NOTE below Table 23). This means all the text below the NOTE below Table 23 about permissions is now contextless and confusing... 

The correct linkage is to the 2nd bullet in 7.6.5.3 "Public-key encryption algorithms".

Rather than move lots of text around I suggest the following purely-editorial correction:
* insert a new subclause heading as 7.6.5.2 "Public-key encryption permissions" directly below the NOTE below Table 23. This new heading is a referencing point for all the current text (incl. Table 24) on permissions
* consequently renumber the current 7.6.5.3 to 7.6.5.4 "Public-key encryption algorithms"
* in the 2nd bullet in the newly numbered 7.6.5.4 "Public-key encryption algorithms" add a back-reference to our new subclause: (see 7.6.5.2 "Public-key encryption permissions").
* as a consequence of the renumber, fix-up Table 27 Recipients description. There are no other cross-references to 7.6.5.x subclauses in ISO 32000-2:2020.

So the final heading structure will be:
* 7.6.5 Public-key security handlers
    - 7.6.5.1 General
    - 7.6.5.2 Public-key encryption dictionary
    - 7.6.5.3 Public-key encryption permissions (**new**)
    - 7.6.5.4 Public-key encryption algorithms
title: Public-key encryption permission explanation has lost its context (editorial)

body:
I know we've discussed this one previously, but it doesn't seem to have been captured as an issue.

32000-2 8.6.5.8 allows the use of any value for a rendering intent, not just the 4 standard ones (see also [Issue 63](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/63)).

PDF/X-4 and earlier prohibited the use of a value for RI other than the standard 4 (e.g. 15930-9:2010 6.23), but this requirement was dropped in PDF/X-6. Some of us vaguely remembered that was done because it was anticipated that PDF 2.0 would prohibit non-standard rendering intents, but we didn't close the loop late in the process to make certain ... and it doesn't.

I recommend that we capture an intent to prohibit non-standard rendering intents in X-6.
title: Clarify rendering intents that can be used in PDF/X-6

body:
32000-2:2020 9.2.4 says that the widths stored in the font dictionary "shall be consistent with the actual widths given in the font program".

15930-9:2010 6.8.4 says (my emphasis):

> For every font embedded in a conforming file, the glyph width information in the font dictionary and in the embedded font program shall be consistent for every glyph referenced for rendering. **_Glyphs that are referenced only with rendering mode 3 are exempt from this requirement_**.

That exemption seems wrong on two levels:

1. It gives a confusing impression that it's contradicting a normative reference by loosening a requirement.

2. Consistency is desirable even with rendering mode 3 so that any following marks that are not in mode 3 will appear in the right place. The underlying rule is to enable some tools to read widths from the font dictionary and some from the embedded font and give equivalent results from both approaches. I don't see any reason to assume that a tool that normally reads widths from the embedded font would switch to using the font dictionary instead for rendering mode 3.

I recommend that the whole of para 1 of 6.8.4 is simply deleted as replicating a requirement from 32000-2.
title: Odd exception in PDF/X-6 font width requirements

body:
**Description**

7.3.7 "Dictionary objects" makes the following two statements:

(A)
> A dictionary entry whose value is null (see 7.3.9, "Null object") shall be treated the same as if the entry does not exist.

(B)
> Multiple entries in the same dictionary shall not have the same key.

This does not clearly define the semantics of something like the following:

    << /Foo null /Foo null >>

Is this forbidden by rule (B) or allowed (equivalent to `<< >>`) due to rule (A)?

**Additional Context**

Note that null values can occur implicitly due to unresolvable references, so if the above example were allowed as `<< >>`, rule (B) could not be verified in general without full cross-reference resolution and unknown "cross-reference stream entry types" (cf. #194) would mean that the following could be valid or invalid depending on which version of PDF the reader supports.

    << /Foo 666 0 R /Foo (bar) >>

**Suggestion**

Clearly define rule (B) as taking precedence over rule (A) by moving it into the first paragraph of section 7.3.7 and wording it more directly.

> A dictionary object is an associative table containing pairs of objects, known as the dictionary's entries. The first element of each entry is the key and the second element is the value. The key shall be a name (...) and each key shall occur only once.

In addition, rule (A) might be augmented to explicitly rule out any confusion.

> A dictionary entry whose value is null (see 7.3.9, "Null object") shall be treated semantically the same as if the entry does not exist. Note that multiple entries for the same key shall still not occur, even with null values.
title: Dictionary entries with null values

body:
**Describe the bug**

There is an internal inconsistency in the wording of Section 7.8.2 "Content streams". Its paragraph 1 makes the following statement:

> A content stream ... consists of a sequence of instructions ...
> The instructions shall be represented in the form of PDF objects,
> using the same object syntax as in the rest of the PDF document.

It seems clear that operators are not PDF objects. However, paragraph 3 reiterates:

> [A content stream] consists of PDF objects denoting operands and operators.

This can be read in two ways: (a) "PDF objects denoting operands and PDF objects denoting operators" or (b) "PDF objects denoting operands and other things called operators". I am assuming that the term "PDF object" in the context of this specification can only reasonably be taken to refer to objects as defined by section 7.3.

Paragraph 5 clarifies:

> An operator is a PDF keyword ...
> [They] shall be distinguished from a name object by the
> absence of an initial SOLIDUS character (2Fh) (/).
> Operators shall be meaningful only inside a content stream.

The term "PDF keyword" is not specifically defined, so it presumably means the same thing as the generic term "keyword" as used, for example, in section 7.3 "Objects".

**Recommendation for correction**

Replace the offending sentence in paragraph 1 as follows:
```diff
- The instructions shall be represented in the form of PDF objects, using the same object syntax as in the rest of the PDF document.
+ The instructions make use of PDF objects which shall be represented using the same syntax as in the rest of the PDF document.
```

Reword the sentence in paragraph 3 as follows:
```diff
- It consists of PDF objects denoting operands and operators.
+ It consists of PDF objects denoting operands and keywords denoting operators.
```

Remove the word "PDF" from the term "keyword" in paragraph 5:
```diff
- An operator is a PDF keyword specifying some action
+ An operator is a keyword specifying some action
```
title: Content stream operators are "PDF objects"?

body:
The syntax for content stream operators is not explicitly defined. This is a problem with *compatibility sections* as introduced by the last paragraph of 7.8.2 "Content streams":

> They bracket a compatibility section, a portion of a content stream within which unrecognised operators shall be ignored without error.

It is not clear if this means that the following would be allowed:

    BX 1 2 \o EX

Clearly `1` and `2` are objects and thus operands, followed by `\o`, a sequence of regular characters that is not an object. Paragraph 5 of 7.8.2 notes:

> An operator keyword shall be distinguished from a name object by the absence of an initial SOLIDUS character (2Fh) (/).

This sounds like operator keywords might be meant to follow the same syntax as name objects after the initial solidus but stops short of saying so.
title: Syntax of content stream operators between BX/EX

body:
First of all: this is a typo I found in PDF 1.7 spec.   I don't know this issue persists in 2.0 spec, because unfortunately the document is not for free, but I am point this out just in case because the paragraph in 1.7 spec may be reused in 2.0.

**Describe the bug**

body:
When a content stream is split across multiple stream objects by specifying an array in a page's **Contents** entry, the description of **Contents** in Table 31 states:

> If the value is an array, the effect shall be as if all of the streams in the array
> were concatenated with **at least one white-space** character added
> between the streams' data, in order, to form a single stream.

(Emphasis mine.) This sounds sensible. It ensures that the stream boundaries coincide with token boundaries. However, it leaves it up to the implementation to decide which whitespace character(s) to "imagine" between the streams. That would be fine if all whitespace was treated the same between tokens, but as far as I can tell from 7.2 "Lexical conventions" and 7.3.4 "String objects", a literal string such as `(Hello World)` is not considered a single token.

Therefore, a content stream as in the following appears to be not well-defined:

    4 0 obj
        << /Type /Page /Contents [5 0 R 8 0 R] ... >>
    endobj

    5 0 obj
        << /Length 30 >>
    stream
    BT /F1 24 Tf 100 100 Td (Hello
    endstream
    endobj                                                                                                                                                                    

    8 0 obj
        << /Length 12 >>
    stream
    World) Tj ET
    endstream
    endobj

Is the string in question `Hello World`, `Hello\nWorld`, or `Hello    \n  \n \n\n\nWorld`?
Or is the above illegal somehow?

**Recommendation for correction**

Clearly define what is to be inserted when joining the streams.
E.g. replace the phrase "at least one white-space character" in Table 31 with "exactly one SPACE (20h) character".

**Additional Context**

Test file: [hello2-fixed.pdf](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/files/9311486/hello2-fixed.pdf)

 - `evince` renders "HelloWorld" (no white-space).
 - `xpdf` renders "HelloWorld" (no white-space).
 - Firefox renders "HelloWorld" (no white-space).
 - Chrome renders "Hello World" (one space character).
title: Splitting a content stream in the middle of a string

Clause 7.6.2 has a list of strings that are never encrypted:
> * The values for the ID entry in the trailer
> * Any strings in an Encrypt dictionary
> * Any strings that are inside streams such as content streams and compressed object streams, which themselves are encrypted
> * Any hexadecimal strings representing the value of the **Contents** key in a Signature dictionary

The last bullet is worded in a very roundabout way... 

Table 255 — Entries in a signature dictionary defines **Contents** as:
> (_Required_) The signature value. When **ByteRange** is present, the value shall be a hexadecimal string (see 7.3.4.3, "Hexadecimal strings") representing the value of the byte range digest. For public-key signatures, Contents should be either a DER-encoded PKCS # 1 binary data object, a DER-encoded CMS binary data object or a DER-encoded CMS SignedData binary data object.
For document timestamp signatures, Contents shall be the TimeStampToken as specified in _Internet RFC 3161_ as updated by Internet RFC 5816. The value of the **messageImprint** field within the TimeStampToken shall be a hash of the bytes of the document indicated by the **ByteRange** and the **ByteRange** shall specify the complete PDF file contents (excepting the Contents value).
Space for the Contents value shall be allocated before the message digest is computed (see 7.3.4, "String objects").

So is it correct that the **Contents** is now only ever a hex string in PDF 2.0?
If so then the 7.6.2 last bullet should just be "The value of the **Contents** key in a Signature dictionary (see Table 255)"?
title: Conditions when Contents key in Signature dictionary is unencrypted?

Recently I got several PDF Documents which contained several Field Arrays. So as a compliant reader how should I deal with this? Take the first one or last one and ignore the rest? Merge both? I would says that this violates the spec but it is not explicitly forbidden. Current definition:

> Fields | array | (Required) An array of references to the document’s root fields (those with no ancestors in the field hierarchy).

Proposed improvement:

> Fields | array | (Required) An array of references to the document’s root fields (those with no ancestors in the field hierarchy). A Fields array should occur only once inside a PDF file.
(inspired by the `Title` block)

OR

> Fields | array | (Required) An array of references to the document’s root fields (those with no ancestors in the field hierarchy). If a Fields array is present more than once, only the last shall be used.
(inspired by the `NA` array)
title: Multiple Form Field Arrays inside one PDF

body:
We recently hit a PDF for remediation which had a 150MB file attached as a data URL in a `goToURL` Action - the file was stored as a String.

I suspect we can all agree is this is not a good approach! But actually, it's not currently clear if we have a method in PDF to _select_ a non-PDF embedded files - even if select just means display it in the File Attachment tab, or open a prompt to save it to disk.

* `Launch` take a file specification, but seems intended for external files rather than internal. It's also disallowed in PDFA.
* `GoToE` works with embedded files, but only PDF files: a `D` array defining the destination in that file is required.

The ongoing project to handle email archiving in PDF will likely find value in being able to refer to a non-PDF attachment. So I think there is a good case for either adding another action type which _selects_ the embedded file, or ensuring that the `Launch` action is refreshed (ie. the documentation and/or properties are updated) to ensure it's clear that launching an embedded file is allowed.

I have a slight preference for a  new action, because (eg) a `LaunchE` action could be allowed in PDF/A-5 while`Launch` remains disallowed. Another possibility is relaxing the requirements on `GoToE` so that the `D` array is optional, and linking to a non-PDF file is allowed, although we then have the question of whether such a file would be valid in PDF/A-3 or A-4.

For reference I attach one of my tests - the first link is a `GoToE` action to the embedded PNG file, the second is a `Launch` action to the same. Neither work in the PDF viewers I tested, although I think the `Launch` action is technically valid.

[embedded-link.pdf](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/files/9479947/embedded-link.pdf)
title: Enhancement: add an action type that allows referring to a non-PDF embedded file.

body:
Regarding the strings used as key in a name tree, ISO 32000-2:2020, Table 36 "Entries in a name tree node dictionary" mandates that

> The keys shall be sorted in lexical order, as described below.

The referenced descriptive text below the table reads as follows:

> The Names entries in the leaf (or root) nodes shall contain the tree’s keys and their associated values, arranged in key-value pairs and shall be sorted lexically in ascending order by key. Shorter keys shall appear before longer ones beginning with the same byte sequence. Any encoding of the keys may be used as long as it is self-consistent; keys shall be compared for equality on a simple byte-by-byte basis.

The term _lexical(ly)_, which is used twice, is meaningful only in combination with a fixed encoding. However, the requirement _self-consistent_ is not very clear, and once an encoding is fixed the term _lexical_ doesn't add any requirement or explanatory value. It may actually be wrong if two byte strings are compared numerically where one string accidentally starts with a BOM and might be interpreted as text (one might argue that "lexical" is undefined anyway for byte strings).


**Proposed clarification**

In the paragraph below Table 36 change

"Any encoding of the keys may be used as long as it is self-consistent;"
to
"All keys shall use the same string type and encoding (see Figure 7  "Relationship between string types");"

For text strings this clarifies the intended existing requirement of having the same encoding. For ASCII strings and byte strings the "same type" requirement is necessary to avoid incorrect comparison.

For example, the string "A" may be represented as ASCII or UTF-8 string as follows:

ASCII string:		0x41
UTF-8 string:		0xEF 0xBB 0xBF 0x41

Lexically both strings are identical, but numerically they are not.


**Proposed editorial changes**

- Table 36, row "Names": change
"The keys shall be sorted in lexical order, as described below."
to
"The keys shall be sorted as described below."

- In the paragraph below Table 36 change
"...shall be sorted lexically in ascending order by key."
to
"...shall be sorted in ascending order by key."
title: String type and encoding in name trees

In Table 87 (Additional Entries in Image Dictionary), for the `SMask` entry, it reads:
>If present, this entry shall override the current soft mask in the graphics state, as well as the image’s Mask entry, if any. However, the other transparency-related graphics state parameters — blend mode and alpha constant — shall remain in effect.

However, neither statement is duplicated in the `SMaskInData` entry.   

It is, however stated later on in 11.6.4.3, bullet three
>If SMaskInData is present with a value other than 0, the embedded soft-mask shall override any explicit or colour key mask specified by the image dictionary’s Mask entry, and it shall override, for this image object only, the current soft mask in the graphics state.

Apparently some implementations (e.g. Chrome) didn't read far enough and apply both Mask and SMaskInData.  

Recommend that we copy the text from the `SMask` entry into the `SMaskInData` entry for consistency.
title: SMaskInData overrides Mask - but it's not clearly stated

body:
**Description**
The PDF specification does not make a clear statement whether the syntax rules of a stream filter must be obeyed if the stream in question is not used anywhere. The closest I can find is in section 7.4.1 "General":

> A PDF writer may encode data in a stream (for example, data for sampled images) to compress it or to convert it to a portable ASCII representation (or both). 
> A PDF reader shall invoke the corresponding decoding filter or filters to convert the information back to its original form.

The first sentence ("may encode...") lets one suspect that the second sentence applies to any stream object, used or not. The second sentence ("shall invoke...") could be taken to imply that a deviation from the filter syntax as described by the appropriate subsection of 7.4 would be a decoding error that makes the file invalid. It would be nice to have the intended interpretation made explicit.

**Context**
To elaborate, the spec does not (as far as my reading goes) prohibit a file from containing objects that are never used anywhere. For example, a presumably useless stream object like this would be valid:

    1 0 obj
    << /Length 5 >>
    stream
    !!!!!
    endstream
    endobj

Section 7.3.8 "Stream objects" introduces the Filter entry which is further described in Section 7.4 "Filters". The latter section describes the expected format for each filter. This includes some statements such as, for example, the following in section 7.4.3 "ASCII85Decode filter":

> Any other characters, and any character sequences that represent impossible
> combinations in the ASCII base-85 encoding, shall cause an error.

This statement, due to the part "shall cause an error" can be taken to imply that a file is invalid if it contains a stream object, used or unused, that lists `/Filter /ASCII85Decode` in its stream dictionary and contains such an "impossible combination".

However, there occur other statements about filter syntax that may not be quite as clear, because they do not explicitly mandate "shall cause an error". An example is also in section 7.4.3:

> As a special case, if all five bytes are 0, they shall be represented by the character 
> with code 122 (z) instead of by five exclamation points (! ! ! ! !).

So, if the above example object were still not used anywhere, but called for the ASCII85Decode filter, would the file as a whole be valid or invalid?

    1 0 obj
    << /Length 5 /Filter /ASCII85Decode >>
    stream
    !!!!!
    endstream
    endobj

**Proposed solution**
Add a sentence to the Filter entry in Table 5 (section 7.3.8 "Stream objects"):
> The stream data shall follow the appropriate format(s) as specified in 7.4, "Filters".
title: Invalid Filter data in unused stream objects

body:
**Description**
This issue is similar to #216 but concerns the Type field of a stream object. This field is not described in Table 5 of section 7.3.8 "Stream objects", but mandated by individual stream types. Table 16 in section 7.5.7 "Object streams", for example, states that object streams must have `/Type /ObjStm` in their stream dictionary.

To go with the example of object streams: It is my understanding that a stream becomes an object stream by virtue of being referenced as such in a cross-reference stream, rather than due to it carrying a Type field of "ObjStm". So a file that contains a stream object like the following but never references it anywhere would be valid, even though the object does not comply with the syntax for an object stream. Is this correct/intended?

    1 0 obj
    << /Length 3 /Type /ObjStm >>
    stream
    XXX
    endstream
    endobj
title: Data syntax for unused streams with respect to Type

ISO 32000-2:2020 Table 255 **SubFilter** cell has an italic "(PDF 1.6)" indicator for the list of values in the 2nd para. ISO 32000-1:2008 is the same, presumably because Adobe PDF 1.7 said "_PDF 1.6 defines the following values for public-key cryptographic signatures: adbe.x509.rsa_sha1, adbe.pkcs7.detached, and adbe.pkcs7.sha1_" . Adobe PDF 1.3 and PDF 1.4 fail to mention any values for **SubFilter** (even searching for just "x509" returns zero results) - Adobe PDF 1.3 Table 7.53 and Adobe PDF 1.4 Table 8.60 do not list any values. Adobe PDF 1.5 Table 8.93 was the first PDF reference that explicitly mentioned the 3 values. So from a specification-centric PoV the first doco for values _adbe.x509.rsa_sha1_, _adbe.pkcs7.detached_, _adbe.pkcs7.sha1_ should be PDF 1.5, not PDF 1.6. So it should be:

> The following values for public-key cryptographic signatures should be used: _adbe.x509.rsa_sha1_ (_PDF 1.5_), _adbe.pkcs7.detached_ (_PDF 1.5_), _adbe.pkcs7.sha1_ (_PDF 1.5_), _ETSI.CAdES.detached_ (_PDF 2.0_) and _ETSI.RFC3161_ (_PDF 2.0_).

I also note that the sentence starting "Other values may be ..." in the 3rd para should really start a new paragraph in ISO 32000-2:2020 as the "Other values ..." is not only applicable for PDF 2.0.
title: Table 255 Signature dictionary SubFilter minor corrections

body:
**Describe the bug**
```
7.3.7 Dictionary Objects (Paragraph 1)
[ ... ] A dictionary entry whose value is null (see 7.3.9, "Null object") 
shall be treated the same as if the entry does not exist. [ ... ]

7.3.9 Null Objects
[ ... ]	Specifying the null object as the value of a dictionary entry (7.3.7, "Dictionary objects") 
shall be equivalent to omitting the entry entirely.
```

The same expected behavior: ignoring entries in dictionaries with value `null` is described in two distinct manners. It may be the interpretation of a non-native speaker, but I feel there is a nuance between the two phrasings. 

I would suggest to use the same definition and phrasing for both to make sure the actual behavior is consistent. Ideally, the definition used in 7.3.7 would be used as it feels the most conclusive to me and doesn't depend on "treating".
title: Null Entries in dictionaries are described differently in 7.3.7 and 7.3.9

body:
"Table 228 — Additional entries common to all fields containing variable text" and related text in clause "12.7.4.3 Variable text" does not explicitly state **precisely** which kinds of fields are "variable text" and thus where Table 228 keys are expected. 

AFAICT there are no explicit requirements anywhere in "12.7 Forms" that limit Table 228 keys to specific kinds of Fields, and the definition of "variable text" in 12.7.4.3 is hand-wavy at best (e.g. the NOTE gives the example of ECMAscript) and is not sufficiently prescriptive to limit things. 

The best seems to be the second paragraph of 12.7.4.3:
> In such cases, the PDF document cannot provide a statically defined appearance stream for displaying the field. Instead, the PDF processor shall construct an appearance stream dynamically at rendering time.

But in Table 166 for Annots, we changed PDF 2.0 to require appearance streams by stating the following for **AP**:
> Every annotation (including those whose **Subtype** value is _Widget_, as used for form fields), except for the two cases listed below, shall have at least one appearance dictionary. ...

It would be far better to be explicit, either by stating in 12.7.4.3 which fields are considered "variable text", or having explicit requirement statements in each of the subclasses in 12.7.5.x with any additional conditions (i.e. on a per-field basis).

(Arising from Arlington issue https://github.com/pdf-association/arlington-pdf-model/issues/29)
title: Unclear which fields are considered "variable text" for Table 228

Table 99 **RBGroups** entry states "_An array consisting of one or more arrays, each of which represents a collection of optional content groups whose states shall be intended to follow a radio button paradigm. ... 
An empty array [] explicitly indicates that no such collections exist_."

So an empty array (zero elements: `[ ]`) is explicitly mentioned but is not allowed!

body:
Syntactic (_not semantic!_) rules for valid attribute objects spread across clauses 14.7.6 and 14.8.5 is very difficult to discover and understand - and there are some errors:

* there is no definitive list of all formally defined values for the required key **O** (owner). 
"Table 360 - Entries common to all attribute object dictionaries" defines _NSO_ and _UserProperties_, and "_one of the values from 14.8.5_" which is a 23-page subclause!! So is this really meaning **only** the values listed in Table 376? Or are there also other valid values of **O** not in Table 376, but buried somewhere else in the text of 14.8.5? 
If it is just Table 376 it would be far far better to reference it precisely from Table 360 rather than some mega-clause.
And it would be good if Table 376 included (or noted) _NSO_ and _UserProperties_ for completeness, with a cross-reference back to Table 360.

* throughout all subclauses of 14.8.5,  Layout, Table, PrintField and Artifact are formatted as bold which indicates a key name, when, in fact, they are **O** (owner) key values and should really be italic. This is confusing.

* 14.8.5.3 attribute inheritance vs explicit exclusion requirements based on the value of **O** in various 14.8.5.x subclauses is unclear. 
For example, 14.8.5.4.1 (layout attributes) states "_Attributes in this category shall be defined in attribute objects whose **O** (owner) entry has the value Layout or whose owner is any other owner excluding **List**, **Table**, **PrintField** and **Artifact**._". But 14.8.5.3 on attribute inheritance lacks explanation in terms of normative requirements: "_an attribute that is specified for an element shall apply to all the descendants of the element in the structure tree unless a descendent element specifies an explicit value for the attribute_". 
So does this mean that if you want to inherit an attribute that is prohibited by the value of **O** (owner) then you need to push it further up the structure tree to another node that has some other **O** (owner) that permits it? 
In which case, 14.8.5.3 should probably note that not all elements in the structure tree may allow for the inclusion of certain inheritable attributes based on requirements in other subclauses.
Or can you have the "wrong attributes" for the purposes of inheritance? 
In which case the various file format requirements like ".. _shall be defined in attribute objects whose **O** (owner) entry..._" should change to something like a processor requirement to "apply"...

* Table 377, second column is titled "Attributes" and the entries are formatted as normal text. I believe these are precise dictionary key names that can occur in attribute objects, rather than a description of the attribute so it would be better if:
     1. the entries were bold - as that is the convention for key names throughout 32K
     2. the column title was "Attribute Key" so it is crystal clear these are normative key names and not descriptive
     3. each row should have a corresponding cross-reference to one of Table 378 to Table 381 (since Table 377 duplicates the inheritance requirement it is important that the synchronisation is acknowledged).

* Table 379 and Table 385 conflict on which values of **O** (owner) **BBox** can be validly defined: 
Table 379 defines **BBox** and is constrained by the 2nd sentence in 14.8.5.4.1: "_Attributes in this category shall be defined in attribute objects whose **O** (owner) entry has the value Layout or whose owner is any other owner excluding **List**, **Table**, **PrintField** and **Artifact**._". 
Table 385 also defines **BBox** and is constrained by "... _attribute objects whose **O** (owner) entry has the value Artifact or whose owner is any other owner excluding **Layout**, **List**, **PrintField** and **Table**._" 
So it appears that when **O** (owner) is either _Layout_ or_Artifact_, or whose owner is any other owner excluding **List**, **PrintField** and **Table** (e.g. _NSO_ or the external format values in Table 376), **BBox** is allowed!
title: Syntactic rules for valid attribute objects across clauses 14.7 and 14.8 is very difficult to understand and has mistakes

body:
PDF/X-6 section 6.19 discusses spectral data as embedded CxF/X-4 files inside PDF. It says

> A conforming writer should ensure that the spectral data present in the file is consistent with the values in the Output Intent ICC profile.” 

But the output intent describes process colorants and CxF is mostly used to describe spots. I recommend that sentence be extended to say

> A conforming writer should ensure that the spectral data present in the file is consistent with the values in the Output Intent ICC profile and with alternate colour spaces and DeviceN colour space attributes dictionaries.

That requirement is not present in PDF/A-4, and is probably not appropriate for adding into 32000-2 itself.
title: Extend recommendations around CxF in PDF/X-6

body:
It is possible to embed an iccMAX profile inside an ICC v4 profile. The v4 profile can then be embedded into a PDF file. Neither 32000-2 itself nor any of other subset standards say anything about this situation, although it could conceivably lead to very different visual appearances from different products.

In many ways this is similar to embedding CxF/X-4 data in PDF, which can also lead to different products producing different output. 32000-2 itself says:
> This document intentionally does not specify how a PDF processor may make use of the data provided in the SpectralData dictionary, and a PDF processor may ignore such data altogether.

And PDF/X recommends that the CxF data should be consistent with output intents (see [issue #227](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/227)).

So, should there be a comment about the potential of varying output if a v4 profile includes an iccMax profile, either in 32000-2 itself, or just in PDF/X-6 (together with the CxF recommendation)?
title: iccMAX profiles embedded within v4 profiles in PDF

body:
Annex E.2, 2nd bullet under "Second class" states ".. _except keys added to a document information dictionary (see 14.3.3, "Document information dictionary") or a thread information dictionary (in the **I** entry of a thread dictionary; see 12.4.3, "Articles")._". This is an incomplete list of officially allowed places in PDF where developers may legally add their own custom names that do **not** have to be 2nd-class names.

A list of other places with either explicit or implied wording (in no specific order) - there may well be others:

* Encrypted Payload dictionary, Table 28, **Subtype** key
* 12.6.4.12 Named actions, 1st para "... _further names may be added in the future_".
* Optional Content Usage dict, Table 100, **CreatorInfo** entry: "_Suggested values include but shall not be limited to_ ..."
* Navigators, **Layout** entry, para about Table 160: "_This mechanism is inherently extensible and allows inclusion of custom named layouts ..._"
* Rubber stamp annot, Table 184, **Name** entry: "_Additional names may be supported as well._"
* File attachment annot, Table 187, **Name** entry: "_Additional names may be supported as well_"
* Printer's Mark annot, Table 398, **MN** entry: "_An arbitrary name identifying the type of printer’s mark, ..._"

body:
I would like to ask and clarify the radio button behavior in combination with the /Opt array. It is defined as:

> An array containing one entry for each widget annotation in the Kids array of the radio button or check box field. Each entry shall be a text string representing the on state of the corresponding widget annotation.

As I understand "one entry for each widget annotation" means that the indices are mapped between Kids and Opt arrays. Is that correct?

```
4 0 obj
<</FT/Btn/Ff 49152
/Kids[16 0 R 21 0 R 22 0 R]
       |       |       |   
/Opt[(Yes)   (No)  (Maybe)]       
/T(Decision)>>
endobj

```
So the corresponding appearance is defined like this:
```
16 0 obj
<</AP<</N<</Yes 17 0 R/Off 18 0 R>>>>/AS/Off/Parent 4 0 R/Subtype/Widget/Type/Annot [...]>>
endobj
```

My second question is: What if the appearance is defined as `/N<</SomethingElseThanYesOrIndex 17 0 R` Who wins? Meaning what should be written into the /V and /AS values? The entry of the Opt array (=Yes) or the name of the AP dictionary in the widget (=SomethingElseThanYes )? 

Additionally the standard defines:

> When this entry is present, the names used to represent the on state in the AP dictionary of each annotation may use numerical position (starting with 0) of the annotation in the Kids array, encoded as a name object (for example: /0, /1). This allows distinguishing between the annotations even if two or more of them have the same value in the Opt array. 

This means the name of the appearance could also be /0 (instead of /Yes)

```
16 0 obj
<</AP<</N<</0 17 0 R/Off 18 0 R>>>>/AS/Off/Parent 4 0 R/Subtype/Widget/Type/Annot [...]>>
endobj
```
However in the following case:

```
4 0 obj
<</FT/Btn/Ff 49152
/Kids[16 0 R 21 0 R 22 0 R 23 0 R 24 0 R 29 0 R]
       |       |       |     |     |      |
/Opt[(Yes)   (No)  (Maybe) (Yes)  (1)    (1)]       
/T(Decision)>>
endobj

```

The "_may_ use" of the standard turns to "must use" in my opinion. Otherwise how can the different yeses be differentiated?
Maybe to add some clarifications regarding those two issues would clarify this (e.g.):

> If an Opt array is used its values take precedence over the names defined in the widget AP dictionaries.

and

> If two or more annotations have the same value in the Opt array, using numerical positioning is required.
title: Radio button form field and Opt array

body:
ISO 32000-2:2020 3.15 says:

> deprecated
> a part of ISO 32000 that should not be written into a PDF 2.0 document, and should be ignored by a PDF processor (3.49)
> Note 1 to entry: In some cases variations on these restrictions on continued use of a deprecated feature are explicitly stated in this document.

ISO 15930-9:2020 (PDF/X-6) says:

> Any feature in ISO 32000-2 that is marked as deprecated should not appear in a PDF/X-6 file, but a conforming processor shall process the file as if the features were not present.

I was trawling 32000-2 to find any specific deprecated features that might cause problems as a result of that shall requirement.

32000-2 says that the Adobe-Korea1-2 character collection for CID-keyed fonts is deprecated (1st para below Table 117 and elsewhere). Take care that “Adobe-Korea1” is used as a synonym for “Adobe-Korea1-2”, as described in 4.2.

So that means that a PDF/X-6 processor reading a file that references Adobe-Korea1-2 “shall process the file as if that [reference] were not present”; I don’t understand how developers can build on that statement to generate correct and consistent output. Even a baseline 32000-2 processor “should” ignore the reference.

All of this means that we need:

1. a clear statement of required or recommended behaviour when processing a 32000-2 file that, against recommendations, references Adobe-Korea1-2. I believe that it should be done as normative text in 32000-2 9.10.2. Leonard tells me that it’s not appropriate to simply use Adobe-KR-9 instead, but that a processor should use some form of mapping table from Korea1-2 to KR-9. I’m not enough of a font expert to formulate a reasonable statement.

2. A statement for consideration in the event that a dated revision of 15930-9 is ever developed, possibly as a new section 6.8.6 to state that the Adobe-Korea1-2 character map shall not be used in a PDF/X-6 file.

I suspect that all of the same arguments and responses would also be appropriate for the deprecated Adobe-Japan2-0 character collection.
title: How should a processor deal with a file referencing a deprecated character collection?

ISO 32000-2:2020 3.15 says:

> a part of ISO 32000 that should not be written into a PDF 2.0 document, and should be ignored by a PDF processor (3.49)
> Note 1 to entry: In some cases variations on these restrictions on continued use of a deprecated feature are explicitly stated in this document.

ISO 15930-9:2020 (PDF/X-6) says:

> Any feature in ISO 32000-2 that is marked as deprecated should not appear in a PDF/X-6 file, but a conforming processor shall process the file as if the features were not present.

I was trawling 32000-2 to find any specific deprecated features that might cause problems as a result of that shall requirement.

32000-2 says in Table 59 that the operator ‘F’ is “Equivalent to f; deprecated in PDF 2.0 and included only for compatibility. Although PDF readers shall be able to accept this operator, PDF writers should use f instead.”

In the context of 32000-2, with the ‘should’ in 3.15, that works fine. But it’s a bit messy for PDF/X-6 with its ‘shall’ requirement and no statement that the description of a deprecated feature may provide specific processor behaviour.

I recommend that, if we should ever do an amendment or dated revision for 15930-9, an explicit prohibition of the ‘F’ operator be added, probably in 6.7.1.
title: Messy processor requirements for deprecated 'F' operator in PDF/X-6

* Adobe PDF 1.5 Table 8.94 says **DigestMethod** was Optional with a default of _MD5_.
* Adobe PDF 1.7 Table 8.103 says **DigestMethod** was Optional with a default of _MD5_, but Implementation Note 144 says it was really required by Adobe’s implementation.
* ISO 32000-1:2008 Table 253 says **DigestMethod** was "(Optional; PDF 1.5 required)" but with no default value defined. Only _MD5_ and _SHA1_ values are defined.
* ISO 32000-2:2017 Table 256 says **DigestMethod** was Optional but with a default value of MD5 for PDF 1.5-1.7 (so no default stated for PDF 2.0). It also introduced the extra values _SHA256_, _SHA384_, _SHA512_ and _RIPEMD160_.
* ISO 32000-2:2020 Table 256 changed **DigestMethod** to Required and that PDF 1.5-1.7 had a default value of _MD5_ (so no default stated for PDF 2.0)
* The resolution of [Errata #117](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/117) was to change **DigestMethod** to optional and indicate as deprecated in PDF 2.0 (as shown in a modified [Table 256](https://pdf-issues.pdfa.org/32000-2-2020/clause12.html#Table256)).
* [Errata #117](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/117) was approved by WG8 in April 2022 and is included in ISO 32000-2:2020 Amendment 1 (XFDF).
* ISO/DTS 32001 clause 5.1.3 added new values to **DigestMethod** and defined a new default value (_SHA256_) for PDF 2.x
* In WG8 document N0953 against ISO/DTS 32001, comment BE-006 highlighted this fact and proposed removal, but the PL at the time resolved with “Not accepted. As this TS explicitly targets ISO 32000-2:2020 & the signature reference dictionary is not deprecated for ISO 32000-2:2020, PL believes these update hash algorithms should be allowed for use in a signature reference dictionary.”. There were no further reviews of ISO/DTS 32001 prior to submission to ISO CS.
* IS/TS 32001 is now [published by ISO](https://www.iso.org/standard/45874.html) with the additional new values for **DigestMethod** and defines a default value for PDF 2.0 for the deprecated **DigestMethod** key:
    > (PDF 2.x) In addition to those values previously defined, this value may be one of _SHA3-256_, _SHA3-384_, _SHA3-512_ or _SHAKE256_. Default value for PDF 2.0: _SHA256_ (PDF 2.0).


It appears that **DigestMethod** has no function in ISO 32000-x, so the change in ISO/TS 32001 is effectively a “no op”, but is nonetheless extremely confusing. This was originally noticed by N0954 BE-006 and then re-discovered because of trying to model ISO/TS 32001 logically into the Arlington PDF Model.

It would be good to clarify the situation.
title: ISO/TS 32001 and ISO 32000-2:2020 Amendment 1 are very confusing

body:
Here is yet another issue with hybrid PDFs (see #115 and #146)

The text after Table 19 in clause 7.5.8.4 "Compatibility with applications that do not support compressed reference streams" says:
>When a PDF reader opens a hybrid-reference PDF file, objects with entries in cross-reference streams are not hidden. When the PDF reader searches for an object, if an entry is not found in any given standard cross-reference section, the search shall proceed to a cross-reference stream specified by the XRefStm entry before looking in the previous cross-reference section (the Prev entry in the trailer).
>NOTE _Hidden objects, therefore, have two cross-reference entries. One is in the cross-reference stream. The other is a free entry in some previous section, typically the section referenced by the Prev entry._
>A PDF reader shall look in the cross-reference stream first, find the object there, and shall ignore the free entry in the previous section.

This wording does not specify what the PDF reader should do in the following use case:
- the object entry is marked as free in the latest xref table (not the previous one!)
- the same object entry is present in xref stream

Should such object be treated as deleted (so the reference to it is equivalent to null) or as real one as specified by the xref stream? 

 As a side note, the term _hidden object_ is not defined anywhere, but used 5 times in this clause. From the context it probably means the objects that are located in the compressed object streams and referenced from the xref streams, which makes them "hidden" from the PDF 1.4 parsers.
title: Conflicts between xref table and xref stream in hybrid-reference files

Suppose a PDF 2.0 document is to be signed using SHA-256 (not SHA3!) for computing the hash over the document. The signing certificate is signed by its issuer using algorithm ecdsa-with-SHA3-256 (here we have SHA3). Shall the ISO 32001 developer extensions dictionary be added in that case?

The issuer's certificate isn't directly involved in signing the document (as per 5.1.1 of ISO 32001), but it might be embedded in the signature (as intermediate certificate in Contents).

Anyway, software validating the signature has to support SHA3 in this case for validating the certificate chain (just as it has to support SHA3 for documents hashed with SHA3). This makes a point for requiring adding the ISO 32001 developer extensions dictionary in the case being presented here.
title: ISO 32001 developer extensions dictionary needed for use of a signing certificate signed with ecdsa-with-SHA3-256?

If I have:
D:20221128110300
is this functionally equivalent to 
D:20221128110300Z
or is it dependent on my local time zone?

Section 7.9.4 has the following text:
"the LATIN CAPITAL LETTER Z signifies that local time is equal to UT. If no UT information is specified, the relationship of the specified time to UT shall be considered to be GMT. Regardless of whether the time zone is specified, the rest of the date shall be specified in local time."

I ask because I'm looking at a bug report where the current behavior leans on the latter part of this statement to treat "D:20221128110300" as 2022.11.28 11:03:00 -06'00' on my machine, while I interpret the (somewhat muddled) middle part of the statement as indicating it shall be treated as: 2022.11.28 11:03:00 +00'00'

Specifically, the intent of this sentence:
"If no UT information is specified, the relationship of the specified time to UT shall be considered to be GMT" 
seems to be: 
"If no UT information is specified, the missing timezone offset shall be assumed to be the same as Greenwich Mean Time's  timezone offset (+0'00)."

21.8.5.3 of ISO 32000-2:2020 implies that a TimeStampToken expires when its signing certificate expires:

"A timestamp token present either in a signature timestamp attribute or in a document timestamp
dictionary may expire due to the expiry of its certificate [...]"

However, according to RFC 3161 (a normative reference for ISO 32000-2), a TimeStampToken never expires. Appendix B reads

"The date/time indicated by the TSA MUST be within the validity period of the signer's certificate."

There are no other requirements related to the validity period of the signing certificate. It's even not possible to revoke a TimeStampToken by revoking the signing certificate after generation of the TimeStampToken:

"Should the certificate be revoked, then the date/time of revocation shall be later than the date/time indicated by the TSA."

Was that implied definition of expiry of TimeStampTokens made up for ISO 32000-2 or is there some normative reference I' don't know about? Or is that implied definition a mistake in ISO 32000-2?

body:
This comes from an ongoing discussion on the PDF/UA mailing list.

In question is a document that contains a `Structure Element` (table 355) with a `C` entry - either a string or array - which identifies one or more _classes_. However there is no corresponding entry in the `ClassMap` value of the `Structure Tree Root` (table 354).

The spec describes the lookup process like so:

ISO 32000-2:2020, 14.8.5.1

> The class name is in turn looked up in the class map, a dictionary identified by the ClassMap entry in the structure tree root, yielding an attribute object or array of objects corresponding to the class.

ISO 32000-2:2020, 14.7.6.1

> An attribute object shall be a dictionary or stream that [...]

So the argument is that, as specified, a missing entry is invalid - it is not an "attribute object".

---

I'm of the opinion that this is an unnecessarily strict requirement. There is a long, long history in PDF of missing items being used to represent missing data. It seems crazy that if an element specifies one or more classes that intentionally have no attributes, that tools then have to defined an empty attribute holder just to represent this. It's brittle, verbose and adds no semantic value.

I would propose changing the text so something like:

> The class name is in turn looked up in the class map, a dictionary identified by the ClassMap entry in the structure tree root. **If present, it yields** <strike>yielding</strike> an attribute object or array of objects corresponding to the class.

I'd also like to note that:

1. There are semantic reasons to add a class with no attributes.
2. I'm not aware of any tools that currently create an empty attribute map when they do this, so there are many PDFs in existence with classes that have no attributes - the vast, vast majority do note create an empty map. So this adjustment would be moving the spec to reflect reality

Other opinions exist of course, I'm sure they will be summarised in replies to this issue.
title: Do Structure Element classes require an entry in the ClassMap?

body:
**Describe the bug**
7.4.4.2, last Paragraph states:
> [The encoder] shall issue a clear-table code when the table becomes full;

Reading this literally, it seems that the rule says that a clear code must be issued immediately after code number 4095 is assigned in step d) of the encoding cycle given in Paragraph 4. That would mean, however, that code 4095 can never actually be used, raising the question whether the intended meaning was to issue the clear code when the table would otherwise _overflow_, i.e. one output cycle later.

This is, of course, analogous to the meaning/issue of EarlyChange. Note, though, that Table 8 which describes that parameter does not mention clear codes. It only talks specifically about code length.

One way to clarify the rule would be to refer explicitly to the encoding sequence as defined in Paragraph 4. For example: "If the table is already full in step d) of the encoding sequence, the next code emitted shall be a clear code".
title: Rule for issuing LZW clear codes is unclear/confusing

body:
"Table 211 - Entries in a URI dictionary" only generically specifies the **Base** key as an ASCII string without being explicit about any requirements of a base URI. It appears from experimentation with multiple popular implementations that a trailing `/` is required for a **Base** URI or otherwise only the host portion gets used (and any path portion is dropped). For interoperability it would be better to be more precise about whether processing is expected/required or whether simple concatenation of **URI** to **Base** is expected to work (file format requirement). Or otherwise an informative note saying behaviour is implementation dependent...

Using https://pdfa.org/community/pdf-technical-working-group as an example: the **Base** settings used were:
* https://pdfa.org/community
* https://pdfa.org/community/

with the relative **URI** in URI action (Table 210) being:
* pdf-technical-working-group
* pdf-technical-working-group/
* ./pdf-technical-working-group
* ./pdf-technical-working-group/
* ../community/pdf-technical-working-group
* ../community/pdf-technical-working-group/

Wrong behaviours included https://pdfa.org/pdf-technical-working-group and https://pdfa.org/communitypdf-technical-working-group which led me to this conclusion.

PS. Note that the URL https://pdfa.org/pdf-technical-working-group will work but only because there is a redirect to https://pdfa.org/community/pdf-technical-working-group, but is technically an incorrect URL for the above **Base** and **URI** combinations.

My experiments led to me think the correct answer is that **Base** (only) needs to end with a trailing `/` and that simple concatenation of **Base** and **URI** is all that is expected (so fundamentally a file format requirement that the two parts are then defined compatibly).
title: URI dictionary Base requirements are unstated leading to different behaviour

"Table 205 — Entries specific to a target dictionary" defines the **P** entry to be either an integer or byte string. The description then states "_... If the value is a string, it specifies a named destination in the current document that provides the page number of the file attachment annotation._"

But named destinations are supported in 2 ways:
* (_since PDF 1.1_) via PDF name objects, via the Doc Catalog **Dests** entry, where the destination name is directly the key in this dictionary
* (_since PDF 1.2_) via PDF string objects, via the Doc Catalog **Names** dictionary and then the **Dests** name-tree as specified in Table 32. And of course noting that name trees actually use strings as their index...!

Both methods are clearly described in 12.3.2.4 Named Destinations.

So I think the Target dictionary **P** entry should also include "name" as a type to support all forms of named destination.

PS. This seems to be the only place in PDF where a named destination is constrained.
title: Table 205 Target P entry does not support all methods for named destination

There are parameters in the D(efault) OCCD, that are used by the most commonly used viewers: **BaseState**, **ON** and **OFF**. In addition to these there is the **View** dictionary in the **Usage** dictionary in the OCG itself.

It is not clear in the spec what happens when an OCG is in the **ON** array in the **D** OCCD and at the same time has an **Usage** dictionary with a **View** dictionary with **ViewState** set to **OFF**. It is neither said that there must not be any such conflicts.

Afaics there are no applications that create or use the **ViewState**. We may:
- deprecate **View** and **ViewState** in the **Usage** dictionary or
- give priority to one of the two parameters

In the latter case we should also specify the default for **ViewState** if the parameter is missing, which should probably be **ON**.

body:
section 12.27.1 [Runtime] General contains the following description:

"An object that represents the run-time instance of the player. Each Runtime object can have its own unique script engine and set of annotations. The variable runtime is a global reference to this object."

I think this passage could use some clarity on what constitutes a set of annotations that would be associated with a runtime.
Is it all 3D annotations of a document? all 3D and RichMedia annotations of a document?  or is it all 3D annotations that share a 3D reference dictionary? Can you have more than one runtime per document? Can you have an AcroForm that interacts with more than one [3D Player] Runtime in the same document?

This came up in the context of a PDF GoTo3DView actions, which requires a Producer to specify a "target annotation for which to set the view." However this required parameter is curiously missing from Runtime.getView (sections 12.27.3.8 and 12.27.3.9) and RunTime.setView (sections 12.27.3.18 and 12.27.3.19).

Also note that Table 121 in section 12.27.2 seems to have a notion of an "active 3D annotation", for the canvasCount property, which is does not seem to be exposed, while viewCount's description is more ambiguous: "The number of named views for annotation." 

Lastly, as a side issue, "player" seems to only be used in this one sentence in the spec and does not seem to be otherwise defined.
title: ISO 21757-1:2020 section 12.27.1 [Runtime] General needs clarification

body:
**Describe the bug**
H.2 contains a PDF file that "is almost the minimum acceptable PDF file". However, even though the file identifies itself as a PDF 2.0 file, it does not contain an `/ID` entry in its trailer, which is required by 7.5.5, Table 15.

Also, the text mentions:

> It is not strictly the minimum acceptable because it contains a page content stream (**Contents** in the page object), and a metadata stream.

However, it does not mention that the page object is also optional. 7.7.3 does not prohibit empty page trees, even though many PDF readers in practice refuse to accept PDF files with no pages.
title: Issues with minimal PDF file example

body:
**Describe the bug**
Occasionally, the standard says that a line of text must contain some particular keyword or data. However, its wording is often unclear on whether that same line can contain other data. First, in 7.5.2:

> If a PDF file contains binary data, as most do (see 7.2, "Lexical conventions"), the header line shall be immediately followed by a comment line containing at least four binary characters—that is, characters whose codes are 128 or greater.

Can a "comment line" contain arbitrary data before the percent sign? If so, can any of the four binary characters be placed before the percent sign, and is the data before the percent sign interpreted as part of the file body? If not, can any white-space be placed before the percent sign? This should be clarified.

In 7.5.4:

> Each cross-reference section shall begin with a line containing the keyword **xref**.

Can this line contain any data before or after the `xref`? If not, this should be clarified as "containing only the keyword".

In 7.5.5:

> The two preceding lines shall contain, one per line and in order, the keyword **startxref** and the byte offset from the beginning of the PDF file to the beginning of the **xref** keyword in the last cross-reference section or the beginning of the previous cross-reference stream.

Can these two lines contain any data before or after the `startxref` or byte offset? If not, this should be clarified as "shall contain only".
title: Which lines can contain extraneous data?

body:
In ISO 32000-2:2020, 7.2.4 states,

> Any occurrence of the PERCENT SIGN (25h) outside a string or inside a content stream (see 7.8.2, "Content streams") introduces a comment.

This implies that a percent sign inside a stream always introduces a comment. 7.2.3 states, "The rules defined in this subclause apply to all characters in the file except within strings, streams, and comments," but the statement in 7.2.4 does not appeal to the classification of characters defined in 7.2.3 and is not bound by its limitations. This is a breaking change from PDF-1.7, which instead states "outside a string or stream" in 7.2.3.

If a percent sign inside a non-content stream does not always introduce a comment, then there is still the question of whether a percent sign within the decoded data of an object stream can introduce a comment. 7.5.7 states that "the **N** objects are stored consecutively" in an object stream following the list of byte offsets. Does 7.2.4 apply to parsing these objects after decoding the stream data? 7.2.1 suggests that objects as syntactic entities are formed from tokenized bytes, using the ordinary syntax rules which accept comments:

> At the most fundamental level, a PDF file is a sequence of bytes. These bytes can be grouped into tokens according to the syntax rules described in subclauses 7.2.2, "Representation" through 7.2.4, "Comments". One or more tokens are assembled to form higher-level syntactic entities, principally objects, which are the basic data values from which a PDF file is constructed.

However, if comments are permitted in object streams, then further clarification is needed in 7.5.7. In particular, what if one object in an object stream is trailed followed by a comment with no EOL marker, and the next byte offset points into that comment? For instance,

```
1 0 obj
<< /Type /ObjStm
   /Length 17
   /N 2
   /First 8
>>
stream
2 0 3 6
123 % 456
endstream
endobj
```

7.5.7 Note 7 suggests that "processing of each object in an object stream starts at the specified byte offset in the decompressed stream and ends prior to the byte offset of the next object or when the end of stream is encountered", which would permit this. But attempting to parse the list of objects in one go would skip object 3.

(There's also another question, of whether an object stream can begin with white-space, since the wording only explicitly permits white-space separating the integers specifying the byte offsets. But this may be adequately implied already by the ordinary syntax rules.)
title: Comments in stream data

body:
PDF 2.0 specifies CapHeight entry in FontDescriptor dictionary (Table 120) to be _"Required for fonts that have Latin characters, except for Type 3 fonts"._

There are two issues here: a font subset may include only lowercase Latin characters, and this parameter would not have sense for it. Second, the term "Latin charater" is not defined in the spec. And I'm not sure if it would be correct to define it only as an ASCII character in the range [a-zA-Z].

As a potential resolution, the text might be modified so say: _"Required for fonts that have Latin characters in the range A-Z, except for Type 3 fonts"_.
title: CapHeight required only for fonts with Latin characters is ambiguous

In 12.2, Viewer Preferences, for /NonFullScreenPageMode, we would expect every value except /FullScreen to be available.

title: UseAttachments missing from NonFullScreenPageMode

body:
In section 7.9.2.4 "Byte string type" of the PDF 2.0 spec it is stated:

>The byte string type shall be used for binary data that shall be represented as a series of bytes, where
each byte may be any value representable in 8 bits. Byte string type is a subtype of string type. For
example, byte strings are used to define a file identifier (see 14.4, "File identifiers") that is specified in
ID entry of PDF file trailer (see "Table 15 — Entries in the file trailer dictionary"). In such case byte
string is written in hexadecimal form (see 7.3.4.3, "Hexadecimal strings") and looks like

> \<B6FB54F3F8554D478DC874F11DAD0F11>

Apart from (probably) some small typos in the last two sentence ("...in *the* ID entry of *the* PDF...", "In such *a* case *a* byte string...") this description is greatly expanded from the PDF 1.7 version which only contains the first two sentences.

What is not clear to me now is whether the given example means that byte strings should now always be in hexadecimal form and may not use the literal string form anymore.

It is my understanding that the description of a dictionary entry contains information on whether a (byte) string should be encoded specially, i.e. either in hexadecimal form or literal string form. See e.g. the description of key `/Contents` in table 255 in section 12.8.1 where it says that `/Contents` should be encoded in hexadecimal form. The key `/ID` mentioned in the example has no such wording in its description.

If my understanding is correct, i.e. if byte strings can be written in both forms except where one of the forms is explicitly requested, I would propose removing the last sentence ("In such case...").
title: Is a byte string always written in hexadecimal form?

body:
Section 9.10.3 says the following about the `dstString` of the `bfrange` operator on page 359:

> In this case, the last byte of the string shall be incremented for each consecutive code in the source code range.
> 
> When defining ranges of this type, the value of the last byte in the string shall be less than or equal to 255 - (srcCode2 - srcCode1). This ensures that the last byte of the string shall not be incremented past 255; otherwise, the result of mapping is undefined.

While the [Adobe Technical Note #5411 "ToUnicode Mapping File Tutorial"](http://www.audentia-gestion.fr/ADOBE/5411.ToUnicode.pdf) is not on the [list of normative references](https://pdfa.org/iso-32000-normative-references/), it doesn't say anything about this restriction. On the contrary, it includes the following example on page 37:

~~~
<1379> <137B> <90FE>
~~~

This would map <1379> to <90FE>, <137A> to <90FF> and <137B> to <9100>, if I understand correctly. So in this case the last byte of the string *would* be incremented past 255.

Furthermore, TN#5411 mentions in section 1.4.1: *"Also, when using “bfrange” operators, care must be taken not to cross first-byte boundaries for the CID values in a single mapping line."* This restriction bears resemblance to the one mentioned in the PDF spec, although for a different part (the `srcCode1 srcCode2` part).

The question for me is now whether the restriction in 9.10.3 is an additional restriction just for ToUnicode CMaps in PDF or if this is an error.
title: Clarification request regarding `bfrange` operators in ToUnicode cmaps

body:
In 7.6.4.4.9 f):

"Encrypt the 16-byte block using AES-256 in ECB mode with an initialization vector of zero, using the file encryption key as the key"

should read

"Encrypt the 16-byte block using AES-256 in ECB mode using the file encryption key as the key"

A similar correction is needed to 7.6.4.4.12.

(ECB mode doesn't use initialization vectors, however some encryption libraries do use an IV of zero to put the library into ECB mode - that's just an API implementation choice, though, and not relevant in a spec like this one).

Example of someone being confused by this, and some discussion:

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/76118349/iv-for-aes-in-ecb-mode-algorithm-2-a-in-the-pdf-2-0-spec/
title: ECB mode doesn't use an Initialisation Vector

body:
Current definition of ColorSpace subdictionary in resource dictionary (Table 34) says:

> A dictionary that maps each resource name to either **the name of a device-dependent colour space** or an array describing a colour space (see 8.6, "Colour spaces")

However, apart from "the name of a device-dependent colour space" the resource name can also be mapped to **/Pattern** name object. 

This is also explicitly stated in the description of the operands for **CS/cs** operators in 8.6.3 (2nd paragraph after Table 61) and a similar text in Table 73 - Colour operators:

> Within a content stream, the **CS** or **cs** operator establishes the current colour space parameter in the graphics state. The operand shall always be name object, which either identifies one of the colour spaces that need no additional parameters (**DeviceGray**, **DeviceRGB**, **DeviceCMYK**, or some cases of **Pattern**) or shall be used as a key in the **ColorSpace** subdictionary of the current resource dictionary (see 7.8.3, "Resource dictionaries"). In the latter case, the value of the dictionary entry in turn shall be a colour space array or name. A colour space array shall never be inline within a content stream.

I would suggest modifying the description of ColorSpace entry in Table 34 as:

> A dictionary that maps each resource name to either the name of a colour space with no additional parameters (**DeviceGray**, **DeviceRGB**, **DeviceCMYK**, or **Pattern**), or an array describing a colour space (see 8.6, "Colour spaces").
title: /Pattern is not permitted as a value in ColorSpace subdictionary of  resource dictionary (Table 34)

body:
In the description of the `Link` element, final few paragraphs if 14.8.4.7.2 on p764, we have this:

> The following items may be children of a link element:
> * One or more content items or other ILSEs (except other links) if `A`, `Dest` and `PA` keys of all of them have identical values
> * One object reference (see 14.7.5.3, "PDF objects as content items") to one link annotation associated with the content

A _content item_ is defined to mean a) a marked-content sequence, or b) an object reference. And _ILSE_ means another Structure Element (accurate enough definition for this discussion)

So there are lots of problems here;

1. The first point says I can include "one or more content items", which includes OBJR to link annotations, and the second point says I can only include one. If the bullet points are to be joined with "and", it's contradictory. If joined with "or", the second is redundant. And the paragraph preceding the list gives no hint as to which applies.
2. The `A`, `Dest` and `PA` keys are prohibited on all content in the first point, which includes ILSEs - on which the `A` key defines attributes! We don't want that. The intent is that all _link annotations_ within the Link element have the same values for these keys, but that's not what's written.

and lastly, all of this is wrapped in a "may contain" rather than should/shall, which means this specific-but-incorrect rule is just a hint. Which I don't think is the intent either.

I'll suggest some options for alternative wording, in the full knowledge that Matthew will jump on it and improve it. I've specifically used "should" for the restriction that all links point to the same thing.

Option 1, replace that text with this

> The following items may be children of a link element:
> * One or more content items or other ILSEs (except other links)
>
> If a link element contains object references (see 14.7.5.3, "PDF objects as content items") to more than one link annotation, all should have identical values for the `A`, `Dest` and `PA` keys


Option 2 is to remove everything from after Note 1 at the bottom of Table 368 to the point just before 14.8..4.7.3, and instead put this in the Description for the Link element in table 368, where it most definitely belongs. Suggested replacement text for the Description:

> An association between content enclosed by the **Link** structure element and a corresponding link annotation (see 12.5.6.5, "Link annotations"). In tagged PDF, **Link** provides functionality comparable to HTML hypertext links. A **Link** structure element may have one or more content items or other ILSEs (except other links) as children.
>
> If more than one link annotation is referenced in a **Link** structure element, they should all have identical values for the `A`, `Dest` and `PA` keys

This way it's aligned to the way Annot and Form are described.

----

Edit: I'm aware this is largely a copy/paste from 32000-1, which had a note - "use of the Link structure element to enclose multiple link annotations is deprecated". That note has now been removed, which goes some way to explaining how the text got into this state.
title: Link Structure Element restrictions in 14.8.4.7.2 are slightly nonsensical

* A name that indicates the first (F), last (L), next (N), previous (P), or default (D) entries in the VA array _or Views array._

There are four more mentions of the VA array in the remaining text following the table that should likewise be similarly expanded .
