body:
This isn't a bug exactly, but it does feel like an oversight.

Table 376 lists various standard structure owners for attributes in a tagged PDF. We have owners for various standards - HTML, CSS - but we _don't_ have an owner for MathML, despite it being a first-class namespace in PDF 2.0

As an example, if I have the following MathML:

```html
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block">...</math>
```

I currently have a choice when turning this into a StructElem: I can use UsersProperties:

```
<<
 /Type /StructElem
 /S /math
 /NS 33 0 R  % the MathML namespace
 /A [
  <<
    /O /UserProperties
    /P [ << /N (display) /V (block) >> ]
  >> ]
>>
```
or I can use the MathML namespace
```
<<
 /Type /StructElem
 /S /math
 /NS 33 0 R  % the MathML namespace
 /A [
  <<
    /O /NSO
    /NS 33 0 R
    /display (block)
  >> ]
>>
```

Neither of these are quite right: the attributes are not defined in the MathML namespace (in the XML sense; they don't need a namespace prefix), and UserProperties loses their semantics.


Is this important? It's certainly going to matter when deriving HTML from PDF or when using well-tagged PDF, and it will impact on accessibility if those attributes are critical to the understanding of the equation - which is the case for (eg) `mathvariant` in MathML4 (see https://www.w3.org/TR/mathml4/#presm_commatt - _"Note that this class is more than styling, it typically conveys semantic intent"_)

Because of this I can't see any place to fix it other than 32000 itself. My proposal would be to add a `MathML` entry to table 376, where it would be "attributes governing MathML structure elements". We already changed `CSS-3.00` to `CSS-3` in the 2020 dated revision, so I hope this isn't too controversial. Failing that, I'd settle for some best-practice guidance.
title: Why isn't MathML a standard structure owner for attributes?

Clause 12.3.2.4 Named destinations, the last sentence in the para between NOTEs 1 and 2 states:

> The value of this entry shall be a dictionary in which each key is a destination name and the corresponding value is either an array defining the destination, using the syntax shown in "Table 149 — Destination syntax", or a dictionary with a **D** entry whose value is such an array and may optionally contain an **SD** entry as defined in "Table 201 — Action types".

body:
If a StructElem is a member of two classes, and both classes define an attribute value, which takes priority? Earlier classes in the class list, later classes in the class list, or some other priority rule? The spec tells us that directly defined attributes (in the `A` key) take priority over attributes defined in classes, but nothing more is said on priority.

A concrete example: what is the Placement attribute for the `P` element - Block or Inline?

```
1 0 obj
<<
 /Type /StructElem
 /S /P
 /C [ /ClassA /ClassB ]
 ...
>>

2 0 obj
<<
  /Type /StructTreeRoot
  /ClassMap <<
    /ClassA << /O /Layout /Placement /Block >>
    /ClassB << /O /Layout /Placement /Inline >>
  >>
  ...
>>
```

I suspect this one's for you, @mrbhardy. For reference here's the text relating to this from 32000-2:2020 - section 14.7.6.2

> If many structure elements share the same set of attribute values, they may be defined as an attribute class sharing the identical attribute object. Structure elements shall refer to the class by name. The association between class names and attribute objects shall be defined by a dictionary called the class map, that shall be kept in the ClassMap entry of the structure tree root (see "Table 354 — Entries in the structure tree root"). Each key in the class map shall be a name object denoting the name of a class. The corresponding value shall be an attribute object or an array of such objects.

> The C entry in a structure element dictionary (see "Table 355 — Entries in a structure element dictionary") shall contain a class name or an array of class names (typically accompanied by revision numbers as well; see 14.7.6.3, "Attribute revision numbers"). For each class named in the C entry, the corresponding attribute object or objects shall be considered to be attached to the given structure element, along with those identified in the element’s A entry. If both the A and C entries are present and a given attribute is specified by both, the one specified by the A entry shall take precedence.
title: Value of an attribute defined by multiple classes associated with a StructElem is undefined

body:
Spec says:

"The ASCII base-85 encoding shall use the ASCII characters ! through u ((21h) - (75h)) and the character z (7Ah), with the 2-character sequence ~> (7Eh)(3Eh) as its EOD marker. The ASCII85Decode filter shall ignore all white-space characters (see 7.2, "Lexical conventions")"

Can we have a newline between the ~ and the > or does that mean it's no longer a "2-character sequence"? Depends how one reads it.

Example file available here: https://github.com/qpdf/qpdf/issues/973

It looks reasonable to me: ASCII85Decode is meant for human readability, so putting in newlines every 80 characters is a resonable approach for a PDF writer to take. Depending on the algorithm, this line splitting might happen when the `~>` sequence is already baked in, so a newline may come between the `~` and the `>`.

Recommend appending ", even within the EOD marker." to the final sentence of this paragraph. You can make an argument that there's no ambiguity here, but multiple implementations have been caught out by this, so I think it's worth clarifying by emphasis.
title: In 7.4.3, clarify whether ASCII85Decode can have a newline in the middle of EOD sequence

body:
See also [PDF/A TWG Issue 31](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdfa-twg/issues/31) and [veraPDF-corpus Issue 263](https://github.com/veraPDF/veraPDF-corpus/issues/263).

XMP metadata in PDF needs to always be UTF-8. 

ISO 16684-1:2019 (XMP) states:
> The choice of Unicode encoding (UTF-8, UTF-16, or UTF-32) is beyond the scope of this document. Other file embedding or usage standards may specify the Unicode encoding.

"Adobe XMP Specification Part 3, Storage in files" (_dated Jan 2020, no equivalent ISO standard!_) states in clause 1.6.1:
> For PDF files, the XMP packet is embedded in a metadata stream contained in a PDF object (beginning with PDF 1.4). The XMP must be encoded as UTF-8.

However in various updates to ISO 32000 and PDF ISO subsets the normative references to Adobe XMP Specification Part 3 got lost so this requirement also got lost. It needs to be reintroduced (as a "shall" requirement to clause 14.3.2 in ISO 32000-2:2020).
title: XMP metadata in PDF needs to always be UTF-8

Clause 7.3.3 states:

> An integer shall be written as one or more decimal digits optionally preceded by a sign. The value shall be interpreted as a signed decimal integer and shall be converted to an integer object.

Should this really include that a valid PDF integer can have leading zeros?
e.g. `0123` or even `00000123`

And similar wording for numbers permits `00001.23` too.
Is this intended/intentional?
title: Can a PDF integer have leading zeros?

body: The Operands column of Table 352 (Marked content operators) in section 14.6 (Marked content), lists the operand for the BMC operator in row 3 as _Tag_ (capitalized). The Description column uses _tag_ which agrees with lower-case operand names elsewhere.

body:
The standard allows the BX/EX compatibility section operators in content streams at both the content stream level and within text objects, according to Figure 9 (section 8.2 Graphics objects) - similar to q/Q (graphics state) and BMC/EMC (marked content). It says that pairs of BX/EX can be nested (7.8.2, last paragraph), but contrary to q/Q (cf. 9.4.1, last paragraph) and BMC/EMC (cf. 14.6.1, last paragraph) , it does not state that nesting must be "balanced" with respect to BT/ET, i.e. whether the following would be legal:

    BX ... BT ... EX ... ET

Is this intentional or an oversight?

The same question _also_ applies to the following combinations:

 - BX/EX vs. q/Q
 - BX/EX vs. BMC/EMC
 - q/Q vs. BMC/EMC

As far as I can see from Figure 9, the four pairs BT/ET, BX/EX, q/Q, and BMC/EMC are those with the relevant nesting behavior. Specifically, all are allowed at both the content stream level and in text objects while the other kinds of objects in the figure (paths, clipping paths, in-line images, external objects, and shading objects) do not seem to have operator overlap.

PS: I have not mentioned BDC, assuming it is equivalent to BMC with regards to this issue.
title: Nesting rules for BX/EX operators with respect to BT/ET and q/Q

body:
14.6.1, Note 1 states:
> This [sequence bracketed by BMC/BDC and EMC] is a sequence not simply of bytes in the content stream but of complete graphics objects.

However, the marked content operators are allowed inside text objects which would seem to imply that in such a case they cover a partial graphics object.

I am assuming that a (complete) text object is what is bracketed by the BT and ET operators based on their description in 9.4.1 (paragraph 3) and Table 105 in 9.4.1, as well as Figure 9 in 8.2 "Graphics objects".
title: Apparent contradiction in wording for marked content operators

body:
I'm trying to create a presentation PDF file that has a heading and a few bullet points and said points should appear when navigating on the page. Basically this is the exact use case described in 12.4.4.2. I have not managed to make this happen as the documentation is quite limited and possibly even misleading.

[The PDF file I managed to create is here](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/files/11826184/subpage.pdf).

The basic setup is that the bullets are in optional content groups that are hidden by default. Then there is a subpage navigation setup that should show the bullets one by one (and hide them when going backwards).

What makes debugging this even harder is that most PDF viewers ignore subpage navigation. Okular, Chromium, Firefox and Apple Preview ignore subpage navigation info. The only viewer that does anything with this is Acrobat Reader and even that behaves weirdly. There are also very few if any sample documents with PresSteps defined (that I could find, at least) so one can't even look into existing docs on how things should work. Neither LibreOffice nor Keynote try to create subpage navigation tags. The most common solution seems to be to simulate that by creating multiple pages instead.

12.4.4.2 says the following:

> When a user navigates to a page, if the page dictionary has a PresSteps entry, the node specified by that entry shall become the current node.

and then:

> If the user requests to navigate forward (such as an arrow key press) and there is a current navigation node, the following shall occur

> The sequence of actions specified by NA (if present) shall be executed.

 Just a few paragraphs later in the same chapter it says:

> If the user requests to navigate to another page (regardless of whether there is a current node) and that page’s dictionary contains a PresSteps entry, the following shall occur

> If the navigation request was forward, or if the navigation request was for random access (such as by clicking on a link), the actions specified by NA shall be executed and the node specified by Next shall become the new current node, as described previously.

These two statements seem to be contradictory. The first action either is or is not taken for seemingly the same operation. At least I can't reasonably understand what the difference between the two is (or if it even exists and the latter should always be done).

If you open the document in Acrobat Reader, start presenter mode and navigate to the second page, the first bullet is already visible. This means that the NA action on the first navigation step has been performed. However if you close the document, reopen it, navigate to the second page and then enable presenter mode, the bullet item is also shown. Even though the user comes to the page via "navigation" rather than "requesting to navigate to a new page". This is all very confusing, as these steps are contradictory and seemingly both apply at the same time but in practice the latter seems to always happen.

I have no idea what the underlying issue here is. My doc might well be malformed somehow, but with the current documentation it is really difficult to determine what the correct syntax should be.
title: Documentation on sub page navigation seems to be insufficient

body:
The first sentence in the last para of subclause 14.7.6.1 states:
> The **C** entry in a structure element dictionary (see "Table 355 — Entries in a structure element dictionary") shall contain a class name or an array of class names (typically accompanied by revision numbers as well; see 14.7.6.3, "Attribute revision numbers").

Attribute revision numbers are deprecated in PDF 2.0 so there is no "typically" any more. We also note deprecation whenever a topic is mentioned, rather than relying on a user to follow links. So a better sentence construction would be:
> The **C** entry in a structure element dictionary (see "Table 355 — Entries in a structure element dictionary") shall contain a class name or an array of class names (possibly accompanied by revision numbers (_deprecated in PDF 2.0_); see 14.7.6.3, "Attribute revision numbers").
title: Attribute revision numbers are deprecated in PDF 2.0

body:
See https://github.com/veraPDF/veraPDF-library/issues/1355 and https://github.com/pdf-association/arlington-pdf-model/issues/90.

One of the issues in https://github.com/veraPDF/veraPDF-library/issues/1355 is that the _key_ in the `name-tree` is `null` and name tree keys are defined as "_where each keyi shall be a string_" and "_The keys shall be sorted in lexical order_". `number-tree` use slightly different wording for the key type ("_each keyi is an integer_" - "is" vs "shall") but the same wording for the sorting requirement ("_The keys shall be sorted in numerical order_").

So `name-tree`/`number-tree` keys cannot be `null` (fails "shall be a string"/"is an integer") and no allowance is made in either the lexical or numeric sorting algorithms for `null` keys - for example, whether they need to come first, last, or are skipped over entirely. And what would it mean if you had a `null` key but a non-`null` value??? Is that meaningful? (I note in https://github.com/veraPDF/veraPDF-library/issues/1355 that both the key and value are both `null`).

So referring to Tables 36 and 37:
* can name-tree and number-trees have keys that are `null`? 

~~I think the answer is yes (it's relatively common as @bdoubrov points out) so we need to allow `null` as an explicit key type for both. And name and number trees should both use the same "shall"-style wording for consistency.~~

* what are the requirements (if any) for the lexical and numeric sorting for keys that are `null`?

~~I think the answer is that keys that are `null` can appear anywhere but are ignored (not involved/skipped over) when considering lexical or numeric sorting. Not sure how to best phrase this - either we can say that only keys that are string/integer are sorted, or we say something about keys that are `null`...~~

* does a `null` key with a non-`null` value mean anything special?

~~I think no. It's syntactically valid but stupid as the value is "inaccessible" via a name/number tree lookup - so no real difference to a key and value both being `null`. This is probably worth a short informative NOTE.~~
title: Name- and number-tree handling of Name and Num array "keys" which are null

body:
Related to Errata #157 and [Arlington Issue #90](https://github.com/pdf-association/arlington-pdf-model/issues/90), but specifically for logical structure. This is effectively checking the rules for any objects that can be an array (either directly or as a value in a name or number-tree) - can the following array objects in logical structure contain `null` objects as array elements? 

* **StructTreeRoot/K** array - can this have `null` array elements?

* **StructTreeRoot/ParentTree** - specifically when the value in the number-tree is an array "_For a page object or content stream containing marked-content sequences that are content items, the value shall be an array of references to the parent elements of those marked-content sequences._" - can an element in that array be `null`? It would appear at least one popular implementation uses 'null`...

* **StructElem/K** - noting that the array format can be an array of various kinds of dicts, or an array of integers

* **StructElem/A** - noting also that this array can have an optional revision number after a dict/stream entry so there is potential ambiguity as to whether a `null` is a dict/stream or revision  in the array elements

* **StructElem/C** - noting also that this array can have an optional revision number after a name so there is potential ambiguity as to whether a `null` is a name or revision in the array elements

* **StructElem/Ref**
title: Semantics of null array elements in logical structure objects that can be arrays

body:
32000-2 prohibits the use of the name None for a component in an NChannel colour space, but that is only stated in a rather convoluted way that is separate from the clearer statement that None may be used in a DeviceN colour space.

Section 8.6.6.5, two paragraphs above Note 4 says 

> "The component names shall all be different from one another, except for the name None, which may be repeated as described later in this subclause. The special name All, used by Separation colour spaces, shall not be used. "

The paragraph below note 6 says:

> "The colour component name None, which may be present only for DeviceN colour spaces that do not have the NChannel subtype, indicates ..."

I suggest extending the first of these paragraphs with the italic text as below:

> "The component names shall all be different from one another, except for the name None, which may be repeated as described later in this subclause. _The special name None shall not be used in DeviceN colour spaces that have the NChannel subtype._ The special name All, used by Separation colour spaces, shall not be used. The names Cyan, Magenta, Yellow and Black are reserved to name the subtractive  process colourants of a CMYK device."

The second paragraph may then be simplified by deleting the parenthetical "which may be present only for DeviceN colour spaces that do not have the NChannel subtype" to avoid duplication.
title: Clarify prohibition of None in NChannel colour spaces

body:
Tables 128 (Type 1 halftone dictionaries), 130 (Type 10 halftone dictionaries) and 131 (Type 16 halftone dictionaries) state:

>This entry [the TransferFunction entry] shall be present if the dictionary is a component of a Type 5 halftone (see 10.6.5.6, "Type 5 halftones") and represents either a nonprimary or nonstandard primary colour component (see 10.5, "Transfer functions").

That means that if the halftone dictionary is referenced from a Type 5 halftone dictionary it shall have (under the specified conditions) a TransferFunction entry.

However, Table 132 (for such Type 5 halftone dictionaries) specifies a "Default" entry:

>A halftone that shall be used for any colourant or colour component that does not have an entry of its own. The value shall not be 5. If there are any nonprimary colourants, the default halftone shall have a transfer function.

That seems to suggest that instead of each nonprimary (...) colourant having it's own TransferFunction there may be a Default instead (or maybe that even is the only way to cover such colourants). This needs to be harmonized.

Table 129 (Type 6 halftone dictionaries) has a Note: 

>PDF versions to 1.7 required that this entry be present if the dictionary is a component of a Type 5 halftone (see 10.6.5.6, "Type 5 halftones") and represents either a non-primary or non-standard primary colour component.

Since that provision is still in place in PDF 2.0 the note should probably be removed (or adjusted).

Perhaps the idea was to remove the requirement in Table 132 for Type 5 Halftone dictionaries (which has happened) and to adjust tables 128 through 131 (which has only happened in table 129)? I would support that idea but it would then have to be executed.

If that is the outcome of this, we need to adjust PDF/A-4 and PDF/X-6 (https://github.com/pdf-association/pdfa-twg/issues/13).

If the outcome is that we keep the requirement for nonprimaries we should limit it to spot colors in CMYK (or non standard subtractive color spaces). We would then have to adjust the text above as well as the text in the first bullet after table 132.

After the above we should discuss #311.
title: The requirements for TransferFunctions in the different halftone types should be aligned and cleaned up

body:
This should be discussed AFTER #310

The first para after the two bullets says:
'When a halftone dictionary of some other Type appears as the value of an entry in a Type 5 halftone dictionary, it shall apply only to the single colourant or colour component named by that entry’s key.'
That makes totally sense since Type 5 halftone dictionaries use different "sub halftone dictionaries" for all colourants.
The text goes on:
'This is in contrast to such a dictionary’s being used as the current halftone parameter in the graphics state, which shall apply to all colour components.'
It should say "dictionary" instead of "dictionary's".
It then goes on:
'If nonprimary colourants are requested when the current halftone is defined by any means other than a Type 5 halftone dictionary, the gray halftone screen and transfer function shall be used for all such colourants.'
It is not clear what this should say in a chapter that specifies Type 5 halftone dictionaries?
title: Text in "10.6.5.6 Type 5 halftones" is not clear

**Describe the bug**

In the past, I experienced that PDF-1.7 denotes the first page by 0 in `PrintPageRange` (otherwise Acrobat will print page 2 with `/PrintPageRange [ 1 1 ]`), although its spec says that the first page should denoted by 1.

I don’t have access to the newest PDF-2.0 spec, but I was told that the spec hasn’t been modified in this method of page numbering for `PrintPageRange`.

I wonder whether the spec should be fixed to reflect that `PrintPageRange` uses zero-based page numbering, or to explain that PDF-2.0 now uses one-based page numbering (contrary to PDF-1.7).

Many thanks for your help.
title: is `PrintPageRange` zero-based?

body:
From @DietrichSeggern 

> in my opinion the situation with TransferFunctions in PDF/A, PDF/X and PDF 2.0 is not consistent. The whole discussion goes back to a veraPDF test case that is attached. [Here](https://github.com/veraPDF/veraPDF-corpus/issues/238).
> 
> The veraPDF test case has an RGB output intent and is drawing in RGB - and it has applied a Type 5 halftone, with nested Type 1 halftones called Red, Green and Blue. The nested halftones do not have a TransferFunction key.
> 
> The question is whether Red, Green and Blue are considered to be “nonprimary or nonstandard primary colour components”. If not the referenced halftone dictionaries would have to have a TransferFunction entry as discussed [here](#310 ).
> 
> PDF/A - and according to [this](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdfa-twg/issues/13#issuecomment-1632661073) also the next PDF/X-6 dated revision - have this provision and note:
> “The TransferFunction key in a halftone dictionary shall be used only as required by ISO 32000-2:—.
> NOTE 1 The TransferFunction key in a halftone dictionary can only be present if it is a component in a Type 5 halftone dictionary representing a colorant other than Cyan, Magenta, Yellow or Black.”
> The note suggests that Red, Green and Blue are never “nonprimary or nonstandard primary colour components”. However, in [this discussion](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/310#issuecomment-1646001887) Martin insists that they actually are. A Note would obviously not be appropriate to change something in a subset that is different in PDF2.0.
> 
> I have no specific standpoint on these questions, they have no impact on real PDFs. But we need to know whether the test case is a “fail” or a “pass" in PDF/A-4 (and PDF/X-6). In my opinion 
> - we should NOT copy the note from PDF/A-4 to PDF/X-6 and leave PDF/X-6 as it is (which means Red, Green and Blue are primaries in DeviceRGB).
> - we should strike the whole provision (that is cited above) in PDF/A. It is nothing that will have any impact on PDFs in archives. If a “print PDF” is being archived it will usually follow PDF/A-4 and PDF/X-6 at the same time. 
> 
> I know that we already agreed to discuss this in SF and perhaps that is just the right next step. But I wanted to make sure that we have some common understanding of this complicated question that is not used in any real PDFs, but can’t be ignored for PDF/A and PDF/X.
title: TransferFunction requirements in Type 5 Halftones in PDF/A and PDF/X

body:
The attached sample file (DefaultColourSpaces.230802.pdf) defines DefaultRGB and DefaultCMYK colour spaces in the page-level Resources dictionary. When text is painted at the page level those are used correctly (by reputable PDF viewers), swapping red and green and cyan and magenta so that the words are drawn in the 'wrong' colour.

Below that a grid of 12 form XObjects are drawn. In forms A-C, and G-I the form contents stream uses sc and does not directly select a colour space. In forms D-F and J-L the forms use rg and k, and therefore do select colour spaces directly.

For forms A, D, G and J there is no Resources dictionary in the form, so the page-level Resources are the current resources for the form stream.

For forms B, E, H and K there is a Resources dictionary in the form, but it does not include any default colour spaces. As resource dictionaries are inherited monolithically that means that there is no default colour space in scope while processing the form content stream.

Forms C, F, I and L have Resources dictionaries that include the same default colour spaces as the page.

Acrobat shows the default colour spaces being applied for all forms except for E and K. The consensus in discussions to date is that this is correct; the default colour space resource should be applied when the colour space is selected (see the 1st para on page 195 of 32000-2:2020, in section 8.6.5.6). Specifying colour values without changing the colour space should not trigger a new search for a default colour space.

But Peter Wyatt's research has shown that a number of reputable PDF viewers get the inheritance into forms wrong. This issue is to ask if anyone can see any way in which the current text could/should be clarified.

[DefaultColourSpaces.230802.pdf](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/files/12240882/DefaultColourSpaces.230802.pdf)
title: Review text to ensure that inheritance of defaulted colour spaces is clear

body:
Table 112 (Entries in an encoding dictionary) in section 9.6.5.1 states about the `Differences` entry of an encoding dictionary, that the entry "should not be used with TrueType fonts".

Section 9.6.5.4 (Encodings for TrueType fonts) has a section beginning with "The following paragraphs describe the treatment of TrueType font encodings beginning with PDF 1.3."  In this section, it is described how a table that maps from character codes to glyph names is constructed.  As part of this process, the description states "Any entries in the Differences array shall be used to update the table."

These two parts of the PDF spec seem to contradict each other, since the table states not to use the differences array, and the later section indicates the differences array can be used to describe the encoding.

The text should be clarified to remove this contradiction.  Maybe the table is meant to say "should not be used with TrueType fonts for PDF versions before PDF 1.3"?  Or maybe the text is section 9.6.5.4 should be updated to describe how to describe the encoding without using the differences array?

Use of differences arrays seems to be supported in practice.  The attached PDF file includes a TrueType font which uses a differences array, and the text displays correctly in Adobe Acrobat Reader, in the Preview app on MacOS, and in the PDF viewer built into Google Chrome (also on MacOS).

[truetype.pdf](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/files/12278258/truetype.pdf)
title: contradicting information about the encoding of TrueType fonts

body:
Table 25 (Entries common to all crypt filter dictionaries) describes the `Length` field of a crypt filter dictionary as "Required; deprecated in PDF 2.0".  The term "deprecated" usually means that a feature **should not** be used in new code, whereas "required" usually means that the feature **should** be be used.  The combination of the two terms is at least confusing, and possibly contradictory.

Maybe the text should be changed to just read "required", without the "deprecated" add-on?  Or maybe it should read "required before PDF 2.0; deprecated in PDF 2.0"?  Otherwise, it should be clarified for implementors whether software generating PDF 2.0 documents should or should not write a `Length` field.

The attached PDF files show that omitting the Length field is supported in some but not all PDF readers.  "a.pdf" (with `Length` field) works in all readers I tried.  "b.pdf" (without `Length` field) works in Acrobat Reader and the PDF reader built into Google Chrome (on MacOS), but does not work in the MacOS Preview app.

[a.pdf](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/files/12279152/a.pdf)
[b.pdf](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/files/12279153/b.pdf)
title: What does it mean to be "required" and "deprecated" at the same time?

body:
Spun out from https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/293

7.3.8.2 (Stream extent) says:

> Every stream dictionary shall have a Length entry that indicates how many bytes of the PDF file are used for the stream’s data. (If the stream has a filter, Length shall be the number of bytes of encoded data.) In addition, most filters are defined so that the data shall be self-limiting; that is, they use an encoding scheme in which an explicit end-of-data (EOD) marker delimits the extent of the data.

While every implementation that I know includes the bytes of the EOD marker in Length, it's not explicitly stated here. It would be easy to argue that the EOD marker is not "encoded data".

I'm sure there are clever ways to tweak the existing sentence on EOD, but KISS! I suggest adding another sentence to say "the Length value shall include the bytes of the EOD marker."
title: Clarify that a stream length includes EOD

body:
ISSUE

`B` entry in Table 31 in 7.7.3.3 ("Page objects") states:
"The beads shall be listed in the array in *natural reading order*." [emphasis is mine]

whilst body text in 12.4.3 ("Articles") prescribes the beads in that array to be "in drawing order":
"for each page on which article beads appear, the page object (see 7.7.3, "Page tree") shall contain a B entry whose value is an array of indirect references to the beads on the page, *in drawing order*." [emphasis is mine]

CORRECTION

Considering that article threads are specifically intended to convey logical relations over physical discontiguity, "in drawing order" should be replaced with "in natural reading order".
title: Articles (12.4.3): Wrong thread beads order

body:
ISSUE 1 - Entry constraint (normative)

The body text in 12.10.3 states:
"The geographic coordinate system shall be described in either *or both* of two well-established standards" [emphasis is mine]

whilst entries within Table 270 (Entries in a geographic coordinate system dictionary) imply that the two standards are mutually exclusive (cannot be "both"):
- `EPSG` entry states:
"Shall not be present if WKT is present."
- `WKT` entry states:
"Shall not be present if EPSG is present."

CORRECTION

If the entry descriptions in Table 270 are correct, the chunk "or both" in the body text of 12.10.3 should be deleted, thus:
"The geographic coordinate system shall be described in either of two well-established standards"

----

ISSUE 2 - EPSG url (informative)

The body text in 12.10.3 references:
http://www.epsg.org/

which is obviously obsolete (web clients like Firefox display a warning because of switching from unsecure HTTP protocol to HTTPS).

CORRECTION

should be updated to:
https://epsg.org/
title: Geographic coordinate system dictionary (12.10.3): Entry constraint (normative) and EPSG url (informative)

body:
ISSUE

The descriptions of several entries in Table 35 ("PDF data types") of 7.9.1 ("General" - "Common data structures") lack terminological uniformity: some entries correctly reference their base object type (eg, `array` is described as "Array object") or base data structure (eg, `name tree` is described as "Name tree (dictionary)"), whilst other entries do not (eg, boolean, numbers and string data types). Furthermore, the description of `date` entry ("Date (ASCII string)") is plain wrong (dates are `text string` (see 7.9.4, "Dates")).

CORRECTION

The descriptions of the following entries in Table 35 ("PDF data types") should be amended as indicated:
- ASCII string:
`String object whose bytes contain ASCII characters`
- boolean:
`Boolean object`
- byte string:
`String object whose series of bytes shall represent [...]`
- date:
`Date (text string)`
- integer:
`Integer numeric object`
- number:
`Numeric object (integer or real)`
- PDFDocEncoded string:
`String object whose bytes contain PDFDocEncoding characters`
- string:
`String object that is not a text string. Beginning [...]`
- text string:
`String object whose bytes shall represent characters [...]`
- text stream:
`Text stream (stream)`
title: PDF data types (Table 35, 7.9.1): Inconsistent entry descriptions

body:
I couldn't find a definition of "fields containing variable text" in ISO 32000-2:2020. There are only a couple of examples in the NOTE of 12.7.4.3.

Adobe Acrobat, for instance, puts a DA entry into the field dictionary of radio button fields, see the attached document created with Adobe Acrobat. For check boxes, the appearance created by Adobe Acrobat uses a character from the ZaDB font for the check mark, so check boxes use text, but not variable text.

Moreover, Adobe Acrobat also puts a DA entry into one of the widget annotations for the radio button (see the attached document), but DA is defined for FreeText and Redact annotations only. Is DA not being defined for widget annotations a bug in ISO 32000 (standard not following existing practice) or is Adobe Acrobat's usage of DA in the widget annotation incorrect?

Adobe Acrobat actually uses the widget annotation's DA entry when recreating the appearance streams due to NeedAppearances.

[rb-da.pdf](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/files/12320902/rb-da.pdf)
title: Fields containing variable text (DA for radio buttons, field dictionary, widget annotation dictionary)

body:
**Description**
In **"7.6.4.3.4  Algorithm 2.B: Computing a hash (revision 6 and later)", step (a):**

Clause (a) ends with "If checking the user password or creating the user key, K1 is the concatenation of the input password and K."

Now (in the opposite case, i.e. *not* "checking the user password or creating the user key) the previous text says that (summarizing/paraphrasing) K1 shall be 64 repetitions of (input password + K + the 48-byte user key).  *Clear enough*.

But it is *unclear* whether, in the "if checking the user password or creating the user key" case, K1 shall be:

- Either as (a) currently reads, "the concatenation of the input password and K",
- ** OR **
- (what I think is meant) _64 repetitions of_ (the concatenation of the input password and K).

Clause (a) right now literally implies K1 is just "one" repetition "if checking the user password or creating the user key" which I believe is incorrect and is upsetting/confusing to the reader.

**Proposed Remedy**
PROPOSAL:  Change the last sentence of (a) to read: "If checking the user password or creating the user key, K1 is 64 repetitions of the concatenation of the input password and K."
(If that is what is meant).

ANTIPROPOSAL:  If I am wrong, and it is actually _intended_ that "If checking the user password or creating the user key, K1 is the concatenation of the input password and K", then change the last sentence of (a) to read:  "If checking the user password or creating the user key, K1 is simply the concatenation of the input password and K, without any repetition."

**Additional context**
The publicly-available codebase "OpenPDF" ( https://github.com/LibrePDF/OpenPDF/ ) implements 64 repetitions for both cases (which I would expect from technical/crypto background).  Thus this favors my "PROPOSAL" intention and not that of the "ANTIPROPOSAL" above.
title: Ambiguous/confusing wording in Algorithm 2.B (a) ISO32000-2:2020-with-errata

body:
Together "7.2 Lexical conventions" and "7.3.3 Numeric objects" fail to fully describe (or is at least very obtuse) how adjacent numbers need to be delimited (i.e. separated). For example, do `+`, `-` or even `.` some of the time, delimit the start of a new number from a previous number, or is a whitespace character always required (nothing states this that I can see!)? 

e.g. `0.12-34-5.6.7` - does this validly represent the four numbers: 0.12, -34, -5.6 and 0.7? Or just 0.12 and a syntax error? Or ...?

The specification is very clear when a number object is preceded by or followed by an object that needs one of the explicit delimiter characters from Table 2. But it is unclear what the requirements are for adjacent numbers...  and implementations do vary a lot!! 

"7.3.3 Numeric objects" states "_An integer shall be written as one or more decimal digits optionally preceded by a sign._" and "_A real value shall be written as one or more decimal digits with an optional sign and a leading, trailing, or embedded PERIOD (2Eh) (decimal point)._" which implies the above is valid as 4 numbers, but it would be good to clarify for consistency between implementations.
title: PDF fails to fully describe how adjacent numbers need to be delimited (i.e. separated).

body:
### SUB-ISSUE 1: File identifiers definition

Subclause 14.4 (File identifiers) states:
> The value of this entry shall be an array of two byte strings. The first byte string shall be a permanent identifier based on the contents of the PDF file at the time it was originally created [...]

To me, *the requirement of being based on the contents of the PDF file is arbitrary and misleading*; the fact that, since PDF 2.0, even the suggested MD5-based hashing algorithm has dropped its main content-related input ("The values of all entries in the file's document information dictionary [...]" (see PDF 1.7)) speaks volumes — now it retains merely "The size of the PDF file in bytes" as a barely content-related input!

As later stated, *the sole relevant attribute of a computed identifier is **uniqueness*** (which implies the statistical robustness of the generative algorithm against collisions):
> PDF writers should attempt to ensure the uniqueness of file identifiers.

Even the NOTE to subclause 14.4 in PDF 1.7 stressed that "all that matters is that the identifier is likely to be unique"... What about standard generative algorithms like, say, [UUID](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universally_unique_identifier) as alternatives to the suggested MD5-based hashing algorithm?
I do not advocate to dismiss the suggested hashing algorithm, just to reword subclause 14.4 in order *to make more clear the distinction between specification* (identifier uniqueness) *and implementation* (algorithms suitable to meet the specification).

Therefore, IMO, the sentence in subclause 14.4 should be reformulated, like so:
`The value of this entry shall be an array of two unique byte strings, each at least 16 bytes long. The first byte string shall be a permanent identifier, not to change when the PDF file is updated. The second byte string shall be a changing identifier, computed when the PDF file is updated (see 7.5.6, "Incremental updates").`

While the last paragraph ("PDF writers should attempt to ensure the uniqueness [...]") would be replaced by:
`Identifier uniqueness should be attempted by employing a suitable generative algorithm, such as UUID (described in Internet RFC 4122); this may also be achieved by means of a message digest algorithm such as MD5 (described in Internet RFC 1321), using the following information:`
`- the current time;`
`- a string representation of the PDF file's location;`
`- the size of the PDF file in bytes.`

-----

### SUB-ISSUE 2: File identifiers mapping to XMP metadata
Apparently, there is a *lack of documentation at core PDF level regarding the relation between PDF file identifiers and document identifiers in XMP metadata*: while Table 349 in subclause 14.3.3 (Document information dictionary) suggests a precise mapping between information entries and document-level XMP metadata, there is no indication for the reconciliation between file identifier's (permanent and changing) byte strings and semantically-corresponding document identifiers (`DocumentID` and `InstanceID`) in Media Management namespace. Although higher-level PDF specs in ISO stack (such as PDF/A) are designed to add constraints atop the core PDF spec, *the latter could nonetheless provide a general mapping suggestion the same way it already does for the document information dictionary entries* (after all, even the mapping of those entries is mentioned both at core PDF and PDF/A levels!).

In XMP metadata, document identifiers are typed as `GUID`, which the XMP spec (part 1 (ISO 16684-1:2011), Annex A) describes eloquently (emphasis is mine):
> This document defines three GUIDs that are intended to help manage copies of a resource [(xmpMM:DocumentID, xmpMM:InstanceID, xmpMM:OriginalDocumentID)], to identify a specific state when desired, and to associate related copies of the same conceptual resource. [...]
The use of robust GUIDs is encouraged; having globally unique values is important. In practical terms, this means that the probability of a collision is so remote as to be effectively impossible. *Typically, 128-bit or 144-bit numbers are used*, encoded as hexadecimal strings.
*This document does not require any particular methodology for creating a GUID, nor does it require any specific means of formatting the GUID as a simple XMP value.*
The only valid operations on XMP IDs are to create them, to assign one to another, and to compare two of them for equality. Comparisons use the Unicode string value as-is, using a direct byte-for-byte check for equality.
IETF RFC 4122 ( http://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc4122.txt ) describes ways to create and format GUID strings. For privacy, the use of a MAC address is not recommended. See section 4.1.6 of RC 4122 for details and alternatives.

According to the description here above, PDF file identifier byte strings seem compatible with document identifiers in XMP Media Management namespace — furthermore, AFAIK, PDF/A allows freedom of identification scheme (identifiers may be externally based (eg, ISBN) or internally based (eg, UUID)). *Could it be acceptable in general cases* (ie, without specific constraints) *to assign the permanent file identifier byte string of a given PDF file to the corresponding `xmpMM:DocumentID` property, and its changing file identifier byte string to the corresponding `xmpMM:InstanceID` property?*

This way, it would be possible to have, by default, a single pair of identifiers, without unnecessary redundancies, like so (byte strings here below are obviously fictitious):

```
trailer
<<
  /Size 5275
  /Root 118 0 R
  /Info 2751 0 R
  /ID [<33333333333333333333333333333333><44444444444444444444444444444444>]
  /Prev 259675
>>
. . .
2152 0 obj<< /Subtype /XML /Length 4751 /Type /Metadata >>
stream
<?xpacket begin="﻿" id="XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX"?>
<x:xmpmeta xmlns:x="adobe:ns:meta/">
<rdf:RDF xmlns:rdf="http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#">
<rdf:Description xmlns:xmpMM='http://ns.adobe.com/xap/1.0/mm/'
  xmpMM:DocumentID='33333333333333333333333333333333'
  xmpMM:InstanceID='44444444444444444444444444444444'/>
. . .
</rdf:RDF>
</x:xmpmeta>
<?xpacket end="w"?>
endstream
endobj
```
title: File identifiers (14.4): Observations and possible improvements

IMHO, subclause 7.11 (File specifications) is not well-organized: subclause 7.11.2.2 (Absolute and relative file specifications) describes file specifications belonging to *any file system* (both platform-independent file names and URLs), yet it is under 7.11.2 (File specification strings), which is *specific to platform-independent file names*. Furthermore, while File specification strings (7.11.2) are described *before* File specification dictionaries (7.11.3), URL specifications (7.11.5) are described *after* them, despite BOTH specification types are referenced within File specification dictionaries (7.11.3).

### PROPOSAL
Therefore, with the same intent of a similar proposal (#263), I suggest to reorganize subclause 7.11 this way:

7.11, "File specifications"
7.11.1, "General": same as current 7.11.1 (General)
7.11.2, "File specification types"
7.11.2.1, "File specification strings": contents of current 7.11.2.1 (General)
7.11.2.2, "URL specifications": contents of current 7.11.5 (URL specifications)
7.11.3, "File specification syntax": contents of current 7.11.2.2 (Absolute and relative file specifications)
7.11.4, "File specification dictionaries": contents of current 7.11.3 (File specification dictionaries)
7.11.5, "Embedded file streams": contents of current 7.11.4 (Embedded file streams)
7.11.6, "Collection items": contents of current 7.11.6 (Collection items)

---
NOTE: [For convenience](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/329#issuecomment-2148730995), original SUB-ISSUE 1 (File specification dictionaries (7.11.3) - Table 43 (Entries in a file specification dictionary)) has been moved to https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/433. Consequently, this issue now covers only original SUB-ISSUE 2 (File specifications (7.11) - Subclause organization improvement).
title: 7.11 (File specifications): Subclause organization improvement

> Certain language-related dictionary entries [(`Lang` entries)] are text strings that specify language identifiers

> All marked-content operators except EMC shall take a tag operand indicating the role or significance of the marked-content element to the PDF processor. All such tags should have second-class names registered with ISO ...

I believe that the intention here is to also allow first-class names, defined in the specification itself.  For example, example 1 in section 14.8.2.2.2 (Specification of Artifacts) suggests that artifacts could be marked using `/Artifact BMC`, and `/Artifact` is not a second-class name.

body:
Section 14.6.1, after note 3, states:

> Marked-content operators may appear only between graphics objects in the content stream. They may not occur within a graphics object or between a graphics state operator and its operands.

While this seems clear, there are many examples in the spec, where marked context operators are used within text objects.  For example, the text after table 352 explicitly states that `BT BMC ... EMC ET` is valid, and section 14.9.5 (Expansion of abbreviations and acronyms) has an example where two `BDC ... EMC` pairs are used within the same text object.  (More similar uses within `BT ... ET` are easily found by searching for `BDC`.)

According to the list in section 8.2 (Graphics objects), text objects are one of the five types of PDF graphics objects and according to section 9.4.1, a "text object begins with the BT operator and ends with the ET operator".  Thus, the use of marked-content operators within `BT ... ET` pairs seems to contradict the statement that marked-content operators may appear only between graphics objects.

My guess is that marked-content operators within text objects are in fact allowed, and section 14.6.1 should be clarified to reflect this.
title: contradicting information about possible locations for marked content operators

`Pg` entries of Marked-content reference and Object reference dictionaries are defined in divergent ways:

- for Marked-content sequences as content items (14.7.5.2), Table 357 (Entries in a marked-content reference dictionary):
> [...] This entry overrides any **Pg** entry in the structure element containing the marked-content reference; it shall be required if the structure element has no such entry.

- for PDF objects as content items (14.7.5.3), Table 358 (Entries in an object reference dictionary):
> [...] This entry overrides any **Pg** entry in the structure element containing the object reference; it shall be used if the structure element has no such entry.

IMO, the latter definition is unnecessarily loose: it states that object-reference-specific `Pg` entry "shall be *used* if the structure element has no such entry", opting for the semantically weaker term *"used"* instead of the much more precise term *"required"* employed by the marked-content reference counterpart.

It seems clear that the description of `Pg` entry in Table 358 needs to be amended this way:
`This entry overrides any Pg entry in the structure element containing the object reference; it shall be required if the structure element has no such entry.`
title: Structure content (14.7.5): Pg entry inconsistency

body:
**Third-class** paragraph (E.2 (Classes of PDF names)) ends with redundant and ambiguous words:
> [...] Third-class names shall all begin with a specific prefix reserved for private extensions. This prefix, which is XX, shall be used as the first characters in the names of all private data added by the developer. It is not necessary to register third-class names in the PDF Names list.

In my opinion:
- the second sentence is *almost a rewording of the first one*: a prefix is a prefix, no need to specify that it is "the first characters in the names"! Furthermore, it already implicitly stated that third-class names concern private data — if they are "reserved for private extensions", they are necessarily used to define private data, what else?
- the third sentence uses the *misleading expression "not necessary"*, which implies that the registration *may* be possible: to my understanding, this is NOT true (the paragraph earlier states that such names "may be used only in PDF files that are part of an internal process", so it doesn't make sense to expose them to a public registry, otherwise they would overlap second-class names!)

### CORRECTION

This is my reformulation proposal:
`[...] Third-class names shall all begin with a specific prefix, which is XX, reserved for all private data added by the developer. By definition, third-class names cannot be registered in the PDF Names list.`
title: Extending PDF (Annex E): Third-class names

NOTE 1 in subclause 7.5.6 reads:

> The main advantage to updating a PDF file in this way is that small changes to a large document can be saved quickly. There are additional advantages *such as when editing a document across an HTTP connection or using OLE embedding (a Microsoft Windows™ specific technology)*, a PDF processor cannot overwrite the contents of the original PDF file. [...]

The emphasized phrase was introduced in PDF 1.4 (2001). While "editing a document across an HTTP connection" may be a perfect fit as an example, "using OLE embedding" IMHO nowadays lacks relevance to be mentioned inside a universal, cross-platform standard format like ISO PDF — OLE is an... ole proprietary technology, feels a bit arbitrary for it to make its way inside this specification, *especially considering that platform-specific definitions* like those in Launch actions (12.6.4.6) or File specifications (7.11.3) *have been deprecated since PDF 2.0*.

### CORRECTION

This is my reformulation proposal:
`The main advantage to updating a PDF file in this way is that small changes to a large document can be saved quickly. There are additional advantages such as when editing a document across an HTTP connection, a PDF processor cannot overwrite the contents of the original PDF file. [...]`
title: Incremental updates (7.5.6): Unnecessary mention of proprietary technology

body:
Here I am reporting a possible bug to correct (SUB-ISSUE 1), and requesting a clarification on an apparent contradiction related to it (SUB-ISSUE 2).

### SUB-ISSUE 1: Cardinality of parent structure elements of PDF objects as content items

Describing the structural parent tree from the point of view of a **PDF object as content item** (such as image XObject), subclause 14.7.5.4 (Finding structure elements from content items) states:
> The tree shall contain an entry for each object that is a content item of at least one structure element [...].

To my understanding, *the phrase "at least one" is misleading, since a PDF object that is a content item is required* (see also Table 359 (Additional dictionary entries for structure element access)) *to be associated to ONE AND ONLY ONE parent structure element*, as later stated:
> The key for each entry shall be an integer given as the value of the StructParent [...] entry in the object [...]. [...] the value [for each entry] shall be an indirect reference to the parent structure element.

This statement is unequivocal, especially considering that, on the other hand, for a content stream (page object or form XObject) containing marked-content sequences that are content items "the value shall be an array of indirect references to the sequences' parent structure elements."

### SUB-ISSUE 2: Parent structure element of a PDF object as content item in case of multiple separate object references

All the above held, the following statement in NOTE 2 of subclause 14.7.5.3 (PDF objects as content items) depicts a more complex case which, to my understanding, leads to a contradiction:
> If the referenced object is rendered on multiple pages, each rendering requires a separate object reference.

As you know, a PDF object as content item is included in the structure tree (see 14.7.2 (Structure hierarchy)) as an **object reference** (see 14.7.5.3 (PDF objects as content items)). Since a PDF object as content item can be associated, via structural parent tree, to ONE AND ONLY ONE parent structure element, NOTE 2 implies that its single parent structure element will have to contain ALL its separate object references, each one for the distinct page where it is rendered (am I right?). *However, such conclusion seems to disrupt the whole purpose of logical content order (the ordering for semantic purposes)* as described by subclause 14.8.2.5 (Page content order and logical content order)... What's wrong with it?

What is the **correct way to place in the logical structure multiple separate object references (one per page) of the same PDF object as content item**? (EXAMPLE 1 in 14.7.5.4 (Finding structure elements from content items) only shows the simple case of a single object reference; IMO, *that example should be expanded to address also the case depicted in NOTE 2, ie multiple separate object references, one per page* — BTW, apparently that example is the only one in the whole ISO PDF spec to mention object references, so it is crucial to integrate it)
title: 14.7.5 (Logical structure, PDF objects as content items): parent structure elements and object references

body:
The PDF specification does not explain how the CIDSystemInfo dictionary for ToUnicode CMaps should be constructed.  The introduction of section 9.10.3 claims that the format is "fully documented in Adobe Technical Note #5014", but #5014 does not have any information specific to ToUnicode cmaps, and only discusses the CIDSystemInfo dictionary in terms of compatibility to the corresponding CIDFont (which does not apply to ToUnicode cmaps, since no font is involved here).  Similarly, I have not found any information how the CMapName should be chosen.

The spec should be updated to either explain how the CIDSystemInfo dictionary and CMapName should be chosen, or should point more explicitly to an external document which explains this.

The example in section 9.10.3 uses `/CIDSystemInfo << /Registry (Adobe) /Ordering (UCS2) /Supplement 0 >>`.  I wonder whether this example is actually correct, since the vast majority of ToUnicode files embedded in the PDF files on my system uses `UCS` instead of `UCS2`.  If `UCS2` is indeed incorrect, the example should also be fixed.

In practice it seems to me that most (all?) pdf-viewers ignore the CIDSystemInfo dictionary and CMapName for ToUnicode cmaps.  So a possible solution may be for the spec to say that these values can be chosen arbitrarily when writing a PDF document, and should be ignored when reading?
title: CIDSystemInfo for ToUnicode CMaps

While the purpose of marked-content sequences is absolutely clear because of their extensive coverage within ISO PDF, ***marked-content points** seem quite obscure*: AFAIK, in the whole spec there is no statement nor example explaining why marked-content points exist and what use they are intended for. Till ISO PDF 1.7 there was a subclause (14.6.3 (Marked Content and Clipping)) which made some sketchy example fleetingly mentioning marked-content points, nothing more.

IMHO, *subclause 14.6.1 (General, Marked content) should clearly state the purpose of marked-content points, along with practical examples* (the same way as marked-content sequences are currently described by ISO PDF). Otherwise, if marked-content points have become neglected and obsolete, that should be stated as well (deprecation?).
title: Marked content (14.6.1): Marked-content point clarification

body:
Table 35 (PDF data types) in 7.9.1 (General, Common data structures) declares `date` type as `ASCII string`, *despite its dedicated subclause (7.9.4 (Dates)) defines it as `text string`*.

As [already emerged in a related issue](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/322#issuecomment-1674933919), for some obscure reason, that definition has changed over time, inadvertently creating a rift between the ancient declaration in Table 35 (`ASCII string`) and the current definition in subclause 7.9.4 (`text string`). I assume that the ancient declaration was so deeply engrained in everybody's mind that nobody cared about this blatant contradiction.

### CORRECTION

IMHO, subclause 7.9.4 definition should be reverted to `ASCII string`.
title: Common data structures (7.9): 'date' type contradiction

body:
Table 35 (PDF data types) in 7.9.1 (General, Common data structures) confusingly declares `string` type as "Any string that is not a text string", *despite its dedicated subclause (7.9.2 (String object types)) defines string object as "further qualified as a text string, ASCII string, or byte string."*.

As [already emerged in a related issue](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/322#issuecomment-1674933919), for some obscure reason, that declaration has changed over time (`string` type was declared as plain simple "String object" till PDF 1.6 (see TABLE 3.31 (PDF data types))), inadvertently creating a rift between the current declaration in Table 35 ("Any string that is not a text string") and the current definition in subclause 7.9.2 ("a text string, ASCII string, or byte string").

### CORRECTION

IMHO, *the inconsistent declaration in Table 35 should be reverted to its original expression* (`string` type as "String object"), and *a new type should be introduced in Table 35 to unambiguously encompass all non-`text string` string types* ("Any string that is not a text string", ie `ASCII string` and `byte string`). As a consequence, all the `string`-typed dictionary entries conforming to this restrictive definition (such as `CheckSum` in Table 45) should be revised accordingly with the new data type.
title: Common data structures (7.9): 'string' type contradiction

body:
Across subclauses 14.7 (Logical structure) and 14.8 (Tagged PDF), `O` entry of attribute object dictionaries (see Table 360 in subclause 14.7.6 (Structure attributes)) is defined in multiple, confusing ways (bolding is mine):

- as "**conforming product** that owns the attribute information" (subclause 14.7.6.1 (General, Structure attributes))
- as "**PDF processor** creating the attribute data" (Table 360 (Entries common to all attribute object dictionaries))
- as "**owner** [...] which determines the interpretation of the attributes defined in the object's dictionary" (subclause 14.8.5.2 (Standard attribute owners))

IMHO, *the last definition is the only accurate one, as "conforming product" and "PDF processor" are misleadingly restrictive* (the Standard attribute owners in subclause 14.8.5.2 have nothing to do with what the rest of the spec calls "PDF processors", yet they are owners as well).

### CORRECTION

My proposal is to harmonize the ways attribute information owners are referred to in ISO PDF:

- subclause 14.7.6.1 (General, Structure attributes): replace "conforming product that owns the attribute information" with "`owner of the attribute information`"
- `O` entry, Table 360 (Entries common to all attribute object dictionaries): replace as follows:
`(Required) The name of the owner of the attribute data. The value shall either be NSO, UserProperties (see "Table 361 — Additional entries in an attribute object dictionary for user properties"), one of the values from 14.8.5, "Standard structure attributes", or the name of the PDF processor conforming to the guidelines described in Annex E, "Extending PDF".`
`[...]`
title: Logical structure, attributes (14.7.6): 'O' entry inconsistency

Related to Errata #322.

Check usage of the word "real" throughout ISO 32000-2 specification (74 occurrences), especially in the middle "Type" column of tables that define dictionary entries. Section 8.4.5 (Graphics state parameter dictionaries) describes how graphics state parameter dictionaries are constructed.  Table 57 lists all possible dictionary keys.  All keys are marked as optional.  The entry for `UseBlackPtComp` states "The default value is: Default".

My understanding was that graphics state parameter dictionaries only change the parameters explicitly mentioned in the dictionary, and leave state corresponding to missing keys unchanged.  If this reading is correct, then giving a default value in table 57 makes no sense.

My suggestions would be:

1.  Remove the statement "The default value is: Default" from table 57.  (Note that table 51 already states that the initial value of the corresponding graphics state parameter is `Default`.)
2. Make it explicit that the `gs` operator does not change graphics state parameters not mentioned in the dictionary.  (I currently can't find anywhere in the spec which says this explicitly.)
title: Default values for entries in graphics state parameter dictionaries?

body:
`OutputIntents` entry (see document catalog dictionary (7.7.2) and page dictionary (7.7.3.3)) is defined as an array of output intent dictionaries which are distinguished by subtype (either predefined (`GTS_PDFX`, `GTS_PDFA1`, and `ISO_PDFE1`) or additional (see Annex E ("Extending PDF"))).

AFAIK, *the spec doesn't prescribe whether **multiple output intent dictionaries of the same subtype*** (eg, `GTS_PDFA1`) *can be added to an array*; real-world PDF files typically contain output intent dictionaries of *distinct* subtype (eg, `GTS_PDFA1` and `ISO_PDFE1`) only, so one might assume that adding multiple output intent dictionaries of the same subtype is pointless (but syntactically possible!). If this consideration is correct, the obvious question is: *why was `OutputIntents` entry defined as an array instead of a dictionary keyed by subtype?* (the latter would have been much more convenient (no output intent duplication for the same subtype, easy retrieval by subtype))
title: Output intents (14.11.5): combination constraints unclear

Section 7.8.2 (Content Streams) explains the term "operator" as follows:

> An operator is a PDF keyword specifying some action that ...

but I did not find any definition of "PDF keyword" in the notes.  It would be good to add a more explicit definition of what is a valid operator.

Maybe `xxx` is an operator, if and only if `xxx` is not empty and `/xxx` is a valid way to write a name?  Assuming that "operator keyword" is the same as "operator", this would be consistent with

> An operator keyword shall be distinguished from a name object by the absence of an initial SOLIDUS character (2Fh) (/).

One aspect of this question is whether `#63` is a valid way to write the `c` (curveto) operator.

body:
Section 14.1 says

> Procedure sets ... (deprecated in PDF 2.0)

Further down on the same page section 14.2 says about Procedure Sets

> This feature has been deprecated since PDF 1.4.

For tidiness, these two statements should agree on the PDF version when Procedure Sets were deprecated.

I looked through some old specs to see which version this might be:

- PDF 1.2 says "The Resources dictionary for each context must contain a ProcSet key whose value is an array consisting of the names of the ProcSets used in that context."
- PDF 1.3 lists `ProcSet` as "optional" in table 3.20.
- PDF 1.4 lists `ProcSet` as "optional" in table 3.21 and says in section 9.1 "Note: Beginning with PDF 1.4, this feature is considered obsolete. For compatibility [...] PDF producer applications should continue to specify procedure sets [...]. However, viewer applications should not depend on the correctness of this information."
- PDF 1.7 lists  `ProcSet` as "optional" in table 33 and says in section 14.2 "Note: Beginning with PDF 1.4, this feature is considered obsolete. For compatibility [...] PDF producer applications should continue to specify procedure sets [...]. However, viewer applications should not depend on the correctness of this information."
- ISO-32000-2 (2020) claims in table 34 that `ProcSet` has been deprecated in PDF 2.0, and the language that PDF producers should specify procedure sets has been removed.

So probably the solution would be for section 14.2 to say "This feature has been deprecated in PDF 2.0" (instead of "... since 1.4").
title: minor contradiction in sections 14.1 / 14.2

body:
Section 8.4.2 states that the `q` operator pushes the entire graphics state on the stack, and `Q` then can restore the entire graphics state.  Does `Q` restore the text matrix?

More specifically, should the following content stream print "XXX" underneath "OOO" or should "XXX" and "OOO" overlap?

```
BT
/F 24 Tf
100 300 Td
q
(OOO) Tj
0 -30 TD
Q
(XXX) Tj
ET
```

(Full PDF attached: [test.pdf](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/files/13502343/test.pdf) )

Some observations:
- Section 8.4.1 says that the graphics state holds the current "graphics control parameters".
- Table 51 says that there are "nine graphics state parameters" and section 9.3.1 says that "there are nine parameters in the text state".  The list of these 9 parameters (table 102) does not include the text matrix.
- The text after table 51 mentions the text matrix as one of "three additional text-related parameters".
- section 9.4.1 says that these "three parameters may be specified only within a text object and shall not persist from one text object to the next".
- If `q`/`Q` save the text matrix, is `BT ... q ... ET ... BT ... Q ... ET` allowed?
- Adobe Acrobat Reader and Google Chrome seem to restore the text matrix when `Q` is issued.
- Preview on Mac seems to get confused by the attached PDF file, misplacing the "OOO".
title: Is the text matrix part of the "graphics state"?

Within the graphics state model, the dictionary associated to the `gs` operator (ExtGState) supports only a subset (`Font` entry corresponding to `Tf` operator) of the **text state parameters** associated to individual operators (see 9.3, "Text state parameters and operators"); *since text state operators can be applied at content stream level* (see Figure 9, "Graphics objects" in 8.2, "Graphics objects") *like any other graphics state operator, it looks pretty weird that such parameters are excluded from ExtGState*.

Moreover, it would be convenient to include in ExtGState **any other appropriate graphics state parameter** associated to individual operators, such as **colour-related** ones (color space, color — see Table 51), as well.

### PROPOSAL

My proposal is to **extend ExtGState dictionary to support *any* appropriate graphics state parameter**, in particular:
- **all the text state parameters** associated to the operators listed in Table 103
- **all the colour state parameters** listed in Table 51 (color space, color)

---
NOTE: The initial comment was updated to include any appropriate graphics state parameter, in particular colour-related ones.
title: 8.4.5 (Graphics state parameter dictionaries, aka ExtGState): extend to full superset of parameters associated to individual operators

body:
Table 50 and section 10.7.2 describe the flatness tolerance as positive number.  In contrast, table 56 states that the argument of the `i` operator (for setting the flatness tolerance) is a number in the range 0 to 100 (and also states that "a value of 0 shall specify the output device’s default flatness tolerance").  Table 57 describes the value of the `FL` entry in a graphics state parameter dictionary (another way of setting the flatness tolerance) simply as a "number".

These descriptions allow for the possibility that the flatness tolerance might be set to values larger than 100 using a graphics state parameter dictionary.  It is also unclear whether setting flatness to 0 via a graphics state parameter dictionary will be interpreted as the device’s default flatness tolerance.  It would be nice to clarify whether or not the two ways of setting the flatness tolerance are different in these regards.

Suggested solution: Move or copy the text "flatness is a number in the range 0 to 100; a value of 0 shall specify
the output device’s default flatness tolerance" from table 56 to section 10.7.2, applying these explanations to the parameter itself rather than to the argument of the `i` operator.
title: possible mistake in given range of the flatness tolerance
