The table for this type has as its first entry

type    |  CompressedEntityType        | (Optional; if compressed_iso_spline is FALSE) PRC_HCG_Circle

The fact that the type is optional is problematic, since  PRC_HCG_Circle is part of an abstract type and it is necessary to read the type to determine which one of the curves we need to decode.      If you can't read the type, how do you know if you have a circle or a line??   

The curve type PRC_HCG_Line (Table 233) also relies on the setting of compressed_iso_spline.
It has an entry

start_end_data | StartEndData | (Optional; ; if compressed_iso_spline is FALSE) Save the start/end trim data


compressed_iso_spline is undefined except for a statement in the circle section where it says:

compressed_iso_spline is TRUE if the circle is being used as the trim boundary of an PRC_HCG_IsoNURBS; otherwise it is FALSE

That is a very poor definition.  What about if the line is being used for a trim boundary?   It clearly has an impact on what gets decoded.  But this definition says it is TRUE if the *circle* is being used as the trim boundary of a PRC_HCG_IsoNURBS.   So how and why would the PRC_HCG_Line decode come into play?

body:
In PDF 2.0, annotations can be either "open" or "closed".  For example, for Text annotations, the spec has the following explanation in Section 12.5.6.4 (Text annotations):

> When closed, the annotation shall appear as an icon; when open, it shall display a popup window containing the text of the note in a font and size chosen by the interactive PDF processor.

Text annotations also have a flag **Open**, "specifying whether the annotation shall initially be
displayed open" (Table 175).

The popup window, which can be shown by opening the Text annotation is an annotation itself.  Section 12.5.6.14 (Popup annotations) does not define what it means for a popup annotation to be open or closed, but a plausible guess is that "open" means visible and "closed" means invisible.  Popup annotations have a separate **Open** flag, "specifying whether the popup annotation shall initially be displayed open" (Table 186).

The spec does not explain how the two separate **Open** flags interact.
- If **Open** is false for both the Text annotation and its popup, it seems clear that the popup *should not* be initially shown.
- If **Open** is true for both the Text annotation and its popup, it seems clear that the popup *should* be initially shown.
- What should happen if one **Open** flag is true and the other is false (true/false or false/true)?  Is this allowed?  What should PDF viewers do in these cases?

The spec should be clarified to explain the meaning of these **Open** flags in more detail.
title: "Open" field for Text/Popup annotations

body:
The PDF 2.0 spec, near the end of section 12.5.2 (Annotation dictionaries), [states](https://pdf-issues.pdfa.org/32000-2-2020/clause12.html#H12.5.2):

> When rendering the appearance dictionary, a PDF reader shall ignore the values of the C, IC, Border, BS, BE, CA, ca, H, DA, Q, DS, LE, LL, LLE, MK, and Sy keys.

This seems to indicate that **CA** and **ca** are ignored.  Consistently with this, the entries for **CA** and **ca** state

> The specified value shall not be used if the annotation has an appearance stream (see 12.5.5, "Appearance streams"); in that case, the appearance stream shall specify any transparency.

There is also some discussion in issue #23.

In contrast, section 12.5.5 (Appearance streams) states:

> The transparency group shall be composited with a backdrop consisting of the page content along with any previously painted annotations, using the values of the **BM**, **ca** and **CA** entries in the annotation dictionary (see "Table 166 — Entries common to all annotation dictionaries") and a soft mask of None.

This seems to directly contradict the "shall ignore" statement from section 12.5.2.  Maybe this apparent contradiction stems from a distinction between rendering the appearance dictionary and compositing it onto the page?  But in this case the "the appearance stream shall specify any transparency" would not make much sense, and also "shall not be used" seems not compatible with this interpretation.  The spec should be clarified to make it clear whether or not **ca** and **CA** are used when rendering appearance streams.
title: contradicting information about rendering PDF annotations

body:
The [current version](https://pdf-issues.pdfa.org/32000-2-2020/clause12.html#H12.5.2) of the PDF 2.0 spec (in section 12.5.2, Annotation dictionaries) states:

> When rendering the appearance dictionary, a PDF reader shall ignore the values of the [...], **H**, [...] keys.

I have found three different **H** keys in appearance dictionaries:

- The "highlighting mode" (None, Invert, Outline, Push) for Link annotations (Table 176),
- the "amount to translate the associated content horizontally, as a percentage of the width of the target media" for Watermark annotations (Tables 193 and 194), and
- the "highlighting mode" (None, Invert, Outline, Push, Toggle) for Widget annotations (Table 191).

The **H** entry for Widget annotations also states that "A highlighting mode other than [Push] shall override any down
appearance defined for the annotation."

Only the Watermark annotation's **H** key directly affects visual rendering (translation), while the Link and Widget H keys affect interaction behavior.  Given this inconsistent usage of the **H** key in annotation dictionaries, I wonder whether really all three of these keys are meant to be ignored if an appearance dictionary is present.  Given that only the **H** entry of Watermark annotations has a direct effect on "appearance", maybe only this one is to be ignored?  The spec should clarify which of these **H** fields need to be ignored.
title: Ignoring "H" fields in annotations which have an appearance stream

Section 12.5.6.6 (Free text annotations) of the PDF 2.0 spec describes the **RD** field in a freetext annotation dictionary as follows:

> A set of four numbers describing the numerical differences between two rectangles: the Rect entry of the annotation and a rectangle contained within that rectangle. [...] The four numbers correspond to the differences in default user space between the left, top, right, and bottom coordinates of Rect and those of the inner rectangle, respectively.

Most PDF viewers I have tried (including Acrobat Reader) use the order "left, bottom, right, top" instead of the order "left, top, right, bottom" described in the spec.  I have not found a single PDF viewer which implements the order of values in the spec.  For this reason, I think it would be best to adjust the spec to say

> ... between the left, bottom, right, and top coordinates of ...

A test file is attached.  The test file draws two copies of an outer rectangle, together with an inner rectangle, and then tries to place an annotation onto the inner rectangle.  The inner rectangle of the annotation uses a bold, dashed outline so that it is easy to see the location on the page.

- The top panel uses the **RD** values suggested by the spec; I have not found a viewer which places this annotation on the inner rectangle.
- The bottom panel uses the modified **RD** values suggested here; some viewers manage to place this annotation on the inner rectangle.

[test.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/21596733/test.pdf)
title: RD field for FreeText annotations

It shall be of the form software_name:software_version, where software_name identifies the software by name. It shall not contain spaces. software_version identifies the version of the software. This is a paragraph of text.

ISO 32000-2:2020 describes CreationDate and ModDate in Table 45 thus:
```
CreationDate   [...] The date and time when the embedded file was created. [...] 
ModDate        [...] The date and time when the embedded file was last modified. [...] 
```
This wording dates back to PDF Reference 1.3. Unfortunately, it is ambiguous: are these the creation/modification date and time of the file (in/from the file system) at the time it was embedded or are these the creation/modification time of the stream in the PDF document?

Experiments indicate that in Adobe Acrobat (the behavior of which the PDF Reference was supposed to describe)  ModDate comes from the file sytem whereas CreationDate is the date and time of the creation of the stream in the PDF document. This difference in the semantics of CreationDate and ModDate is not reflected in the wording.

**Describe the bug**

When a ExtGState resource is invoked into a graphic state, 32K does not give any guidance as to the order in which the keys of the dictionary are processed.

**Describe the bug**
In the [pre-ISO 2006 version](https://opensource.adobe.com/dc-acrobat-sdk-docs/pdfstandards/pdfreference1.7old.pdf) of the PDF 1.7 spec, dates with a timezone offset end with a trailing apostrophe in Clause 3.8.3, Dates. This apostrophe is defined in four places:

- The ASCII string at the top
- The last bullet in the list explaining its constituent components
- The first sentence of the following paragraph starting with "The apostrophe character..."
- The example at the end of the clause

In errata published by Adobe in 2007 [(archival link)](https://web.archive.org/web/20100601205933/http://www.adobe.com/devnet/pdf/pdfs/pdf_17_errata.pdf), the first sentence in the paragraph starting with "The apostrophe character..." is removed. All other references to the character are left intact.

In Clause 7.9.4 of the 2008 version of the PDF spec (ISO 32000-1:2008), all references to the trailing apostrophe are removed.

In Clause 7.9.4 of the PDF 2.0 spec (ISO 32000-2:2020), Note 2 says this:
> PDF versions up to and including 1.7 defined a date string to include a terminating apostrophe. PDF processors are recommended to accept date strings that still follow that convention.

_Given this inconsistency, should a conforming PDF 1.7 writer write an apostrophe at the end of a date offset?_

**Additional context**
I first came across the issue in the context of [Typst's](https://typst.app) PDF backend pdf-writer. [A user reported](https://github.com/typst/pdf-writer/issues/73) that the date offsets are not correctly parsed by Apple Preview because we did not use an apostrophe at the end. When implementing, we used the 2008 PDF 1.7 spec as our primary reference.
title: Trailing apostrophe in PDF 1.7 (2006 vs. 2008 spec)

body:
Location: Clause 7.5.8 “Cross-reference streams”, Example 4 (narrative text preceding the object/xref stream listings)

Issue summary
The narrative sentence describing the three fields of cross-reference stream entries contains a grammatical error and an ambiguous phrase that likely misstates “second field.” This can confuse implementers about the meaning of the three fields for Type 2 (compressed object) entries.

Problematic text (as published)

“The first field of, along with a cross-reference table field is the number of the object stream (15), and the third field is the position within the sequence of objects in the object stream (0, 1, and 2). The cross-reference stream also contains a Type 1 entry for the object stream itself.”

Issues:

“The first field of,” leaves of without an object (grammatical error).

“along with a cross-reference table field” is unclear and likely intended to mean “the second field” (and it should refer to the cross-reference stream, not a table).

Proposed correction (minimal, unambiguous wording)

“The first field is 2; the second field is the number of the object stream (15); and the third field is the position within the sequence of objects in the object stream (0, 1, and 2). The cross-reference stream also contains a Type 1 entry for the object stream itself.”

Rationale

For compressed objects (Type 2) in a cross-reference stream, the three fields are:

entry type = 2; 2) object stream number (here 15); 3) index/position within that object stream (here 0, 1, 2).

The corrected sentence aligns with the Example 4 data and the normative semantics of cross-reference stream entry types and fields.

This is an editorial fix (clarifies text only); no technical behavior changes.

Impact
Avoids misinterpretation of cross-reference stream entries and eliminates ambiguity for readers implementing PDF 2.0 xref stream parsing.
title: Erratum request for ISO 32000-2:2020 — Example 4 text in object-reference stream description

body:
This issue is a recommendation that we formalise, or at least document, an approach taken by the LaTeX team when converting to/from MathML in it's XML form, and MathML as it's stored in the StructureTree.

### Background

XML has a concept of "attributes with a namespace" and "attributes with no namespace" - **not** a default namespace, literally "no namespace". 

```xml
Examples of "attributes with no namespace"
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block">
<m:math xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block">

Example of "attributes with a namespace" - requires a prefix on the attribute. 
<m:math xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" m:display="block">
```

PDF 2.0 does not have this concept; every attribute is assigned to a namespace owner.

In https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/286 this was discussed and it was agreed that PDF namespaces and XML namespaces are different - we added this note:

> NOTE The attribute owner, defined through the O and NS entries in the attribute object, define an owner for each attribute, but do not provide information on transformation of those attributes into other formats. When considering formats such as HTML and MathML, attributes would be transformed to meet the syntactic requirements of those formats.


### Proposal

I'm essentially suggesting that we revisit the resolution from https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/286, and extend that note, or add another.

Conversion between XML and the PDF Structure Tree happens. The note is telling people not to make any assumptions about how to process namespaces when doing this - that's OK, but is still avoiding the problem of what people are expected to do when converting between these two formats. It's not specifically a MathML issue, but it's the most obvious namespace where this applies.

Fortunately @davidcarlisle proposed what I think is a rather elegant solution in the 2025-03-06 PDF/UA TWG meeting, specifically:

> if a PDF attribute has the same *namespace object* as the element it's attached to, treat the attribute as having "no namespace" when converting to XML. Otherwise, treat the attribute as being in that namespace when converting to XML.

This is very neat because it solves the ambiguity described in https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/286 but requires no changes to the PDF spec - it's just a guidance for PDF processors. But it's not documented anywhere in the PDF spec, and I really think that needs to change (although I believe it might be part of an upcoming LaTeX best-practice guide).

The consequences if we don't do this is that anyone extracting MathML *from PDF to XML* will quite possibly generate incorrect MathML. The same statement applies to HTML and any other content originating from an XML syntax that we might reasonably expect to see stored in PDF.

The only other way around this is namespace-specific knowledge, which I don't think is reasonable. If someone adds some ChemML content to a PDF, I shouldn't have to know ChemML to correctly namespace the attributes when deriving XML. This is _not_ a problem when deriving HTML, but only because HTML _does_ have this namespace-specific knowledge - and HTML is limited to MathML, SVG and HTML.

### Proposed Action

The addition of another note, or an addendum to the existing note, reading something like this:

> PDF processors extracting attributes to XML may consider attributes with an identical NS entry to the structure element to be attributes without a namespace, and attributes with a different NS entry to be attributes in the specified namespace.

I have made this as non-normative as I can; it's guidance, nothing more. Wordsmithing, I'm not sure if "attributes without a namespace" would be better phrased as "attributes in the empty namespace" - the former is a bit closer to the W3C spec language, the latter is pretty common too.
title: Consider a recommendation for how to resolve ambiguity converting a Structure Tree to XML

body:
1.Use of “can contain” instead of “may contain”.
In the context of ISO-style wording, “may” is typically used to express permission or an optional possibility, while “can” is more about capability.
Here, the sentence:
**The PDF dictionaries can contain a Type entry with the value Halftone …**
is describing what is allowed in the PDF dictionaries, so “may contain” is more appropriate and consistent with the normative style used elsewhere in the specification.

2.“with the following exceptions:” is followed by prose instead of a clear list.
After: … with the following exceptions:
there are actually two distinct exceptions:

- the optional Type entry with value Halftone
- the representation of spot/transfer functions and threshold arrays
However, they are written as continuous prose without any bullets or clear separation. This makes the “exceptions” harder to scan and less readable, especially for implementers who are comparing with the PostScript halftone dictionaries.

3.Two different exceptions are compressed into one long line.
In:
**Spot functions and transfer functions are represented by function objects instead of PostScript language procedures. Threshold arrays are specified as streams instead of files.**
two separate constraints are placed in a single run-on sentence. For clarity and consistency with the “following exceptions” lead-in, it would be preferable to split them into separate bullet points.

Proposed revised NOTE 1:

NOTE 1 The dictionaries representing these halftone types contain the same entries as the corresponding PostScript language halftone dictionaries (as described in clause 7.4 of the PostScript Language Reference, Third Edition), with the following exceptions:

-  The PDF dictionaries may contain a Type entry with the value Halftone, identifying the type of PDF object that the dictionary describes.
-  Spot functions and transfer functions are represented by function objects instead of PostScript language procedures.
-  Threshold arrays are specified as streams instead of files.
title: Suggestion to improve wording and structure of NOTE 1 in 10.6.5.1 General

* Changing the Document: not allowed

body:
I do not understand some of the wording used in this paragraph and would be grateful for confirmation or correction of my interpretation and its implications, particularly since I find it hard to believe that they reflect the intention of the standard.

"A field dictionary that does not have a partial field name of its own shall not be considered a field but simply a Widget annotation"

Let's call such dictionaries Representations for clarity. I am not clear on the phrase "to be considered", but my interpretation is that the term "field" as used in the standard excludes Representations, and the term "widget annotation" and by extension "annotation" includes Representations.

Representations "should differ only in properties that specify their visual appearance"

My interpretation of this is that, while not recommended, Representations are allowed to differ in other properties, such as those that affect the permitted values of the underlying field (which sounds odd).

"actual field dictionaries with the same fully qualified field name shall have the same field type ..."

I have no idea what "actual field dictionaries" or "non-actual field dictionaries" (which must exist by implication unless the "actual" is pure literary flourish) are supposed to be.

Absence of 1.7 statement "It is possible for different field dictionaries to have the same fully qualified field name if they are descendants of a common ancestor with that name and have no partial field names (T entries) of their own."

My interpretation is that the implied requirement in earlier versions of the standard that field dictionaries with T entries have unique fully qualified names no longer exists.

Some of the implications of the new wording as I see it are:

- 12.7.2 para 1: "A field that has children that are fields is called a non-terminal field". As Representations are not fields, they are no longer terminal fields. 

- 12.7.2 para 2: "when a field has only a  single associated widget annotation, the contents of the field dictionary and the annotation dictionary may be merged ...".  As Representations are not fields, this merging is no longer allowed for Representations. This seems to imply  that many pre-1.7 files containing forms are now non-conforming. 

- Table 226 Kids entry: The definition is incomplete since it is silent with regards to Representations.

- Table 228 entries are no longer allowed in Representations.

- Table 191 : The Parent entry can no longer contain a reference to a Representation, as a Representation is no longer a field.

- Table 31 Annots entry: Representations are now permitted to be included in the Annots array of a page object, despite lacking all the entries required of annotation dictionaries.
title: Clarification of section 12.7.4.2 Field Names paragraph 3

**Describe the bug**
Section 8.2.5.29.2, "Non-mathematical scientific formulae" differentiates non-mathematical formulae from mathematical formulae, but the mechanism added in PDF 2.0 to define Math is now extensible beyond classical mathematics (e.g. Chemistry can be presented using MathML).

We say that:

> Non-mathematical scientific formulae shall be enclosed within Formula structure elements and shall have either an Alt entry or an ActualText entry in its structure element dictionary.

This mandate that non-mathematical shall (in UA and the Accessibility Conformance level for WTPDF) have Alt and ActualText can cause poor behaviors in processors that could consume the MathML for non-Math use cases.

We should consider updating UA and WTPDF to have a broader understanding of what is supported in the "Math" use cases and what it means to be non-mathematical.

[Issue 711](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/711) describes the limitations of the current WTPDF and PDF/UA in regards to non-mathematical formula.  It is focused on addressing cases where MathML can solve non-Math use cases and recommends that we re-define the non-Math term.

However, that works because PDF 2.0 recognizes the MathML namespace and explicitly permitted.  PDF 2.0 does not limit the use of MathML to a specific use case, just provides the namespace mechanism. 

This issue is to discuss how we can solve beyond the cases where MathML support a given use case and bring in broader industry-standard namespaces to support addition uses cases (e.g. Music).

Describe the bug Clause: 14.8.3 — Basic layout model Sub-clause: 14.8.3.3 — Progression direction Paragraph: First paragraph

The paragraph links block-progression direction and inline-progression direction to the writing system in use via the WritingMode structure attribute. However, the current wording is ambiguous for right-to-left (RTL) scripts such as Arabic, Persian (Farsi), Urdu, and other RTL languages.

In practice, many PDF creation tools—including Microsoft Word exported via “Save as PDF” and Adobe Acrobat—do not correctly apply RTL semantics even when the document language is explicitly set to Arabic and the layout direction is set to right-to-left from Word’s Layout tab before exporting. The resulting PDFs frequently contain: •	visual glyph painting in left-to-right order using Tj / TJ operators
	•	inconsistent or missing WritingMode •	mismatches between visual order and logical reading order
	•	reversed inline progression for screen readers
	•	broken reflow and extraction This ambiguity leads to inconsistent processor behavior and severe accessibility failures for blind users relying on screen readers. ￼ Recommendation for correction 1. Clarify how inline-progression and block-progression directions must be interpreted for RTL scripts when:
	• WritingMode is present
	• WritingMode is absent
	• WritingMode is ignored by processors
	•	text is painted visually in LTR order 2. Provide a normative example for an Arabic or Persian paragraph showing correct tagging, WritingMode , and intended progression directions. 3. Specify mandatory fallback behavior when structural semantics and painting instructions conflict. 4. Add explicit PDF/UA conformance requirements ensuring alignment between logical order, progression direction, screen reader order, and reflow. ￼ Additional context Tested using Microsoft Word + Adobe Acrobat, with: •	Document language set to Arabic
	•	Layout direction set to right-to-left Despite this, exported PDFs still contained incorrect logical order and reversed reading progression for RTL scripts such as Arabic.
Thank you for your efforts
title: Issue with RTL language iso 32000 -2 2020

body:
**Affected specification area**
ISO 32000-2:2020 — Content representation and annotations (general limitation, not confined to a single clause)

**Description of the issue**
PDF documents frequently contain internet-related information such as domain names, URLs, and email addresses directly embedded in text content (e.g. “wikipedia.org”, “https://example.com”, “contact@example.com”).

In the current PDF specification, such internet-related information is treated as ordinary text unless it is explicitly converted into link annotations. As a result, internet-related entities that are visually obvious to human readers are not represented as structured, machine-readable content objects.

This creates a structural limitation: PDF documents that are widely distributed via the internet are not “internet-aware” at the content level. Internet-related references remain semantically invisible, difficult to extract reliably, and indistinguishable from arbitrary text strings without heuristic analysis.

**Why this is problematic**
- Domain names, URLs, and email addresses embedded in content cannot be reliably identified or extracted without heuristics (e.g. regex, layout analysis)
- Semantic interpretation of internet-related content is not possible
- Hyperlinks are tightly coupled to annotations rather than content meaning
- Automated processing, compliance checks, digital preservation, and AI-based analysis are negatively affected

**Recommendation for correction**
Clarify or extend the content model to allow internet-related entities (such as domain names, URLs, and email addresses) to be explicitly represented as identifiable, machine-readable content elements, independently of annotations.

This does not require defining interaction behavior (e.g. clickable links), but rather enabling structured recognition of internet-related content within the document model.
title: Lack of Internet-Aware Content Representation in PDF

> The specified font value shall match a resource name in the Font entry of the default resource dictionary (referenced from the DR entry of the interactive form dictionary; see "Table 224 — Entries in the interactive form dictionary").

Section 12.5.6.9 (Polygon and polyline annotations) of the PDF-2.0 specification describes the **Vertices** field in the annotation dictionary as follows (as "fixed" in #444, see also [here](https://pdf-issues.pdfa.org/32000-2-2020/clause12.html#H12.5.6.9)):

> (Required) Shall be ignored if Path is present.  An array of numbers specifying the alternating horizontal and vertical coordinates, respectively, of each vertex, in default user space.

It also defines **Path** (also "fixed" in #444):

>  (Optional; PDF 2.0) An array of n arrays, each supplying the operands for a path building operator (m, l or c).
> If this key is present the Vertices key shall be ignored.
> Each of the n arrays shall contain pairs of values specifying the points (x and y values) for a path drawing operation.  The first array shall be of length 2 and specifies the operand of a moveto operator which establishes a current point.  Subsequent arrays of length 2 specify the operands of lineto operators. Arrays of length 6 specify the operands for curveto operators.  Each array is processed in sequence to construct the path.  The current graphics state shall control the path width, dash pattern, etc.

I believe that this is a mistake in the spec (and in particular in the way #444 was resolved), and that **Path** should be fixed or removed.

(I'm putting this out for Polygon annotation, but very similar arguments may apply to the other annotation types which define **Path** fields.)

Here are the reasons why I think that the current spec is wrong here:

1. I have not found a single PDF viewer which implements the behaviour described in the current spec: The test file [test.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25420165/test.pdf) (human-readable) shows two gray squares in the background, and a polygon annotation drawing a slightly smaller blue square.  I've adjusted **Vertices** to describe a square inside the left background square, and **Path** to describe a square inside the right background square.  Most viewers show a blue square on the left (Acrobat Reader, GhostScript, Firefox, ...), others show nothing at all.  I have not found a single reader which places the blue square on the right.

2. In another issue, @lrosenthol [seemed to indicate](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/445#issuecomment-2843019609) that **Path** is intended for handling click testing, not appearance.

3. The statement "The current graphics state shall control the path width, dash pattern, etc." does not make sense, see #607 .

4. The statement "Arrays of length 6 specify the operands for curveto operators" is also suspicious: "polygons" should not be allowed to have curved outlines.  If curves were intended, why not just introduce a generic path annotation?

5. The timing is also suspicious: **Path** was introduced in PDF 2.0, which is the same version that made its rendering information redundant by requiring appearance streams.
title: Path field in Polygon annotations

The discussion of https://github.com/pdf-association/crypto-provenance-twg/issues/14 in the previous PDF TWG meeting came to the conclusion that there is an apparent need to clarify that comments are not allowed in hex strings.

This can be implemented by adding a NOTE to section 7.3.4.3 "Hexadecimal strings" like this

> NOTE: Allowing white-space characters in a hexadecimal string does not imply that comments are allowed, too. Comments are only defined outside strings, see section 7.2.4 "Comments".

(But see #273 for more need of clarification of comment usage.)

-----

There is no need, though, to forbid white spaces in hex strings, not even in the special hex strings carrying signature containers. Because the size of signature containers often cannot be known before actual signature creation, these hex strings usually do have some excess space. Whether this excess space is filled with white spaces or with trailing zeroes, does not make a difference here.

For adbe.pkcs7.* signatures ISO 32000-2 section 12.8.3.3.1 says «Since the length of CMS objects is not entirely predictable, the value of **Contents** shall be padded with zeros at the end of the string (before the ">" delimiter) before writing the CMS to the allocated space in the PDF file.» But this requirement is given specifically for those signatures, not generally.
title: Clarify comment usage in hex strings

body:
ISO32000-2 Table 49 defines properties for developer extension dictionaries, intended to document extensions to PDF. The key is a prefix (eg `ADBE` and `ISO_`, two examples that have defined extensions) and the value is a dictionary as defined in this table:

|Key|Type|Value
|---|--|--
|Type|name|optional ... shall be DeveloperExtensions
|BaseVersion|name|required ... the name of the PDF version to which this extension applies (eg `/2.0`)
|ExtensionLevel|integer|required ... an integer defined by the developer to denote the extension being used. 
|URL|string|optional ... a URL that refers to documentation for this extension
|ExtensionRevision|text string|optional ... additional revision information on the extension

This assumes the extension registrar uses a numbering system (like ADBE, where extension level is "3", or like ISO, where `ExtensionLevel` might be "32002"). <strike>The next section 7.12.5 further defines `ExtensionLevel` to say it **shall** be be "ordered ... monotonically increasing sequence over time", which is clearly an unnecessary and unenforceable claim - one that already doesn't apply to either ISO or Adobe!</strike>

I don't think the PDF Association, or anyone else that might define a developer extension, should be required to use a <strike>monotically increasing</strike> numeric system to manage extensions to PDF. We have URL/URI/URNs for this purpose.

So my suggestion would be:

1. Change `ExtensionLevel` from "Required" to "Optional" - or if that's too much, "Required if prefix is ISO_ or ADBE, optional otherwise"
2. Change `URL` from "Optional" to "Optional if ExtensionLevel is set, required otherwise", and change the definition to "a URL that refers to _the definition_ for this extension".
3. <strike>Delete everything after the the first sentence in 7.12.5</strike>
4. Change 7.12.6 from "a URL to the documentation that is provided" to "a URL for the definition"

This gives extension registrars the option of using a number-based system like ISO, or a URL-based system. 

Alternatively we could redefine `ExtensionLevel` to be "number, name or string" to let it take a URL, but this feels like more of a breaking change for any API that processes developer extensions.


----

Second aspect: Extension Dictionaries that define new compression schemes (eg Brotli) run the risk of being not found if they stored in an ObjectStream that is compressed with the new compression scheme. As with https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/110, we could cover this situation with an advisory note after Table 14 saying that a developer extensions defining such an extension **should** not be stored in Object Streams. For sake of argument:

> Note: as Developer Extension dictionaries define new capabilities in PDF, care must be taken to ensure they are accessible for PDF processors unaware of those capabilities. An example would be ensuring that a Developer Extension defining a new compression algorithm is not stored in an object stream compressed with that algorithm.

----

The third and final part of this is that if the Extension Dictionary defines a new encryption scheme, the URL defining the extension would itself be encrypted. Proposed solution for this is that we change the type of URL from `string` to `name or string`, as we do in (eg) Tables 151 and 400.

----
EDIT: as Michael noted below, the monotonic requirement has already been revised - I have struck out the aspects relating to that.
title: Developer Extensions Dictionary is too prescriptive

We generate a PDF and apply a certification signature (our organization’s certificate). This certification signature is PAdES Baseline-B and sets DocMDP permissions to level 2 (P2) so that an end user can sign afterward.

**Question**
Is there a standard / interoperable way to require that a signature added under DocMDP P2 is invisible only, while still allowing a valid PAdES B-LT signature? If this is not possible, could someone explain why (at the PDF/standard level) and what the intended model is?

body: This is a proposed addition to PDF to solve a problem that has come from working on EA-PDF, specifically EA-PDF _collections_. These are a stored as a single PDF Portfolio containing multiple PDF attachments, one attachment per email. When displaying a PDF Portfolio in a PDF viewer, a collections-aware PDF viewer will rely on the data structures in ISO32000 12.3.5 to present the attachments - this describes how properties within a _collection item dictionary_ on each Embedded File can be used to create an index. It works well - as well as the EA-PDF spec there is an example in ISO32000 at the end of 12.3.5 showing how various columns relating to email might be defined. Here's how it looks in Acrobat So far, so good. The problem is that email is threaded, and while we can display columns for subject, data, sender etc, what we can't do is display any sort of hierarchy in that top section, which I'll call the _collection navigator_ pane. This turns out to be fairly critical for several reasons. 1. Email is threaded - of course - and the subject often changes with a "Re:" before replies, so sorting by subject is no substitute. 2. The alternative is creating a threaded index in the container PDF - you can see that's what we've done in PDF we're displaying, above. The problem is the index can be _huge_ - the PDF I showed has 65,000 email attachments and the index itself was 2,500 pages, all of it reproducing information that could easily be derived. The other problem with an index in the container PDF is - it's fixed. Adding to the collection means recreating the index. **This is nothing to do with Collection _Folders_** - those are a way of organising attachments into folders, but a folder is not itself an attachment. So there is no solution to be found there. To illustrate, what I'm suggesting is that we're able to display something like this mockup in the collection navigator To enable this I'd like to propose a new addition to ISO32000-2 Table 155, which defines the columns that are displayed in the collection navigator. The type of each column is defined with the `Subtype` field in that table, which can currently be text, dates, numbers etc. I'm proposing a new value for `Subtype`, something like `Tree`, where the value of the item in the Embedded File's _collection item dictionary_ is an object-reference to another Embedded File that is considered to be the "parent" of this Embedded File. Reasons for suggesting this approach 1. There's nothing EA-PDF specific about it - it's a general solution. 2. It allows for multiple different hierarchies - no need for this with email, but there might be for other collection types. 3. It doen't interfere with Collection folders. 4. It's fairly backwards compatible: any viewer that doesn't recognise the new Column subtype would just ignore it. 5. There is only one source of truth: if we only store a "Parent" and not an array of "Kids", there is no way for an item to be in a hierarchy more than once. The tree would be constructed and the children of any node sorted based on the secondary column, i.e. date, sender etc. That's my pitch. If there's interest I'd be happy to formalize this proposal - as an extension to PDF with a PDF declaration? Or some other way?
title: Extend Document Collection Schema to support hierarchical structures.

body:
## Kerning
The current definition for `/ReversedChars` says that the intent is to mark a "show string" of text as reversed, and that "If the sequence encompasses multiple show strings, only the individual characters within each string shall be reversed."

It demonstrates this with an example

```
/ReversedChars
BMC
( olleH) Tj
-200 0 Td
( .dlrow) Tj
EMC

represents the text "Hello world"
```

OK, fine - but if we introduce kerning, what does this represent?

```
/ReversedChars
BMC
( olleH) Tj
-200 0 Td
[( .dlr) -30 (ow)] TJ
EMC
```

It's either "Hello World" or "Hello rld.wo", depending on whether "show string" means a single string, or the concatenation of all the individual strings passed to a single text show operator. There is a definition at the end of 9.2.1:

> A content stream paints glyphs on the page by specifying a font dictionary and a string object that shall be interpreted as a sequence of one or more character codes identifying glyphs in the font. This operation is called showing the text string; the text strings drawn in this way are called _show strings_.

But it doesn't mention the TJ operator, and the term "show string" is only ever used in the context of the /ReversedChars - it's not mentioned in the definitions of the TJ and Tj operators.

I would strongly suggest that a "show string" is defined as the concatenation of all strings passed to an individual text-showing operator - or kerning in arabic and hebrew is going to get a lot more complicated. And not just kerning - this also applies to...

## Non-spacing marks
The spec also doesn't address how non-spacing marks are handled, eg arabic vowel markers. All the PDF creators I have tested that emit R2L content in reverse order, are emitting the base glyph first followed by any non-spacing marks. This is the order the glyphs are emitted from the OpenType layout algorithm (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/typography/script-development/arabic), so that's to be expected.

However the simplistic examples (shown above) don't address non-spacing marks - we're told that "In order for such text to be extracted or read out aloud, the sequence of the characters as found in the show string operator shall be reversed before using them."

If we naively reverse a sequence containing non-spacing marks that follow the base glyph, they will be moved to before the base glyph and the output will be incorrect. So we need to change something. Either:

1. "character" is defined to be a sequence of a base glyph plus one or more non-spacing marks, so marks always follow a base glyph even if the string is reversed.
2. a note is added that any show-strings must be edited so non-spacing marks are moved before the base glyph.

I'm not a big fan of option two; it requires a non-obvious and slighty weird post-processing step for text layout which is certainly not in any PDF layout engine today, and the PDF spec says the intent of showing text left-to-right is to avoid the need for "tedious and costly" processing. I think it makes a lot more sense to make this a processing requirement for anyone reversing the text, rather than a creation requirement.

---
Related issue: https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/718
title: /ReversedChars, kerning and non-spacing marks in RTL languages.

**Describe the bug**

**Clause/section number: 1**4.3.1, first bulleted item

The text in 14.3.1 appears to use inconsistent terminology.

The introductory paragraph of 14.3.1 defines two concepts:

**document metadata:** general information about the document, such as title, author, and creation/modification dates
**object-level metadata**: metadata associated with individual objects in a document

However, in the first bulleted item, the text says:

“For document data and for object-level metadata: In a metadata stream (PDF 1.4) associated with the document or a component of the document ...”

The use of document data here appears inconsistent with the terminology established immediately above. Since this subclause is specifically describing how metadata can be stored, and since the second bullet says “For document metadata only…”, the phrase document data is likely incorrect and may have been intended to be document metadata.

As written, “document data” may be interpreted more broadly as document content or general document data, which does not seem to match the scope of this subclause.

Recommendation for correction:

Revise the first bulleted item from:

“For **document data** and for object-level metadata: ...”

to:

“For **document metadata** and for object-level metadata: ...”

This would make the terminology consistent with the definitions in 14.3.1 and with the second bulleted item.
title: Possible terminology inconsistency in ISO 32000-2, 14.3.1 “General” — “document data” may need to be “document metadata”

**Describe the bug**
The ISO 32000-2:2020 spec indicates in "12.5.6.10 Text markup annotations" table 182, that the QuadPoints entry should specify the points in this order:

> The coordinates for each quadrilateral shall be given in the order: 𝑥1 𝑦1 𝑥2 𝑦2 𝑥3 𝑦3 𝑥4 𝑦4

But, the correct order used by Adobe and pretty much everybody else is:

x4 y4 x3 y3 x1 y1 x2 y2

It seems the industry has reached a consensus that the QuadPoints should written two lines. First you write the line above the text and followed by line below the text. Also, this assumes the text is left-to-right. The order is not very important for highlight (any order will be acceptable in this case). But it is very important for underline. So, point order is top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right

Especially, since the text could be rotated 180 degrees, and in that case, the underline would have to be drawn ABOVE the text. See the attached ABC-underline.pdf

[ABC-underline.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26945175/ABC-underline.pdf)

**Additional context**
Add any other context about the problem here, including sample PDF files.

Clause 2, Normative references, cites:

INCITS 4-1986 (R2017), Information Systems — Coded Character Sets — 7-Bit Standard Code for Information Interchange (7-Bit ASCII).

We are preparing a Chinese national adoption of ISO 32000-2:2020. During the national review process, a reviewer suggested replacing or supplementing this reference with the Chinese national standard GB/T 1988—1998, Information technology — 7-bit coded character set for information interchange.

However, GB/T 1988—1998 is based on ISO/IEC 646:1991, while ISO 32000-2:2020 cites INCITS 4-1986 (R2017), not ISO/IEC 646:1991.

Our understanding is that ISO/IEC 646:1991 and INCITS 4-1986 are closely related, and that the International Reference Version of ISO/IEC 646 is aligned with US-ASCII. However, ISO/IEC 646 also allows national versions and application-oriented versions, while INCITS 4-1986 appears to identify the fixed 7-Bit ASCII character set.

Since PDF syntax relies on fixed ASCII characters and their code values, we would like to confirm whether the reference to INCITS 4-1986 (R2017) was intentional.

Could you please advise whether, for a national adoption of ISO 32000-2:2020, the normative reference to INCITS 4-1986 (R2017) should be retained as-is?

In particular, would replacing INCITS 4-1986 (R2017) with ISO/IEC 646:1991, or with a national standard based on ISO/IEC 646:1991, be considered technically equivalent for the purposes of ISO 32000-2:2020?

If the reference to INCITS 4-1986 (R2017) is intended to specifically identify fixed 7-Bit ASCII as used by PDF syntax, we plan to retain the original reference and explain the relationship with GB/T 1988—1998 only in the national drafting explanation.

In some cases, ISO 32000-2:2020 requires text strings to be compared for equality. For instance, when signing a signature field that has a signature field lock dictionary with Action being Include or Exclude, field names (which are text strings) need to be compared for equality.

Unfortunately, ISO 32000-2:2020 does not specify how to compare text strings. J.3.3 only states the obvious and does not mention text strings.

Example: Which of these **text** strings shall compare equal?
`<41>`
`<fe ff 00 41>`
`<fe ff 00 1b 65 6e 00 1b 00 41>`
`<ef bb bf 41>`
`<ef bb bf 1b 65 6E 1b 41>`
`<ef bb bf 1b 6d 65 1b 41>`

They all contain just one letter, A, therefore this example does not even involve Unicode normalization.

I guess most implementation will convert to some Unicode representation before comparing, probably some or all of them without Unicode normalization. Some of them remove language escape sequences, others probably don't.

A document might use inconsistent encodings for text strings if it has been manipulated by different PDF implementations. For instance, a PDF library may encode field names as UTF-16 in its API (Java!) and use PDFDocEncoding when writing to the document strings that can be encoded with PDFDocEncoding. If an application uses such a library to retrieve a field name from the document and then passes that field name as-is to an API that adds a field to the Fields entry of a signature field lock dictionary, a field name that is encoded with UTF-16BE in the field dictionary will be encoded with PDFDocEncoding in the signature field lock dictionary. Some libraries remove language escape sequences before passing text strings to the application. In that case (using the same application), the field name may have a language escape sequence in the field dictionary, but not in the signature field lock dictionary.

ISO 32000-2:2020 should specify how to compare text strings for equality.
title: ISO 32000-2:2020 does not specify how to compare text strings

While experimenting with Adobe Acrobat for https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/757, I noticed that if a PDF document has a root field named "a" that just contains a T entry and a Kids entry (in particular, no Ff entry) which defines terminal fields "a.b" and "a.c" and the siganture field lock dictionary of a signature field specifies just field "a" to be locked, Adobe Acrobat will lock both "a.b" and "a.c" by setting the ReadOnly bit in their Ff entry.

If listing a non-terminal field in the Fields array of a signature field lock dictionary really is supposed to include or exclude (depending on the Action entry) all or just immediate children of that field, that requirement should be specified explicitly in ISO 32000-2:2020. Currently, it only specifies this in Table 236:

`Fields   An array of text strings containing field names.`

Which is a bit sparse. It even does not specify that those field names are fully qualified field names, but for Adobe Acrobat, they are: In the example above, "b" does not lock "a.b".

BTW, only "partial field name" and "fully qualified field name" are defined by ISO 32000-2:2020, "field name" seems not to be defined.

BTW, 12.7.5.5 does not specify what mechanism shall be used to prevent changing the value of the fields.
title: Non-terminal fields in Fields array of signature field lock dictionary, field names vs fully qualified field names

> The comment consists of all characters after the PERCENT
SIGN and up to but not including **the end-of-the-line marker.**

`end-of-the-line marker` is not mentioned further in the document, but is usually referred to as `end-of-line (EOL) marker`. Notice the missing `-the` in the definition.

```diff
The comment consists of all characters after the PERCENT
-SIGN and up to but not including **the end-of-the-line marker.**
+SIGN and up to but not including **the end-of-line (EOL) marker.**
+(See 7.2.3, "Character Set")

body:
Table 237 does not specify what mechanism shall be used for locking the document if LockDocument in the signature field seed value dictionary is set to /true. Also, "lock the document" is nowhere defined, as far as I can tell.

Obviously, a PDF processor cannot use the LockDocument entry of a signed signature field to find out whether the document is locked or not because it does not know whether the user has overridden LockDocument if LockDocument is /auto and LockDocument is not a required constraint. (Assuming the signing software did not change LockDocument from /auto to /false or /true depending on the user's choice. Note that modifying LockDocument might invalidate existing signatures as there's no specification of what changes are allowed after signing.)

Probably, DocMDP with P=1 is what is intended. But then, LockDocument would overlap with the MDP entry and a new problem arises: If LockDocument is /false or the user overrides /auto (which is the default value), will the P value in the MDP entry be overridden by LockDocument with 0?

Does LockDocument being /true (or the user choosing to lock the document for /auto) override the P value in the MDP entry with 1? This won't work if there is already a signature because this would create a certification signature and a certification signature must be the first signature.

Or does DocMDP override LockDocument? In what way?

Is updating the DSS and adding document timestamps allowed for documents locked due to LockDocument? Despite 12.8.5.3, some software (e.g., Adobe Acrobat when I last tried that) does not allow updating the DSS and adding DTS for DocMDP with P=1!

Has anyone actually implemented LockDocument? I don't think any two developers will come up with compatible implementations for the current specification of LockDocument.

In short: the documentation of LockDocument should specify how to lock the document.
title: Mechanism to be used for LockDocument in signature field seed value dictionary

A well-known implementation creates redaction annotations with `/QuadPoints []`.

Now, the standard appears to allow this: 

"An array of 8 × 𝑛 numbers specifying the coordinates
of n quadrilaterals in default user space that comprise the region in which
the link should be activated. The coordinates for each quadrilateral are
given in the order:

𝑥1 𝑦1 𝑥2 𝑦2 𝑥3 𝑦3 𝑥4 𝑦4

specifying the four vertices of the quadrilateral in counterclockwise order.
For orientation purposes, such as when applying an underline border
style, the bottom of a quadrilateral is the line formed by (x1, y1) and (x2, y2).

If this entry is not present, or the PDF processor does not recognise it, or if
any coordinates in the QuadPoints array lie outside the region specified
by Rect then the activation region for the link annotation shall be defined
by its Rect entry."

I'd suggest we say `n` cannot be zero. Using `/QuadPoints []` as a sort of null value seems like a poor idea.

Example file:

[redaction_annotation_unapplied.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28651311/redaction_annotation_unapplied.pdf)

body: Overprint was introduced in PDF 1.2. The mechanism has not changed since then and is in the PDF Spec still specified in "8.6.7 Overprint control". Note that transparency settings do not have an impact on the result of overprinting. Then transparency was introduced and with it a chapter that explains how to implement overprinting in the transparent imaging model. This is specified in "11.7.4.3 Compatibility with opaque overprinting". The problem or oversight is that when implementing 11.7.4.3 overprinting cannot happen for objects that are in an isolated transparency group with objects outside of that group. That is not mentioned at all in 8.6.7 nor does 11.7.4.3 say anything about this difference. I think that change was never anticpated. Overprinting is an important ingredient to printing. Specifically you do not want to knock out any background behind black objects. This now becomes an issue since the very widely used cloud based layout platform, Canva, introduces lots of isolated transparency groups into their PDFs so that all black objects will always knockout. We have tested all widely used output engines, apparently all have implemented overprinting based on 11.7.4.3 Attached are two simple PDFs, one with an isolated transparency group, one without. The screenshot demonstrates the difference in Acrobat, Output Preview with Black off. I can see three possible solutions: - Ideally the Spec would be changed so that isolated transparency groups would have no impact on overprinting. I think this change in overprint behavior was never intended nor foreseen. Unfortunately that would mean that all output engines would have to be changed. - If we do not want to go that far there should be some clarification that establishes this as the normative algorithm. - At least should there be some information that whether or not transparency group isolation settings have an impact on overprint is implementation specific. [Black in Transparency Group Isolated.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28750460/Black.in.Transparency.Group.Isolated.pdf) [Black in Transparency Group not Isolated.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28750461/Black.in.Transparency.Group.not.Isolated.pdf)
title: Result of overprint is different if implemented based on 8.6.7 or 11.7.4.3

body:
Table 236 of ISO 32000-2:2020 says this about the P entry of the signature lock dictionary:

```
  If MDP permission is already in effect from an earlier incremental save
  section or the original part of the document, the number shall specify
  permissions less than or equal to the permissions already in effect based
  on signatures earlier in the document. That is, permissions can be denied
  but not added. If the number specifies greater permissions than an MDP
  value already in effect, the new number is ignored.
```
But it does not say that the P entry defines an MDP permission, so this text may or may not apply to the P entry in the signature lock dictionary. This is the only instance of "MDP permission" in ISO 32000-2:2020, that is, "MDP permission" is not defined!

Let's assume the P entry in the signature lock dictionary **does** provide "MDP permission". Then, suppose we do this to a document:

- add a signature field S1
- sign field S1 (approval signature)
- add a signature field S2 with P=2 in the signature lock dictionary
- sign field S2 (approval signature)
- clear the signature S2 (by removing the V entry) -- we need to save incrementally due to S1
- change P in the signature lock dictionary of S2 from 2 to 3
- sign field S2 (approval signature)
- add an annotation

Now, is signature S2 valid or not? According to Table 236, P=2 is still in effect as it affects "any incremental changes to the document following the signature of which this key is part" and it overrides P=3 (because 2 is less than 3), so signature S2 is now invalid. I found no software that actually implements signature validation this way.

The document still contains some incremental updates where S2 is signed with P=2. Probably that value of P is intended to apply only to those incremental updates where that **signature** (ie, instance of the V entry) is still active, not to any/all incremental updates that have S2 signed (possibly with a different V entry). But I don't think this conclusion cannot be drawn from the current wording.
title: P in the signature lock dictionary, MDP permission, and cleared signatures

body: **Additional context** This is written against the PRC ISO standard 14739-1, First edition, dated 2014‐12‐15. **Describe the bug** Trying to understand how to parse the `CompressedKnot` structure. The 2014 spec says about `CompressedKnot.knot`: _"The `DoubleWithVariableBitNumber` is written using `tolerance_parameter` and `number_bit_parameter + 1`"_ also _"The format of the data is either `Double` or `DoubleWithVariableBitNumber` in the file depending upon the Boolean test (`number_bit_parameter > 30`)"_. According to https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/706 "uBitNumber shall be less than 31 (see §9.14 constraint)" for a `DoubleWithVariableBitNumber`. Now assuming `number_bit_parameter==30`, the `DoubleWithVariableBitNumber` encoding is selected for `CompressedKnot.knot` with 31 (`number_bit_parameter + 1`) bits. This contradicts with _"uBitNumber shall be less than 31 (see §9.14 constraint)" for a `DoubleWithVariableBitNumber`_. PS.: Note, the same logic pattern appears for the number of bits allocated to `CompressedWeights.compressed_weights`.
title: PRC: CompressedKnot

Table 236 of ISO 32000-2:2020 for P=1: No changes to the document are permitted; any change to the document shall invalidate the signature.

Period. No exceptions.

Table 257 of ISO 32000-2:2020 for P=1: No changes to the document shall be permitted; any change to the document shall invalidate the signature.

Period. No exceptions.

12.8.5.3 of ISO 32000-2:2020: When evaluating the DocMDP restrictions (see 12.8.2.2, "DocMDP") the presence of a document timestamp and/or DSS information shall be ignored.

Two problems:

12.8.5.3 contradicts Table 257. Perhaps Table 257 should reference 12.8.5.3.

12.8.5.3 does not say that the P entry of Table 236 in 12.7.5.5 shall be ignored! Table 236 is about "MDP permissions" (whatever that is), not DocMDP.

Unfortunately, Adobe Acrobat resolves that contradiction in favor of Table 236 and Table 257, making LTA/LTV signatures impossible for both types of P=1.
title: Do DSS and TDS invalidate signatures with P=1?

# PRC: WriteDouble's back-reference shortcut has an interoperability hazard worth a NOTE (§9.19)

**Section:** §9.19 "Procedure for WriteDouble"
(`iso-prc/sections/09-io-algorithms.adoc:243`, listing at `iso-prc/code/write_double_procedure.cpp`).

**Change type:** Informative addition. **This is not a defect in the specification** — the listing is
self-consistent. It is a hazard the text does not warn about, and which cost us a month to find.

**Verified against:** the working source at `pdf-association/3dpdf-twg`, `main` @ `ba2bdc1`
(2 September 2026). No NOTE of this kind is present.

---

## The mechanism

`write_double_procedure.cpp` emits the mantissa bytes with a back-reference shortcut. For each byte
after the first, it searches the bytes already emitted for an identical value:

```c
if(pb!=pbStart &&
  (pbResult=SEARCHBYTE(BEFOREBYTE(pb),*pb,DIFFPOINTERS(pb,pbStart)))!=NULL)
{
  write_bits(0,1);                            /* back-reference */
  write_bits(DIFFPOINTERS(pb,pbResult),3);    /* distance */
}
else
{
  write_bits(1,1);                            /* literal */
  write_bits(*pb,8);
}
```

A distance of 1 — "repeat the immediately preceding byte" — is reachable and legal by this listing.

## The hazard

**A distance-1 back-reference is mishandled by Adobe Acrobat.** Files carrying it load with an empty
model tree and empty canvas, with no error message, while the same geometry written with the byte
emitted literally loads and displays correctly.

### How we established it

This was not inferred from symptoms. The failing case was a real file (a turbine tessellation,
26,540 and 8,868 triangles) that opened correctly in one third-party reader and blank in Acrobat.

1. We compared our output against an **independent, unrelated open-source PRC encoder** to find where
   the two diverged.
2. We then ran a **bit-level bisection** over the divergences — 4,900 candidate positions narrowed to
   the single one responsible.
3. That position was a distance-1 back-reference inside a `WriteDouble` mantissa. Removing only that
   shortcut — emitting the byte literally instead — fixed both the original real-world file and a
   synthetic reproduction, confirmed in Acrobat.

So the causal isolation is at the level of individual bits, not files.

## Why this belongs in the document even though the listing is correct

An implementer writing an encoder from §9.19 will naturally implement the shortcut as given, because
it is given. There is nothing in the text to suggest that one of its legal outputs is a practical
hazard, and the failure it produces is silent and total — a blank model tree, no diagnostic, on a
file that is byte-for-byte conforming to the listing.

The document already carries informative NOTEs elsewhere for exactly this kind of
"legal-but-inadvisable" situation.

## CR-14a — proposed NOTE

Insert after the `write_double_procedure.cpp` listing in §9.19:

> **NOTE** — The back-reference form of this procedure permits a distance of 1, repeating the
> immediately preceding byte. Although conforming, this form has been observed to be mishandled by at
> least one major reader, which fails to display the model with no error indication. Encoders may
> prefer to emit the byte literally when the back-reference distance would be 1; the output remains
> conforming and is measurably more interoperable. Readers shall accept both forms.

The last sentence matters: the NOTE should not imply that distance-1 is invalid, because files
containing it exist and a reader must handle them.

## Scope of the claim, and what would extend it

The NOTE above is deliberately worded to be true independently of anything we have not measured. It
says the form is permitted, that it *has been observed* to be mishandled by at least one reader, that
encoders may prefer the literal form, and that readers must accept both. Each of those is established:
the first from the listing, the second by bit-level isolation, the third by the fix, the fourth by the
fact that such files exist.

What we have **not** measured is whether established producers emit distance-1 back-references. We
have deliberately not claimed they do or do not, and the NOTE does not depend on it either way.

That measurement would only let us say something *stronger* than the NOTE does — for example
recommending against the form outright, if it turned out no established producer uses it. It is
cheaply obtained (decode `WriteDouble` fields across a corpus and record back-reference distances by
producer) and we are willing to run it. But the NOTE as drafted does not need it, and we would not
want its absence to hold up an advisory that is correct as written.

## Related

[#770](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/770) and
[#776](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/776) concern §10.2 and are separate; this
issue is §9.19 only. An independent implementation reconstructed the exponent table of §9.19 and
verified it against the specification's listing entry by entry, 2,077 of 2,077, so the table itself
is confirmed correct and is not in question here.
title: PRC: WriteDouble Mantissa Encoding clarity section 9.19

# PRC: `HuffmanTreeCalculation` is declared and never defined, and the required tree shape is non-optimal

**Section:** §10.2 "Huffman algorithm"
(`iso-prc/sections/10-tessellation-compression.adoc:8`, listing at `iso-prc/code/huffman.cpp`).

**Change type:** Normative addition.

**Verified against:** the working source at `pdf-association/3dpdf-twg`, `main` @ `ba2bdc1`
(2 September 2026).

---

## The gap

In `iso-prc/code/huffman.cpp`:

- **line 3** declares `void HuffmanTreeCalculation(...);` — ending in a semicolon;
- **line 27** calls it, from inside `Huffman()`;
- **nowhere** defines it.

The listing is therefore incomplete as printed: the normative example invokes a function the document
does not contain. And the missing function is not incidental — it is the step that decides every
output bit. `Huffman()` only serialises the table that `HuffmanTreeCalculation` produces.

## The tree is not the conventional optimal one

This is the part that matters most, because an implementer who fills the gap with a textbook Huffman
construction produces output that is a valid prefix code and still wrong for this format.

Every real, independently-produced PRC file we have examined uses a tree with an **unconditionally
wasted leading bit** — Kraft sum 0.5, every real leaf's code beginning with bit 1. The construction
that produces it is a conventional greedy build followed by one extra merge against a zero-frequency
phantom leaf placed as the root's 0-branch.

**This is now measured, not sampled.** We instrumented a decoder to dump, for every Huffman-coded
array in a corpus of real files, the producer's own stored leaf table together with the symbol
frequencies implied by the decoded array. That yields **86,986 arrays from 141 files spanning two
independent producer families**, and each one is a labelled test case: these frequencies produced
this table. Across all of them:

| Property | ours | second implementation |
|---|---|---|
| **Fact 1.** Kraft sum of the stored code lengths is exactly 0.5 | 86,986 / 86,986 | **101,100 / 101,100 — 100.000%** |
| **Fact 2.** Every real leaf's code begins with bit 1 — the phantom is the root's 0-branch | 86,986 / 86,986 | **100.000%** |
| *Corollary.* Removing the leading bit leaves a complete tree (Kraft 1.0) | 86,986 / 86,986 | **100.000%** |
| **Fact 3.** Step 1's tree is length-optimal for its frequencies | 81,102 / 81,102 | not checkable — see below |

**Two of those rows are independent facts and the third is a corollary of them, which we should say
rather than let a reviewer discover.** If every code begins with bit 1, stripping that bit maps each
code of length `L` to one of length `L−1`, which doubles the Kraft sum — so 0.5 becomes exactly 1.0
as a matter of arithmetic. Rows one and two force row three. It was worth verifying and it was
verified, but it is a consistency check on the other two, not a third confirmation. Presenting three
results at 100.000% invites the conclusion that there is more independent evidence here than there
is.

**The results have since been reproduced independently**, over **101,116 Huffman arrays in 212
files** from a corpus that does not overlap ours, by a decoder that parses the same per-array leaf
tables. Sixteen arrays across six files were excluded there as malformed — their declared maximum
code length is impossible (zero with hundreds of leaves, or values in the billions; one declares
fourteen codes of length one, a Kraft sum of 7.0 where a prefix code admits at most two). Those same
arrays fail every check, and all six files decode badly on independent grounds unrelated to Huffman
tables, so they read as decoder desynchronisation rather than producer output. The honest headline is
therefore **100.000% of well-formed arrays, with sixteen malformed arrays in six files set aside**.

The length-optimality row is the one a second reader could not check, and the reason matters: that
implementation does not reconstruct trees from frequencies at all — it reads the stored table, so it
has nothing to compare a length-optimal tree against. That is precisely the argument CR-16c rests on
below. A decoder never needs the construction.

Taking Fact 3 on its own: the stored code lengths always achieve the minimum weighted path length for
the frequencies actually present. So step 1 is genuinely the conventional greedy construction — not
a variant, not a length-limited or otherwise constrained code — and the phantom merge of step 3 is
the *only* departure from the textbook algorithm.

**Isolated causally, not inferred.** Splice testing — swapping only the tree construction while
holding every other byte constant — reproduces Adobe Acrobat rejecting the file with a standard
optimal tree and accepting it with the phantom-wrapped variant.

A reader does not need any of this: `puLeafCodeValues` gives each leaf's complete code explicitly. It
is a writer-side requirement only, which is why the ambiguity is invisible to a decode-only
implementation and surfaces only when producing new files.

## CR-16a — insert the missing body

After the forward declaration, before the `Huffman()` listing:

> `HuffmanTreeCalculation` shall construct the code table as follows:
>
> 1. Build a Huffman tree by repeated minimum-frequency-pair merging over the distinct values present
>    in `pcArray` — the conventional greedy construction that the example in Figure 20 follows.
> 2. If the input has exactly one distinct value, add one zero-frequency phantom leaf, with any code
>    value different from the real one, before proceeding, so that step 1 has at least two leaves to
>    merge.
> 3. After step 1 produces its root, perform exactly one further merge, unconditionally: combine that
>    root against one additional zero-frequency phantom leaf, placing the **phantom leaf as the new
>    root's left (bit-0) child** and step 1's result as the right (bit-1) child.
> 4. `uNumberOfLeaves`, `puLeafValues`, `puLeafCodeLength` and `puLeafCodeValues` describe only the
>    real leaves from step 1. The phantom leaves added in steps 2 and 3 contribute no entry — they
>    exist only to shape the real leaves' code values and lengths.

## CR-16b — insert a NOTE

> **NOTE** — The wasted leading bit is by design. Every conforming encoder's tree for this algorithm
> has Kraft sum 0.5: the true root's 0-branch is always the unused phantom leaf of step 3, so every
> real leaf's code begins with bit 1. A reader need not reconstruct this shape — `puLeafCodeValues`
> gives each leaf's complete code — but a writer that instead builds a standard complete tree
> produces a bit-level mismatch with every currently known real PRC producer, and such output has
> been observed to be rejected outright by at least one major reader.

## The tie-break: now measured, and our recommendation is to leave it unspecified

Step 1 says "repeated minimum-frequency-pair merging" but does not state **what happens when
frequencies tie**. Different tie-break rules yield different code assignments for the same input, so
two encoders following this text can still produce different bytes. Our previous comment said we
could not determine the rule and offered to run the experiment. **We have now run it**, on the corpus
described above, and the result changes what we think the document should say.

### What the measurement establishes

**The reconstruction model is exact wherever no tie arises.** Of the usable arrays, **43,306 contain
no weight tie at any merge**. On every one of them, rebuilding the tree from the recovered
frequencies reproduces the producer's stored code lengths exactly — **43,306 / 43,306 (100.000%)**,
and identically under every candidate rule, since with no tie there is nothing for a rule to decide.
This validates the whole chain: the frequencies we recover are the frequencies the encoder saw, and
the phantom-wrap reading is correct. Whatever remains unexplained is therefore *only* the tie-break.

**The producers are deterministic.** A deterministic encoder must map a given `{value: frequency}`
input to exactly one code assignment. Grouping every array by that input finds **4,519 inputs that
occur more than once**, and **not one of them disagrees with itself** — zero inconsistencies, in
either producer family. So a rule does exist; this is not an unstable sort or a hash-order accident.

**But no simple rule reproduces it.** We tested **188 candidate rules** across five structurally
different model families: priority-queue comparators keyed on frequency then symbol value, subtree
size, subtree height, leaf-versus-internal, or creation order; the two-queue construction with both
front-preferences; four conventions for how an internal node inherits a symbol value; the
maintained-sorted-array construction with four insertion positions; and an exhaustive sweep of all
132 lexicographic comparators over the six node features above. The best result is **92.66%** for one
producer family and **91.93%** for the other. Nothing reaches 100%.

The best-fitting model is the same shape for both families — a maintained sorted array, leaves
ordered by ascending frequency then ascending symbol value, with each merged node inserted *before*
existing entries of equal weight. That the best model is positional rather than a comparator key is
itself informative: no total order on node properties does as well, which is what one would expect if
the behaviour is an artifact of a particular list implementation rather than a designed rule.

### Why we now recommend *not* specifying it

**A decoder never needs the rule.** `uNumberOfLeaves`, `puLeafValues`, `puLeafCodeLength` and
`puLeafCodeValues` carry the complete code table in the file. A conforming reader builds its tree from
those stored codes and never re-derives one from frequencies — so two encoders that break ties
differently produce files that are *both* decoded correctly by the same reader.

The corpus supports this directly, and the second implementation puts it more strongly than we did.
We reported that no array's stored codes match the canonical assignment for their lengths. They
report that **not a single leaf in any array coincides with its canonical code** — the
partially-canonical count is zero, across 101,101 arrays carrying any code. So the stored codes could
not possibly be reconstructed from lengths alone, in any array either of us has examined, and a
reader must be using the stored table.

The tie-break therefore affects **bit-exact reproducibility between encoders**, and nothing else. It
is not an interoperability requirement.

Given that, mandating a specific rule would carry a real cost and no benefit: it would render every
existing producer non-conforming on a point no reader can observe. The honest and useful thing is to
say so explicitly.

## CR-16c — state that the tie-break is unspecified

Append to CR-16a's step 1:

> Where two or more nodes have equal frequency, the choice of which to merge is **not specified by
> this document**. Different encoders resolve such ties differently and may therefore produce
> different — equally valid — code assignments for identical input.
>
> **NOTE** — This latitude is not observable by a conforming reader. The complete code table is
> written to the file (`uNumberOfLeaves`, `puLeafValues`, `puLeafCodeLength`, `puLeafCodeValues`) and
> a reader reconstructs the tree from those stored codes, never from the frequencies. The tie-break
> affects only whether two independent encoders produce byte-identical output for the same input, and
> conformance does not require that they do.

This costs the document nothing, closes a gap an implementer would otherwise fall into, and is
consistent with every file we have measured.

### What we did not establish

We did not identify the actual rule either producer uses, and we are not claiming it is unknowable —
92% from a positional model is close enough that a determined effort would likely finish it. We
stopped because the remaining 8% would change no recommendation: the rule is producer-specific, and
CR-16c is the right text whether or not one producer's rule is eventually named. If the working group
would rather the rule were named than declared unspecified, we would need to know whose behaviour
should become normative — a question for the group, not a measurement.

## Relationship to #776

[#776](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/776) reports that §10.2 has no read-side
procedure at all. Taken with this issue: **§10.2 currently specifies neither how to build the tree nor
how to read it back — only how a finished tree is serialised into a bit field.**

If only one is taken in this revision we would suggest #776, since a decoder implementer has nothing
to converge toward, whereas an encoder implementer can at least compare output against real files.
But the two together are the coherent fix.

## Evidence class

The absence is readable from the source. The required tree shape is measured byte-exactly across
86,986 Huffman-coded arrays from 141 real files and two independent producer families, at 100.000% on
every structural property CR-16a asserts, and is additionally isolated by splice testing against a
major reader's accept/reject behaviour. The tie-break is measured to be deterministic per producer,
not reproduced by any of 188 candidate rules, and — the point that matters for the document —
unobservable to any conforming reader. CR-16c states that rather than guessing at it.
title: PRC: Missing `HuffmanTreeCalculation` - Encoding Requires a Specific Tree Shape
