# PRC: orientation of implicit iso-face curves is not stated (§7.9.21.5.1)

**Section:** §7.9.21.5.1 "General" (`iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:3343`), under
§7.9.21.5 "Compressed Face".

**Change type:** Clarification / informative addition.

**Verified against:** the working source at `pdf-association/3dpdf-twg`, `main` @ `ba2bdc1`
(4 September 2026). No commit in that repository references this issue.

**Scoped deliberately below the two neighbouring issues.** This is a text-completeness observation,
**not** an observed decode failure. We believe the intended behaviour is uniquely determined by loop
closure, so this asks the document to state an inference rather than reporting that the format is
ambiguous. It is offered because it cost an implementor time, and because the adjacent sentence takes
care to specify the same property for the explicit case.

---

## Finding

§7.9.21.5.1 introduces the implicit/explicit distinction and then specifies orientation for only one
of the two (`07-base-entities.adoc:3343`):

> A curve is implicit if it is computed using iso-face properties. For example, the third and fourth
> curves in an _ISO_CYLINDER_ are implicit curves. Other curves are explicit. **Explicit curves are
> stored with the same orientation as the loop that references them first** in the compressed B-rep
> data.

The final sentence resolves orientation for explicit curves by reference to how they were *stored*.
That resolution is unavailable for implicit curves, which are never stored — yet an implementor must
give the reconstructed third and fourth curves a direction in order to build a coherent loop, and
those curves may subsequently be referenced by an adjacent face, at which point their orientation
becomes observable.

In practice we believe the traversal order of the closed loop determines it uniquely: with the loop
corners labelled V0 (join of curves 1 and 2), V1 (far end of curve 2), V2
(`common_third_fourth_vertex`) and V3 (far end of curve 1), curve 3 must run V1 to V2 and curve 4 V2
to V3 for the loop to close. We have not found a case where that inference fails.

## CR-25a — state the implicit case alongside the explicit one

**Location:** §7.9.21.5.1 "General", immediately after the existing sentence on explicit curves.

**AFTER:**

> Explicit curves are stored with the same orientation as the loop that references them first in the
> compressed B-rep data. **Implicit curves are not stored, and take the orientation required for the
> loop that computes them to be continuous: each implicit curve runs from the end of the preceding
> curve in the loop to the start of the following one. Where an implicit curve is subsequently
> referenced by an adjacent face, it is referenced with the orientation so determined.**

## Evidence class, stated honestly

This is the weakest of the three findings in this stretch of text and is labelled accordingly.
nanoPRC does not currently reconstruct implicit curves — it records reference indices without
dereferencing them — so we cannot offer an implementation result either way. We are not claiming the
format is ambiguous, only that the text is silent where its immediate neighbour is not.

If the committee reads the loop-closure argument as obviously sufficient and would rather not add
text, we would not press it.

## Relationship to #727 and the #769–#776 series

This finding comes from the same specification review as
[#727](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/727), and is filed separately for the
same reason that review's earlier findings became
[#769](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/769)–[#776](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/776):
each is independently actionable and independently closable, and bundling them delays the
straightforward ones behind the contested ones.

It is **not** a continuation of #727's open question. #727 concerns `is_face_planar` interpretation
within `PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D_Compressed` — tessellation — and remains open pending a discriminating
fixture. This issue concerns the compressed B-rep exact-geometry text and does not depend on how
#727 resolves. The two share a provenance, not a subject.

## Scope

This issue is §7.9.21.5.1 only. Two neighbouring findings in the same stretch of text are filed
separately: `PRC_HCG_Ellipse` having a normative encoding but no structure, and the dangling
`number_of_bits_to_store_reference` cross-reference in §7.9.21.8.

**Provenance.** Surfaced while working through the compressed-B-rep curve material alongside the
nanoPRC maintainer (CascadiaVoxel LLC, AGPLv3, https://github.com/mvrhel/nanoPRC), who is
implementing the compressed exact-geometry path and hit this against a real file. Verifiable by
reading the specification alone; no implementation dependency.
title: PRC: orientation of implicit iso-face curves is not stated (§7.9.21.5.1)

body:
# PRC: Texture Coordinates in `PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D` Have No Stated Dimension and a Contradicted Index Scale (§7.8.5.1, Tables 138/139)

[New 8 September 2026]

Two coupled defects in the **uncompressed** tessellation text. They are presented together because
neither can be resolved without the other: the index scale cannot be stated without first stating
the coordinate dimension, and the dimension is never stated anywhere in the document.

| CR | Topic | Location | Change type |
|---|---|---|---|
| CR-29 | `triangulated_index_array` is documented as "always a multiple of 3", but Table 139 places texture-coordinate indices in that same array, where the scale is 2 | §7.8.5.1 "General" (ISO/CD 14739-1.4:2026(en), p.63–64); Table 139 "PRC tessellation types" (p.66–67) | Normative correction |
| CR-30 | The dimension of `texture_coordinates` is never stated, and the only cross-reference offered points at a table that does not describe it | §7.8.5.1 "General" (p.64); Table 138 "PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D" (p.65); Table 95 "PRC_TYPE_GRAPH_TextureApplication" (p.45) | Normative addition |

**Provenance.** Found while assisting the nanoPRC maintainer (CascadiaVoxel LLC, AGPLv3,
https://github.com/mvrhel/nanoPRC) in scoping a texture-coordinate **writer** for the uncompressed
tessellation. The reader already existed; implementing the writer required knowing the convention
the reader had been reverse-engineered against, and the specification does not supply it. Both CRs
are confirmed against the specification text; CR-29 additionally carries measurement against real
files, since specification text alone is insufficient to determine the convention in use.

**Scope note.** Nearly all existing PRC tessellation issues on this tracker concern the *compressed*
path (`PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D_Compressed`, §8.8, Tables 217–242 — e.g. #727, #750, #772, #774). The
uncompressed `PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D` of §7.8.5 has had little attention, and these two defects sit
squarely in it.

---

## CR-29 — `triangulated_index_array`: the "multiple of 3" rule cannot hold for texture indices

**Sections:** §7.8.5 "PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D", §7.8.5.1 "General" (p.63–64); Table 139 "PRC tessellation
types" (p.66–67).

**Change type:** Normative correction.

**Status:** Confirmed by specification text (internal contradiction), and the correct scale
determined by measurement against real files.

### Background

§7.8.5.1 "General" (p.63) defines the array:

> "The `triangulated_index_array` is an array of integers that are an index into the `coordinates` or
> `normal_coordinates` arrays. Because these arrays represent triples of numbers of the (x, y, z) of
> a point or the (nx, ny, nz) values of a normal vector, the index is always a multiple of 3."

Two claims are made: an enumeration of what the array indexes (`coordinates` or
`normal_coordinates`), and a scale rule that follows *from* that enumeration.

### Finding

Table 139 "PRC tessellation types" (p.66–67) places a third kind of index in the same array. For
`PRC_FACETESSDATA_TriangleTextured`:

> "This is the same as `PRC_FACETESSDATA_Triangle` except that there are texture coordinate indices
> between normal and point indices. […] For example, a simple triangle with one texture coordinate
> index is described by (normal,texture,point,normal,texture,point,normal,texture,point)."

and for `PRC_FACETESSDATA_TriangleOneNormalTextured`:

> "For example, a simple triangle with one texture coordinate index is described by
> (normal,texture,point,texture,point,texture,point)."

So `triangulated_index_array` contains texture-coordinate indices as well, which §7.8.5.1's
enumeration omits. The consequence is not merely an incomplete list: the stated scale rule is
derived from the operands being 3-tuples, and texture coordinates are not 3-tuples (CR-30). A
reader that applies "always a multiple of 3" uniformly will decode texture indices incorrectly, and
on the files measured below will index outside the texture-coordinate array entirely.

### Measurement

Two files from the public prc-db corpus (https://github.com/ralovich/prc-db), chosen because they
use *different* face layouts, so the result is not an artefact of one encoder's habits.

**`prcs/welding_robot_kinematics_animation.stream-45.prc`** — `must_calculate_normals = 1`,
`number_of_normal_coordinates = 0`, so per Table 139 each vertex contributes `(texture, point)`;
`used_entities_flag = 0x200` (`TriangleTextured`), `number_of_texture_coordinate_indexes = 1`,
12 triangles, `number_of_triangulated_indices = 72` — consistent with 36 vertices x 2 entries.
`number_of_texture_coordinates = 40`.

Decoding the leading pairs, dividing the point index by 3 as specified and the texture index by 2:

| raw (texture, point) | texture / 2 | point / 3 |
|---|---:|---:|
| 34, 51 | 17 | 17 |
| 22, 33 | 11 | 11 |
| 32, 48 | 16 | 16 |
| 24, 36 | 12 | 12 |
| 10, 15 | 5 | 5 |
| 18, 27 | 9 | 9 |
| 4, 6 | 2 | 2 |
| 26, 39 | 13 | 13 |

Every texture value is even and divides to an index within the 20 available texture coordinates.
Under the stated "multiple of 3" rule the first entry would be 34/3, which is not an integer; taken
unscaled it would be 34, outside a 20-entry array.

**`prcs/PartList-Helico.stream-435.prc`** — `must_calculate_normals = 0`,
`number_of_normal_coordinates = 1908`, so each vertex contributes the full `(normal, texture,
point)` triple; `used_entities_flag = 0x200`, `number_of_texture_coordinate_indexes = 1`, 18 array
entries per face. `number_of_texture_coordinates = 1272`.

| raw (normal, texture, point) | normal / 3 | texture / 2 | point / 3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0, 0, 3 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| 3, 2, 6 | 1 | 1 | 2 |
| 6, 4, 0 | 2 | 2 | 0 |
| 9, 6, 9 | 3 | 3 | 3 |

Again every texture value is even. Note also that 1272 texture doubles and 1908 normal doubles give
636 texture coordinates and 636 normals — equal counts, which holds only at 2 doubles per texture
coordinate against 3 per normal.

**Conclusion:** texture-coordinate indices in `triangulated_index_array` are stored pre-multiplied
by **2**, not 3. Two files, two different face layouts, no exceptions.

### Proposed change

Replace the second sentence of the `triangulated_index_array` bullet in §7.8.5.1 "General" with
text that scales per operand. Suggested wording:

> "The `triangulated_index_array` is an array of integers that are an index into the `coordinates`,
> `normal_coordinates` or `texture_coordinates` arrays, according to the position of the entry
> within the pattern given for each tessellation type in Table 139. Each index is stored
> pre-multiplied by the number of values per element of the array it indexes: indices into
> `coordinates` and `normal_coordinates` are multiples of 3, because those arrays hold (x, y, z) and
> (nx, ny, nz) triples; indices into `texture_coordinates` are multiples of 2, because that array
> holds (u, v) pairs (see CR-30)."

---

## CR-30 — the dimension of `texture_coordinates` is never stated, and its cross-reference is wrong

**Sections:** §7.8.5.1 "General" (p.64); Table 138 "PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D" (p.65); §7.5.6
"PRC_TYPE_GRAPH_TextureApplication", Table 95 "PRC_TYPE_GRAPH_TextureApplication" (p.45).

**Change type:** Normative addition, plus an editorial cross-reference correction.

**Status:** Confirmed by specification text alone.

### Finding

`texture_coordinates` is mentioned in exactly two places in the prose of §7.8.5.1 (p.64):

> "The `number_of_texture_coordinates` field is the size of the texture coordinate array."
>
> "The `texture_coordinates` field contains and array of texture coordinates (see Table 95)."

and in Table 138 "PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D" (p.65) as `Array <Double> [number_of_texture_coordinates]`.

Neither states how many doubles constitute one texture coordinate. `number_of_texture_coordinates`
is described only as "the size of the texture coordinate array", which — consistent with how
`number_of_coordinates` and `number_of_normal_coordinates` are used for positions and normals — is a
count of **doubles**, not of coordinates. So the field name and its description disagree about the
unit, and the element size needed to reconcile them is absent.

The offered cross-reference does not supply it either. **Table 95 is
`PRC_TYPE_GRAPH_TextureApplication`**, whose rows are `base`,
`biased_material_generic_index`, `biased_texture_definition_index`, `biased_next-texture_index` and
`biased_uv_coordinates_index`. It describes how a material selects a texture and which UV set to
use. It says nothing about the layout, dimension or interpretation of the `texture_coordinates`
array, so the reference at p.64 leads nowhere useful.

The only textual signal anywhere in the document is nomenclature — `uv_coordinates_index`, and
§7.5.6's "the set of UV coordinates to consider" (p.45) — which implies two dimensions without
stating it.

Note that Table 95's own example distinguishes multiple texture-coordinate *indexes* per vertex from
multi-dimensional coordinates:

> "EXAMPLE A simple triangle with TWO texture coordinates index is described by
> (normal,{texture1,texture2},point, …) […] The `uv_coordinates_index` field indicates which of
> texture1 or texture2 is used."

That is, `number_of_texture_coordinate_indexes > 1` selects among several UV *sets*, each of which
is still a UV pair. It is therefore not a mechanism by which a texture coordinate could have three
components, and should not be mistaken for one.

The measurement under CR-29 settles the dimension empirically: `number_of_texture_coordinates` of
40 and of 2 occur in real files, neither divisible by 3, and the equal 636/636 texture/normal counts
in `PartList-Helico` hold only at 2 doubles per texture coordinate.

### Proposed change

1. In §7.8.5.1 "General" (p.64), state the element size and correct the cross-reference:

> "The `number_of_texture_coordinates` field is the size of the `texture_coordinates` array, counted
> in doubles.
>
> The `texture_coordinates` field is an array of doubles holding `number_of_texture_coordinates / 2`
> texture coordinates, each a (u, v) pair. The UV set selected for a given face is identified by
> `uv_coordinates_index` in `PRC_TYPE_GRAPH_TextureApplication` (see 7.5.6)."

2. Remove the "(see Table 95)" reference from the `texture_coordinates` bullet, or retarget it to
   §7.5.6 as above. Table 95 does not describe this array.

### Why this matters beyond editorial tidiness

An implementor writing this array today must choose an element size and an index scale with no
normative statement of either. The reference implementation this was found through carries an
explicit admission of the problem in its source — a comment reading "Not sure about the texture
indices though" at the point where the scale is applied. It happens to apply the correct factor of
2, but arrived at it empirically rather than from the specification, and a second implementation
reading the same text has no reason to reach the same answer.
title: PRC: Texture Coordinates in `PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D` Have No Stated Dimension and a Contradicted Index Scale

body:
Clause 7.8.9.8 `CompressedTextureParameter` does not state how many values make up one UV
coordinate in `texture_parameters`, nor what unit `texture_parameters_size` counts in. Both are
required to read the array properly.

Specifically, the prose currently says only this:

> **texture_parameters** is an array of float which contains coordinates of UV textures. This array
> is also filled during mesh traversal.

"Coordinates of UV textures" implies two values per coordinate, but neither the prose nor the table
says so, which makes it a bit ambiguous, so clause 7.8.9.8 should probably more explicitly state:

1.  `texture_parameters` is a flat array of  **pairs** of `FloatAsBytes` values, in (u, v) order.
2.  `texture_parameters_size` counts **values** (floats), so the number of UV pairs is `texture_parameters_size / 2`.
title: PRC: (clause 7.8.9.8)  ambiguous sizing for `CompressedTextureParameter`

body:
*Clause 7.5.4, `PRC_TYPE_GRAPH_Material` field descriptions; and the `colors` array in
`PRC_TYPE_ASM_FileStructureGlobals`.*

The colour array is declared as an array of `RgbColor` entries — `colors`, of type
`Array<RgbColor>[color_count]`, where `RgbColor` is three `Double` values. Every field that addresses it
is described as "an index into the RGB array" or "the index into the colour array", which reads as an
index of colour entries.

Conforming writers instead express these indices in the array's **individual double values**, three per
colour. A reader implementing the text literally therefore selects the wrong colour, or computes an
index beyond the end of the array, on every file — while consuming exactly the correct number of bits.
There is no desync and no error condition, so nothing downstream reports it.

The fields affected are `ambient_index`, `diffuse_index`, `emissive_index` and `specular_index` in
`PRC_TYPE_GRAPH_Material`; `color_index` in `PRC_TYPE_GRAPH_Style`; and the colour identifier of the
`Color` markup entity. The defect is in how the array is addressed rather than in any one field, so the
recommendation states the rule once, at the array.

**Recommendation**

Add the following sentence to the description of the `colors` array in
`PRC_TYPE_ASM_FileStructureGlobals`:

> Indices into this array are expressed in individual double values rather than in `RgbColor` entries.
> An index *i* identifies the colour at position (*i* − 1) / 3 in the array.
title: PRC: Colour indices are described as indexing the colour array, but are expressed in its individual double values

body:
*Clause 7.9.21.10 `CompressedPoint`, including its NOTE and the normative Read/Write Algorithm
`WriteCompressedPoint` / `ReadCompressedPoint`.*

The clause states its quantisation tolerance three times and its `uNbBits > 30` fallback twice, and in
both cases the statements disagree. In each case the part labelled normative is the one that is wrong,
so an implementer who follows the procedure produces output the rest of the clause forbids.

**Contradiction 1 — which tolerance scales the point.** The opening prose and the normative algorithm
both use `brep_data_compressed_tolerance`. The clause's own NOTE forbids exactly that, and gives the
reason: the variable "is not defined in all calling contexts". It is not. A `CompressedPoint` inside
`PRC_TYPE_TOPO_SingleWireBodyCompress` has no such field — that structure carries `curve_tolerance` —
and because `curve_trimming_face` is always FALSE there, every point in a wire body is a
`CompressedPoint`. So the normative algorithm names a field that does not exist in a context where it
is the only encoding used. The clause already defines the correct term, `compression_tolerance`, as
"`brep_data_compressed_tolerance` when the enclosing parent is `PRC_TYPE_TOPO_BrepDataCompress`, or
`curve_tolerance` when the enclosing parent is `PRC_TYPE_TOPO_SingleWireBodyCompress`".

The failure is silent. A reader following the normative algorithm inside a wire body has no field to
read; if it substitutes a default, every coordinate in the body is scaled wrongly while the bitstream
stays structurally valid and the entity count stays correct. Nothing in the file detects it.

**Contradiction 2 — the `uNbBits > 30` fallback.** Two sentences roughly twenty lines apart say
opposite things. The first: "When `uNbBits > 30` … each coordinate is instead written by `WriteDouble`.
In neither case is `PRC_TYPE_TOPO_UniqueVertex` written or read." The second: "If `uNbBits` is greater
than 30, the compressed point is stored as a `PRC_TYPE_TOPO_UniqueVertex`; otherwise it is stored as a
`Point3DWithVariableBitNumber`." The normative algorithm agrees with the first. The two produce entirely
different bitstreams for the same input, and a reader cannot tell from the text which is intended. 

The second contradiction is likely a leftover from before the `WriteDouble` fallback was introduced,
since the sentence recommended for deletion describes the pre-fallback behaviour.

**Recommendation**

1. In the opening paragraph of `CompressedPoint`, replace `brep_data_compressed_tolerance` with
   `compression_tolerance`, so the sentence reads:

   > When *uNbBits* ≤ 30, the three coordinates are encoded by *WritePoint3DWithVariableBitNumber*
   > using *uNbBits* bits and tolerance dTol = compression_tolerance / 100.

2. Delete the sentence:

   > If uNbBits is greater than 30, the compressed point is stored as a _PRC_TYPE_TOPO_UniqueVertex_;
   > otherwise it is stored as a Point3DWithVariableBitNumber .

3. In the preamble to the Read/Write Algorithm, replace the sentence identifying the tolerance with:

   > The following algorithms define the normative encoding and decoding of a *CompressedPoint*. The
   > *compression_tolerance* is the tolerance value carried by the enclosing parent structure, as
   > defined above: *brep_data_compressed_tolerance* when the enclosing parent is
   > *PRC_TYPE_TOPO_BrepDataCompress*, or *curve_tolerance* when the enclosing parent is
   > *PRC_TYPE_TOPO_SingleWireBodyCompress*.

4. In both procedures, rename the parameter and the two `dTol` assignments accordingly:

   > PROCEDURE WriteCompressedPoint(x, y, z : Double; +
   > {nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp} compression_tolerance : Double): +
   > {nbsp} +
   > {nbsp}{nbsp}dTol ← compression_tolerance / 100
   >
   > PROCEDURE ReadCompressedPoint(compression_tolerance : Double) +
   > {nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp}{nbsp} → (x, y, z : Double): +
   > {nbsp} +
   > {nbsp}{nbsp}dTol ← compression_tolerance / 100

5. Consequent on 1, 3 and 4, delete the final sentence of the NOTE, which then has nothing left to
   prohibit:

   > The variable brep_data_compressed_tolerance must not be used directly in this formula, as it is not
   > defined in all calling contexts.

   The remainder of the NOTE — the per-parent explanation — should be retained.
title: PRC: Clause 7.9.21.10 `CompressedPoint` contradicts itself twice, and the normative algorithm is on the losing side of both

body:
*Clause 7.3.5.2, `PRC_TYPE_ASM_FileStructureGlobals`.*

The table declares two independent count-and-array pairs: `texture_app_count` with
`texture_applications`, followed by `material_count` with `materials`.

Conforming writers emit **one** count followed by **one** array whose entries are type-tagged and
dispatched on the tag — `PRC_TYPE_GRAPH_Material` (702) or `PRC_TYPE_GRAPH_TextureApplication` (711).
The two entity types are interleaved in a single array.

A reader implementing the table literally desyncs at `material_count`: having consumed
`texture_app_count` entries from the head of the combined array, it reads its second count out of the
middle of that array's data. Because this is the globals section, the damage is not local — the colour
palette, every line pattern and every style follow it, and all are lost.

The table appears to describe the structure a reader ends up with rather than the data on the wire.

**Recommendation**

In `definitions/base-entities/structure_and_assembly.yaml`, replace the four attributes
`texture_app_count`, `texture_applications`, `material_count` and `materials` with:

```yaml
  - name: material_count
    data_type:
      kind: UnsignedInteger
    description: Number of entries in the materials array
    required: true
  - name: materials
    data_type:
      kind: Array
      inner_kind: PRC_TYPE_GRAPH_MaterialOrTextureApplication
      occurrence: material_count
    description: |
      Array of materials and texture applications, interleaved in a single array.

      Each entry begins with its entity type, which selects how the remainder of the entry is
      read: PRC_TYPE_GRAPH_Material or PRC_TYPE_GRAPH_TextureApplication. Texture applications
      are not counted or stored separately.
    required: true
```
title: PRC: `PRC_TYPE_ASM_FileStructureGlobals` declares texture applications and materials as two arrays; conforming writers emit one type-tagged array

body:
*Clause 7.4.3 `PRC_TYPE_MISC_CartesianTransformation2d` (Table 88), attribute `rotation`.*

`rotation` is declared as `Array<Vector2D>` with occurrence 2, described as the x-axis giving
`mat[0][0] mat[1][0]` and the y-axis giving `mat[0][1] mat[1][1]`.

Conforming writers store **one** `Vector2D` — the x-axis, as (cos θ, sin θ). The y-axis is not written;
it is the perpendicular of the x-axis, which is determined because this attribute is present only when
`PRC_TRANSFORMATION_NonOrtho` is FALSE.

A reader implementing the table literally consumes four doubles where two were written, and desyncs
everything that follows in the same structure.

The declaration is inconsistent with its own sibling. `non_ortho_matrix`, in the same table, is also
`Array<Vector2D>[2]` and genuinely does carry two vectors — a non-orthogonal matrix's second column is
not derivable from its first. `rotation` is the orthogonal case, where it is. The two are declared
identically although only one of them can be, and the specification already applies the same economy in
three dimensions, where `PRC_TYPE_MISC_CartesianTransformation3d` stores two of three axes and derives
the third by cross product.

The `[2]` appears to describe the resulting matrix columns rather than the number of vectors written.

**Recommendation**

In `definitions/base-entities/misc_data.yaml`, replace the `rotation` attribute with:

```yaml
  - name: rotation
    data_type:
      kind: Vector2D
    description: |
      Define the rotation, as the x-axis of the resulting matrix.

      xaxis -> mat[0][0] mat[1][0]

      The y-axis is not stored. It is the perpendicular of the x-axis, and gives
      mat[0][1] = -mat[1][0] and mat[1][1] = mat[0][0]. The vector is a unit vector.
    required: false
    require_conditions: "*behavior* and PRC_TRANSFORMATION_Rotate is TRUE and *behavior* and PRC_TRANSFORMATION_NonOrtho is FALSE"
```
title: PRC: 2D transformation: the orthogonal `rotation` is declared as two `Vector2D` but only the x-axis is written

body:
*Clause 7.8.7.2 `VertexColors` (Table 143), the `number_of_colors` derivation; and Table 140
`PRC_TYPE_TESS_Face`, the `vertex color data` row.*

**1. The derivation names a field that is not the quantity it needs.** `VertexColors` is delta-encoded
and carries no element count on the wire. The clause derives one:

> The **number_of_colors** stored in the **color_data** shall be calculated from the number of point
> indices and is found in the:
> - **wire_indexes** array in the case of a PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D_Wire;
> - **size_of_triangulateddata** in the case of a PRC_TYPE_TESS_Face.

The first half names the right quantity — the number of point indices. The second names
`size_of_triangulateddata`, which is the **length of the `triangulateddata` array**: Table 140
establishes this by using it as that array's own occurrence count,
`Array <UnsignedInteger>[size_of_triangulateddata]`. One identifier cannot be both an array's length
and the count of point indices inside it.

The two readings differ by a factor of nine on a real file. Because the array is delta-encoded with no
terminator, the wrong count **desynchronises the bitstream**: the reader finishes the entity in the
wrong place and everything after it is noise.

The wire half is underspecified rather than wrong. "Found in the `wire_indexes` array" cannot count
anything on its own, because that array interleaves `number_of_indices_per_wire_edge` headers with the
indices themselves.

**2. Table 140 makes the colour block unconditional.** Its `vertex color data` row is `(Required)` with
no condition, while the identical row in Table 142 reads `(Optional; if has_vertex_colors is TRUE)`.
Implemented literally, Table 140 says every face carries a colour block.

**Recommendation**

1. Replace the derivation sentence and its two bullets with:

   > The **number_of_colors** stored in the **color_data** is not stored explicitly and shall be
   > derived from the number of point indices in the enclosing entity.
   >
   > For a *PRC_TYPE_TESS_Face*, it is the number of point indices addressed by the face's primitive
   > blocks as selected by **used_entities_flag**: three per triangle for a triangle list, and one per
   > point for each triangle fan or triangle strip, summed over every block present on the face. It is
   > not derived from **size_of_triangulateddata**, which is the length of the **triangulateddata**
   > array and not a count of the point indices within it. The value does not depend on
   > **must_recalculate_normals**: that flag removes normal indices from the triangulated index array
   > and never point indices, so the number of point indices is the same whether it is set or not.
   >
   > For a *PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D_Wire*, it is the number of point indices in the **wire_indexes** array,
   > excluding the **number_of_indices_per_wire_edge** headers interleaved with them. Implicit points
   > and the segment case are as described for **is_segment_color**.

2. In `definitions/base-entities/tessellation.yaml`, change the `vertex color data` row of
   `PRC_TYPE_TESS_Face` to match the equivalent row of `PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D_Wire`:

```yaml
  - name: vertex color data
    data_type:
      kind: VertexColors
    description: "*vertex color data*"
    required: false
    require_conditions: "if *has_vertex_colors* is TRUE"
```

**What this issue is not asking for**

**Do not add an explicit element count to the array.** No existing writer emits one, so a count field
would change the wire format and orphan every file already written. The array is recoverable as it
stands; what is missing is the rule, not the data.
title: PRC:  `VertexColors`: the element count is derived from a field that cannot supply it, and Table 140 makes the block unconditional

body:
*Clause 7.8.7 (`has_loops`), clause 7.9.21.3 (`origin_array`), and clause 7.9.21.2
(`number_vertex_references` / `number_edge_references`) — the NOTE block in each.*

Three NOTE blocks in clause 7 state requirements, using `shall` or `shall not`.  As drafted, these three
oblige a conforming implementation to do nothing — including in two cases where the note is the only
convenient statement of a rule a reader cannot otherwise settle.

| note | the requirement it states |
|---|---|
| `has_loops` presence | "Readers encountering files with authoring_version < 7039 **shall** treat *has_loops* as FALSE and **shall not** attempt to read *has_loops* from the bitstream." |
| `origin_array` presence | "Readers encountering files with authoring_version < 7031 **shall** treat origin_array as [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] and **shall not** attempt to read origin_array from the bitstream." |
| dual-cache indexing | "A reader encountering more compressed vertices or edges than *number_vertex_references* or *number_edge_references* respectively **shall not** treat the excess as an error… Index resolution **shall** apply the threshold-and-offset rule…" |

The first two are presence conditions: they determine whether a field is read from the bitstream at
all. A reader that treats them as informative and reads the field anyway desynchronises on every file
written before the stated authoring version. That is a conformance rule sitting in the one part of the
clause that cannot carry one.

**Recommendation**

For each, state the obligation in the clause body and retain the note as explanation. The substance is
already drafted; only its location changes.

1. In the description of `has_loops`, add:

   > *has_loops* is present only in files whose PRC authoring version, recorded in the
   > *PRC_TYPE_ASM_FileStructure* header, is greater than or equal to 7039. In a file whose authoring
   > version is less than 7039, *has_loops* shall be treated as FALSE and shall not be read from the
   > bitstream.

   and reduce the NOTE to:

   > NOTE: The authoring version is the sole mechanism for detecting the presence of *has_loops*; there
   > is no secondary flag.

2. In the description of `origin_array`, add:

   > *origin_array* is present only in files whose PRC authoring version, recorded in the
   > *PRC_TYPE_ASM_FileStructure* header, is greater than or equal to 7031. In a file whose authoring
   > version is less than 7031, *origin_array* shall be treated as [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] and shall not be
   > read from the bitstream.

   and reduce the NOTE to:

   > NOTE: The authoring version is the sole mechanism for detecting the presence of *origin_array*;
   > there is no secondary flag.

3. In the descriptions of `number_vertex_references` and `number_edge_references`, add:

   > A reader encountering more compressed vertices or edges than *number_vertex_references* or
   > *number_edge_references* respectively shall not treat the excess as an error; the total count
   > spans both caches. Index resolution shall apply the threshold-and-offset rule given in these two
   > descriptions.

   and reduce the NOTE to:

   > NOTE: The fields *number_vertex_references* and *number_edge_references* define the boundary
   > between these caches within the single serialised stream. Implementations that treat
   > *number_vertex_references* as the total vertex count will fail to index all the ana-vertex
   > references.
title: PRC: Three NOTEs in clause 7 state requirements,

body:
*Clause 7.8.9, `PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D_COMPRESSED`, the `point_reference_array` field description.*

The description states two things about the `CompressedIndiceArray` written in this position:

> the Boolean value which indicates whether the character array is compressed is not stored. Its value
> is implicit and set to number_of_reference_points > 3, where number_of_reference_points is the number
> of non-zero elements in the *points_is_reference_array*. **Its size is implicit and set to number of
> non-zero elements in the *points_is_reference_array*.**

The first part is correct and is the only statement of the recovery rule anywhere in the specification;
it should be kept.

The second part is contradicted by the bitstream. **The size is written.** `WriteCharacterArray` emits
an `UnsignedInteger` size in *both* of its forms — the compressed branch writes the Huffman word count
and the uncompressed branch writes the character count — and the `bWriteCompressStrategy` exemption
suppresses only the Boolean, not the size. A reader implementing the sentence literally skips a field
that is present.

The failure is silent and severe. Implementing it literally consumes zero bits when
`number_of_reference_points` is 0 — which is correct by coincidence, because the size then encodes as a
single zero bit — and too few bits otherwise. In the case we measured it consumed 3 bits where 32 were
due, so `must_recalculate_normals` was read 29 bits early and returned FALSE where TRUE was written,
the remainder of the entity collapsed, the following entity's type field read as a null, and every
tessellation after the first was dropped. The file still decoded *successfully*, with most of its
geometry missing and no guard tripped.

**Recommendation**

In the `point_reference_array` description, replace the final sentence so the paragraph reads:

> *point_reference_array* *CompressedIndiceArray* (see WriteCompressedIndiceArray) invokes
> *WriteCharacterArray* (see WriteCharacterArray). In this case, the Boolean value which indicates
> whether the character array is compressed is not stored. Its value is implicit and set to
> number_of_reference_points > 3, where number_of_reference_points is the number of non-zero elements
> in the *points_is_reference_array*. The size of the character array is written, as it is in both
> forms of *WriteCharacterArray*; only the compression Boolean is omitted.
title: PRC: `point_reference_array`: the array size is documented as implicit, but it is written on the wire

## Defect

Fourteen curve entities carry a `transform` attribute. Four of them - `PRC_TYPE_CRV_Circle` (7.10.6),
`PRC_TYPE_CRV_Intersection` (7.10.13), `PRC_TYPE_CRV_Line` (7.10.14) and `PRC_TYPE_CRV_PolyLine`
(7.10.17) - declare a `has_transform` Boolean before it and make the transformation conditional upon
that Boolean. The remaining ten declare the transformation as unconditionally required, with no

This is the condition reported for surfaces in #658 and remedied there for that half of the

## Evidence

Two independent implementations read a `has_transform` Boolean before the transformation on nine of

**CR-31.** Our reference for this change request; please quote the issue number.

**Location:** 7.9.12 `PRC_TYPE_TOPO_Face`, its prose and Table 189;
`iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/topology.yaml`, `PRC_TYPE_TOPO_Face`.

## Defect

Table 189 declares `number_of_loops` as Required with the description "Number of loops in this face;
shall be 1 or more", and the prose above the table describes one of the loops as representing the
exterior boundary of the face. A face declaring zero loops therefore has no boundary that the clause
contemplates, and the clause gives a reader no reading for it.

Files declaring zero are not rare, and they come from more than one producer. The specification as
written makes them non-conforming, yet the most widely deployed reader renders them, so implementers
have no basis for choosing between rejecting such a file, drawing the surface whole, or drawing
nothing.

## Evidence

**Measured with nanoPRC's reader over prc-db** (https://github.com/ralovich/prc-db), a collection
of real-world PRC files gathered from public sources across the internet and curated by @ralovich.
The files are the work of many independent producers; neither the curator nor this project wrote
them. Of its 310 files, 307 open. Thirty-six carry uncompressed B-rep faces, 23,004 faces in
total. **Nineteen** of those files declare `number_of_loops = 0` on every face; the other
seventeen conform, with counts of one, two where a face has a hole, and up to thirty-seven. No
file mixes the two conventions. In all nineteen, across **4,193 faces**, the faces carry no
boundary topology of any kind: zero coedges, zero edges, zero vertices - a surface and nothing
else. Eighteen of the nineteen share one writer signature; the nineteenth is a file our own reader
reaches only three of eighty-four declared bodies in, so no writer conclusion is drawn from it.

**What those faces put in `index_of_outer_loop`.** The attribute is Required and is read
unconditionally, before any branch on `number_of_loops`, so it is present on the wire for a zero-loop
face and the question of what it holds is answerable. Measured across the same thirty-six files: all
**4,193** zero-loop faces carry **-1**, with no other value observed in any of the nineteen files.
The same sweep reads 18,811 loop-bearing faces, of which 12,521 carry a negative index - permitted,
since 7.9.12 requires the index to be defined only when `PRC_CONTEXT_OuterLoopsFirst` is TRUE - and
6,290 carry a non-negative one. **None of the 6,290 is out of range**, which is the control on the
read: had the attribute been decoded wrongly, out-of-range values would appear among them. The two
groups sum to 23,004, the face total independently reported by the same tool.

This is what licenses the `-1` in the proposed text below: it records existing practice across at
least two writers rather than inventing a value.

**From a second implementation's corpus** (219 further files). Four declare `number_of_loops = 0`
and `is_trimmed = FALSE` across 2,040 faces, all on `PRC_TYPE_SURF_NURBS` surfaces. As Table 294
gives that surface type no `UVParameterization` of its own, and `is_trimmed`/`trimmed_surface` is the
only other means of bounding a face, nothing in those files bounds the patches. A minimal synthetic
pair isolating the same condition in a single face, differing only by the loop, accompanies that
report.

**Observed behaviour of the reference viewer**, contributed by that implementation and stated here as
their measurement: all four files open without error, populate the model tree and render.

## Proposed change

Two changes, both required together.

### Change 1 of 2 - Table 189, the `number_of_loops` row

Current text of the Data Description column:

```
(Required) Number of loops in this face; shall be 1 or more
```

Replace with:

```
(Required) Number of loops in this face. A value of 0 indicates a face that is not bounded by loops;
see 7.9.12.
```

The same string appears in `topology.yaml`. Current text:

```yaml
  - name: number_of_loops
    data_type:
      kind: UnsignedInteger
    required: true
    description: Number of loops in this face; shall be 1 or more
```

Replace with:

```yaml
  - name: number_of_loops
    data_type:
      kind: UnsignedInteger
    required: true
    description: "Number of loops in this face. A value of 0 indicates a face that is not bounded by loops; see 7.9.12"
```

### Change 2 of 2 - 7.9.12, the list of characteristics

Current text of the final two list items:

```
-- An unordered list of loops delimiting the bounded portion (interior) of the face.

-- One of the loops represents the exterior boundary of the face and the other loops (if any) represent interior
     loops (holes) within the face. If PRC_CONTEXT_OuterLoopsFirst is set to TRUE in the topological context
     the face is contained in, the index of the outer loop shall be defined.
```

Replace with:

```
-- An unordered list of loops delimiting the bounded portion (interior) of the face. The list may be empty.

-- If the list is not empty, one of the loops represents the exterior boundary of the face and the other loops
     (if any) represent interior loops (holes) within the face. If PRC_CONTEXT_OuterLoopsFirst is set to TRUE in
     the topological context the face is contained in, the index of the outer loop shall be defined.

-- If the list is empty, the face is not bounded by loops and its extent is the parameter domain of the face.
     A reader shall accept such a face and shall treat its extent as that domain.
     index_of_outer_loop shall be set to -1 for such a face and shall be ignored by a reader.
```

## Effect if accepted

A zero-loop face becomes conforming, its meaning is stated, and a reader's obligation towards it is
stated, so the three behaviours implementations currently choose between are reduced to one. Faces
declaring one or more loops are unaffected: every sentence describing them is preserved verbatim.
title: PRC: number_of_loops "shall be 1 or more" is contradicted by conforming-looking files, and the reference viewer draws them [CR-31]

body:
**CR-32.** Our reference for this change request; please quote the issue number.

**Location:** 7.9.21.7.1 General, the paragraph defining vertex loops.

## Defect

7.9.21.7.1 provides for the vertex loop, defines its shape, and 7.9.21.7.2 confines it to analytic
faces by stating that the loop of an iso-face cannot be degenerate. What the clause does not state is
whether a reader is required to render a face whose only boundary is such a loop.

The construct is not avoidable for the geometry it exists to serve. A full sphere cannot be bounded
by an ordinary rectangular boundary, because its poles are singular and the circles at the extremes
of the second parameter collapse to points. A writer emitting a closed sphere or torus as exact
B-rep has no conforming alternative available. The most widely deployed reader nevertheless declines
to draw such a face, so that writer's output is silently blank, and neither implementation can point
to a sentence that settles which of them is wrong.

## Evidence

**From a second implementation**, and stated here as their measurement rather than ours. Four files
containing no tessellation entities whatever were opened in the reference viewer:

| file | surface | its only loop | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cone-real-loop` | cone | a real boundary loop | renders |
| `sphere-zone-real-loop` | sphere, closed and periodic | a real seam-split boundary loop | renders |
| `sphere-degenerate-loop` | sphere, closed | one-point vertex loop | blank |
| `torus-degenerate-loop` | torus, closed | one-point vertex loop | blank |

The second file is the control: a latitude band bounded by two latitude circles and two seam edges,
closed and periodic in the same parameter as the full sphere, differing from it only in not carrying
a degenerate loop. It renders. The distinguishing condition is therefore the degenerate loop, and not
closedness, periodicity or the absence of tessellation. It follows that the reference implementation
both tessellates exact B-rep geometry and declines this particular construct.

**A census run with nanoPRC's reader over prc-db** (https://github.com/ralovich/prc-db), a
collection of real-world PRC files gathered from public sources across the internet and curated by
@ralovich, the files themselves being the work of many independent producers. It is offered for
scale rather than for the substance of the request. Across the 307 of its 310 files that open,
thirty-six carry uncompressed B-rep faces holding 20,816 loops. Of those, 1,158 loops in eight
files consist of a single coedge, so the precursor shape is common; none of the 1,158 is
degenerate. The detector was verified against the four fixtures above, which it scores 1, 1, 1 and
0 respectively, so the zero is a measurement and not a silence. The construct therefore appears to
be written by one implementation rather than to be in general use. That bears on priority, not on
substance: the specification provides for the construct, so a reader's obligation towards it
should be stated whether or not files exercising it are common today.

## Proposed change

One paragraph gains one sentence.

Current text:

```
Vertex loops are used to represent a loop consisting of a single vertex, such as those that can exist on the apex
of a cone, or a sphere touching a plane. They are represented by a degenerate line which has identical start
and end vertices.
```

Replace with:

```
Vertex loops are used to represent a loop consisting of a single vertex, such as those that can exist on the apex
of a cone, or a sphere touching a plane. They are represented by a degenerate line which has identical start
and end vertices. A vertex loop does not bound the face; a reader shall treat a face whose loops are all vertex
loops as extending over the whole of its parameter domain, and shall render it accordingly.
```

## Effect if accepted

A reader's obligation is stated where the construct is defined. Writers emitting closed spheres and
tori as exact B-rep gain an assurance that conforming readers will draw them, and the reference
implementation's present behaviour becomes a defect in that implementation rather than a permitted
choice.
title: PRC: the degenerate vertex loop of 7.9.21.7.1 is not drawn by the reference viewer [CR-32]

body:
Clause 7.2 Lexical conventions does not mention whether the leading PLUS `+`, MINUS `-`, or PERIOD `.` in numbers causes one number to end and another to start (i.e. act as numeric token separators), or if this is a syntax error. That is, whether whitespace is mandatory between consecutive numbers. Testing shows that implementations vary on this point, which results in different appearances (since consecutive numbers occur a lot in content streams). 

e.g.
`12.34.56 ` -> "+12.34" followed by "+0.56" or "12.34" followed by an error?
`-12.34-56` -> "-12.34" followed by "-56" or "-12.34" followed by an error?
`+12.34+56` -> "+12.34" followed by "+56" or "+12.34" followed by an error?

This same question also applies to PDF arrays in objects where consecutive numbers can appear.

All(?) processors seem to handle PLUS `+`, MINUS `-`, or PERIOD `.` starting a number WITHOUT requiring any whitespace when the preceding char is an official delimiter (e.g. `)`, `>`, `]`)

This issue occurs far more often than I'd like in content streams.
title: Do consecutive numbers need whitespace or do `+`/`-`/`.` act as a delimiter?
