**CR-33.** Our reference for this change request; please quote the issue number.

**Location:** 7.5.5.1 `PRC_TYPE_GRAPH_Picture` General, the paragraph immediately following
Table 93 (`iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc`, the paragraph after the
`PRC_TYPE_GRAPH_Picture` data-definition block); and Table 93 itself, generated from
`iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/graphics.yaml`, `PRC_TYPE_GRAPH_Picture`.

## Defect

The paragraph carries three problems, all in three sentences. The third is the substantive one.

**First**, the field names are written with spaces in the second and third sentences -- "pixel
width and pixel height" -- where Table 93 immediately above and the first sentence of the same
paragraph write **pixel_width** and **pixel_height**. A reader cannot tell whether "pixel width"
names the field or describes a quantity.

**Second**, the third sentence has lost its operators. As printed it reads "shall be at least
pixel width **pixel_height** number of components per pixel", which is three nouns in a row and
not an expression. The intended product is legible from context but is not stated.

**Third, and the reason for this request:** the sentence "When **format** is 0 or 1, pixel width
and pixel height fields are ignored" tells a writer that it may store anything in those fields,
and tells a reader nothing about what to do with the values it finds. Neither half is safe. Real
writers are divided on what to put there, and the most widely deployed reader does not ignore the
fields at all -- it honours them in preference to the dimensions recorded inside the encoded
image.

The consequence is a file that conforms to the sentence as written and does not display. A writer
that takes "ignored" at its word and stores, say, the dimensions of a different image, or a
placeholder, produces a picture that the dominant implementation will size incorrectly, with no
sentence in the document to say it was wrong to do so.

## Evidence

### What the reference viewer does

Two files were written that differ in nothing except the two fields under discussion. Each
contains one textured quad, one picture, and an identical texture chain.

| file | image in the buffer | record declares | Adobe Acrobat |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 256x256 PNG | 255x255 | displays |
| B | 255x255 PNG | 256x256 | empty model tree |

If the fields were ignored, both would behave alike, and B would display, since its buffer holds a
perfectly good PNG. The declared values decide the outcome, so they are not ignored.

### What real writers do

Every PNG and JPEG picture in two independent corpora was decoded and its true dimensions compared
against the values in its picture record:

| | pictures | declare true dimensions | declare 0 | declare a value that disagrees |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| corpus A | 1159 | 793 | 366 | 0 |
| corpus B | 476 | 55 | 421 | 0 |
| **combined** | **1635** | **848** | **787** | **0** |

Corpus A is the 310-file collection published by @ralovich
(https://github.com/ralovich/prc-db), whose files come from a wide range of producers and
creators; the curator publishes them but did not author them. Corpus B is a separate 384-file
collection held privately, with some overlap.

Two things follow. Producers are genuinely split, so both behaviours are in circulation and any
correction has to accommodate both. And **no producer in either corpus stores a value that
contradicts its image** -- the permission the current sentence grants is not exercised by anyone.
What writers actually do is either state the truth or state nothing, which is narrower than the
text allows, and narrower in exactly the way a reader needs.

## Proposed change

Two changes, both in 7.5.5.1.

### Change 1 of 2 - the paragraph following Table 93

**Current text**

> **pixel_width** and **pixel_height** are the size of the picture expressed in pixels. When
> **format** is 0 or 1, pixel width and pixel height fields are ignored. When **format** is one of
> {2,3,4,5} the size of the picture buffer when uncompressed shall be at least pixel width
> **pixel_height** number of components per pixel.

**Replacement text**

> **pixel_width** and **pixel_height** are the size of the picture expressed in pixels.
>
> When **format** is 0 or 1, the encoded image records its own dimensions, and **pixel_width** and
> **pixel_height** shall either be equal to those dimensions or both be 0. A writer shall not store
> dimensions that differ from those of the encoded image. A reader shall take the dimensions from
> the encoded image when both fields are 0, and may rely on the fields otherwise.
>
> When **format** is one of {2,3,4,5}, the size of the picture buffer when uncompressed shall be at
> least **pixel_width** x **pixel_height** x the number of components per pixel.

The replacement makes no existing file non-conforming: every picture measured above either states
its true dimensions or states 0, and both remain permitted. It removes only the case no producer
was observed to emit, which is also the only case that silently misrenders.

The source is AsciiDoc, so the current text above is shown as it renders. In
`sections/07-base-entities.adoc` the paragraph reads, verbatim:

```adoc
*pixel_width* and *pixel_height* are the size of the picture expressed in pixels. When *format* is 0 or 1, pixel width and pixel height fields are ignored. When *format* is one of {2,3,4,5} the size of the picture buffer when uncompressed shall be at least pixel width *pixel_height* number of components per pixel.
```

Note that the inconsistent styling and the missing operators are present in the source, not
introduced by rendering: "pixel width and pixel height" carries no markup, and "at least pixel
width *pixel_height* number of components per pixel" has no operators between its terms.

Replacement, in the same form:

```adoc
*pixel_width* and *pixel_height* are the size of the picture expressed in pixels.

When *format* is 0 or 1, the encoded image records its own dimensions, and *pixel_width* and *pixel_height* shall either be equal to those dimensions or both be 0. A writer shall not store dimensions that differ from those of the encoded image. A reader shall take the dimensions from the encoded image when both fields are 0, and may rely on the fields otherwise.

When *format* is one of {2,3,4,5}, the size of the picture buffer when uncompressed shall be at least *pixel_width* {times} *pixel_height* {times} the number of components per pixel.
```

### Change 2 of 2 - the two attribute descriptions in Table 93

Table 93 is generated from `definitions/base-entities/graphics.yaml`. Both fields currently carry a
description that only repeats the field name, so the table says nothing about the rule above.

Current text:

```yaml
  - name: pixel_width
    data_type:
      kind: UnsignedInteger
    required: true
    description: "*pixel_width*"
  - name: pixel_height
    data_type:
      kind: UnsignedInteger
    required: true
    description: "*pixel_height*"
```

Replace with:

```yaml
  - name: pixel_width
    data_type:
      kind: UnsignedInteger
    required: true
    description: "*pixel_width*; 0 when *format* is 0 or 1 and the dimensions are taken from the encoded image"
  - name: pixel_height
    data_type:
      kind: UnsignedInteger
    required: true
    description: "*pixel_height*; 0 when *format* is 0 or 1 and the dimensions are taken from the encoded image"
```

This change is presentational only and adds no requirement the paragraph does not already state. It
is included because a reader consulting the table alone would otherwise see two fields described
solely by their own names, with no indication that 0 is a permitted and meaningful value.

## Notes

The measurements were made with nanoPRC, an independent C99 PRC reader and writer, by decoding
each embedded PNG and JPEG buffer and comparing the decoded dimensions against the picture record.
The two Acrobat files were produced by writing a single image and varying only the two declared
fields.

The reference-viewer behaviour above was found while investigating a separate defect in nanoPRC's
own output, which is not the subject of this request and is not claimed to be a defect in the
specification.
title: PRC: pixel_width and pixel_height are declared ignored for PNG and JPEG, but readers need a rule [CR-33]

body:
**CR-30.** This change request is identified as CR-30 in the reports and correspondence it
arises from; please quote that identifier in any reply so the two stay tied together.

**Location:** 7.9.21.9.5 `PRC_HCG_CompositeCurve`, the second sentence
(`iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc`, the paragraph introducing
`PRC_HCG_CompositeCurve`).

**Please read the last section before the rest.** The reading proposed here is an argument from
structure by two implementers. Neither of us has knowledge of what the sentence was intended to
mean, and if the committee has that knowledge and it differs, the intent should win and this
request should be refused.

## Defect

7.9.21.9.5 reads, in full:

```
The PRC_HCG_CompositeCurve structure defines a compressed composite curve (see Table 239). It must not be
used on edges or coedges.
```

A compressed B-rep contains no `PRC_TYPE_TOPO_Edge` (7.9.9) and no `PRC_TYPE_TOPO_CoEdge` (7.9.10)
entity. The prohibition therefore names two entity types that do not occur in the structure the
clause describes, and a reader cannot tell from the text which of two incompatible restrictions is
intended:

1. **It concerns uncompressed topology.** A compressed curve can be referenced from an uncompressed
   `PRC_TYPE_TOPO_Edge` through a `RefOrCompressedCurve`, and the sentence restricts that. On this
   reading the sentence says nothing about the inside of a compressed B-rep, and a composite curve
   may trim a compressed face.
2. **It concerns the compressed B-rep's own edges.** On this reading the entities 7.9.21 calls edges
   are compressed curves referenced from faces, and a composite curve used as a trimming curve is
   prohibited.

The two readings produce different writers and different readers. A writer following reading 1 emits
files a reader following reading 2 must reject.

## Evidence

### The clause's own vocabulary points both ways

Measured across all 1,413 lines of 7.9.21: "edge" occurs three times, "coedge" once.

**Toward reading 2.** 7.9.21 does use "edge" for entities inside a compressed B-rep, and points at
the curve clause when it does -- "number_edge_references represents the number of referenced edges in
the brep; see 7.9.21.9", where 7.9.21.9 is `CompressedCurve`. The only other use is in the same
register, "the two other trimming edge curves", describing an iso-face's trimming curves.

**Toward reading 1.** "coedge" occurs exactly once in the whole of 7.9.21 -- inside the prohibition
itself. A compressed B-rep has no coedge concept under any reading. "edges or coedges" is the
standard pairing from 7.9.9 and 7.9.10, which reads as vocabulary carried over from the uncompressed
clauses rather than language chosen for this one.

We think that two-way split is the finding rather than a failure to look harder, and we do not
propose to resolve the clause on it.

### A structural argument, contributed by a second implementation

Stated here as their reasoning rather than ours, and offered as reasoning rather than measurement:

**A compressed face's trimming is already a composition mechanism.** An ana-face's loops are walked
as a sequence of curves terminated by `PRC_HCG_NewLoop` or `PRC_HCG_EndLoop`. The loop *is* the
composite. Placing a `PRC_HCG_CompositeCurve` inside one nests a sequence of curves within a sequence
of curves, with two different terminators and no stated rule for how they interact.

**On an iso-face the prohibition is not merely useful but necessary.** 7.9.21.5.1 defines an iso-face
as a surface trimmed by four iso-parametric curves, and Table 216 fixes the count at four, with the
`sense_array` assigning each to a natural boundary -- Umin, Vmin, Umax, Vmax. A composite curve is by
construction multi-segment and therefore not a single iso-parametric boundary. There is no slot in
that structure a composite could legally occupy.

**So under reading 2 the sentence has work to do on both compressed face types, and under reading 1
it has none anywhere inside 7.9.21** -- which is the clause the sentence sits in. That is weak on its
own, since clauses do sometimes constrain things defined elsewhere, but it points the same way as the
rest.

### What no corpus can settle

Neither implementation has found a file that exercises the question. It cannot be decided by
measurement, which is why it is put as a clause problem.

## Proposed change

One sentence.

**Current text**

```
It must not be used on edges or coedges.
```

**Replacement text**

```
It shall not be used as a trimming curve of a compressed face, and shall not be referenced from the iso-edge
or ana-edge cache of a PRC_TYPE_TOPO_BrepDataCompress.
```

The replacement also changes "must not" to "shall not", which is the form ISO/IEC Directives Part 2
requires for a prohibition and which the surrounding clauses use.

## Effect if accepted

The prohibition names entities that exist in the structure the clause describes, so a writer of
compressed B-rep can tell whether it applies, and a reader can tell what to reject. Nothing is said
about uncompressed topology, which under this reading the sentence never governed.

If the committee's answer is instead reading 1, the same defect still needs fixing and the
replacement would be:

```
It shall not be used as the curve of a PRC_TYPE_TOPO_Edge or of a PRC_TYPE_TOPO_CoEdge. It may be used as a
trimming curve of a compressed face.
```

We are not asking for a choice between these. We are proposing the first and recording the second so
that a decision the other way has drafting ready rather than a fresh request.

## On the standing of this request

Neither implementation involved has any knowledge of what the sentence was intended to mean, and
neither is in a position to say what the original specification work had in view. The argument above
is structural: it says the prohibition makes sense of the compressed structures as they are
documented, and does not make sense of anything in the clause under the alternative reading.

If a committee member knows the intent, that knowledge should decide this and not the argument above.
If nobody does, then what is being asked is what the sentence should say now, and we would rather it
said one of the two things above than what it says today.
title: PRC: a compressed composite curve may trim a compressed face, and the curves inside it are stored in full and take no place in the list of curves [CR-30]

body:
Clause 7.8.9.8, `CompressedTextureParameter`, paragraphs 2 and 3 (the paragraphs beginning
*"**binary_texture_data** represents a bit field"* and *"**reference_array** is used to reference UV
parameters"*), together with Table 176 and Table 177.

A bit in `binary_texture_data` is **emitted** once per corner encountered during mesh traversal —
three per triangle. What the bit **compares** is whether the UV parameter was already stored *for
that vertex*. Both paragraphs describe only the comparison, and that description is the only thing
in the clause from which a reader can infer the emission, so the natural reading gives one bit per
vertex rather than three per triangle.

The word "vertex" is not wrong where it stands: the comparison genuinely is per vertex. The defect
is that one sentence carries both quantities and names only one of them.

**Recommendation for correction**

Replace the second paragraph of 7.8.9.8, which currently reads:

> *binary_texture_data* represents a bit field. During mesh traversal, if the current vertex has a
> texture, a bit texture_is_reference is set in this array. This bit is true if the same UV
> parameter has already been stored during mesh traversal for the same vertex. In this case, the
> reference index is stored in reference_array. Otherwise, this bit is set to FALSE and UV
> parameters are stored in Texture_parameters.

with:

> *binary_texture_data* represents a bit field containing one *texture_is_reference* bit for each
> corner encountered during mesh traversal, in traversal order. *texture_is_reference* is TRUE 
> if the UV parameter for the current corner's vertex has already been stored during the treatment
> of another triangle, in which case the reference index is stored in *reference_array*. Otherwise 
> *texture_is_reference* is FALSE and the UV parameter is stored in *texture_parameters*.

and the third paragraph, which currently reads:

> *reference_array* is used to reference UV parameters. The references on UV parameters are done
> per vertex. A UV parameter for the current vertex is referenced only if the same UV parameter has
> already been stored for the same vertex during the treatment of another triangle. This treatment
> is performed during mesh traversal, the same way as the treatment for normals.

with:

> *reference_array* is used to reference UV parameters already stored, and contains one entry for
> each corner whose *texture_is_reference* bit is TRUE. The comparison is made per vertex: the UV
> parameter for the current corner is referenced only if the same UV parameter has already been
> stored for the same vertex during the treatment of another triangle. This treatment is performed
> during mesh traversal, the same way as the treatment for normals.

Optionally, add the resulting consistency condition, which gives readers the validation rule the
clause currently lacks:

> *reference_array_size* + *texture_parameters_size* / 2 shall equal the number of bits in the bit
> field, every corner being accounted for either as a reference or as a stored UV pair.

Two further points, both in Table 177 and editorial in that no bit on the wire changes:

1. `last_integer_used_bit_number` contradicts its own description, which reads *"The number of
   padding bits appended to the bit field to bring its length to a multiple of 32."* The length
   formula subtracts it, so it is a count of **padding** bits; the name says "used bit number",
   which is the complement. An implementer following the name computes `size * 32 - (32 - padding)`
   and is wrong by a constant on every entity whose last word is partly used. If the field holds
   padding bits, `padding_bit_count` says so. If the intent was the used bits in the last word,
   the formula needs changing instead. We assume the former because that is what the arithmetic
   does, but the clause as written supports the opposite reading.

2. `texture_binary_data` (Table 177) is a transposition of `binary_texture_data` (Table 176), the
   field whose type contains it. A rename is proposed separately as
   [pdf-association/3dpdf-twg#15](https://github.com/pdf-association/3dpdf-twg/pull/15); it is
   mentioned here only so the two are not resolved independently. Nothing above depends on it.
title: PRC: Clause 7.8.9.8: "vertex" describes both the emission and the comparison, and they differ by a factor of three

body:
**Reviewed with Datalogics (Patrick Gallot), with three suggestions applied.**

**Change type: advisory / informative addition, not a normative correction.** Unlike CR-16, which
supplied a complete validated replacement for a missing function body, this CR does not claim to
have found the fully general algorithm. It documents a real, quantified, reader-impacting finding
together with a partial empirical improvement and an honest residual gap, so that the committee and
implementor community have visibility into both rather than waiting on a closed answer.

**Verified against** the TWG working source at commit `934f079`, fetched 24 September 2026.
Citations are by file and line rather than by section or table number, because those are in motion
while the document is edited.

---

## Background

The field is defined at `iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/tessellation.yaml:566-572`. Its
description covers cardinality only:

> The number of normals is implicit, depending on the number of triangles and faces. Vertices have
> always as many normals as the number of faces to which they belong.

`normal_is_reversed` is present when `must_recalculate_normals == TRUE` — that is, when no
per-vertex normals are supplied and a decoder must reconstruct them from geometry. Neither this
entry nor, so far as we have found, any other part of the base specification or the companion
pseudo-code document gives an **encoder** any guidance on how to derive the value.

This is a distinct question from CR-15, which concerns decoder-side timing of when an
already-encoded bit is consumed. This CR concerns what an encoder should compute in the first place,
for the specific case where no external per-vertex normal source exists to compare against.

Compounding the guidance gap, `iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:2836` currently states:

> The *normal_is_reversed* field is reserved for future use.

That directly contradicts its established real-world role as an actively consumed, load-bearing
field in every `must_recalculate_normals == TRUE` implementation we are aware of, and it relates to
the cardinality question already open as #750. The findings below suggest the field's basic
documented status, not only derivation guidance for it, needs correction.

A superficially reasonable approach — and the one nanoPRC used before this finding — is an
independent per-triangle geometric decision: compute a smoothed per-vertex proxy normal, an
equal-weighted average of adjacent face normals since no better source exists in the normal-free
case, and compare it by dot-product sign against the triangle's own local winding. That mirrors
what the `must_recalculate_normals == FALSE` case does when a real per-vertex normal is available.

## Finding: the independent per-triangle decision is empirically unreliable

Measuring the reconstructed normal as a real decoder computes it — geometric winding of the
triangle's own decoded position, corrected by whatever the encoder wrote — against true geometry:

| measurement | result |
|:--|:--|
| wrong-value rate, independent per-triangle decision | **52%** on a 227,000-triangle real file |
| wrong-value rate, same method, four smaller real files | **100% of affected triangles** |

The check is against true geometry, not merely internal self-consistency or agreement with another
encoder's output.

## Empirical improvement: chain-inheritance

Inheriting the value from a growing triangle's parent in the traversal, rather than deciding each
triangle independently:

| measurement | result |
|:--|:--|
| 227,000-triangle file | 52% → **5.1%** |
| four smaller files | 100% → **~0%** |
| real Adobe Acrobat blank-model-tree rejections fixed | **2 of 4** previously-failing files |

## Residual gap — stated because it is not closed

Chain-inheritance is **not** a complete solution. A residual gap of roughly 5% remains on complex
meshes. It has a known, validated root cause which we have not resolved, and we are flagging it as
an open question rather than presenting it as settled. We would rather file an incomplete finding
with the gap named than hold it until it is closed.

## CR-22a — proposed advisory NOTE

**Location:** the companion *Pseudo-code Additions* document, adjacent to the
`MustRecalculateNormals == TRUE` branch discussion (Function 6, cross-referenced from CR-15c). We
cannot give a file and line for this one because the companion document is not in the TWG working
source; if it would help, tell us where it now lives and we will re-cite it accordingly.

**Proposed text (informative, not normative):**

> **NOTE — Encoder guidance for `normal_is_reversed` when no per-vertex normal source is
> available.** This document describes the field's presence and cardinality but does not prescribe
> how a conforming encoder should derive its value. Implementor experience indicates that an
> independent, per-triangle decision — comparing each triangle's own winding against a
> locally-smoothed proxy normal, in the absence of any true per-vertex normal source — is unreliable
> in practice, and implementors are advised to consider inheriting the value from a growing
> triangle's parent in the traversal instead, which measurably improves reliability on real-world
> test data, though neither approach is claimed to be complete or universally correct for all source
> geometry. Multiple different assignments of this field, each internally consistent with a given
> mesh's true geometry, are observed to occur among conforming implementations in practice.
> Accordingly, this specification does not mandate a single derivation algorithm, and decoders
> should not assume any particular derivation strategy.

**Confidence.** Medium-high for the quantitative findings — both wrong-value rates are directly
measured and reproducible. Low-medium for the proposed NOTE wording and for the inference that the
specification should not mandate a single algorithm; both are our interpretation and are open to
committee revision. This CR is submitted primarily to put the data in front of the committee,
including the open residual gap, rather than to propose normative text with high confidence.

## Summary

| Item | Status |
|:--|:--|
| Independent per-triangle proxy-normal decision is empirically unreliable | Confirmed — 52% wrong on a 227K-triangle real file; 100% of affected triangles on four smaller ones |
| Chain-inheritance dramatically improves reliability | Confirmed — 52%→5.1% and 100%→~0%; **not** claimed complete |
| Chain-inheritance fixes real Acrobat blank-model-tree rejections | Confirmed for 2 of 4 previously-failing files |
| Residual ~5% gap on complex meshes has a known root cause | **Not resolved** — open, flagged for future work |
| Specification should mandate one derivation algorithm | **Not proposed** — advisory only, given evidence that multiple valid derivations exist |

## Provenance

Confirmed against the nanoPRC implementation (CascadiaVoxel LLC, AGPLv3,
https://github.com/mvrhel/nanoPRC) by a true-geometry consistency check, and for a subset of cases
against Adobe Acrobat directly.

@datalogics-pgallot reviewed this text on 14 August 2026 and proposed three changes, all of which
were applied before filing: the NOTE was reworded to drop a requirement-shaped clause that did not
belong inside informative text; and he proposed a venue split, keeping this CR in-spec while a
broader acceptance-behaviour catalogue goes into a separate implementer note. We agreed to that
split and it is reflected above.

The delay between his review and this filing is ours alone, and we apologise for it.
title: PRC: `normal_is_reversed` has no encoder guidance, and independent per-triangle derivation is empirically unreliable [CR-22]

body:
Clause 7.9.21, *Read/Write Algorithm for CompressedPoint*; the two clauses both titled
`WritePoint3DWithVariableBitNumber` at 9.10 and 9.19; and clauses 9.13
`WriteIntegerWithVariableBitNumber` and 9.15 `WriteDoubleWithVariableBitNumber`.

**First, what is not wrong.** 9.13 and 9.15 are not in conflict. They encode different types and
each is self-consistent with the width convention its own callers use:

| | width derived by | writer | bits occupied |
|---|---|---|---|
| integer path | `GetNumberOfBitsUsedToStoreInteger` — signed, sign included | 9.13 writes sign + `n-1` | `n` |
| double path | a magnitude count | 9.15 writes sign + `n` | `n + 1` |

9.14 writes exactly its `uBitNumber` bits, so both are exact. Either convention is workable. No
change is requested to either clause.

**1. The defect is that one normative algorithm mixes them.** The `WriteCompressedPoint` procedure
in 7.9.21 derives its width in the *integer* convention and then spends it in the *double* one:

```
uMaxCoordinate ← MAX(|x|, |y|, |z|) / dTol + 1
uNbBits        ← GetNumberOfBitsToStore(uMaxCoordinate) + 1      -- magnitude bits, +1 for sign
…
WritePoint3DWithVariableBitNumber(x, y, z, dTol, uNbBits)        -- routes to 9.15
```

`uMaxCoordinate` is a magnitude, so `uNbBits` is magnitude-bits-plus-one — the sign is already paid
for. 9.15 then writes a sign bit of its own and treats `uNbBits` as the magnitude width. Followed
literally the procedure emits **one bit more per coordinate than it accounted for**, three per
point, in the most frequently used compressed structure in the format.

The matching `ReadCompressedPoint` does not resolve it: it delegates to
`ReadPoint3DWithVariableBitNumber(dTol, uNbBits)` without stating how many bits that consumes.

**2. `WritePoint3DWithVariableBitNumber` is defined twice, under the same title, with different
contracts** — at 9.10 and at 9.19 — which is what lets the mismatch pass unnoticed. 9.10 takes a
point and a tolerance, derives the width itself, writes it as a 6-bit prefix, and routes each
coordinate through 9.13 (so `n` is the total). 9.19 takes the width as a parameter, writes no
prefix, and routes through 9.15 (so `n` is the magnitude). A cross-reference selects one of two
encodings that differ by a bit per coordinate, and nothing at either site says which is intended.
The 7.9.21 pseudocode's own references are already adrift of this: it cites §9.17 and §9.18 for
`WriteDouble` and `WritePoint3DWithVariableBitNumber` where the current heading order gives 9.18
and 9.19.

**3. Two of the three bit-counting functions used in normative text are undefined.** The
specification defines `GetNumberOfBitsUsedToStoreUnsignedInteger` (9.1) and then invokes two others
that appear nowhere: `GetNumberOfBitsUsedToStoreInteger`, in 9.8 and three times in 9.10, and
`GetNumberOfBitsToStore`, in the 7.9.21 pseudocode above. Since what separates these names is
precisely whether the sign bit is counted, the undefined ones are exactly those that would have
settled defect 1.

**What it costs.** Every field whose width is given as a bit count is ambiguous by one bit per
value. Table 238 is the clearest case: `point_number_bits` and `tangent_number_bits` are each
specified as *"GetNumberOfBitsUsedToStoreUnsignedInteger() + 1"*, and whether that `+1` is the sign
bit or sits on top of one decides whether a coordinate occupies `point_number_bits` bits or one
more. That is three bits per point on a curve with no length prefix and no padding, so the next
field starts in the wrong place and everything after it is misread. The failure is silent: the
decode does not throw, it drifts.

**This is not hypothetical.** Two independently written readers made opposite choices and each
believed it was following the clause.

The two readers disagreed on the Hermite curve's `point_number_bits`. One reads that count as
total-including-sign and reports it exercised on 11,317 Hermite curves across 17 files of a public
collection; the other read it as magnitude-only until recently. Both cite the same sentence. *That
measurement covers the Hermite field only* — stated separately here because it does not extend to
`CompressedPoint`'s `uNbBits`, which is what this ticket is about.

**On `CompressedPoint` the two readers now AGREE, and they agree on a combination neither clause
states.** Both take the 6-bit width prefix and the over-30 threshold from 7.9.21's
`WriteCompressedPoint`, then decode each coordinate through the 9.15
`WriteDoubleWithVariableBitNumber` layer treating the width as **sign-inclusive** — one sign bit, then
`number_of_bits - 1` of magnitude. Neither implementation arrived at that by reading the other's
source; each carries a comment to the effect that the width is the whole field with the sign
included. Two independent readers converging on a hybrid that no single clause describes is stronger
than either one's practice on its own, and it is the mechanism behind recommendation 1's second
option: the route the document describes is not the route real files require.

**A related defect in the same clause, separable from the sign-bit question.** 7.9.21's
`WriteCompressedPoint` carries an explicit fallback — at a width of 30 bits or fewer the point is
packed, otherwise it is written as three plain doubles. The corresponding constraint in 9.19 states
the threshold and describes **no fallback at all**. Real files need one: across two collections the
widths actually observed on that branch are 31, 32, 35, 36, 50 and 58, the four widest of which
require a differently-tagged structure rather than the plain-double path. So the route 7.9.21 uses is
incomplete for real data whichever way the sign-bit question resolves. Numbered as item 6 below.

**A third stale cross-reference, and the worst-placed.** Alongside the 7.9.21 pseudocode citing
§9.17 and §9.18 where the heading order gives 9.18 and 9.19, **9.19's opening sentence says "using
the variable-bit-number encoding defined in §9.14"** while its body calls
`WriteDoubleWithVariableBitNumber`, which is §9.15. §9.14 is
`WriteUnsignedIntegerWithVariableBitNumber` — the layer that carries the magnitude and *excludes* the
sign bit. In a clause whose whole ambiguity is whether the sign bit is counted, the cross-reference
points the reader at the sign-free layer. The companion "(see §9.14 constraint)" nearby is correct,
since 9.14 does carry the "shall be less than 31" sentence.

**Recommendation for correction**

1. **Make 7.9.21's `WriteCompressedPoint` consistent with the writer it calls.** Either drop the
   `+ 1` from the width derivation, so that `uNbBits` is the magnitude count 9.15 expects, or route
   the coordinates through the integer form (9.10/9.13) for which a sign-inclusive `uNbBits` is
   correct. The second matches what existing files appear to contain — see below — but either
   makes the procedure self-consistent, and only one bit per coordinate separates them.

2. **State in each of 9.13 and 9.15 whether `uBitNumber` includes the sign bit.** Neither clause
   says so, and they differ; one sentence apiece would prevent the same mismatch recurring at
   another call site. No change to the encodings themselves is being asked for.

3. **Remove or retitle one of the two `WritePoint3DWithVariableBitNumber` clauses.** If both
   encodings are genuinely in use, they need distinct names — the deriving form and the
   width-parameterised form are different procedures and cannot share an identifier that other
   clauses cross-reference.

4. **Define `GetNumberOfBitsUsedToStoreInteger` and `GetNumberOfBitsToStore`**, or restate their
   call sites in terms of the defined 9.1 with the sign bit added explicitly.
   (For a reviewer checking this: `GetNumberOfBitsUsedToStoreInteger` does **not** appear in the
   `.adoc` or `.yaml` sources at all. It lives in the `include::../code/*.cpp` files, used once in
   9.8 and three times in 9.10, and is defined nowhere. Grepping the section sources alone will
   suggest the function is absent and the claim wrong.)

5. **In Table 238, state the width of a stored coordinate in bits**, rather than leaving it to be
   inferred from the formula that produced `point_number_bits`. The same applies to any other table
   that carries a `*_number_bits` field.

6. **Give 9.19 the over-30 fallback that 7.9.21's `WriteCompressedPoint` already has**, or state
   where a reader should go when the width exceeds it. As written, 9.19 gives the threshold and no
   alternative path, and real files exceed it — observed widths on that branch are 31, 32, 35, 36,
   50 and 58. This is independent of the sign-bit question and can be resolved separately.

7. **Correct 9.19's opening cross-reference from §9.14 to §9.15.** Its body calls
   `WriteDoubleWithVariableBitNumber` (9.15); §9.14 is the unsigned-integer layer, which excludes the
   sign bit. The nearby "(see §9.14 constraint)" is correct and should stay.

**Additional context**

*What existing files appear to contain.* Our reader consumes a `CompressedPoint` coordinate in
`uNbBits` bits **total** — sign plus `uNbBits - 1` of magnitude, the integer-path reading — and
decodes the compressed B-rep of several hundred files in two collections on that basis. Read the
other way, every such file would be misaligned by three bits at the first point. We therefore
believe real writers follow the integer route, which is the one the 7.9.21 pseudocode does not
specify.

The same choice arises for Table 238's `point_number_bits` and `tangent_number_bits`, whose
derivation is worded identically (*"GetNumberOfBitsUsedToStoreUnsignedInteger() + 1"*). Our reader
read those as magnitude-only until today and changed to total-including-sign on evidence: one more
file in a 529-file corpus becomes decodable, none regress, and it agrees with a second independent
implementation that reports the same reading exercised on 11,317 Hermite curves across 17 files.
We changed it on measurement, not on the document, because the document supports both.

The reason we can offer the corpus evidence but not a reading is that no writer we have access to
can settle it either: a writer that computes the width and consumes it in the same process is
self-consistent under either convention, so round-tripping proves nothing. It takes two independent
implementations to see the defect at all, which is why it has survived.


**Source locations**

Resolved against the PDF Association TWG working source at commit `84d98e1` (27 September 2026),
the same commit the reviewer used. Clause numbers are the heading order in
`iso-prc/sections/09-io-algorithms.adoc` and are given alongside, but the file and line is what
stays checkable when the numbering moves again.

| what | clause | file:line at `84d98e1` |
|---|---|---|
| `GetNumberOfBitsUsedToStoreUnsignedInteger` | 9.1 | `sections/09-io-algorithms.adoc:5` |
| `WritePoint3DWithVariableBitNumber` (first) | 9.10 | `sections/09-io-algorithms.adoc:124` |
| `WriteIntegerWithVariableBitNumber` | 9.13 | `sections/09-io-algorithms.adoc:157` |
| `WriteUnsignedIntegerWithVariableBitNumber` | 9.14 | `sections/09-io-algorithms.adoc:173` |
| `WriteDoubleWithVariableBitNumber` | 9.15 | `sections/09-io-algorithms.adoc:189` |
| `WriteDouble` | 9.18 | `sections/09-io-algorithms.adoc:229` |
| `WritePoint3DWithVariableBitNumber` (second) | 9.19 | `sections/09-io-algorithms.adoc:256` |
| the §9.14 cross-reference of item 7 | 9.19 opening | `sections/09-io-algorithms.adoc:258` |
| `WriteCompressedPoint` | 7.9.21 | `sections/07-base-entities.adoc:4159` |
| `ReadCompressedPoint` | 7.9.21 | `sections/07-base-entities.adoc:4183` |
| `point_number_bits` | Table 238 | `definitions/base-entities/topology.yaml:1492` |
| its `GetNumberOfBitsUsedToStoreUnsignedInteger() + 1` formula | Table 238 | `definitions/base-entities/topology.yaml:1496` |

Two notes for anyone checking these. The 9.19 opening at `:258` reads *"using the variable-bit-number
encoding defined in §9.14"* while the procedure below it calls `WriteDoubleWithVariableBitNumber`,
which is at `:189` — that is item 7. And `GetNumberOfBitsUsedToStoreInteger`, of item 4, appears in
none of the `.adoc` or `.yaml` sources: it is in the `include::../code/*.cpp` files only.
title: PRC: Clause 7.9.21 / Clause 9: the CompressedPoint algorithm derives a bit count in one convention and spends it in the other

body:
*`CompressedShell` -- `<<tab-entities-CompressedShell>>`, Table 202 in the N808 CD. The table is
generated from `iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/topology.yaml`, so its number is assigned at build
time; the entity name and the field names are the stable reference.*

The table gives `number_of_faces` as:

| field | as written |
|---|---|
| `single_face` | (Required) True if there is only a single face in the shell |
| `number_of_faces` | **(Optional; if `single_face` is TRUE)** Number of faces in the shell **if there is more than a single face** |

The presence condition says the count is present when `single_face` is TRUE. The description in the
same cell says it carries a count only when there is more than one face. Both cannot hold: when
`single_face` is TRUE there is by definition one face, and the count the description describes does
not exist.

The gate must read **"if `single_face` is FALSE"**.

In the working draft the two halves sit in the same YAML node, which makes the contradiction plainer
than the rendered table does:

```yaml
- name: number_of_faces
  data_type: NumberOfBitsThenUnsignedInteger
  description: Number of faces in the shell if there is more than a single face.
  required: false
  require_conditions: "if *single_face* is TRUE"
```

**A SECOND CONSEQUENCE IN THE SAME ENTITY, which the gate fix alone does not resolve.** The two
arrays that follow both take their length from that field:

```yaml
- name: faces        occurrence: number_of_faces
- name: is_iso_face  occurrence: number_of_faces
```

When `single_face` is TRUE, `number_of_faces` is absent under either reading -- so both arrays
reference a field that does not exist in the stream, and nothing states that their length is 1.
Correcting the presence condition leaves that gap open. We read it as 1 and so, by the corpus
evidence below, does every writer; it is simply not written down.

A reader implementing the condition literally consumes a `NumberOfBitsThenUnsignedInteger` -- five
bits plus its payload -- that is not present in the stream, and desyncs on **every single-face
shell**. By count that is the large majority of compressed shells, so the literal reading does not
degrade gracefully; it loses the body.

**Recommendation**

Change the presence condition of `number_of_faces` in Table 202 from

> (Optional; if `single_face` is TRUE)

to

> (Optional; if `single_face` is FALSE)

The field description needs no change -- it already describes the FALSE-gated behaviour.

**Additional context**

Corpus measurement over our PRC collection, which is assembled from publicly available 3D PDFs:

| | occurrences | files | is a count present? |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `single_face = TRUE` | **24,016** | 19 | **no, in every case** |
| `single_face = FALSE` | 766 | 53 | yes, in every case |

Measured 2 October 2026 over 529 files, of which 67 carry at least one `CompressedShell`.
title: PRC: Table 202 `number_of_faces`: the presence condition is inverted, and contradicts its own description

body:
Section 14.11.7 (Open prepress interface (OPI)) of the PDF 2.0 spec describes the **GrayMap** field in Table 406 as follows:

> (Optional) An array of 2n integers in the range 0 to 65,535 (where n is the number of bits per sample) recording changes made to the brightness or contrast of the image.

I think that "2n" should be "2^n" here.  The gray map is a lookup table which gives one output value for each possible pixel value, and an image with n bits per sample has 2^n possible pixel values.

The OPI 1.3 specification ([OPI_13.pdf](https://web.archive.org/web/2019/https://www.adobe.com/content/dam/acom/en/devnet/postscript/pdfs/OPI_13.pdf), page 11, description of `%ALDImageGrayMap`) supports this:

> A bitmap will have two GrayMap values (corresponding to pixel values 0 and 1); a 4-bit grayscale image will have 16 values; and an 8-bit image will have 256 values.

The examples on pages 13 and 14 of that document also have 16 values for `%ALDImageType: 1 4` and 256 values for `%ALDImageType: 1 8`.
title: Length of GrayMap in OPI 1.3 dictionaries

body:
**Describe the bug**

ISO 32000-2:2020, 9.10.3 "ToUnicode CMaps", first and second bullet; Table 125a "Additional entries in a ToUnicode CMap stream dictionary" (added by #462).

1. **Codespace in a ToUnicode CMap that uses another one.** The second bullet of 9.10.3 requires that the CMap file "contain begincodespacerange and endcodespacerange operators". The first bullet and the UseCMap entry of Table 125a allow a ToUnicode CMap to be based on another ToUnicode CMap. Adobe TN #5014 (normative reference, cited by 9.10.3 as the full syntax documentation), 5.4, says that the using CMap adopts the codespace of the used CMap, and: "It causes an error to try to redefine the adopted codespace." A child CMap that follows 9.10.3 must therefore declare a codespace that TN #5014 treats as an error to redefine. The text does not say whether an identical redeclaration is allowed, whether a different one is allowed, or whether the child may (or must) omit the codespace operators.

2. **UseCMap names a predefined CMap.** Table 125a, UseCMap: "The name of a predefined CMap, or a stream containing a CMap." There are no predefined ToUnicode CMaps. All CMaps in Table 116 map character codes to CIDs (9.7.5.2, NOTE 1), but 9.10.3, third bullet, requires mappings to Unicode with `beginbfchar`/`beginbfrange`. This was pointed out in the last comment of #462, after the TWG agreement; the published Table 125a still has the text.

3. **Text copied from Table 118 that does not apply.** Table 125a keeps two phrases from Table 118 that make no sense for a ToUnicode CMap: in CIDSystemInfo, the parenthesis about "Identity-H or Identity-V CMaps"; in WMode, the writing mode "for any CIDFont with which this CMap is combined". This was also pointed out in the last comment of #462.

**Recommendation for correction**

- 9.10.3, second bullet: "The CMap file shall contain begincodespacerange and endcodespacerange operators that are consistent with the encoding that the font uses, unless the CMap uses another ToUnicode CMap (usecmap operator, UseCMap entry). Such a CMap adopts the codespace of the used CMap; if it contains codespace operators, they shall define exactly the same codespace ranges."
- Table 125a, UseCMap: "(Optional) A stream containing the ToUnicode CMap on which this CMap is based. If this entry is present, the referencing CMap shall specify only the mappings that differ from the referenced CMap." If names are to remain allowed, state which names are meant, since Table 116 contains none that can be used here.
- Table 125a: delete the Identity-H/Identity-V parenthesis in CIDSystemInfo. For WMode, either state that it has no effect for a ToUnicode CMap or delete the row.

**Additional context**

Found while implementing a validator.

Related: #462 (closed, ISO approved; created Table 125a), #635 (open; PDF/A rule on CMaps that reference other CMaps, applied to ToUnicode), #344 (open; CIDSystemInfo for ToUnicode CMaps), #780 (open; under-specified ToUnicode CMaps).
title: 9.10.3 / Table 125a: codespace operators and UseCMap target in ToUnicode CMaps that are based on another CMap

body:
**Describe the bug**

ISO 32000-2:2020, 8.9.7 "Inline images": the first paragraph below Table 90 (as corrected by #20) and NOTE 2. The ID operator is followed by a single white-space character "Unless the image uses ASCIIHexDecode or ASCII85Decode as its final or only filter". NOTE 2 uses the same wording.

Table 5 (Filter) says that multiple filters "shall be specified in the order in which they are to be applied", that is, in decoding order. In that order the "final" filter is the last array element, which receives the output of the other filters and not the bytes that follow ID. The filter that reads the bytes after ID, and to which the white-space exception logically applies, is the first array element. It is the "final" filter only in encoding order, which is the order 7.4.1 uses in its own example ("LZW and ASCII base-85 encoding (in that order)", giving `[/ASCII85Decode /LZWDecode]`).

Example: for `/F [/A85 /Fl]`, does the exception apply (A85 is the final filter when encoding) or not (Fl is the final filter when decoding)? Both readings occur: #543, for example, reads "final filter" as "the first name in the Filter list".

**Recommendation for correction**

In both places, replace "its final or only filter" / "the final or only filter" with:

> "the first (or only) filter in its Filter array, that is, the filter that is applied first when decoding"

**Additional context**

Found while implementing a validator.

#20 (closed, ISO approved) introduced the wording "final or only filter" in the paragraph; the array order was not discussed there.
title: 8.9.7 (as corrected by #20): "final or only filter" is ambiguous with respect to the order of the Filter array

body:
**Describe the bug**

ISO 32000-2:2020, 9.7.6.2 "CMap mapping", second paragraph; 9.7.5.4 "CMap example and operator summary" (embedded CMaps follow Adobe Technical Note #5014); 9.10.3 "ToUnicode CMaps", paragraphs on `beginbfrange` below EXAMPLE 2.

Codespace ranges are defined per byte: according to 9.7.6.2 a code matches if "the value of each of its bytes lies between the corresponding bytes" of the bounds. A multi-byte codespace range is therefore a rectangle, not an interval.

For the mapping range operators (`begincidrange`, `beginnotdefrange`, `beginbfrange`) ISO 32000-2 does not say which codes lie between `srcCode1` and `srcCode2` when the two codes differ in a byte other than the last one, nor in which order those codes are numbered:

- 9.10.3 implies a linear interval: "Consecutive codes starting with srcCode1 and ending with srcCode2", with m = srcCode2 − srcCode1 + 1 destination strings, and the limit 255 − (srcCode2 − srcCode1) for the last byte of dstString also uses the numeric difference.
- TN #5014 (normative reference), 5.2, says the domain of code mappings "may be multidimensional if the codespace is multidimensional". This suggests the per-byte rectangle used for codespaces, but TN #5014 does not define how CIDs are numbered over such a rectangle. TN #5014, B.4, notes that ATM-J only supports range operations in which the last byte varies, which implies that other implementations may accept more.
- TN #5411 (in the Bibliography since #277), 1.4.1, cautions for `bfrange` that "care must be taken not to cross first-byte boundaries".

Example (codespace `<0000> <FFFF>`): `<0110> <0220> 100` in a `cidrange` block is 273 codes (CIDs 100 to 372) under the linear reading, but 2 × 17 = 34 codes under the rectangle reading. `<01FE> <0201>` is 4 codes under the linear reading, but not a valid range under the rectangle reading (the second byte has low > high). Writers and readers cannot tell which result is intended, and validators cannot decide whether such a range is valid.

For reference: every range line in Adobe's published predefined CMap files and Adobe-*-UCS2 ToUnicode mapping files differs from its partner only in the last byte; even Identity-H is written as 256 ranges `<xx00> <xxFF>`.

**Recommendation for correction** (two alternatives, for the TWG to choose)

A. Restrict. With this rule the linear and the rectangle readings give the same result, and it matches TN #5411 1.4.1, TN #5014 B.4 and Adobe's own CMap files. Add as a new item in the list of 9.7.5.4, and refer to it from 9.10.3:

> "In a range mapping (begincidrange, beginnotdefrange, beginbfrange), srcCode1 and srcCode2 shall have the same length and shall differ only in their last byte. The range consists of the codes whose leading bytes equal those of srcCode1 and whose last byte lies between the last bytes of srcCode1 and srcCode2 inclusive, in increasing order."

B. Define the linear reading. Add to 9.7.5.4:

> "In a range mapping, srcCode1 and srcCode2 shall have the same length. The range consists of all codes of that length whose value, read as a big-endian unsigned integer, lies between those of srcCode1 and srcCode2 inclusive; the n-th code of the range is mapped to the n-th destination. All codes of the range shall lie within the codespace."

(The last sentence of B corresponds to TN #5014, 5.2, which requires the domain of the code mappings to lie entirely within the codespace.)

**Additional context**

Found while implementing a validator.

Related: #277 (closed, ISO approved). Its body quotes the TN #5411 first-byte caution, but the resolution only added a NOTE about the dstString rule. #559 (open, 9.7.6.2 logically incomplete; empty codespace and short strings). #780 (open, under-specified ToUnicode CMaps, including the codespace). None of these defines source-code ranges whose codes differ in a leading byte.
title: 9.7.5.4 / 9.7.6.2 / 9.10.3: meaning of cidrange, notdefrange and bfrange when srcCode1 and srcCode2 differ in a leading byte

body:
**Describe the bug**

ISO 32000-2:2020, 8.6.5.5 "ICCBased colour spaces": the last bullet of the list below Table 66, which requires profiles to conform "to the specification version indicated by the Profile version number in its header", read together with Table 66 as replaced by #181.

Corrected Table 66 maps profile header versions to two specifications only: "2.x.y.z" to ICC.1:2001-04 and "4.x.y.z where x ≤ 3" to ISO 15076-1:2010. This follows the #181 rationale that profiles with the same major version are compatible, so PDF only needs the latest v2 and v4 specifications.

The bullet, which was not changed by #181, still points to the specification of the exact header version:

- A profile with header version 4.2.0.0 would have to conform to ICC.1:2004-10 (profile version 4.2.0.0), which is not a normative reference of ISO 32000-2. Table 66, on the other hand, assigns it to ISO 15076-1:2010, which says in 7.2.4 that the version number consistent with it is "4.3.0.0".
- The same applies to 2.0 to 2.3 profiles: ICC.1:2001-04, 6.1.3, gives "2.4.0" as its profile version number.

For any profile whose minor version is not the one of the listed specification, it is therefore unclear which specification applies, and whether it conforms at all.

**Recommendation for correction**

Replace the bullet by:

> "A profile shall conform to the ICC specification listed in "Table 66 - ICC profile versions supported by ICCBased colour spaces" for its profile header version. A profile whose minor or bug-fix version is lower than that of the listed specification shall not be considered non-conforming because of its version field alone."

**Additional context**

Found while implementing a validator.

Related: #181 (closed, ISO approved; Table 66 replacement and new normative reference ICC.1:2001-04), #228 (closed, ISO approved; NOTE 2 on tags from later ICC versions).
title: 8.6.5.5: "Profiles shall conform to the specification version indicated by the Profile version number" is inconsistent with corrected Table 66 (#181)

**Describe the bug**

ISO 32000-2:2020, 9.7.4.3 "Glyph metrics in CIDFonts".

The paragraph on the W array (below the two W formats) says that specifying a given CID value more than once "should not be done". In that case, "the first specification is the one that shall be used".

The paragraphs on the W2 array (vertical metrics) use the same two kinds of group (`c [...]` and `cfirst clast ...`), but contain no corresponding statement. A W2 array that gives metrics for the same CID more than once therefore has no defined result: first wins, last wins, or error.

**Recommendation for correction**

Add after the description of the two W2 formats (before EXAMPLE 3):

> "Specifying a given CID value more than once in W2 should not be done. In the case where it is done, the first specification is the one that shall be used."

**Additional context**

Found while implementing a validator. The W rule was added in ISO 32000-2:2020; ISO 32000-1 has no rule for either array.
title: 9.7.4.3: "the first specification is the one that shall be used" is stated for W only; W2 has no rule for a CID given more than once

body:
**Describe the bug**

ISO 19005-4:2020, 6.2.10.7 "Unicode character maps", third item of the list of exceptions. It covers Type 0 fonts whose descendant CIDFont uses "the Adobe-GB1, Adobe-CNS1, Adobe-Japan1 or Adobe-KR-9 character collections".

Three collections are named without a supplement, but Adobe-KR is named with supplement 9. ISO 32000-2, 9.7.5.2 (paragraph below Table 117), names all four with supplements ("Adobe-CNS1-7, Adobe-GB1-5, Adobe-Japan1-7 and Adobe-KR-9"). ISO 32000-2, 9.10.2 (the method that this exception relies on), names the collections without supplements, including "Adobe-KR". Table 114 says that the Supplement "shall not be used in determining compatibility between character collections".

It is therefore unclear whether a CIDFont with Registry "Adobe", Ordering "KR" and a Supplement other than 9 falls under the exception.

**Recommendation for correction**

Replace "Adobe-KR-9" with "Adobe-KR", so that the four collections are named the same way as in ISO 32000-2, 9.10.2. Whether the deprecated Adobe-Korea1, which 9.10.2 still lists, should also be covered is left to the TWG (see also #231).

**Additional context**

Found while implementing a validator. The impact is low, because 6.2.10.7 is a recommendation ("should include a ToUnicode entry"), but validators that report the recommendation have to decide which fonts are exempt.

Related, but none of them covers this list: #77 (supplement numbers of predefined CMaps in 6.2.10.3.1), #231 (deprecated character collections), #342 (supplement numbers in ISO 32000-2, 9.10.2).
title: ISO 19005-4:2020 6.2.10.7: "Adobe-KR-9" is named with a supplement number, the other character collections without one

body:
**Describe the bug**

ISO 19005-4:2020, 6.7.2.1 "General" (Metadata streams), second paragraph and NOTE; clause 2 "Normative references".

6.7.2.1 requires that XMP packets "shall be well-formed as defined by XMP (ISO 16684-1)". The NOTE refers to attributes that are deprecated "in ISO 16684-1". Clause 2 lists ISO 16684-2, but not ISO 16684-1, and ISO 16684-1 is not in the Bibliography either. The edition that applies can only be inferred indirectly, through the undated normative reference to ISO 16684-1 in ISO 32000-2 (and its terms "XMP" and "XMP packet").

**Recommendation for correction**

Add ISO 16684-1 to clause 2 of ISO 19005-4. Either make it undated, or, if a particular edition is intended, make it dated. Confirm that the requirements of 6.7 hold for that edition.

**Additional context**

Found while implementing a validator. Editorial, low priority.
title: ISO 19005-4:2020 6.7.2.1: ISO 16684-1 is used normatively but is not listed in clause 2

body:
# PRC: the `PRC_HCG_AnaCylinder` prose names two fields that do not exist

**Reviewed with Datalogics (Patrick Gallot), who asked us to file it.**

**Change type: editorial correction**, with one optional clarifying addition. Nothing on the wire
changes.

**Verified against** the TWG working source at commit `84d98e1`. Every "current text" block below
was compared character for character against `git show 84d98e1:<path>`. Citations are by file and
line, because clause and table numbers are moving while the document is edited.

---

## Defect

The clause describing the analytic cylinder, at `iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:3468`,
says the axis is defined from *point_on_axis* and *cylinder_axis_direction*. The data definition
it points to, at `iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/topology.yaml:746-767`, has no fields with
those names. Its two fields after `face` are `point` (`:758`) and `direction` (`:763`).

The name *point_on_axis* does occur once elsewhere in the document, as a local variable in the
evaluation pseudocode for `PRC_TYPE_SURF_Revolution` (`adoc:6003`). That is unrelated to the
analytic cylinder, and it makes the stray name harder to dismiss as a typo.

The mismatch has a practical cost beyond the wording. Both fields are typed `CompressedPoint`. A
reader who sees two fields of the same point type, one of them described in the prose as a
*point_on_axis*, is nudged toward reading the second one as a second point on the axis and
subtracting the two. The analytic cone next door (`topology.yaml:815-834`) does carry two points,
`axis_point` and `apex_point`, and is used exactly that way (`adoc:3509`). So the cone reinforces
the wrong reading.

## Evidence

This is not hypothetical. An independent implementer reading this clause built a reader that
treated `direction` as a second point. It produced zero-length axes, and the implementer later
withdrew that reading.

The table's reading is the right one. nanoPRC reads `direction` exactly as the table declares it,
as one `CompressedPoint` immediately after `point` (`src/prc_parse_extra_geometry.c:2105-2119` at
upstream `aef8a68`). On 28 September we added a temporary probe there that printed each decoded
vector and its length, and ran it over two collections, one public and one private. The probe has
since been removed.

**Denominator:** 68,427 `PRC_HCG_AnaCylinder` faces in 66 files. 16,624 of them are in 20 files of
the public collection and 51,803 are in 46 private files. A further 230 faces from one file whose
parse reported failure are excluded.

| Measure | Result |
|---|---|
| Faces whose `direction` decodes to the zero vector | 0 of 68,427 |
| Faces whose `direction` is within 0.001 of unit length | 68,427 of 68,427 (worst deviation 0.000502) |
| Faces whose `direction` is an exact axis-aligned unit vector | 58,628 of 68,427 (85.68%); `(0,0,1)` alone on 13,408 |

A misaligned read, or a field that was really a second point, could not come out unit length on
every one of 68,427 faces. The residual deviation is the size expected from tolerance
quantisation. The dominance of axis-aligned directions is what drilled and turned features produce.

**Limit of this evidence.** nanoPRC parses both fields but does not yet build a cylinder from them.
The tessellation case for this entity is a stub. So nanoPRC's naming is not evidence of anything;
only the measured values are.

## Proposed change

The two changes are independent. Change 1 corrects the defect. Change 2 is optional and only
removes the remaining invitation to misread `direction`; it can be rejected on its own.

### Change 1 of 2: the prose

Location: `iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:3468`

Current text:

```
The analytic cylinder axis is defined from *point_on_axis* and *cylinder_axis_direction* (see <<tab-entities-PRC_HCG_AnaCylinder>>). The cylinder radius is computed using loop vertices to obtain an average radius when projected onto the axis.
```

Replace with:

```
The _PRC_HCG_AnaCylinder_ structure is shown in <<tab-entities-PRC_HCG_AnaCylinder>>.
The cylinder axis passes through *point* and is parallel to *direction*. *direction* is a vector, not a second point on the axis. The cylinder radius is computed using loop vertices to obtain an average radius when projected onto the axis.
```

The first sentence of the replacement is the same one used to introduce each sibling entity
(`PRC_HCG_AnaPlane` at `adoc:3456`, `PRC_HCG_AnaTorus` at `:3479`, `PRC_HCG_AnaSphere` at `:3496`,
`PRC_HCG_AnaCone` at `:3508`). The last sentence is unchanged.

### Change 2 of 2 (optional): the field description

Location: `iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/topology.yaml:763-767`

Current text:

```
  - name: direction
    data_type:
      kind: CompressedPoint
    required: true
    description: Direction of cylinder axis
```

Replace with:

```
  - name: direction
    data_type:
      kind: CompressedPoint
    required: true
    description: Direction of cylinder axis, a vector stored in the CompressedPoint encoding; not a second point on the axis
```

## Effect if accepted

* The prose names the fields the table defines, so a reader can match the two without guessing.
* The difference between this entity and `PRC_HCG_AnaCone`, which does carry two points, is stated
  rather than left for the reader to infer.
* **Unchanged:** field names, field order, data types and the bit stream. No writer or reader
  changes behaviour. The radius sentence is untouched, and this CR does not say whether `direction`
  must be unit length: the measurements show it always is, but that is a property of the files
  examined, not something this CR asks the document to require.
title: PRC: the PRC_HCG_AnaCylinder prose names two fields that do not exist

# PRC: `IsoNURBSTrimCrv.iso_boundary` names a type that does not exist, and hides that nothing is stored

**Reviewed with Datalogics (Patrick Gallot), who agree with the wording below and have
  implemented it in their writer.**

**Change type: technical clarification.** The bit stream does not change. The current wording sends
a writer or reader looking for curve data that is not there.

**Verified against** the TWG working source at commit `84d98e1`. The "current text" block below was
taken from `git show 84d98e1:<path>` and is reproduced character for character. Citations are by
file and line, because clause and table numbers are moving while the document is edited.

---

## Defect

`IsoNURBSTrimCrv` is the record for one trim curve of a `PRC_HCG_IsoNURBS` face that is not given by
reference. Its first field, `iso_boundary`, is described at
`iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/topology.yaml:943` as TRUE "when the trimming curve is not a
circle or a line, and is of type CompressedBSplineHermite".

Two things are wrong with that:

* **There is no type `CompressedBSplineHermite`.** It is not defined anywhere in the document, and
  the record has no field that could hold one. A reader following the description has nothing to
  read, and a writer has nothing to write.
* **It hides what the curve actually is.** The clause for this face says "The four curve types are
  stored as reference (identifier), line, circle, or other (iso boundary of surface)"
  (`iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:3555`), and `sense_array` says which natural boundary of
  the surface (Umin, Vmin, Umax or Vmax) each trim curve lies on (`07-base-entities.adoc:3544-3553`).
  So when `iso_boundary` is TRUE, the trim curve is the surface's own boundary at that edge. It can
  be worked out from data already in the file, and nothing further is stored.

## Evidence

**Real files store nothing after a TRUE.** Instrument: nanoPRC's reader, which reads no data after
`iso_boundary` = TRUE. Population: the public prc-db collection, 310 files. 15 files carry
`IsoNURBSTrimCrv` records: 1,566 with `iso_boundary` TRUE, in 14 of those files, and 2,935 with it
FALSE, across all 15. The reader stays in step through every one of them. If any data were stored
after a TRUE, every later field in those sections would be misread.

**A second implementation agrees.** Datalogics had implemented the same reading and could not
justify it from the text: implementing the field list and implementing the field description gave
the same number of completed geometry sections across their 529-file collection. They have now
built an `IsoNURBS` fixture following this reading, relying on the `sense_array` clause.

## Proposed change

Location: `iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/topology.yaml:943`

Current text:

```
    description: Boolean with value is set to TRUE when the trimming curve is not a circle or a line, and is of type CompressedBSplineHermite
```

Replace with:

```
    description: Boolean with value set to TRUE when the trimming curve is neither a circle nor a line. The trimming curve is then the natural boundary of the surface given by *sense_array*, and no curve data is stored.
```

## Effect if accepted

* The description names where the curve comes from, which is the part a writer has to act on, and
  says plainly that nothing is stored.
* The reference to an undefined type is removed.
* **Unchanged:** field names, field order, data types and the bit stream. Readers and writers that
  already store nothing after a TRUE behave exactly as before.
title: PRC: IsoNURBSTrimCrv.iso_boundary names a type that does not exist, and hides that nothing is stored

PDF date strings (objects) are described by ISO 32000-2:2020 subclause 7.9.4, which states:

> Date values used in a PDF shall conform to a standard date format, which closely follows that of the international standard ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One), defined in ISO/IEC 8824-1.

This reference to ISO/IEC 8824-1 implies that PDF date strings represent Gregorian calendar dates.

As some recent work in our [PDF Forensics LWG](https://pdfa.org/community/pdf-forensics-lwg/) has shown, some PDFs use alternative calendars. 

Since PDF date strings are primarily used for internal comparison (e.g., **CreationDate**, **LastModified**), for interoperability purposes, indexing, AI understanding, etc., the PDF specification should clarify that PDF date strings use the Gregorian calendar. This means alternate calendaring systems first need to convert to the Gregorian calendar before writing to PDF.

Proposal: add an informative note stating that PDF date strings use the Gregorian calendar.
title: Only by inference PDF date strings use the Gregorian calendar

ISO 32000-2:2020 "Table 253 — Entries in an FDF named page reference dictionary" describes the **F** entry as a "file specification" in the Type column. Does this mean a file specification dictionary (subclause 7.11.3), a file specification string (subclause 7.11.2), or either?  

This identical wording goes back to Adobe PDF 1.3 Reference.

PS. I also looked in XFDF (ISO 19444-1:2019) and although it doesn't mention **TRef**, "Table 25 — File specification attributes" states "... _corresponds to the **F** key in the file specification dictionary._" - in XFDF things have to be a string because it is an XML atttribute so I wasn't able to infer anything concrete from this.

So should the Type column state "dictionary or string" ('cos **F** is string), "dictionary or text string" ('cos **UF** is text string), "dictionary", "string", "text string" or something else to be consistent with all other tables in 32K?
title: FDF named page reference dictionary F entry (Table 253) type description is ambiguous
