## PRC: `number_vertex_references` states the dual-cache rule twice, and the two statements disagree

 **Reviewed with Datalogics (Patrick Gallot). The conflict was found by Datalogics; the nanoPRC
  measurement is ours.**

**Changes since the 22 October draft:** the Defect section no longer says the two implementations
read the kind rule differently. Datalogics found on 22 October that the figure they had sent was
mislabelled: split by cause, their losses go negative too. Both readers take the kind from the face
that holds the reference, and both lose references by going below zero. The Defect section now
states that one failure, and the Datalogics table gives the split.

**Change type: technical correction.** The bit stream does not change. A reader that follows the
field descriptions as written today resolves some vertex and curve references to the wrong entry,
or to none.

**Verified against** the TWG working source at commit `6fb2ed9` (21 October 2026). The "current
text" blocks below were taken from the source at `84d98e1` and are unchanged at `6fb2ed9`; they are
reproduced byte for byte, including trailing spaces. Citations are by file and line, because clause
and table numbers move while the document is edited.

---

## Defect

A compressed B-rep stores each new vertex once, and later refers back to it with a *point_index*.
The vertices are split into two caches: those stored while iso-faces are read, and those stored
while ana-faces are read. `number_vertex_references` gives the size of the first. The document
then says, in two places, how a *point_index* picks its cache, and the two places say different
things.

**The clause prose splits on the index value.** `iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:3271`:

```
The *number_vertex_references* field represents the number of iso-vertices in the compressed brep — the size of the iso-vertex cache. The total compressed vertex stream is partitioned into an iso-vertex cache of this size followed by an ana-vertex cache for the remainder; *point_index* values below this threshold index into the iso-vertex cache, and values at or above this threshold index into the ana-vertex cache with the threshold subtracted. See <<CompressedVertex>>.
```

**The field description splits on the kind of vertex.** `topology.yaml:533-536`, in
`iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/`, says "if the vertex is an iso-vertex, retrieve from the
iso-vertex cache at point_index; if the vertex is an ana-vertex, retrieve from the ana-vertex cache
at *point_index* − *number_vertex_references*".

The field description needs a fact that is not available where it is used: the kind of the vertex
being referred to is not known until the reference has been resolved. A reader therefore has to
substitute something it does know. Two independent implementations, nanoPRC and Datalogics' reader,
both substituted the kind of the face that holds the reference. Both then lose references on real
files, and in the same way: an index below the threshold, read on an ana-face, has the threshold
subtracted and goes below zero. Of nanoPRC's 38,668 lost vertex references, all go negative; of
Datalogics' 12,352, 12,346 do, and the other 6, spread across three files, overrun.

The clause prose does not have this problem, because the value of the index alone selects the
cache.

**The same is true for curves.** `number_edge_references` is the size of the iso-edge cache.
`07-base-entities.adoc:3273` says edges use "the same dual-cache scheme as vertices", with the field
as "the threshold and offset". `topology.yaml:537-548` again splits on the kind: "if the edge is an
iso-edge, retrieve from the iso-edge cache at the stored index; if the edge is an ana-edge, retrieve
from the ana-edge cache at stored_index − number_edge_references".

**The normative sentence points at the wrong one.** `07-base-entities.adoc:3290` says "Index
resolution shall apply the threshold-and-offset rule given in the *number_vertex_references* and
*number_edge_references* descriptions of `<<tab-entities-PRC_TYPE_TOPO_BrepDataCompress>>`". Those
descriptions are the yaml text. So the only "shall" leads to the statement that real files
contradict.

**And the first sentence of each description is looser than what the caches hold.** Both say the
count of vertices or edges "referenced from iso-faces". What was measured, in every compressed
B-rep body of the collection below, is the count *stored* while iso-faces are read. For curves that
includes the third and fourth trim curves an iso-face derives from its two stored curves, and the
trim curves of IsoNURBS faces. A reader that counts only the curves an iso-face stores explicitly,
or leaves out the IsoNURBS trim curves, computes the wrong threshold before any rule is applied.

## Evidence

**Instrument.** nanoPRC's reader with a temporary probe, built from upstream `83ca530` in a scratch
copy and since discarded. Beside the reader's own single list, the probe kept an iso list (vertices
stored while an iso-face was being read) and an ana list, and resolved every *point_index* three
ways. A reference counts as resolved correctly in the strongest test available without a viewer:
when an edge's start vertex is a reference and the previous edge has just ended, the start should be
the same point as that end. Not every case should match, because some edges are traversed in
reverse, so the comparison between rules matters more than any one total.

**Denominator.** The public prc-db collection, 310 files. 197,932 vertex references in 25,627
compressed B-rep bodies, in 20 files; 123,444 start-after-end cases.

**First, what the threshold means.** In all 25,627 bodies, `number_vertex_references` equals the
number of vertices stored while iso-faces were read.

| how *point_index* is resolved | references out of range | start lands on the previous end |
|---|---|---|
| one list, indexed from 0 (no split) | 7,024 | 63,514 |
| **by value**, `07-base-entities.adoc:3271` | **0** | **67,919** |
| by kind of face, `topology.yaml:533-536` as nanoPRC read it | 38,668 | 66,647 |

* **The value rule resolves every reference.** It rescues all 7,024 that overrun a single list and
  makes none go out of range. It changes the resolution of 4,562 references that were already in
  range, all of them in the two files that carry the overruns (ENGINE-TYPE-01-2-LITER_3D.stream-496
  and Portal-Plate-NC-Machine-Work-Instruction.stream-176). In both, more starts land on the
  previous end (22,833 to 25,715, and 1,099 to 2,622). In the other 18 files it resolves every
  reference exactly as a single list does: there, all iso-vertices are stored before any
  ana-vertex, which is why a reader without the split has worked on most files.
* **The kind rule, read as the kind of face, puts 38,668 references out of range** that resolve
  under either other rule. All 38,668 go negative, and none overruns. It does worse than the value
  rule in 17 of the 19 files that have cases, and ties in the other two.

**A second implementation, the same result.** Datalogics implemented both rules in their own reader,
taking the kind from the face that holds the reference, and scored them over their own collection
of 529 files. The figures below are from their reader as it stood on 21 and 22 October 2026. That
reader has been corrected since, in ways that let it read further into some files, so later counts
are larger; the shape of the result is unchanged.

| over the 40 files that read a vertex reference (Datalogics' reader, 21–22 October 2026) | |
|---|--:|
| references read | 61,351 |
| of those, overrunning a single list | 1,570 |
| value rule: overrunning references rescued | 1,346 |
| **value rule: in-range references broken** | **2** |
| kind rule: overrunning references rescued | 1,346 |
| kind rule: in-range references lost | 12,352 |
| ... by going negative | 12,346 |
| ... by overrunning | 6 |
| iso-vertices stored after an ana-vertex | 315 |

Of the 315 vertices stored out of order, 286 are in `Portal-Plate-NC-Machine-Work-Instruction`, ten
other files contribute between one and four each, and five sit in files Datalogics' per-file listing
does not reach. So the two caches are genuinely interleaved in real files, and the rule matters
beyond one file. Datalogics' reader stops earlier than nanoPRC's on
both of the files named above, so their figures are a subset of the same population and not a
second opinion on it.

### Curve references

**Instrument.** The same probe, extended to curves. It recorded every curve as it was stored, by
where it was stored: as one of the two stored trim curves of an iso-face, as a third or fourth curve
derived for an iso-face, as an IsoNURBS trim curve, or inside an ana-face trim loop. Each stored
curve's endpoints were taken from its start and end vertices, resolved by the value rule above. The
test for a referenced curve is that it shares an endpoint with the curve before it in the same trim
loop or iso-face. Direction is ignored, because a referenced curve is often used reversed.

**Denominator.** The same 310 files: 188,237 curve references in 25,683 compressed B-rep bodies, in
20 files; 46,490 references that follow a curve whose endpoints are known.

**What the threshold means.** In all 25,683 bodies, `number_edge_references` equals the number of
curves stored while iso-faces were read, counting the derived third and fourth curves and the
IsoNURBS trim curves. Leaving out the IsoNURBS curves, it fails in 82 bodies.

| how a curve index is resolved | references out of range | shares an endpoint with the previous curve |
|---|---|---|
| one list, indexed from 0 (no split) | 4,594 | 34,420 |
| **by value**, as `07-base-entities.adoc:3273` | **0** | **36,435** |
| by kind of face, `topology.yaml:537-548` as nanoPRC read it | 60,056 | 29,160 |

The pattern is the vertex one. The value rule resolves every curve reference. It ties a single list
in 18 files, does better in the same two files as before (ENGINE-TYPE-01: 15,741 against 14,105;
Portal-Plate: 963 against 584), and is never worse. Read as the kind of face, the kind rule does
worse than the value rule in all 19 files that have cases, and all 60,056 of its failures go
negative.

## Proposed change

The two changes are independent, but they make the same correction, so we would expect them to be
taken together.

### Change 1 of 2: `number_vertex_references`

Location: `iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/topology.yaml:524-536`

Current text:

```
  - name: number_vertex_references
    data_type:
      kind: UnsignedIntegerWithVariableBitNumber
    required: true
    description: |
      Number of iso-vertices in the compressed brep — the count of vertices 
      referenced from iso-faces, forming the iso-vertex cache. This value 
      partitions the total compressed vertex population into two sequential 
      caches: iso-vertices occupy indices [0, *number_vertex_references* − 1] 
      and ana-vertices occupy the remainder. When resolving a *point_index* 
      reference: if the vertex is an iso-vertex, retrieve from the iso-vertex 
      cache at point_index; if the vertex is an ana-vertex, retrieve
      from the ana-vertex cache at *point_index* − *number_vertex_references*. See <<CompressedVertex>>.
```

Replace with:

```
  - name: number_vertex_references
    data_type:
      kind: UnsignedIntegerWithVariableBitNumber
    required: true
    description: |
      Number of iso-vertices in the compressed brep: the count of vertices
      stored while iso-faces, including IsoNURBS faces, are read. These form
      the iso-vertex cache. This value partitions the total compressed vertex
      population into two caches: iso-vertices occupy indices
      [0, *number_vertex_references* − 1] and ana-vertices occupy the
      remainder. When resolving a *point_index* reference, the value of
      *point_index* selects the cache: a value below
      *number_vertex_references* is an index into the iso-vertex cache, and a
      value at or above it is an index into the ana-vertex cache at
      *point_index* − *number_vertex_references*. The kind of face that
      contains the reference does not select the cache. See <<CompressedVertex>>.
```

### Change 2 of 2: `number_edge_references`

Location: `iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/topology.yaml:537-548`

Current text:

```
  - name: number_edge_references
    data_type:
      kind: UnsignedIntegerWithVariableBitNumber
    required: true
    description: |
      Number of iso-edges in the compressed brep — the count of edges referenced
      from iso-faces, forming the iso-edge cache. This value partitions the total compressed
      edge population into two sequential caches: iso-edges occupy indices
      [0, number_edge_references − 1] and ana-edges occupy the remainder.
      When resolving a curve reference: if the edge is an iso-edge, retrieve from the
      iso-edge cache at the stored index; if the edge is an ana-edge, retrieve from the
      ana-edge cache at stored_index − number_edge_references. See <<CompressedCurve>>.
```

Replace with:

```
  - name: number_edge_references
    data_type:
      kind: UnsignedIntegerWithVariableBitNumber
    required: true
    description: |
      Number of iso-edges in the compressed brep: the count of curves stored
      while iso-faces are read. This includes the two trim curves an iso-face
      stores, the third and fourth trim curves it derives from them, and the
      trim curves of IsoNURBS faces. These form the iso-edge cache. This value
      partitions the total compressed edge population into two caches: iso-edges
      occupy indices [0, number_edge_references − 1] and ana-edges occupy the
      remainder. When resolving a curve reference, the value of the stored index
      selects the cache: a value below number_edge_references is an index into the
      iso-edge cache, and a value at or above it is an index into the ana-edge cache
      at stored_index − number_edge_references. The kind of face that contains the
      reference does not select the cache. See <<CompressedCurve>>.
```

With both changes, `adoc:3271` and `adoc:3273` agree with the yaml, and the "shall" at `adoc:3290`
leads to the right rule. No adoc line needs to change.

## Effect if accepted

* The document states one rule for resolving vertex and curve references, and the normative
  sentence at `adoc:3290` points to it.
* The descriptions say what each cache holds, so that two readers compute the same threshold.
* A reader built from the field descriptions no longer loses references on files that store
  ana-vertices or ana-curves before iso ones.
* **Unchanged:** field names, field order, data types and the bit stream. Readers that already split
  on the index value, and readers that use one list on files where iso-vertices come first, behave
  exactly as before.
title: PRC: `number_vertex_references` states the dual-cache rule twice, and the two statements disagree

## PRC: the compressed indice array pseudocode contradicts its tables in three places

**CR-36b. Draft of 22 October 2026, not yet filed.** Items 2, 3 and 4 of the CR-36 draft of
18 October, filed together on Datalogics' review of 21 October because they are all
pseudocode-against-table discrepancies in the same area, and because item 3 is a prerequisite for
**CR-36a** (signed steps), which is filed separately.

For reference: CR-36a, the signed-steps ticket this one's item 3 prepares for, is filed as #849.

**Verified against** the TWG working source at commit `6fb2ed9` (21 October 2026). Quotations are
by file and line.

## 1. Whether `point_reference_array` is compressed is fixed by a table, but the pseudocode lets the writer choose

**Current text.**

- `iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/tessellation.yaml:560`: "the Boolean value which indicates
  whether the character array is compressed is not stored. Its value is implicit and set to
  number_of_reference_points > 3".
- `iso-prc/code/Huffman-func.cpp:12-14`: `bool bIsCompressed = HuffmanCompression(); if
  (bWriteCompressStrategy) WriteBoolean ( bIsCompressed );`. When the Boolean is not written, the
  code still lets the writer's own strategy choose.
- `iso-prc/sections/09-io-algorithms.adoc:76`, NOTE: "Compression can be skipped systematically when
  the array size is lower than 5". For a `point_reference_array` of exactly 4 references,
  compression is required by the table, so the NOTE is wrong there.

**Proposed replacement** for `Huffman-func.cpp:12`:

```cpp
  // When bWriteCompressStrategy is false the choice is not stored, and the
  // caller fixes it: for point_reference_array, compressed exactly when
  // number_of_reference_points > 3 (see PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D_Compressed).
  bool bIsCompressed = bWriteCompressStrategy ? HuffmanCompression()
                                              : bImplicitCompression;
```

with `bool bImplicitCompression` added to the parameter list.

**Proposed replacement** for the NOTE at `09-io-algorithms.adoc:76`:

> NOTE Where the compression choice is stored, compression can be skipped systematically when the
> array size is lower than 5, since the compressed strategy leads to write at least one unsigned
> integer. Where it is implicit (point_reference_array), the rule given with that field applies
> whatever the size.

## 2. "Its size is implicit", yet the size is written

**Current text.** `tessellation.yaml:560`: "Its size is implicit and set to number of non-zero
elements in the *points_is_reference_array*."

`Huffman-func.cpp:32` writes `WriteUnsignedInteger ( uCharArraySize )` in the plain branch whatever
`bWriteCompressStrategy` is. The Huffman stream carries the size too (`huffman.cpp:57-58`). Real
files carry it: nanoPRC's reader reads it on every one of the 1,562 short `point_reference_array`s
in the public prc-db collection and on all the longer ones. If it were absent, every later field
would be misread.

**Proposed replacement:** "Its size is still written as part of the character array, and shall be
equal to the number of non-zero elements in the *points_is_reference_array*."

## 3. Editorial, and a prerequisite for CR-36a: the element width never reaches the Huffman call

`Huffman-func.cpp:1-3` declares `Huffman(pcArray, uCharArraySize, puHuffmanArray,
uHuffmanArraySize)` with no width, and calls it that way at `:22-23`. The definition at
`huffman.cpp:23` takes `uNumberOfBitsForValues` as its third parameter. `WriteCharacterArray`'s own
`uBitNumber` (`Huffman-func.cpp:10`) is never used.

**Proposed replacement:** pass it through, as
`Huffman(pcArray, uCharArraySize, uBitNumber, puHuffmanArray, uHuffmanArraySize);`, and change the
declaration at `:1-3` to match the definition.

This matters beyond tidiness. The width decides how a negative leaf is stored, which is the subject
of CR-36a; until the width reaches the call, the pseudocode cannot express CR-36a's rule.

## Effect if accepted

* The pseudocode, the field table and the NOTE agree on when `point_reference_array` is compressed
  and that its size is written.
* **Unchanged:** the bit stream. All three changes describe what real files already contain.
title: PRC: the compressed indice array pseudocode contradicts its tables in three places

## PRC: a step in a compressed indice array's bit-length table is signed, and the text never says how a negative step is stored

**Reviewed with Datalogics (Patrick Gallot).** The three smaller items are CR-36b (see #822),
  which this ticket depends on for its Huffman half (see "Related").

For reference: CR-36b, named in the Related section above, is filed as #848. Its item 3 (the element width never reaching the Huffman call) is the prerequisite for this ticket's Huffman half.

**Verified against** the TWG working source at commit `6fb2ed9` (21 October 2026). Quotations are
by file and line.

## Why it matters

A writer following the text can produce a compressed tessellation that a strict reader cannot read.
nanoPRC did, from July to October 2026. It stored a negative bit-length step in the 6-bit form
inside an array written as 8-bit characters. Adobe Acrobat and an independent commercial reader both
read it as +63, lost their place, and dropped that part and every part after it from the model tree.
Fixing that one value made seven long-failing files open in Acrobat. The fix is nanoPRC #156.

## Defect

**Current text.** `iso-prc/sections/09-io-algorithms.adoc:116`:

> The following code example shows how to write an array of indices; the indices are always
> positive at input.

`iso-prc/code/WriteCompressedIntegerArray2.cpp:13` stores `pcArray[u] = cTemp - cLastBitCount;`. That
is a difference between two bit counts, so it is negative whenever an index needs fewer bits than the
one before it. The array is then passed to `WriteCharacterArray` with a width of 6, which stores it in
one of two ways:

- **Plain:** `WriteCharacter ( pcArray[u] )` (`iso-prc/code/Huffman-func.cpp:35`), a Character
  "written as a single 8 bits" (`iso-prc/sections/06-basic-types.adoc:88`). So −1 is 0xFF.
- **Huffman:** each leaf value is written in `uNumberOfBitsForValues` bits, the low bits only
  (`iso-prc/code/huffman.cpp:44-45`), which is 6 here. So −1 is 0x3F.

Nothing tells the reader that the value is signed, or how to restore the sign in either form. The
sentence about positive indices tends to suggest the opposite.

## Evidence

**Instrument.** nanoPRC's reader with a temporary count in the indice-array decoder, recording for
each array whether it was stored plain or Huffman-compressed, and each step's raw value before any
sign is restored. The count was checked first against a figure already established by a separate
probe on 18 October (the plain-form row below), which it reproduces exactly. Population: the public
prc-db collection, 310 files, 44,468 indice arrays.

| array, form | arrays | files | negative steps | stored as 6-bit (32 to 63) | stored as 8-bit (128 to 255) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| `point_reference_array`, plain | 1,562 | 25 | 88 | **0** | **88** |
| `point_reference_array`, Huffman | 8,448 | 137 | 3,883,122 | **3,883,122** | **0** |
| `triangle_face_array`, Huffman | 5,776 | 44 | 649,874 | **649,874** | **0** |
| `triangle_face_array`, plain | 28,682 | | 0 | | |

The 88 plain-form negatives are in 16 files. Every writer in the collection stores a negative step
in two's complement in the width of the element: 8 bits when the array is plain, 6 bits when it is
Huffman-compressed. No file stores it any other way.

**A second writer.** Datalogics report that their writer, implemented independently from 9.6 and
from 6's "written as a single 8 bits", already does the same: `v & 0xFF` in the plain branch, and the
low 6 bits as the Huffman leaf. That is a reading of their own source, not a count of their output.

## Proposed change

Location: `iso-prc/sections/09-io-algorithms.adoc:116`

Current text:

```
The following code example shows how to write an array of indices; the indices are always positive at input.
```

Replace with:

```
The following code example shows how to write an array of indices. The indices are always positive at input, but the differences between consecutive bit counts stored in pcArray (all elements after the first) are signed. They are stored in two's complement in the width of the character array element. When the array is written plain, each is a whole Character (8 bits), so −1 is stored as 0xFF. When the array is Huffman-compressed, each is a leaf value of 6 bits, so −1 is stored as 0x3F, and a reader shall sign-extend leaf values of 32 or more. The first element is an absolute bit count, and is never negative.
```

## Related

**CR-36b** (filed alongside) corrects three places where the pseudocode and the tables disagree in
the same area. One of them, its item 3, is a prerequisite for this ticket's Huffman half: the
element width never reaches the Huffman call in the pseudocode, and it is the width that decides how
a negative leaf is stored.

## Effect if accepted

* Writers and readers store and restore negative steps the same way, in both forms.
* **Unchanged:** the bit stream. Every file in the collection above already conforms to the
  replacement text.
title: PRC: a step in a compressed indice array's bit-length table is signed, omits how a negative step is stored

body:
Clause 12.5.5 (Appearance streams), algorithm step: "The transparency group shall be composited
with a backdrop consisting of the page content along with any previously painted annotations,
using the values of the BM, ca and CA entries in the annotation dictionary."

Table 166, CA row (and ca row, word for word): "The specified value shall not be used if the
annotation has an appearance stream; in that case, the appearance stream shall specify any
transparency."

Clause 12.5.2 (as amended by issues #23 and #34, which struck BM from this list) still lists CA and
ca among the keys a PDF reader shall ignore when rendering the appearance dictionary.

The three sentences cannot all be obeyed. Files in the wild (e.g. pdf.js's highlight.pdf) write
/CA 0.8 on the annotation and ca 0.8 inside the appearance stream; applying both would darken
the producer's intent. Proposed resolution: amend 12.5.5's sentence to "using the value of the BM
entry in the annotation dictionary; the CA and ca entries shall not be used where the annotation
has an appearance stream (see Table 166)", or strike CA and ca from Table 166's restriction and
from 12.5.2's list. We implement Table 166's reading today.
title: 12.5.5 and Table 166 disagree on CA/ca for annotations with an appearance stream

body: ## Problem description 14.8.4.4.2 Link elements in 32000 and 14.8.4.7.3 Link elements in 32000-2 (here added through an error related to issue #133) contain the requirement > When a Link structure element describes a span of text to be associated with a link annotation and that span wraps from the end of one line to the beginning of another, the Link structure element shall include a single object reference that associates the span with the associated link annotation. Further, the link annotation shall use the *QuadPoint* entry to denote the active areas on the page. (Note that the texts write **QuadPoint**, but the name of the key is actually **QuadPoints** with an s, see tables 173/176) * When links go over more than one page there are always at least two link annotations. The requirement to use only one single object reference would mean that one would have to drop at least one and make it an artifact. Is that the intended meaning? If yes, which one is the preferred one? (Note that dropping an annotation probably contradicts the requirement in UA-2 which says *Multiple link annotations shall be included in a single Link or Reference structure element if they target the same location and are semantically perceived to be a single link.*) * Using *QuadPoints* to denote active area can led to unusable PDFs. * A PDF viewer is not required to support **QuadPoints**. In such a viewer **Rect** is used to define the active area. * In link annotations using **QuadPoints** the **Rect** array has to encompass the full region covered by the **Quadpoints** otherwise **QuadPoints** are ignored (and so can not denote the active area): > If this entry is not present, or the PDF processor does not recognise it, or if any coordinates in the **QuadPoints** array lie outside the region specified by **Rect** then the activation region for the link annotation shall be defined by its **Rect** entry. * This can led to very large clickable areas in non-supporting PDF viewers: Attached a PDF with a link using **QuadPoints** on the first page. On my mobile using the Adobe viewer (as shown in the screenshot) the link area covers a large part of the page. Basically any place I touch triggers a dialog. The short link in the first column is "hidden" and can not be used. The links on the second page which use multiple link annotations for the splitted link work fine. [quadpoints-overlapping-column.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34198426/quadpoints-overlapping-column.pdf) ## Suggested solution: * Drop the requirement that only a single link annotation should be inside a Link structure element. A requirement that the annotations have the same action and (if present) **Contents** entry should be enough. AT should then be able to announce only one. * Drop the requirement that **QuadPoints** should be used.
title: Problematic Single Object reference and QuadPoint requirement for link annotations in tagged PDF

body:
*Clause 7.10.11 `PRC_TYPE_CRV_Helix01`, its sub-clauses 7.10.11.2 `Type0HelixData` and 7.10.11.3
`Type1HelixData`, and Tables 267, 268 and 269. Clause and table numbers are from the current draft; every field is named as well, so the references survive renumbering.*

> **Edited 23 November 2026**, following the comments below: added 2(c) on `pitch`; revised the end of recommendation 3; added recommendations 4 to 6. Each change is marked *[Added 23 November 2026]* or *[Revised 23 November 2026]*, and replaced text is kept struck through. The rest of the text is as first posted.

One field of this entity means two different things depending on the value of another field, and nothing in its description says so. Two further fields in the same entity are named one thing and defined as another. All three are the same kind of defect — a description that does not say what the field means. **Two of them have already cost a correct implementation in our own group a wrong decision; the third we produced deliberately, to show what it costs.** None of them requires a change to the format.

**1. `start` means two different things depending on `type`, and its published description is the word "start".**

Table 267 gives the field in full as:

| Name | Data Type | Data Description |
|---|---|---|
| `start` | `Vector3D` | (Required) start |

and the prose of 7.10.11 adds only this:

> The Start variable represents a 3D position which is used to define the starting position of the helix.

The two sub-clauses then define it incompatibly.

**In 7.10.11.2, `start` is a point on the helix:**

> The origin and direction define the axis of the helix. The axis of the helix is denoted as the
> *z*-axis. The projection of the start position onto the helix axis determines an
> *origin_on_axis*. The *x*-axis is then defined as the vector from the origin_on_axis to the
> start point. This defines a coordinate system orienting and defining the constant radius helix.

**In 7.10.11.3, `start` is the origin of the frame that orients the helix:**

> A coordinate system whose
> * origin is at the start point,
> * *z*-axis is the unit_z vector, and
> * *x*-axis is the unit_u vector,
>
> orients the helix.

**The two evaluation formulas settle it, and they differ in the first argument of their last line:**

> **7.10.11.2** — `eval_point = transform_point( origin_on_axis, x_axis, z_axis, tmp_point );`
>
> **7.10.11.3** — `eval_point = transform_point( start, x_axis, z_axis, tmp_point );`

A type 0 helix is evaluated from `origin_on_axis`. `start` enters only through the derivation of that point and of the *x*-axis, and the curve passes through `start` by construction. A type 1 helix is evaluated from `start` itself, with `tmp_point` already carrying a radius-sized offset in the local frame — so a type 1 helix **does not pass through `start` at all** unless its radius law evaluates to zero there.

**This is not a redundancy that a careful reader can resolve from context.** Table 269 gives `Type1HelixData` thirteen fields — `unit_z`, `unit_u`, four reserved doubles and three law functions — and **no origin of any kind**. `start` is the record's only positional datum. A writer that reads the shared description literally and places `start` on the curve puts the entire helix one radius away from where it belongs, and the file it writes is perfectly well-formed.

**Measured rather than argued.** Two files of a type 1 helix differing in the single `start` vector and in nothing else — one double, in the geometry section alone — carrying byte-identical cameras, so that what separates the two pictures is the field and not the view: 

| arm | `start` | the reading it encodes | Adobe Acrobat |
|---|---|---|---|
| control | `(0, 0, 0)` | the origin of the orienting frame, as 7.10.11.3 defines it | renders a three-turn helix |
| subject | `(10, 0, 0)` | a point **on** the curve, as the shared description reads | renders a three-turn helix **displaced by one radius** |

**Both are accepted. Neither is refused, flagged or drawn degenerately.** The radius law gives 10, so moving `start` onto the curve moves the entire helix 10 units along `unit_u`, off the axis its writer intended. The only way to know which of the two files was the one that was meant is to know which meaning of `start` its writer had in mind. That is the defect, in two pictures.

**It has already cost a wrong fix, which is why we are raising it rather than absorbing it.** A writer in our own group read the shared description literally, concluded that a legal type 1 helix declaring `start = (0,0,0)` against a radius law giving R=10 was *"a point on no helix of that radius"*, and built a repair fixture moving the start to `(10,0,0)`. Under the 7.10.11.3 formula that displaces the whole helix by 10 along `unit_u`: the repair is the regression. Corrected on
29 October 2026 by reading 7.10.11.3, not by testing, because both files serialise cleanly and differ only once rendered.

**2. The same root cause appears twice more inside this one entity.** In each case a field is named one thing and defined as another, and a writer binding the published evaluation formula to the published structure table has only the field name to bind by.

**2(a). `Type0HelixData`'s `radius` is defined as a rate of change of radius.** Table 268 gives:

| Name | Data Type | Data Description |
|---|---|---|
| `radius` | `Double` | (Required) Radius_evolution |

The prose of 7.10.11.2 agrees with that description — *"The radius evolution is used to define a linear evolution of radius, such as a conic helix"* — and so does its evaluation formula:

> `radius = x_axis.length + param * radius_evolution;`

So the stored value is a **rate of change of radius per unit parameter**, zero for an ordinary helix and non-zero for a cone. Three labels for one quantity, and the field **name** is the only one that disagrees — while `radius_evolution`, the identifier the formula binds, appears nowhere in Table 268.

**The failure is silent and produces a well-formed file.** A writer that reads the name and stores the helix's actual radius R emits a legal `Type0HelixData` in which the radius grows by R per radian: at `param = 2π` the curve is at roughly seven times its intended radius. We built exactly that file — a three-turn helix of radius 15 and pitch 2, with the stored double set to 15, the value the field's name invites, and nothing else changed. Acrobat accepts it with no dialog and no empty model tree, and draws the object the file now specifies: a nearly flat spiral passing a radius of about 109 after one turn and 298 after three, against 38 units of rise. The control, one double away, draws the intended helix. **Nothing anywhere between a writer that trusts the field name and that picture raises anything at all.**

**2(b). `orientation` is named for one sense and defined as the other, and the two formulas spell it differently.** Table 267 gives:

| Name | Data Type | Data Description |
|---|---|---|
| `orientation` | `Boolean` | (Required) Trigonometric orientation (TRUE if helix turns in a clockwise direction and FALSE if it turns in a counter-clockwise direction |

*Trigonometric* orientation conventionally means the **positive** sense, counter-clockwise; the description binds **TRUE to clockwise**. The name and the description point opposite ways, and nothing in the clause says which a reader should implement.

**We measured it.** Two files identical but for this one bit, read side by side at the same camera, draw as mirror images of each other, and the `TRUE` arm turns **clockwise** about the axis seen from the positive *z* direction. **The description is right; the name is what misleads.** A reader cannot reach that answer by reading carefully, because reading carefully is what produces the other one: a reader in our own group implemented the counter-clockwise sense for `TRUE`, from the field's name and from the ordinary meaning of *trigonometric*, and drew every type 0 helix mirrored until this pair showed it, on 3 November. **Two implementations in one group, each wrong on a different
field of this one entity, each from reading a field's name rather than its description.**

**The published description also stops mid-clause, with its parenthesis still open.** Nothing is broken by that — the cell publishes exactly as written — but the content inside the parenthesis is load-bearing, and we cannot tell from outside whether anything was lost after *"counter-clockwise direction"*.

**And the two formulas do not name this Boolean the same way.** 7.10.11.3 tests `trigonometric_orientation`; **7.10.11.2 tests `trignometric_orientation`** — one letter short, an identifier that appears nowhere else in the document except one unrelated sentence in the `PRC_TYPE_MATH_FCT_1D_ArctanCos` clause. A reader implementing the type 0 formula literally is binding to an identifier the document does not otherwise define, and one that differs from the type 1 formula's name for the same Boolean in the same entity. In the same vein, all four occurrences of
`coeffient` in the document's clause text are inside 7.10.11.3's own formula. We mention these as evidence that this entity's identifiers cannot be bound literally, not as edit requests.

*[Added 23 November 2026.]* **2(c). `pitch` is described as a turn width and used as a rise per radian.** The prose of 7.10.11.2 says that "the pitch of the helix is the width of one complete helix turn measured along the helix axis". Its formula says `tmp_point.z = pitch * param`, the rise per unit of the parameter, which is in radians, so one turn rises 2π · `pitch`. The attached control stores `pitch` 2 over three turns and rises 37.7 units in Acrobat (2 · 6π), not 6. Table 268 describes the field only as "Pitch". (Found by t3dr0, below.)

**For the avoidance of doubt, the radius is not specified twice.** The formula in 7.10.11.2 takes `x_axis.length` directly, so the *x*-axis is not normalised and `|start − origin_on_axis|` **is** the radius at `param = 0`. The two quantities compose rather than compete. An earlier reading of ours saw a conflict here and was wrong; we mention it only because the field name invites exactly that reading.

**Recommendation**

These are ~~three~~ six statements the document does not currently make. *[Revised 23 November 2026.]* The wording below is offered as a starting point, not as a patch. 

**1. Say in 7.10.11 that `start` defers to `type`,** and give Table 267's `start` row a description that is a sentence rather than a repetition of the field's name:

> The **start** field is a 3D position whose meaning depends on **type**, which precedes it in the record.
>
> For a **type 0** helix, **start** is a point **on** the helix. Its projection onto the helix axis gives *origin_on_axis*, and the direction from *origin_on_axis* to **start** fixes the *x*-axis and therefore the angular phase at which the helix begins.
> For a **type 1** helix, **start** is the **origin of the local coordinate system** in which the helix is evaluated, as the evaluation formula shows. It is not in general a point on the curve:
> the curve passes through **start** only where the radius law evaluates to zero.

**2. Make Table 268's `radius` row say what the field holds.** The cleanest repair is to rename the field to `radius_evolution`, so that the structure table, the description and the evaluation formula all use one identifier. If renaming is unacceptable at this stage, the minimum is a description that is a sentence — for example *"the rate of change of radius per unit parameter, as used in the evaluation formula; 0 for a constant-radius helix"*. That form changes no bytes and no structure. It would also help for 7.10.11.2 to state that its *x*-axis is **not** normalised, since
the formula consumes its length: that is unambiguous once the formula is read, but the prose is what a writer reads first.

**3. State `orientation`'s sense unambiguously and reconcile it with the field name** — for example *"TRUE if the helix turns clockwise about the axis when viewed from the positive z direction; FALSE if it turns counter-clockwise."* Our measurement says the binding the text already carries is the one a major implementation already applies, so this is a matter of **saying** it rather than of changing it, and the wording matters precisely because the field's name pulls a careful reader the other way. ~~Two smaller things belong with it. Confirm that nothing was lost after *"counter-clockwise direction"* before the parenthesis is closed — we raise the open parenthesis as a signal that a clause may have been cut, not for tidiness, and only you can say whether it was. And have the two sub-type formulas name the Boolean identically.~~

*[Revised 23 November 2026.]* Two smaller things belong with it. Confirm that nothing was lost after *"counter-clockwise direction"* before the parenthesis is closed. And make the formulas carry the sense, since the description alone did not:

- define `transform_point( o, x, z, p )` as *o* + *p.x* · *X* + *p.y* · (*Z* × *X*) + *p.z* · *Z*, where *X* and *Z* are *x* and *z* scaled to unit length;
- in 7.10.11.2 (type 0), exchange the two branches, so that `cos( - param )` and `sin( - param )` go with TRUE — Acrobat turns a type 0 TRUE helix clockwise seen from +*z*;
- in 7.10.11.3 (type 1), keep the branches as written — Acrobat turns a type 1 TRUE helix counter-clockwise — and say so, so that each sub-type states its own sense;
- have the two formulas name the Boolean identically.

*[Added 23 November 2026.]* **4. Say what `pitch` holds.** For example *"the rise along the helix axis per unit of the parameter; one complete turn rises 2π · pitch."*

*[Added 23 November 2026.]* **5. Normalise the type 1 frame, as Acrobat does.** In 7.10.11.3: *"`unit_z` is normalised, and `unit_u` is made orthogonal to it and normalised, before use."* This keeps files with a skewed frame conforming; Acrobat draws them as their orthonormalised controls.

*[Added 23 November 2026.]* **6. State the type 0 axis and radius as the formula uses them.** The evidence is in the comments below.

- In 7.10.11.2, replace "a constant radius helix" and "the constant radius helix": the radius varies linearly with the parameter, `radius = x_axis.length + param * radius_evolution` in the sub-clause's own formula, and is constant only when the evolution is zero — the description of `radius_evolution` itself offers "a conic helix" as the case it serves.
- The radius may be negative; the point then lies on the opposite side of the axis.
- The axis direction need not be of unit length; the *z*-axis is its unit vector, and `pitch` is measured along it.
- When `start` lies on the axis, so that `start` − *origin_on_axis* has no direction, the *x*-axis is the unit vector of *z* × (1, 0, 0); when the axis is parallel to the *x*-axis, so that this vanishes, it is (0, 1, 0).

**What this issue is not asking for**

**No structural change, and no new field.** `type` is a `Character` read *before* `start` in the record, so a conforming reader always knows which meaning applies by the time it reads the value. Nothing on the wire needs to move; every existing file stays valid under whichever reading its writer used. The gap is entirely in the description.

**Additional context**

[helix-type0-control.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34395971/helix-type0-control.pdf)
[helix-type0-orientation-false.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34395970/helix-type0-orientation-false.pdf)
[helix-type0-radius-evolution.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34395998/helix-type0-radius-evolution.pdf)
[helix-type1-start-frame-origin.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34395969/helix-type1-start-frame-origin.pdf)
[helix-type1-start-on-curve.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34395967/helix-type1-start-on-curve.pdf)
title: `PRC_TYPE_CRV_Helix01`: the `start` field has two incompatible meanings, and two further fields in the same entity are named one thing and defined as another

The table 166 "Entries common to all annotation dictionaries" in section 12.5.2 has two entries /ca and /CA. While /ca is a new one introduced with PDF 2.0, /CA exists since PDF 1.4 and describes the opacity value for stroking operations when regenerating an appearance stream.

A widget annotation which can use all of the keys of table 166 has additional entries defined in table 191 in section 12.5.6.19. One of those additional keys is named /CA the normal caption of the widget.

So there is a problem when one wants to specify both the /CA as opacity value and /CA as normal caption for a widget annotation.

I'm no sure if there is a documented way of how to handle such "shadowed" keys. Anyways, I don't think it is a good idea having two keys with different types and meanings.
title: Key /CA from general annotation dictionary shadowed by /CA from widget

body: This is tracking [Cryptography & Provenance TWG issue 25](https://github.com/pdf-association/crypto-provenance-twg/issues/25) ISO/TS 32003, sub-clause 5.2, text below EXAMPLE 1, states: > Encrypted string or stream objects shall be limited to (239 - 256) bytes of plaintext. But NIST SP 800-38D, section 5.2.1.1 "Input data" from https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/38/d/final, specifies that in bits: ISO/TS 32003 needs to be corrected from "bytes" to "bits" as follows: > Encrypted string or stream objects shall be limited to (239 - 256) **bits** of plaintext. C&P TWG agreed with this correction on 17 November 2026.
title: ISO/TS 32003 says "bytes" but NIST SP 800-38D, says "bits"

body:
# PRC: the texture bit field of a compressed tessellation does not say what its bits count, in what order, or what a reference value means

**Reviewed with Datalogics (Patrick Gallot), who offered to draft this change request with us ("you have the working implementation and we have the measurements").** The defect was found independently by both: by Datalogics while writing textured files, and by nanoPRC while fixing its reader.

**Change type: technical clarification, with two corrections.** The bit stream does not change. A
reader built from the text as written cannot decode the texture coordinates of a compressed
tessellation, one field is described with the wrong meaning, and one sentence names the wrong condition.

**Verified against** the TWG working source at commit `567be68` (main, pulled 20 November 2026; the draft of 28 October was checked at `6fb2ed9`, and every quoted block is unchanged). The "current
text" blocks below are reproduced byte for byte. Citations are by file and line, because clause and
table numbers move while the document is edited.

**Related:** #812 (`texture_parameters_size` counts floats, not (u,v) pairs). This ticket uses that
reading and does not repeat it.

---

## Defect

A compressed tessellation (`PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D_Compressed`) that carries texture coordinates stores
them in three parts: a bit field (`binary_texture_data`), a list of reference values
(`reference_array`), and a pool of (u,v) pairs (`texture_parameters`). Each corner of a triangle
either takes a new pair from the pool or reuses a pair already stored on the same vertex. The bit
field says which, corner by corner.

The text does not give a reader enough to decode this:

1. **What the bits count.** `iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:2894` says a bit is set "if the
   current vertex has a texture". It does not say whether there is one bit per vertex, per triangle
   corner, or per corner of a textured face only, so a reader cannot tell how many bits to read or
   which bit belongs to which corner.
2. **The bit order.** `07-base-entities.adoc:2911` says how the bit field is split into 32-bit words,
   but not whether the first bit is the most or the least significant bit of the first word.
3. **What a reference value means.** `07-base-entities.adoc:2896` says only that "the reference
   index is stored in reference_array", and that the treatment is "the same way as the treatment
   for normals". It does not say what the index counts. Compressed normals count back from the most
   recent normal stored on a vertex; texture references in real files do not (see Evidence), so the
   comparison with normals points a reader the wrong way.
4. **`last_integer_used_bit_number` is described with the wrong meaning.** `07-base-entities.adoc:2911`
   and `iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/tessellation.yaml:749` call it the number of padding bits.
   In real files it is the number of bits used in the last word. The two readings agree only when
   the value is 16, or when it is 0 and the last word is full.
5. **The value 0 is written two ways.** When the meaningful bits fill the last word exactly, some
   writers write 0 and stop; others append one further word with no meaningful bits and write 0.
   The text allows a reader to handle neither.
6. **Editorial.** `required:` is left blank on all three `BinaryTextureData` attributes
   (`tessellation.yaml:736`, `:743` and `:748`). All three are always present.

## Evidence

**Instrument.** nanoPRC's reader at upstream `main` `8bd4385`, in a scratch copy with a temporary
probe in the compressed-tessellation decoder. The decoder reads one bit per corner in traversal
order, takes a fresh pair for a clear bit and a referenced pair for a set bit, and the probe reports
for each textured entity: whether the whole block was consumed exactly (every bit, every reference
and every pair used, none left over), the word count, `last_integer_used_bit_number`, and the number
of bits read. The decoding rule is the one in nanoPRC's reader (`src/prc_decode_compressed_tess.c:2300-2514`),
added in nanoPRC PR #151.

**Denominator.** prc-db as it was when this change request was first drafted (310 files). 6,824 textured compressed entities in 64
files. Datalogics' independent census finds the same 6,824.

**What the bits count, and their order.**

| reading | entities that decode exactly |
|---|--:|
| one bit per corner of a textured face, least significant bit of the first word first | **6,824 of 6,824** |
| the same, with any of the other three bit orders | at most 1,486 |

Under the other bit orders, references appear on vertices that have no pair yet. One entity
(`smallBMS-(3D-pdf).stream-13`) has `all_faces_have_texture` FALSE; it decodes exactly only if the
corners of untextured faces take no bit. In every entity,
`reference_array_size + texture_parameters_size / 2` equals the number of corners of textured
faces.

The order of corners within a triangle is the traversal order. At the start of a chain, nanoPRC's
decoder exchanges the first two corners when the first has the higher point index
(`src/prc_decode_compressed_tess.c:1302`); the bits follow the order after that exchange. In
`3D-PDF-Sample-Shoe` (217 such chain starts) and `3D-PDF-Sample-Carburetor` (83), every entity
decodes exactly in that order; read in the order before the exchange, 4 of 53 and 9 of 51 entities
no longer do. Whether that exchange is itself specified belongs to the traversal algorithm, not to
this ticket.

**Both collections, and the partly textured entities (Datalogics, 20 November 2026).** Datalogics' reader decodes the case
Change 1 describes, and checks each entity against the format: exactly *texture_parameters_size* / 2 fresh pairs, and exactly
*reference_array_size* references, consumed, every reference inside its vertex's list. Every entity in either collection that
writes *all_faces_have_texture* FALSE passes, and the NOTE of Change 2 holds on each when the corners of untextured faces are
left out:

| collection | entity | triangles | textured corners | fresh pairs + references |
|---|---|--:|--:|---|
| prc-db | `smallBMS-(3D-pdf).stream-13` | 140 | 102 | 36 + 66 |
| SafeDocs filtering | `2233665`, first | 13,930 | 1,152 | 384 + 768 |
| SafeDocs filtering | `2233665`, second | 5,752 | 732 | 244 + 488 |
| SafeDocs filtering | `2233665`, third | 3,078 | 288 | 96 + 192 |

Counting every corner instead cannot fit: `smallBMS` would need 420 bits where its bit field holds 128, enough for its 102
textured corners, and the largest `2233665` entity would need 41,790 bits where its field holds 1,184. Over both collections
every textured compressed entity now passes: 7,116 of 7,116 in 74 files of prc-db now (606 files, which contain the 310; the first count is a floor for the second), and 6,827 of 6,827 in 44 files
of the SafeDocs filtering (219 files). On 14 November the figures were 7,115 and 6,824; the difference is these four entities.
(The figures above under "Denominator" are those of the original measurement, on the 310-file subset current in October.)

**`last_integer_used_bit_number`.** Read as "bits used in the last word" (and, for 0, either reading
below), the bit count matches the number of textured corners on all 6,824 entities. Read as "padding
bits", it matches on 314: the 244 with the value 16, where the readings coincide, and the 70 below
where 0 means a full last word.

The wrong meaning is not only a matter of wording. One of the two writers whose source is known was
built from the current text and wrote the padding count, words x 32 - corners, with no other branch.
That agrees with the bits-used reading only where the two coincide, and the writer was corrected on
seeing this change request (Datalogics, 27 October 2026).

| value | entities | files | what follows |
|---|--:|--:|---|
| 1 to 31 | 6,567 | | that many bits used in the last word |
| 0, last word full | 70 | 22 | |
| 0, followed by one word with no meaningful bits | 187 | 5 | |

No file uses both forms of 0. Because the number of meaningful bits always equals the number of
textured corners, a reader that counts corners can accept both. Of the two writers whose source we
know, Datalogics' writes 0 for a full last word and appends no word, and nanoPRC's appends the extra
word.

**What a reference value means.** This is the least settled part, and the evidence is stated at its
strength. A set bit's reference value was scored three ways on every entity, by resolving every
corner and counting triangles whose (u,v) span more than a quarter of the image, against the same
rate on triangles where all readings agree:

* **counted from the first pair stored on the vertex (0 = first)**: at or below the agreed-triangle
  rate where the image is not tiled, e.g. `3D-PDF-Sample-Carburetor` 0.3% against 0.8%, and
  `3D-PDF-Sample-Shoe` 7.1% against 10.9%;
* counted back from the most recent pair, as compressed normals do: 81.6% and 58.1% on the same two
  files;
* as an index into the whole pool: worse everywhere.

Of the 124 entities with at least 20 triangles where the readings disagree, 94 are within ten points
of the agreed rate under "counted from the first". The other 30, mostly in
`3D-PDF-Sample-Chasis`, are not explained by any of the three. Rendering agrees with the first
reading: `3D-PDF-Sample-Shoe`, read with it, shows the same coherent texture as Adobe Acrobat, where
pair-per-vertex reading shows a scrambled one.

**An independent range check (Datalogics, 26 October 2026).** Datalogics' reader reads the reference
values for alignment but does not use them: it assigns one (u,v) pair per vertex in decode order. It
is therefore not a second implementation of the "counted from the first" reading, but its census
settles two of the three candidates without resolving a single reference. Over the 6,824 textured
entities, 6,158 carry a reference array, and 31,011,489 reference values were read:

* the largest reference value anywhere is 11 (5,992 of the 6,158 entities have every reference 0;
  then 73 top out at 1, 67 at 2, 15 at 3, single figures above). An index into the whole pool would
  reach values near `texture_parameters_size / 2`, in the thousands: **refuted**;
* 42,493 values are odd. An offset into `texture_parameters` counting floats would always be even:
  **refuted**;
* where a vertex carries one pair, "counted from the first" and "counted back from the most recent"
  give the same answer, so a range check cannot separate those two; the scoring above does.

The same census shows that pair-per-vertex decoding is not merely unsupported but impossible on 198
of the 6,824 entities (in 8 files): there the number of stored pairs differs from the number of
vertices, so a per-vertex index cannot be right whatever the semantics.

(The scoring was measured on 16 October 2026 on nanoPRC `73f03b2`; the entity count and the exact
decoding of all 6,824 were re-measured on `8bd4385` for this draft and are unchanged.)

**A writer.** nanoPRC's writer (PR #154) writes this block: one bit per corner, least significant
bit first, the extra-word form of 0, and a reference value of 0 throughout, since it splits every
vertex at a seam so that each vertex carries one pair. Its files render textured in Adobe Acrobat,
PDF-XChange Editor and FinalMesh. Datalogics' writer reached the same unit and polarity
independently, from the same collection.

## Proposed change

### Change 1 of 5: the bit field

Location: `iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:2894`

Current text:

```
*binary_texture_data* represents a bit field. During mesh traversal, if the current vertex has a texture, a bit texture_is_reference is set in this array. This bit is true if the same UV parameter has already been stored during mesh traversal for the same vertex. In this case, the reference index is stored in reference_array. Otherwise, this bit is set to FALSE and UV parameters are stored in Texture_parameters.
```

Replace with:

```
*binary_texture_data* represents a bit field with one bit, texture_is_reference, for each corner of each triangle whose face has a texture, taken in the order in which mesh traversal visits the corners. Corners of triangles whose face has no texture (see *face_has_texture*) have no bit. The bit is TRUE if the corner uses a UV parameter that has already been stored during mesh traversal for the same vertex; the index of that UV parameter is then the next value of *reference_array*. Otherwise the bit is FALSE and the corner uses the next UV parameter of *texture_parameters*.
```

### Change 2 of 5: what a reference value means

Location: `iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:2896`

Current text:

```
*reference_array* is used to reference UV parameters. The references on UV parameters are done per vertex. A UV parameter for the current vertex is referenced only if the same UV parameter has already been stored for the same vertex during the treatment of another triangle. This treatment is performed during mesh traversal, the same way as the treatment for normals.
```

Replace with:

```
*reference_array* is used to reference UV parameters. The references on UV parameters are done per vertex: each vertex has the list of UV parameters stored for it during mesh traversal, in the order they were stored. A value of *reference_array* is an index into that list, where 0 is the first UV parameter stored for the vertex. A UV parameter for the current vertex is referenced only if the same UV parameter has already been stored for the same vertex during the treatment of another triangle.

NOTE: *reference_array_size* + *texture_parameters_size* / 2 equals the number of corners of triangles whose face has a texture.
```

The NOTE was checked independently by Datalogics, whose check counts all corners (3 per triangle)
because it was written before Change 1: it holds on 6,823 of the 6,824 entities, and the one
failure is `smallBMS-(3D-pdf).stream-13`, the single entity with `all_faces_have_texture` FALSE.
That is exactly the exception Change 1 states (corners of untextured faces take no bit).

### Change 3 of 5: the words

Location: `iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:2911-2912`

Current text:

```
_BinaryTextureData_ represents a bit field (see <<tab-entities-BinaryTextureData>>). It indicates during mesh traversal whether UV coordinates are referenced. (See <<CompressedTextureParameter>> for more details). The bit field is padded with *last_integer_used_bit_number* zero bits so that its total length becomes a multiple of 32, where 0 ≤ *last_integer_used_bit_number* < 32. The padded bit field is then partitioned into 32-bit words and stored as an array of _UnsignedIntegers_, the count of which is
recorded in *texture_bit_words_size*. Each unsigned integer is written as 4 bytes via _MakePortable32BitsUnsigned_ (see <<MakePortable32BitsUnsigned>>).
```

Replace with:

```
_BinaryTextureData_ represents a bit field (see <<tab-entities-BinaryTextureData>>). It indicates during mesh traversal whether UV coordinates are referenced. (See <<CompressedTextureParameter>> for more details). The bit field is stored in 32-bit words, beginning with the least significant bit of the first word. The number of words is recorded in *texture_bit_words_size*. *last_integer_used_bit_number* is the number of bits of the bit field in the last word, from 1 to 31, or 0 if the bit field fills the last word. When the bit field fills the last word, some writers append one further word that holds no bits of the bit field, and also set *last_integer_used_bit_number* to 0. A reader should therefore take the length of the bit field from the number of corners it describes (see <<CompressedTextureParameter>>). Each unsigned integer is written as 4 bytes via _MakePortable32BitsUnsigned_ (see <<MakePortable32BitsUnsigned>>).
```

### Change 4 of 5: the table

Location: `iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/tessellation.yaml:731-749`

Current text:

```
- name: BinaryTextureData
  attributes:
  - name: texture_bit_words_size
    data_type:
      kind: UnsignedInteger
    required:
    description: "The number of 32-bit _UnsignedIntegers_ in *texture_bit_words*. The total number of bits in *texture_bit_words* is therefore *texture_bit_words_size* * 32. The number of meaningful (non-padding) bits is *texture_bit_words_size* * 32 - *last_integer_used_bit_number*."
  - name: texture_bit_words
    data_type:
      kind: Array
      inner_kind: UnsignedInteger
      occurrence: texture_bit_words_size
    required:
    description: "An array of *texture_bit_words_size* 32-bit UnsignedIntegers, each written as 4 bytes via MakePortable32BitsUnsigned (see <<MakePortable32BitsUnsigned>>). The total bit content is *texture_bit_words_size* * 32 bits, of which the last last_integer_used_bit_number bits are padding."
  - name: last_integer_used_bit_number
    data_type:
      kind: UnsignedInteger
    required:
    description: "The number of padding bits appended to the bit field to bring its length to a multiple of 32. Satisfies 0 ≤ *last_integer_used_bit_number* < 32. The number of meaningful bits in texture_bit_words is *texture_bit_words_size* * 32 - *last_integer_used_bit_number*."
```

Replace with:

```
- name: BinaryTextureData
  attributes:
  - name: texture_bit_words_size
    data_type:
      kind: UnsignedInteger
    required: true
    description: "The number of 32-bit _UnsignedIntegers_ in *texture_bit_words*."
  - name: texture_bit_words
    data_type:
      kind: Array
      inner_kind: UnsignedInteger
      occurrence: texture_bit_words_size
    required: true
    description: "An array of *texture_bit_words_size* 32-bit UnsignedIntegers, each written as 4 bytes via MakePortable32BitsUnsigned (see <<MakePortable32BitsUnsigned>>). The bit field begins with the least significant bit of the first word."
  - name: last_integer_used_bit_number
    data_type:
      kind: UnsignedInteger
    required: true
    description: "The number of bits of the bit field in the last word of *texture_bit_words*, from 1 to 31, or 0 if the bit field fills the last word or the last word holds none of it. Satisfies 0 ≤ *last_integer_used_bit_number* < 32."
```

### Change 5 of 5: the condition of *face_has_texture*

Location: `iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:2876`

Change 1 depends on this sentence, through "see *face_has_texture*". It names the opposite condition to the table.

Current text:

```
* The *face_has_texture* field is a Boolean array. It indicates which faces have texture when *no_texture* is TRUE and *all_faces_have_texture* is FALSE.
```

Replace with:

```
* The *face_has_texture* field is a Boolean array. It indicates which faces have texture when *no_texture* is FALSE and *all_faces_have_texture* is FALSE.
```

The sentence is the only place in the clause that has TRUE here. Six lines earlier, `:2870`, "The *no_texture* field is TRUE if
there is no texture", so a face cannot be described as textured when *no_texture* is TRUE. `tessellation.yaml:681` makes the array
present "if *no_texture* is FALSE and *all_faces_have_texture* is FALSE", which is how the four entities above are read by
Datalogics' reader and by nanoPRC's (`src/prc_parse_tess.c:1505-1530` reads *all_faces_have_texture* only when *no_texture* is
clear, and *face_has_texture* only when that is FALSE). One word, TRUE to FALSE. Found by Datalogics (20 November 2026).

## Effect if accepted

* A reader can decode the texture coordinates of a compressed tessellation from the text alone.
* `last_integer_used_bit_number` is described as real files use it, and both existing forms of 0
  remain valid.
* The comparison with normals, which points the other way, is removed.
* The sentence that Change 1 points to names the same condition as the table.
* **Unchanged:** field names, field order, data types and the bit stream. Every file in the
  collection above decodes exactly under the proposed text.
title: PRC: the texture bit field of a compressed tessellation does not say what its bits count, in what order, or what a reference value means

# PRC: raw picture formats -- say which row comes first, what "flate-formatted" means, and what the buffer holds

**CR-42.**

**Verified against** the TWG working source at commit `567be68` (main, pulled 20 November 2026). Quotations are by file and line.

**Builds on CR-33 (#827).** CR-33 says where a reader takes the size of a PNG or JPEG picture (formats 0 and 1) and rewrites the
paragraph at `iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:1121`. This change concerns the other formats, 2 to 5, which that paragraph
leaves with one sentence. The two do not conflict: CR-33 covers formats 0 and 1, CR-42 covers formats 2 to 5.
The editorial change to "RGBA quadruplet" has also been made, so the RGBA wording that the first draft of this CR included is dropped.

## Current text

- `iso-prc/definitions/values/value_type.yaml:12-35`, EPRCPictureDataFormat: values 2 to 5
  (`KEPRCPicture_BITMAP_RGB_BYTE`, `_RGBA_BYTE`, `_GREY_BYTE`, `_GREYA_BYTE`) are each described as
  "flate-formatted pixel data", followed by "Each element is an RGB triplet (3 components)", "Each element is an RGBA quadruplet
  (4 components)", "a single luminance value (1 component)" and "a luminance/alpha pair (2 components)".
- `iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:1121-1127`, as CR-33 now has it. Its last paragraph (`:1127`):

  > When *format* is one of {2,3,4,5}, the size of the picture buffer when uncompressed shall be at least *pixel_width* *
  > *pixel_height* * the number of components per pixel.

  and, before it, `:1121`: "*pixel_width* and *pixel_height* are the size of the picture expressed in pixels." The same rows in
  `iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/graphics.yaml:169` and `:174` now read "Width of the picture in pixels, when *format* is one of
  {2,3,4,5}" and "Height ..." with the format 0 and 1 case stated.

## 1. Row order is not stated, and real readers and writers agree on bottom row first

Nothing says whether the first stored row of a raw picture is the top or the bottom of the image.
PNG and JPEG define their own (top first).

- nanoPRC wrote one 64x64 image three ways (raw RGB, raw RGBA, PNG) onto three quads with identical
  texture coordinates. Adobe Acrobat 2026.002.22031 drew the two raw quads one way up and the PNG
  quad the other: it takes the first stored row of a raw picture as the image's bottom row.
- OpenSCAD2PDF (Patrick Gallot's writer) reached the same result independently from a controlled pair: the same
  pixels, model and texture coordinates, stored once as raw RGB with rows top first and once as PNG.
  The raw one drew upside down and the PNG upright. Its writer now stores raw rows bottom first by
  default (0.9.0 onwards).
- Both writers' raw pictures stored bottom row first draw the right way up in Acrobat, and nanoPRC's
  reader, which reverses raw rows, reads both writers' pictures the right way up.

## 2. "flate-formatted" does not say what is stored, and real files differ

- The phrase does not say whether the data is a zlib stream (RFC 1950: header, deflate data,
  adler32) or a bare deflate stream (RFC 1951). Every deflated raw picture we have seen, from three
  writers, is a zlib stream (header 78 9C).
- Real files also store raw pixels uncompressed. In the public prc-db collection, 34 raw pictures in
  16 files (all 2x2): the 32 RGBA ones in 15 files are stored as they are (each block exactly
  16 bytes); the RGB ones in the two teapot files are zlib streams. Adobe Acrobat displays
  uncompressed raw pictures written by nanoPRC.
- The "at least" in `:1127` allows a buffer larger than the image, with no rule for what the extra
  bytes are.

## 3. For formats 2 to 5 the declared size is the only size

CR-33 now says the fields describe the picture "when *format* is one of {2,3,4,5}". For a raw picture there is no image header:
*pixel_width* and *pixel_height* are the only size information in the file, so a value of 0 leaves a reader with nothing, and the text
does not say that it must not occur.

## Proposed replacement

In `value_type.yaml`, for values 2 to 5, replace "flate-formatted pixel data." with:

> Pixel data compressed as a zlib stream (IETF RFC 1950).

In `07-base-entities.adoc:1127`, the paragraph as CR-33 has it, replace the whole paragraph with:

> When *format* is one of {2,3,4,5}, *pixel_width* and *pixel_height* shall not be 0, and the picture
> data shall inflate to exactly *pixel_width* x *pixel_height* x the number of components per pixel
> bytes. The rows are stored from the bottom row of the image to the top row, each row from left to
> right.
>
> NOTE Some existing files store the pixel data of formats 2 to 5 uncompressed. A reader can
> recognise this when the data is exactly *pixel_width* x *pixel_height* x the number of components
> per pixel bytes long and does not inflate to that size.

Change type: substantive (row order and the exact size are new requirements, though they describe
what existing writers and Acrobat already do; the NOTE keeps existing uncompressed files readable).
title: PRC: raw picture formats -- say which row comes first, what "flate-formatted" means, and what the buffer holds

# PRC: PRC_TYPE_SURF_Blend01 evaluates the pipe on the origin curve, and gives two answers for a missing tangent curve

**Reviewed with Datalogics (Patrick Gallot), who found both defects while drawing Figure 16.** Line numbers checked at 567be68.

**Change type: technical correction.** The bit stream does not change. A reader that follows the pseudocode draws every Blend01 surface displaced by one radius at every v. A reader that follows the prose and the pseudocode's tangent fallback draws a tilted, elliptical cross-section wherever the radius varies.

**Verified against** the TWG working source at commit `567be68` (main, pulled 20 November 2026). Quoted text is reproduced as it stands; citations are by file and line.

---

## Defect

**1. The evaluation formula centres the pipe on the origin curve.** The pseudocode
(`iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:5399-5401`) is:

```
R(implicit_param_v) = origin_curve(implicit_param_v) - center_curve(implicit_param_v)

XYZ = origin_curve(implicit_param_v) + cos(implicit_param_u) * R(implicit_param_v) + sin(implicit_param_u) * [tangent_curve(implicit_param_v) stem:[^^] R(implicit_param_v)]
```

At u = 0 that is 2 x origin - center, a point the clause names nowhere, and the surface is a pipe of the right radius
centred on the origin curve. The prose (`:5365`) requires the opposite, "a variable radius pipe surface centred on the
center curve with the origin curve defining both the radius and 0 location of the u parameter", and the key of Figure 16
agrees with it. With center_curve(v) as the first term the formula satisfies both halves of that sentence: the
cross-section is centred on the centre curve, and at u = 0 it passes through origin_curve(v). The error is a displacement
of exactly one radius at every v, so it never shrinks to something small.

**2. A missing tangent curve is given two different answers.** The prose (`:5363`) and the pseudocode (`:5405`) use the
first derivative of the **origin** curve; Table 289 (`iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/surface.yaml:75`) uses the
**center** curve. The clause says what the tangent is for, "the normal of the cross section plane" (`:5365`), and a pipe's
cross-section plane is normal to its spine, the centre curve. Separately, the pseudocode says "unitized" only in the
fallback branch, while the identity |tangent x R| = |R|, which a circular cross-section needs, holds only for a unit
tangent whichever branch supplied it; Table 289 states no requirement on the field.

## Evidence

- **Real files mean the prose.** Of the 64 Blend01 surfaces in prc-db and Datalogics' SafeDocs filtering, 60 were written
  by Asymptote, whose public tube generator passes the tube's centre line as center_curve and, as origin_curve, the centre
  line offset by the radius along a unit normal. Evaluated by the pseudocode, every such tube lies one radius to the side
  of the spherical caps Asymptote puts on its ends; evaluated by the prose, the caps sit on the tube ends. The Datalogics
  reader followed the pseudocode until 11 November and now follows the prose (Patrick Gallot, 12 November).
- **The tangent fallback, measured on a case.** A straight blend whose radius ramps from 6 to 14 over 40 units: the
  centre-curve derivative gives |tangent x R| = 6.000 against |R| = 6, a circle in a plane normal to the spine; the
  origin-curve derivative, tilted by atan(8/40), gives 5.886, an ellipse in a tilted plane (Patrick Gallot; re-derived
  here as 6 cos(atan 0.2) = 5.88).
- **The 64 real surfaces cannot decide defect 2.** All store no tangent curve, so every one goes through the disputed
  sentence; but in each, origin curve and centre curve run parallel, both candidate derivatives point the same way, and
  both readings draw the same tube.
- **One implementation already works around both.** nanoPRC's Blend01 evaluator takes center_curve(v) as the first term,
  following the prose rather than the pseudocode, and after taking the origin-curve derivative as the fallback tangent it
  rescales tangent x R to the length of R so the cross-section stays round
  (CascadiaVoxel/nanoPRC, `src/prc_tessellation_exact_geom_surfaces.c`, `prc_evaluate_surf_blend01`). The rescaling is
  the symptom defect 2 predicts.

## Proposed change

### Change 1 of 4: the missing tangent curve, in the prose

Location: `iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:5363`

Current text (second sentence):

```
If the tangent curve is not defined (NULL), the first derivative of the origin curve is used instead.
```

Replace with:

```
If the tangent curve is not defined (NULL), the first derivative of the center curve is used instead, since the cross-section plane is normal to the center curve.
```

### Change 2 of 4: the evaluation formula

Location: `iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:5401`

Current text:

```
XYZ = origin_curve(implicit_param_v) + cos(implicit_param_u) * R(implicit_param_v) + sin(implicit_param_u) * [tangent_curve(implicit_param_v) stem:[^^] R(implicit_param_v)]
```

Replace with:

```
XYZ = center_curve(implicit_param_v) + cos(implicit_param_u) * R(implicit_param_v) + sin(implicit_param_u) * [T(implicit_param_v) stem:[^^] R(implicit_param_v)]
```

### Change 3 of 4: the tangent, in the pseudocode

Location: `iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:5405`

Current text:

```
If the tangent curve is NULL, use the unitized first derivative of origin curve instead of the tangent curve.
```

Replace with:

```
T(implicit_param_v) is tangent_curve(implicit_param_v), or, if the tangent curve is NULL, the first derivative of center_curve at implicit_param_v; in either case unitized.
```

### Change 4 of 4: Table 289

Location: `iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/surface.yaml:75`

Current text:

```
    description: "Tangent curve; may be NULL in which case the first derivative of the center curve is used as the tangent curve."
```

Replace with:

```
    description: "Tangent curve; may be NULL in which case the first derivative of the center curve is used as the tangent curve. The tangent is unitized before use."
```

## Effect if accepted

- A reader built from the text draws the pipe centred on its centre curve, through the origin curve at u = 0, with a
  circular cross-section normal to the spine, as Figure 16 shows and as real files are written.
- **Unchanged:** field names, field order, data types and the bit stream. Figure 16 and its key already agree.
- **Not addressed:** whether a stored tangent curve that is not normal to R should be projected; no real file stores one.
title: PRC: PRC_TYPE_SURF_Blend01 evaluates the pipe on the origin curve, and gives two answers for a missing tangent curve
